Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 6, verse 1 (part 1 of 2):

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

Surat al-An'am is Meccan according to the majority of scholars. Ibn 'Abbas and Qatadah said: it is entirely Meccan except for two verses which were revealed at Medina. His statement, exalted is He: ﴿They did not measure Allah with His true measure﴾ [al-An'am 6:91] was revealed concerning Malik ibn al-Sayf and Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf, the two Jews. The other is His statement: "It is He who produced gardens, both trellised and untrellised" [al-An'am 6:141], which was revealed concerning Thabit ibn Qays ibn Shammas al-Ansari. Ibn Juraij said: it was revealed concerning Mu'adh ibn Jabal, and al-Mawardi reported this.

Al-Tha'labi said: Surat al-An'am is Meccan except for six verases which were revealed at Medina: "They did not measure Allah with His true measure" to the end of three verses, and "Say: Come, I will recite what your Lord has forbidden you" [al-An'am 6:151] to the end of three verses. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: these are the muhkam (clear, decisive) verses. Ibn al-'Arabi mentioned that His statement: "Say: I find not" [al-An'am 6:145] was revealed at Mecca on the Day of 'Arafah. The discussion of all of this will come, Allah willing.

It is reported in a khabar (report) that the surah was revealed all at once, apart from the six verses. Seventy thousand angels accompanied it, and with one of its verses there were twelve thousand angels, which is: ﴿With Him are the keys of the unseen; none knows them but He﴾ [al-An'am 6:59]. They descended by night, with a loud sound (zajal), glorifying and praising. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) summoned the scribes, and they wrote it down that same night.

Abu Ja'far al-Nahhas transmitted with an isnad: Muhammad ibn Yahya told us, Abu Hatim Rawh ibn al-Faraj, mawla of al-Hadarimah, told us, Ahmad ibn Muhammad Abu Bakr al-'Umari told us, Ibn Abi Fudayk told us, 'Umar ibn Talhah ibn 'Alqamah ibn Waqqas told me, from Nafi' Abi Sahl [in some manuscripts: Abi Suhayl; in others: Ibn Suhayl; the correct reading is what we have recorded, from al-Tahdhib] ibn Malik, from Anas ibn Malik, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Surat al-An'am was revealed accompanied by a procession of angels that filled the space between the two horizons, with a loud sound of glorification." The earth was shaking for them, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was saying: "Glory be to my Lord, the Mighty," three times. [In the manuscript of al-Jamal, on the authority of al-Qurtubi: then he fell down prostrating.]

Al-Darimi Abu Muhammad mentioned in his Musnad, from 'Umar ibn al-Khattab (may Allah be pleased with him), who said: "Al-An'am is among the choicest (najaib) of the Qur'an." [Najaib al-Qur'an and nawajihi: its most excellent surahs (al-Nihayah).] Also in it, from Ka'b, who said: "The opening of the Torah is the opening of al-An'am, and its ending is the ending of Hud." Wahb ibn Munabbih also said this.

Al-Mahdawi mentioned that the commentators said: the Torah began with His statement: ﴿Praise belongs to Allah, who created the heavens and the earth﴾ [al-An'am 6:1], and ended with His statement: ﴿Praise belongs to Allah, who has not taken a son, and has no partner in dominion﴾ [al-Isra' 17:111], to the end of the verse.

Al-Tha'labi mentioned from Jabir, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "Whoever recites the first three verses of Surat al-An'am, up to His statement: ﴿and He knows what you earn﴾ [al-An'am 6:3], Allah appoints forty thousand angels to him, who write for him the like of their worship until the Day of Resurrection. An angel descends from the seventh heaven with an iron mace, and when Satan wants to whisper to him or inspire something into his heart, he strikes him a blow, and there will be seventy veils between them. On the Day of Resurrection, Allah, exalted is He, will say: 'Walk in My shade, on a day when there is no shade but My shade; eat of the fruits of My Garden, drink from the water of al-Kawthar, and bathe in the water of al-Salsabil. You are My servant, and I am your Lord.'"

In al-Bukhari, from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "If you want to know the ignorance of the Arabs, recite what comes after the hundred and thirtieth verse of Surat al-An'am: ﴿They have certainly lost who killed their children in foolishness without knowledge﴾ up to His statement: ﴿and they were not guided﴾" [al-An'am 6:140]. [See vol. 7, p. 96.]

Note: The scholars said: this surah is a foundation (asl) for disputation with the polytheists, and with others among the innovators (mubtadi'un), and with those who deny the Resurrection and the rising again. This requires that it was revealed all at once, because it is about one meaning of argument, though it is expressed in many ways. On it the theologians (mutakallimun) built the principles of religion, because it contains clear verses which refute the Qadariyyah, unlike the surahs that mention... [in manuscripts B, J, 'Ayn and Ya: "and we will explain this further, clearly, if Allah wills"]. We will expand on this, if Allah wills, by the power and help of Allah, exalted is He.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿Praise belongs to Allah, who created the heavens and the earth and made the darknesses and the light; then those who disbelieve ascribe equals to their Lord﴾ (1).

There are five issues here.

The first: His statement, exalted is He: ﴿Praise belongs to Allah﴾. He, glorified is He, began its opening with praise of Himself and the affirmation of divinity (uluhiyyah). That is, all praise belongs to Him, so there is no partner for Him. If it is said: other surahs also open with "Praise belongs to Allah," so why not suffice with one of them and be free of the rest? It is answered: because each occurrence has a meaning in its own place which another cannot convey, since it is tied to the various blessings; and also because of the argument it contains in this place against those who "ascribe equals to their Lord." The meaning of "praise" has already been discussed in the opening surah (al-Fatihah) [see vol. 1, p. 131 ff.].

The second: His statement: ﴿who created the heavens and the earth﴾. He informs about His power, His knowledge and His will, saying: "who created," that is, originated, brought into being, produced and initiated. Khalq (creation) can mean invention (ikhtira') and it can mean measuring (taqdir), as has already been mentioned, and both are intended here. This is evidence of their having come into existence (huduth). He raised the sky without pillars, and made it level without crookedness (awad) [al-awad: crookedness]. He placed in it the sun and the moon as two signs, adorned it with the stars, and deposited in it the clouds and the vapours as signs. He spread out the earth and deposited in it the provisions and the plants, and scattered in it creatures of every kind as signs. He placed in it mountains as pegs and roads as wide paths, made rivers and seas flow in it, and caused springs to gush from the rocks: as indications of His oneness and great power, and that He is Allah, the One, the Subduer. By creating the heavens and the earth He made clear that He is the creator of everything.

The third: Muslim transmitted, saying: Suraij ibn Yunus and Harun ibn 'Abd Allah told me, both saying: Hajjaj ibn Muhammad told us, saying: Ibn Juraij said: Isma'il ibn Umayyah informed me, from Ayyub ibn Khalid, from 'Abd Allah ibn Rafi', mawla of Umm Salamah, from Abu Hurairah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) took hold of my two hands and said: "Allah, mighty and majestic, created the clay on Saturday, created the mountains in it on Sunday, created the trees on Monday, created the disliked things on Tuesday, created light on Wednesday, scattered the creatures in it on Thursday, and created Adam (peace be upon him) after 'Asr on Friday, at the last of creation, in the last hour of the hours of Friday, between 'Asr and night."

I say: the scholars included this hadith as an explanation of the opening of this surah. Al-Bayhaqi said: the people of knowledge of hadith claimed that it is not preserved (mahfuz), because it contradicts what the people of tafsir and the people of history hold. Some claimed that Isma'il ibn Umayyah only took it from Ibrahim ibn Abi Yahya, from Ayyub ibn Khalid, and Ibrahim is not a reliable authority for argument. Muhammad ibn Yahya reported: I asked 'Ali ibn al-Madini about the hadith of Abu Hurairah, "Allah created the clay on Saturday." 'Ali said: this is a Medinan hadith, transmitted by Hisham ibn Yusuf from Ibn Juraij, from Isma'il ibn Umayyah, from Ayyub ibn Khalid, from Abu Rafi', mawla of Umm Salamah, from Abu Hurairah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) took hold of my hands. 'Ali said: and Ibrahim ibn Abi Yahya clasped my hand and said to me: Ayyub ibn Khalid clasped my hand; and he said to me: 'Abd Allah ibn Rafi' clasped my hand; and he said to me: Abu Hurairah clasped my hand; and he said to me: Abu al-Qasim, [the Messenger of Allah] (ﷺ) clasped my hand, and said: "Allah created the earth on Saturday," and he mentioned the hadith in similar wording. 'Ali ibn al-Madini said: I do not think Isma'il ibn Umayyah took this matter except from Ibrahim ibn Abi Yahya. Al-Bayhaqi said: Musa ibn 'Ubaydah al-Rabadhi has followed him in this, from Ayyub ibn Khalid, but Musa ibn 'Ubaydah is weak. It is also reported from Bakr ibn al-Sharud, from Ibrahim ibn Abi Yahya, from Safwan ibn Sulaym, from Ayyub ibn Khalid, and its isnad is weak, from Abu Hurairah, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "On Friday there is an hour which no servant who asks Allah, mighty and majestic, for something during it will fail to be given it." He said: 'Abd Allah ibn Salam said: Allah, mighty and majestic, began creation: He created the earth on Sunday and Monday, created the heavens on Tuesday and Wednesday, created the provisions and what is in the earth on Thursday and Friday until the 'Asr prayer, and between the 'Asr prayer and sunset He created Adam. Al-Bayhaqi transmitted it.

I say: in it is that Allah, exalted is He, began creation on Sunday, not on Saturday. Likewise it has already been mentioned in al-Baqarah [vol. 1, pp. 255–256 and following] from Ibn Mas'ud and others among the Companions of the Prophet (ﷺ). The difference of opinion there about which was created first, the earth or the sky, has also been discussed fully there. And praise belongs to Allah.

The fourth: His statement: ﴿and made the darknesses and the light﴾. After mentioning the creation of substances (jawahir), He mentioned the creation of accidents (a'rad), because the substance cannot do without them, and whatever cannot do without accidents (hawadith) is itself originated. In the terminology of the theologians, the jawhar (substance) is the indivisible part (al-juz' alladhi la yatajazza') which bears the accident. We have explained it in the book "al-Kitab al-Asna fi Sharh Asma' Allah al-Husna," under His name "al-Wahid." The accident ('arad) is so called because it occurs (ya'ridu) in the body and the substance, so that by it it changes from one state to another. The body (jism) is that which is composed, and the least that is called a body is two composed substances. Although these terms did not exist in the first generation, the meaning of the Book and the Sunnah points to them, so there is no sense in denying them. The scholars have used them, agreed upon them, built their discourse on them, and overcame their opponents with them, as has been mentioned in al-Baqarah.

The scholars differed about the intended meaning of the darknesses and the light. Al-Suddi, Qatadah and the majority of the commentators said: what is meant is the blackness of the night and the brightness of the day. Al-Hasan said: disbelief and faith. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: this is a departure from the apparent meaning. I say: the wording includes it, and in the revelation: ﴿Is one who was dead and We gave him life and made for him a light by which he walks among people like one whose likeness is in darknesses﴾ [al-An'am 6:122]. [See vol. 7, p. 78.] "The earth" here is a noun of genus, so its singular form in the wording is equivalent to its plural; likewise "the light." Similar is ﴿Then He brings you out as a child﴾ [Ghafir 40:67]. [See vol. 12, p. 11.] And the poet said:

"Eat in part of your belly, so that you may be chaste,
for your time is a time of lean years." [The complete verse: "For your time is a time of lean years" (fa-inna zamanakum zaman khamis).]

And it has already been mentioned [...]

Al-Qurtubi's commentary (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran), on surah 6, verse 1 (part 2 of 2):

The poet says: "Eat from part of your belly, so that you become accustomed to it, for time is one of hunger and drought."

As for "ja'ala" (made, placed) here meaning "khalaqa" (created), Ibn 'Atiyyah said that no other meaning is permissible. I say: On this reading, the wording and the meaning agree in the sequence, so the plural is conjoined to the plural and the singular to the singular, the wording becomes harmonious, and eloquence is made evident. And Allah knows best.

It was also said: He put "the darknesses" in the plural and "the light" in the singular because the darknesses are not transitive, whereas the light is transitive.

Al-Tha'labi related that some scholars of meanings said: "Ja'ala" here is superfluous (za'idah), and the Arabs add "ja'ala" in speech, as in the words of the poet:

"And I have made myself see the two as four, and the one as two, when old age has weakened me."

Al-Nahhas said: "Ja'ala" in the sense of "khalaqa" takes only one object. This meaning and the various usages of "ja'ala" have already been discussed fully in (Surat al-Baqarah).

The fifth matter: His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Then those who disbelieve ascribe equals to their Lord﴾. This is a new sentence (mubtada') with its predicate (khabar), and the meaning is: then those who disbelieve set up equals and partners with Allah, though He alone created these things.

Ibn 'Atiyyah said: The "thumma" (then) indicates the ugliness of the disbelievers' act, because the meaning is: His creation of the heavens and the earth is established, His signs have shone forth, and His bounty in that has become clear; then after all of that they ascribe equals to their Lord. This is like saying: "O so-and-so, I gave you, I honoured you, and I did good to you, then you insult me." If the conjunction were with "waw" (and) in this and similar cases, the reproach would not be necessarily implied as it is with "thumma." And Allah knows best.

**Al-Qurtubi's commentary (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on Surah al-An'am (6), verse 2**

His words, may He be exalted: ﴿He it is who created you from clay﴾ — the verse is a statement of fact, and its meaning has two views. The first, which is the most well-known and the view of most of the scholars of creation, is that what is meant is Adam, peace be upon him, and "creation" refers to his offspring. The branch is attributed to its origin, and so He said "created you" in the plural, addressing them as his descendants. This is the view of al-Hasan, Qatadah, Ibn Abi Najih, al-Suddi, al-Dahhak, Ibn Zayd and others. The second view is that the drop of semen (nutfah) was created by God from clay in reality, and then He transformed it until it became a human being; this is mentioned by al-Nahhas.

I say: In sum, when the Mighty and Majestic mentioned the creation of the great world (al-'alam al-kabir), He mentioned after it the creation of the small world (al-'alam al-saghir), which is the human being, and placed in him what is in the great world, as we have explained in al-Baqarah (see vol. 2, p. 202 and following) in the verse of tawhid. And God knows best, and praise be to God.

Abu Nu'aym al-Hafiz narrated in his book, from Murrah, from Ibn Mas'ud, that the angel entrusted with the womb takes the drop, places it on his palm, and says: "O Lord, is it formed or unformed?" If He says "formed," he says: "O Lord, what is the provision, what is the trace, what is the term?" And He says: "Look in the Mother of the Book." So he looks in the Preserved Tablet and finds in it its provision, its trace, its term and its deeds. He takes the dust in which it will be buried in its place and kneads with it its drop. That is the saying of God the Exalted: ﴿From it We created you, and into it We will return you﴾ (Ta-Ha: 55). (See vol. 11, p. 120.)

And he transmitted from Abu Hurayrah, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "There is no child born except that some of the dust of its grave has been sprinkled upon it." 

I say: According to this, every human being is created from clay and from a despised fluid, as God the Exalted has informed in Surah al-Mu'minun (see vol. 12, p. 108). Thus the verses and the hadiths are harmonized, and the difficulty and the contradiction are removed. And God knows best.

As for the report of the creation of Adam, peace be upon him, it has already been mentioned in al-Baqarah (see vol. 1, p. 279), with its derivation, and we will add here a portion of that, his description, his age and his death. Ibn Sa'd mentioned in al-Tabaqat, from Abu Hurayrah, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "The people are the children of Adam, and Adam is from dust." And from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, who said: God created Adam, peace be upon him, from earth called Dajna' (dajna': with a long or short vowel; it is transmitted with a non-emphatic ḥā' and is vocalized in al-Lisan and al-Nihayah with a fatha on the dal; the author of al-Qamus said: it is with a damma and a kasra). Al-Hasan said: And He created his chest (ju'ju') from Daryah. Al-Jawhari said: Daryah is a village of the Banu Kilab on the road to Basra, and it is closer to Makkah. And from Ibn Mas'ud, who said: God the Exalted sent Iblis, and he took from the surface of the earth, from its sweet and its salty parts, and Adam, peace be upon him, was created from it. Thus whatever He created from its sweet part goes to Paradise, even if it is the son of an unbeliever, and whatever He created from its salty part goes to the Fire, even if it is the son of a pious man (in one copy: a prophet). Hence Iblis said: "Shall I prostrate to one whom You created from clay?" (al-Isra': 61), because he [Adam] came with the clay (al-tinah), so he was named Adam, because he was created from the surface of the earth (adim al-ard).

And from Abdullah ibn Salam, who said: God created Adam at the end of Friday. And from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: When God created Adam, his head touched the sky. He said: He then flattened him to the earth until he became sixty cubits in length and seven cubits in breadth. And from Ubayy ibn Ka'b, who said: Adam, peace be upon him, was tall, curly-haired, as if he were a towering palm tree (nakhlah saḥuq; al-saḥuq: the very tall one). And from Ibn 'Abbas, in a lengthy narration: Adam, peace be upon him, performed the Hajj from India to Makkah forty times on foot. When Adam was sent down, his head touched the sky, and therefore he became bald, and he bequeathed baldness to his offspring, and the land animals fled from his height, and they became wild from that day. He did not die until his offspring and the offspring of his offspring reached forty thousand. He died on the summit of the mountain upon which he had been sent down. Shith said to Jibril, peace be upon them both: "Pray over Adam." Jibril said to him: "Go forward yourself and pray over your father," and he pronounced thirty takbirs over him: five for the prayer, and twenty-five as an honor to Adam. It is also said: he pronounced four takbirs over him. The children of Shith placed Adam in a cave and set over it a guard, so that none of the children of Qabil could approach him; those who came to him and asked forgiveness for him were the children of Shith. Adam's lifespan was nine hundred and thirty-six years.

It is said: Is there evidence in the verse that substances (al-jawahir) are of one genus? The answer is yes, because if clay may be transformed into a living human being, capable and knowing, it is permissible for it to be transformed into every state of the substances, since reason levels these in judgment. The transformation of the inanimate into the animate has indeed been established by the indication of this verse.

His words, may He be exalted: ﴿Then He decreed a term﴾ — the object. "And a named term is with Him" — the subject and predicate. Al-Dahhak said: "a term" refers to death, and "a named term with Him" is the term of the Resurrection. The meaning according to this is: He decreed a term and informed you that you remain until death, and He did not inform you of the term of the Resurrection.

Al-Hasan, Mujahid, Ikrimah, Khasif (in al-Tahdhib: it is a diminutive; in al-Qamus: it is like Amir) and Qatadah said — and this is al-Hasan's wording: He decreed the term of the world from the day He created you until you die, and "a named term with Him" means the Hereafter. It is also said: "He decreed a term" refers to what He made known to us, that there is no prophet after Muhammad (ﷺ), and "a named term" is from the Hereafter. It is also said: "He decreed a term" refers to what we know of the times of the crescent moons, the crops, and what resembles them, and "a named term" is the term of death, which a person does not know when he will die. Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid said: the meaning of the verse is "He decreed a term" by the decree of this world, and "a named term with Him" for the beginning of the Hereafter. It is also said: the first is the seizing of souls in sleep, and the second is the seizing of the soul at death, also from Ibn 'Abbas.

His words, may He be exalted: ﴿Then you still doubt﴾ — a beginning and predicate: that is, you doubt that He is one God. It is also said: you dispute about that, that is, you argue with the argument of doubters (in one copy: the polytheists). Disputing (al-tamari) is arguing on the basis of doubt, and from it is His saying: ﴿Will you then dispute with him about what he sees?﴾ (al-Najm: 12).

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 6, verse 3–5:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And He is Allah in the heavens and on the earth﴾. It is said: What is the governing element (ʿamil al-iʿrab) of the adverbial phrase in "fi al-samawat wa fi al-ard"? On this there are several answers. First: that is, He is Allah, the Exalted or the Worshipped, in the heavens and on the earth, just as you say: Zayd is the caliph in the east and the west, meaning his rule. It is also permissible that the meaning is: He is Allah, the One alone who governs in the heavens and on the earth, just as you say: He is in the needs of people and in the prayer. It is also permissible that it is a predicate after a predicate, and the meaning would be: He is Allah in the heavens, and He is Allah on the earth. It has also been said: the meaning is, He is Allah, who knows your secret and your open speech in the heavens and in the earth, so nothing is hidden from Him. Al-Nahhas said: this is among the best of what has been said concerning it. Muhammad ibn Jarir said: "He is Allah in the heavens," and "He knows your secret and your open speech" is in the earth; so "He knows" is the governing element in both readings, and the first is safer and further from difficulty. It has been said other than this. The established principle is His transcendence, exalted is He, above movement, transfer, and occupying places.

(And He knows what you earn) that is, of good and evil. Al-kasb (earning) is an action undertaken to bring about a benefit or to repel a harm, and for this reason the act of God is not called kasb.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And there does not come to them any sign﴾ that is, any indication, such as the splitting of the moon and the like. The "min" here is for the comprehensiveness of the genus, as you say: There is not in the house anyone (min ahad).

(of the signs of their Lord) The second "min" is partitive (lil-tabʿid). And (turning away) is the predicate of "kanu" (were). Al-iʿrad (turning away) is leaving off reflection upon the signs by which they ought to take evidence for the oneness of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, from the creation of the heavens and the earth and what is between them, and that He is returned to, Eternal, Living, Self-Sufficient, free of all things, Powerful, whom nothing can frustrate, Knowing, whom nothing is hidden from; and from the miracles which He established for His Prophet ﷺ, so that by them his truthfulness may be proven in all that he brought.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So indeed they have denied﴾ meaning the polytheists of Makkah.

(the truth) meaning the Qur'an; it has also been said: Muhammad ﷺ.

(So there will come to them) that is, there will befall them the punishment; and by the news (al-inba') is meant the tidings of the punishment, as when you say: Be patient, the news will come to you, meaning the punishment. The intended meaning is what befell them on the Day of Badr and the like. It has also been said: the Day of Resurrection.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 6, verse 3–5:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And He is Allah in the heavens and on the earth﴾. It is said: What is the governing element (ʿamil al-iʿrab) of the adverbial phrase in "fi al-samawat wa fi al-ard"? On this there are several answers. First: that is, He is Allah, the Exalted or the Worshipped, in the heavens and on the earth, just as you say: Zayd is the caliph in the east and the west, meaning his rule. It is also permissible that the meaning is: He is Allah, the One alone who governs in the heavens and on the earth, just as you say: He is in the needs of people and in the prayer. It is also permissible that it is a predicate after a predicate, and the meaning would be: He is Allah in the heavens, and He is Allah on the earth. It has also been said: the meaning is, He is Allah, who knows your secret and your open speech in the heavens and in the earth, so nothing is hidden from Him. Al-Nahhas said: this is among the best of what has been said concerning it. Muhammad ibn Jarir said: "He is Allah in the heavens," and "He knows your secret and your open speech" is in the earth; so "He knows" is the governing element in both readings, and the first is safer and further from difficulty. It has been said other than this. The established principle is His transcendence, exalted is He, above movement, transfer, and occupying places.

(And He knows what you earn) that is, of good and evil. Al-kasb (earning) is an action undertaken to bring about a benefit or to repel a harm, and for this reason the act of God is not called kasb.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And there does not come to them any sign﴾ that is, any indication, such as the splitting of the moon and the like. The "min" here is for the comprehensiveness of the genus, as you say: There is not in the house anyone (min ahad).

(of the signs of their Lord) The second "min" is partitive (lil-tabʿid). And (turning away) is the predicate of "kanu" (were). Al-iʿrad (turning away) is leaving off reflection upon the signs by which they ought to take evidence for the oneness of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, from the creation of the heavens and the earth and what is between them, and that He is returned to, Eternal, Living, Self-Sufficient, free of all things, Powerful, whom nothing can frustrate, Knowing, whom nothing is hidden from; and from the miracles which He established for His Prophet ﷺ, so that by them his truthfulness may be proven in all that he brought.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So indeed they have denied﴾ meaning the polytheists of Makkah.

(the truth) meaning the Qur'an; it has also been said: Muhammad ﷺ.

(So there will come to them) that is, there will befall them the punishment; and by the news (al-inba') is meant the tidings of the punishment, as when you say: Be patient, the news will come to you, meaning the punishment. The intended meaning is what befell them on the Day of Badr and the like. It has also been said: the Day of Resurrection.

﴿Did they not see how many generations We destroyed before them?﴾ The word "كَمْ" (kam, "how many") is in the accusative position, governed by "أَهْلَكْنَا" (ahlaknā, "We destroyed") and not by "أَلَمْ يَرَوْا" (alam yaraw, "did they not see"), because an interrogative word is not governed by what precedes it. Rather, it is governed by what follows it, since the interrogative has the front position in the sentence. The meaning is: "Do they not take warning from those nations We destroyed before them because of their denial of their prophets?" That is, "Did they not know this?"

"Al-qarn" (generation, a people of the same era) is a community of people. Its plural is "al-qurūn." The poet said:

*When the generation in which you were has passed away,*
*and you have been left behind in another generation, then you are a stranger.*

So "qarn" is every people in its age, derived from "iqtirān" (association), meaning people associated with one another in one time. In a hadith from the Prophet ﷺ he said: "The best of people is my generation (qarnī), meaning my companions, then those who follow them, then those who follow them." This is the most authentic of what has been said about it. It has also been said that the meaning is "from the people of a generation," with the word omitted, as in His saying ﴿and ask the town﴾ (Yusuf 12:82). According to this, "qarn" is a period of time. It has been said to be sixty years, seventy, eighty, or a hundred. Most of the people of hadith hold that a qarn is a hundred years, and they argued with the statement of the Prophet ﷺ to Abdullah ibn Busr: "You will live a qarn," and he lived a hundred years. This was mentioned by al-Nahhas. The root meaning of "qarn" is a thing that rises, as in "qarn" for an animal's horn.

﴿We had established them on the earth as We had not established you﴾ is a shift from the third person (ghaybah, absence) to the second person (khiṭāb, direct address). The opposite is in His saying: ﴿until, when you are in the ship and they sail with them with a good wind﴾ (Yunus 10:22). The people of Basra said: He reported about them with His saying "Did they not see," and among them were Muhammad, peace be upon him, and his companions. Then He addressed them together with them. The Arabs say: "I said to Abdullah, 'How generous he is!'" and "I said to Abdullah, 'How generous you are!'" If it had come according to the earlier third person, it would have said: "as We had not established for them." It is permissible to say "makkinhu" and "makkin lahu" (both forms of "establish for"), so the verse came with both dialects together. The meaning is: We gave them of the worldly things what We did not give you.

﴿And We sent the sky upon them in abundant rain﴾. It means abundant rain, expressed by "the sky" because rain descends from the sky. From this is the saying of the poet [[Ma'ud al-Hukama', Mu'awiya ibn Malik. In another version: "nazal al-samā'" (the sky descended). This is the first half of a line whose completion is:

*We grazed it, even if they were angry.*

He was called Ma'ud al-Hukama' because of his saying in this poem:

*I return with its like, the wise after me,*
*when right in calamities strikes.*

*[ ..... ]*

*When the sky falls upon the land of a people.*]]

"Midrār" (abundant, pouring) is a form indicating intensity, like "midhkār" for a woman who has given birth to many males, and "mi'nāth" for a woman who gives birth to many females. It is said: "darra al-laban yadirru," meaning the milk flows abundantly when it comes to the milker. "Midrāran" is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (ḥāl).

﴿And We made the rivers flow beneath them﴾, that is, beneath their trees and dwellings. From this is the saying of Pharaoh: ﴿And these rivers flow beneath me﴾ (al-Zukhruf 43:51). The meaning is: We expanded favours upon them, and they disbelieved in them.

﴿So We destroyed them for their sins﴾, that is, for their disbelief. Thus sins are the cause of retribution and the removal of blessings.

﴿And We produced after them another generation﴾, that is, We brought into being. Let these people beware of destruction too.

The verbal noun of His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And if We had sent down to you a Book on parchment﴾ (qirtas, a written sheet), and so on. The meaning: And if We had sent it down, O Muhammad, before their eyes, as they claimed and demanded, a written speech "on parchment." From Ibn 'Abbas: a book suspended between the heaven and the earth. This shows you that "sending down" has two aspects. The first is that it means the Book was sent down to you in the sense of the angel's descending with it. The second is: "And if We had sent down a book on parchment," held by God between the heaven and the earth. He said "sent down" as an intensification, describing the long duration of the book's staying between heaven and earth. "The Book" is a verbal noun meaning the act of writing. He then made clear that the writing was on parchment, because writing without parchment is not conceivable. "On parchment" means on a page. Qirtas means a page, and it is said qirtas with a damma, and "qartasa so-and-so" means he shot and hit the page attached to the target.

﴿So they touched it with their hands﴾: that is, they witnessed it and touched it with their hands, as they had proposed, and exaggerated in examining and turning it over by feeling it with their hands, so that every doubt would be removed and every difficulty would vanish from them entirely. Yet they persisted in opposition, continued in their disbelief, and said: ﴿This is nothing but clear magic﴾, meaning, "Our eyes have only been dazzled and we have been bewitched." This verse is a reply to their saying: "Until you send down to us a book that we can read" (Al-Isra 17:93). God informed them, by what had preceded in His knowledge, that if He had sent it down they would have denied it.

Al-Kalbi said: It was revealed concerning al-Nadr ibn al-Harith, Abdullah ibn Abi Umayyah, and Nawfal ibn Khuwaylid, who said: "We will not believe you until you cause a spring to gush forth for us from the earth" (Al-Isra 17:90), and the rest of the verse.

The commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 6, verses 8–10:

Allah's words: (They say, "Why was not an angel sent down to him?") They suggested this as well. And "dhalulan" [sic] means "halla" (why not / would that).

(And if We had sent down an angel, the matter would have been decided.) Ibn 'Abbas said: If they saw the angel in his own form, they would die, since they could not bear to see him. Mujahid and Ikrimah said: the Hour would have been established. Al-Hasan and Qatadah said: they would have been destroyed by the punishment of annihilation (al-'adhab al-isti'sal), because Allah has established His custom that whoever asks for a sign, and it is shown to him, and he does not believe, Allah destroys him immediately. That is, (they would not be given respite) means they would not be granted delay or postponement.

Allah's words: ﴿And if We had made him an angel, We would have made him a man﴾, meaning: they would not be able to see the angel in his own form except after he takes on dense bodies, because every kind is at ease with its own kind and shuns other kinds. So if Allah made the messenger to mankind an angel, they would shun coming near him and would not feel at ease with him, and fear and dread of his speech and of guarding against him would seize them, which would keep them from speaking to him and prevent them from questioning him. Then the benefit would not be achieved. And even if He had transferred him from the form of the angels to a form like theirs, so that they would feel at ease with him and settle with him, they would say, "You are not an angel, you are only a human, so we do not believe in you," and they would return to their former state. The angels used to come to the prophets in human form: they came to Abraham and Lot in the form of human beings, and Jibril (Gabriel) came to the Prophet (ﷺ) in the form of Dihya al-Kalbi. That is: if an angel had been sent down, they would have seen him in the form of a man, as is the custom of the prophets; and if he descended in his own form, they would not have seen him. So when We make him a man, it would be confusing to them, and they would say, "This is a sorcerer like you."

Al-Zajjaj said: the meaning of (and We would have confused them) is: [confused] their leaders, just as they confuse their weak followers. They used to say to them, "Muhammad is only a human, and there is no difference between him and you," and so they would confuse them with this and create doubt in them. So Allah, mighty and majestic, informed them that if He sent down an angel in the form of a man, they would find a way to confusion, as they do.

Al-labs (confusion) means mixing. It is said: labastu 'alayhi al-amra, albisuhu labsan, meaning I mixed it up for him. Its original sense is covering with a garment or the like. He said "lalabasna" (We would have confused) with the attribution to Himself, in the sense of creation, and He said "ma yalbisuna" (what they confuse) attributing it to them, in the sense of acquisition.

Then He said, comforting and consoling His Prophet (ﷺ): ﴿And messengers before you were mocked, but what they had been mocking encompassed those who mocked﴾, meaning: there descended upon their nations the punishment by which they were destroyed, as recompense for their mocking of their prophets. "Haqa bi al-shay'" (haqa) means: yahiqu, haiqan, huyuqan, haiqanan, it descended. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And the evil plotting encompasses only its own people﴾ [Fatir: 43]. And "ma" in His words "bima kanu" [what they used to] has the sense of "alladhi" (which). It has also been said that it has the sense of the verbal noun, meaning: the consequence of their mockery encompassed them.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 6, verse 11–12:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Say: Travel through the earth﴾, meaning: Say, O Muhammad, to these mockers, scoffers, and deniers: Travel through the earth, then observe and inquire, so that you may know what punishment and painful torment befell the disbelievers before you. This travel is recommended when it is undertaken for the sake of reflection (i'tibar, taking a lesson) upon the traces of the nations that passed away and the inhabitants of the abodes, and "the outcome" (al-'aqibah) is the final end of the matter. The deniers here are those who deny the truth and its people, not those who deny falsehood.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Say: To whom belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth?﴾ This [also] [[in k.]] is an argument against them. The meaning: Say to them, O Muhammad: "To whom belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth?" If they say, "To whom?", then say: "To Allah." The meaning: once it is established that to Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth, and that He is the Creator of all, either by their acknowledgment or by the establishment of proof against them, then Allah is able to hasten their punishment and to resurrect them after death. But He ﴿has prescribed for Himself mercy﴾, meaning He has promised it out of His bounty and generosity, and therefore they are granted respite. The mention of "Himself" here is an expression of His existence and an affirmation of His promise, and of the absence of intermediaries between Him and it. The sense of the statement is an appeal from Him, Exalted is He, to those who turn away from Him to turn toward Him, and an announcement from Him, glory be to Him, that He is merciful to His servants and does not hasten to punish them, and accepts from them repentance and return.

In Sahih Muslim, on the authority of Abu Hurayrah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "When Allah had decreed creation, He wrote in a Book, concerning Himself, which is placed with Him: Indeed My mercy overcomes My wrath." That is, when He manifested His decree and made it apparent to whomever He willed, He caused a Book to appear in the Preserved Tablet, or wherever He wished; its content is a true report and a promise of truth: "Indeed My mercy overcomes My wrath," meaning it precedes it and exceeds it.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Surely He will gather you﴾. The lam is the lam of oath, and the nun is the nun of emphasis. Al-Farra' and others said: it is permissible that the complete sentence ends at His saying "the mercy," and what follows is a new clause by way of explanation, so that the meaning of "He will gather you" is: He will grant you respite and will delay your gathering. It was also said: the meaning is "He will gather you," i.e., in the graves, until the Day you denied. It was also said: "ila" (to) is in the sense of "fi" (in), i.e., He will gather you on the Day of Resurrection. It was also said: the position of "He will gather you" may be in the accusative as an apposition (badal) to "the mercy," so that the lam has the sense of "an" (that). The meaning is: "Your Lord has prescribed for Himself that He will gather you," i.e., that He gather you. Many grammarians said the same regarding His saying: ﴿Then it appeared to them, after they had seen the signs, that they should imprison him﴾ [Yusuf: 35], i.e., that they imprison him. It was also said: its position is in the accusative governed by "kataba" (He prescribed), just as "anna" is in His saying: ﴿Your Lord has prescribed for Himself mercy: that whoever of you does evil in ignorance﴾ [al-An'am: 54]; this is because it explains the mercy as respite until the Day of Resurrection, according to al-Zajjaj.

﴿There is no doubt in it﴾: there is no doubt (la shakk) in it.

﴿Those who have lost their souls, they do not believe﴾: this is a subject and predicate (ibtida' wa khabar), as said by al-Zajjaj, and it is the best of what has been said about it. You say: "Whoever honors me, for him is a dirham," so the fa' includes the meaning of condition and consequence. Al-Akhfash said: if you wish, "Those who" may be in the accusative position as an apposition (badal) of the kaf and mim in "He will gather you," i.e., He will gather the polytheists who have lost their souls. Al-Mubarrad rejected this and claimed it was an error, because one does not apposit from the addressed or the addressing: one does not say "marartu bika Zayd" or "marartu bi Zayd," since this is not ambiguous so as to require clarification. Al-Qutabi said: "Those who" may be a qualifier (na't) or a badal of "the deniers" mentioned earlier. It was also said: "Those who" is a vocative of a singular noun.

The commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 6, verse 17:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And if God touches you with harm, there is none who can remove it except Him﴾. The touching (al-mass) and removing (al-kashf) are attributes of bodies, and here they are used figuratively (majaz) and in an extended sense (tawassu'). The meaning is: if hardship of poverty or sickness befalls you, O Muhammad, there is none to lift it or turn it away except Him. And if He afflicts you with well-being, ease and blessing (fa-Huwa 'ala kulli shay'in Qadir), He is capable of all things, of good and of harm.

Ibn 'Abbas narrated: I was riding behind the Messenger of God (ﷺ), and he said to me: "O boy, or O my son, shall I not teach you words through which God will benefit you?" I said: "Yes." He said: "Be mindful of God and He will protect you. Be mindful of God and you will find Him before you. Get to know God in ease and He will know you in hardship. When you ask, ask God; and when you seek help, seek help from God. The pen has dried over what is to be. If all of creation gathered to harm you with anything God had not decreed for you, they would not be able to do it. Serve God with gratitude and certainty, and know that in patience with what you dislike there is much good, that victory comes with patience, that relief comes with distress, and that with hardship comes ease."

Abu Bakr ibn Thabit al-Khatib narrated it in his book (al-Fasl wa'l-Wasl), and it is a sound hadith (hadith sahih). It was also transmitted by al-Tirmidhi, and this version is more complete.

**Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 6, verses 18–19:**

His statement, exalted is He: ﴿And He is the Subduer over His servants﴾. Al-qahr is domination (al-ghalabah), al-qahir is the dominant one (al-ghalib), and uqhira al-rajul means that a man is made to be in the state of one subdued and humiliated. The poet said [[He is al-Mukhabbal al-Sa'di, satirizing al-Zibriqan and his people. Jidha' al-rajul means his people.]]:

*"Husayn wished that his jidha' would rule,*
*so Husayn became humiliated and subdued."*

Qahira means he was overcome. The meaning of ﴿over His servants﴾ is the over-ness of dominance through subjugation and overpowering them; that is, they are under His control. It is not a spatial over-ness, just as you say "the sultan is over his subjects," meaning in rank and elevation. Qahr carries an additional meaning not found in qudrah (power), namely preventing others from reaching their aims.

﴿And He is the Wise﴾ in His command, ﴿the Aware﴾ of the deeds of His servants. That is, whoever is characterized by these attributes must not be associated with Him.

His statement, exalted is He: ﴿Say, "What thing is greatest in testimony?"﴾ This was because the polytheists said to the Prophet ﷺ: "Who will testify for you that you are the Messenger of Allah?" So the verse was revealed, according to al-Hasan and others. The word "thing" (shay') here stands in the place of the name of Allah, Exalted, and the meaning is: Allah is greatest in testimony, that is, His singularity in lordship (al-rububiyyah) and the presence of proofs for His oneness are the greatest and most mighty testimony. So He is a witness between me and you that I have conveyed to you and that I have been truthful in what I said and claimed of prophethood. His statement, exalted is He: ﴿And this Qur'an has been revealed to me﴾, that is, the Qur'an is a witness to my prophethood.

﴿That I may warn you thereby﴾, O people of Makkah.

﴿And whoever it reaches﴾, that is, whoever the Qur'an has reached. The pronoun (al-ha') has been omitted because of the length of the speech. It has also been said: "and whoever reaches puberty (al-hulm)." By this it is indicated that whoever has not reached puberty is neither addressed nor obligated in worship. Conveying the Qur'an and the Sunnah is commanded, just as the Prophet ﷺ was commanded to convey them, when He said: ﴿O Messenger, convey what has been revealed to you from your Lord﴾ [[See p. 242 of this part.]] [al-Ma'idah: 67]. In Sahih al-Bukhari (a collection of hadith regarded as the most authentic), from Abdullah ibn Amr, from the Prophet ﷺ: "Convey from me even if it is a single verse, and narrate from the Children of Israel without restriction, and whoever deliberately lies about me, let him take his seat in the Fire." There is also a report: whoever has received a verse of the Book of Allah, the command of Allah has reached him; he either acts upon it or abandons it. Muqatil said: whoever the Qur'an has reached, of the jinn and of mankind, it is a warning to him. Al-Qurazi said: whoever the Qur'an has reached is as if he has seen Muhammad ﷺ and heard from him. Abu Nahik read: ﴿And this Qur'an has been revealed to me﴾ in the active form (musamma al-fa'il), and this is the meaning of the reading of the majority.

His statement, exalted is He: ﴿Do you indeed testify that there are other gods with Allah?﴾ This is an interrogative of reproach and rebuke. It is read as "a-innakum" with two hamzahs, according to the original form. If the second is lightened, you say "ayyinakum." Al-Asma'i transmitted from Abu Amr and Nafi' "a'innakum," and this is a well-known dialect in which an alif is placed between the two hamzahs because of their meeting. The poet said [[He is Dhu al-Rummah. al-Wa'sa' is a soft sandy tract, and Jalajil (with a fatha on the jim) and, in Sibawayh's book, (with a damma), is a specific place. al-Naqa is a sand dune.]]:

*"O gazelle of al-Wa'sa' between Jalajil*
*and the dune, are you a-(anta) or Umm Salim?"*

As for the one who reads "innakum" as a statement, the meaning is that He has confirmed their polytheism upon them. He said: ﴿other gods﴾ and did not say "ukhar" (plural masculine). Al-Farra' said: because "gods" (alihah) is a plural, and the plural may take the feminine, and from this is His statement: ﴿And to Allah belong the Most Beautiful Names, so call upon Him by them﴾ [[See vol. 10, p. 342.]] [Ta-Ha: 51], and His statement: ﴿What then is the state of the former generations?﴾ [[See vol. 11, p. 205.]] [Ta-Ha: 51]. If He had said "al-awwal wa al-akhir" it would also have been correct [[That is, outside the Qur'an.]].

His statement, exalted is He: ﴿Say, "I do not testify."﴾ That is, "I do not testify with you." The object has been omitted because the context indicates it. Its parallel is: ﴿If they testify, do not testify with them﴾ [[See vol. 7, p. 129.]] [al-An'am: 150].

*so Husayn became humiliated and subdued."*

Qahira means he was overcome. The meaning of ﴿over His servants﴾ is the over-ness of dominance through subjugation and overpowering them; that is, they are under His control. It is not a spatial over-ness, just as you say "the sultan is over his subjects," meaning in rank and elevation. Qahr carries an additional meaning not found in qudrah (power), namely preventing others from reaching their aims.

﴿And He is the Wise﴾ in His command, ﴿the Aware﴾ of the deeds of His servants. That is, whoever is characterized by these attributes must not be associated with Him.

His statement, exalted is He: ﴿Say, "What thing is greatest in testimony?"﴾ This was because the polytheists said to the Prophet ﷺ: "Who will testify for you that you are the Messenger of Allah?" So the verse was revealed, according to al-Hasan and others. The word "thing" (shay') here stands in the place of the name of Allah, Exalted, and the meaning is: Allah is greatest in testimony, that is, His singularity in lordship (al-rububiyyah) and the presence of proofs for His oneness are the greatest and most mighty testimony. So He is a witness between me and you that I have conveyed to you and that I have been truthful in what I said and claimed of prophethood. His statement, exalted is He: ﴿And this Qur'an has been revealed to me﴾, that is, the Qur'an is a witness to my prophethood.

﴿That I may warn you thereby﴾, O people of Makkah.

﴿And whoever it reaches﴾, that is, whoever the Qur'an has reached. The pronoun (al-ha') has been omitted because of the length of the speech. It has also been said: "and whoever reaches puberty (al-hulm)." By this it is indicated that whoever has not reached puberty is neither addressed nor obligated in worship. Conveying the Qur'an and the Sunnah is commanded, just as the Prophet ﷺ was commanded to convey them, when He said: ﴿O Messenger, convey what has been revealed to you from your Lord﴾ [[See p. 242 of this part.]] [al-Ma'idah: 67]. In Sahih al-Bukhari (a collection of hadith regarded as the most authentic), from Abdullah ibn Amr, from the Prophet ﷺ: "Convey from me even if it is a single verse, and narrate from the Children of Israel without restriction, and whoever deliberately lies about me, let him take his seat in the Fire." There is also a report: whoever has received a verse of the Book of Allah, the command of Allah has reached him; he either acts upon it or abandons it. Muqatil said: whoever the Qur'an has reached, of the jinn and of mankind, it is a warning to him. Al-Qurazi said: whoever the Qur'an has reached is as if he has seen Muhammad ﷺ and heard from him. Abu Nahik read: ﴿And this Qur'an has been revealed to me﴾ in the active form (musamma al-fa'il), and this is the meaning of the reading of the majority.

His statement, exalted is He: ﴿Do you indeed testify that there are other gods with Allah?﴾ This is an interrogative of reproach and rebuke. It is read as "a-innakum" with two hamzahs, according to the original form. If the second is lightened, you say "ayyinakum." Al-Asma'i transmitted from Abu Amr and Nafi' "a'innakum," and this is a well-known dialect in which an alif is placed between the two hamzahs because of their meeting. The poet said [[He is Dhu al-Rummah. al-Wa'sa' is a soft sandy tract, and Jalajil (with a fatha on the jim) and, in Sibawayh's book, (with a damma), is a specific place. al-Naqa is a sand dune.]]:

*"O gazelle of al-Wa'sa' between Jalajil*
*and the dune, are you a-(anta) or Umm Salim?"*

As for the one who reads "innakum" as a statement, the meaning is that He has confirmed their polytheism upon them. He said: ﴿other gods﴾ and did not say "ukhar" (plural masculine). Al-Farra' said: because "gods" (alihah) is a plural, and the plural may take the feminine, and from this is His statement: ﴿And to Allah belong the Most Beautiful Names, so call upon Him by them﴾ [[See vol. 10, p. 342.]] [Ta-Ha: 51], and His statement: ﴿What then is the state of the former generations?﴾ [[See vol. 11, p. 205.]] [Ta-Ha: 51]. If He had said "al-awwal wa al-akhir" it would also have been correct [[That is, outside the Qur'an.]].

His statement, exalted is He: ﴿Say, "I do not testify."﴾ That is, "I do not testify with you." The object has been omitted because the context indicates it. Its parallel is: ﴿If they testify, do not testify with them﴾ [[See vol. 7, p. 129.]] [al-An'am: 150].

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 6, verse 20:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Those whom We have given the Book﴾. He means the Jews and the Christians who recognized (the truth) and yet were obstinate. Its meaning has already been discussed in (al-Baqarah) [[See vol. 2, p. 162 onward.]]. The word ﴿alladhina﴾ (those who) is in the nominative case as the subject (mubtada'). ﴿Yaʿrifunahu﴾ (they recognize him) is in the position of the predicate (khabar), meaning: they recognize the Prophet ﷺ. This is related from al-Hasan and Qatadah, and it is the view of al-Zajjaj. It was also said: the pronoun refers to the Book, meaning they recognize it in the manner by which it indicates (the truth of it), namely, the attribute by which it points to the soundness of the matter of the Prophet ﷺ and his family. ﴿Alladhina khasiru anfusahum﴾ (those who have lost their souls) is in the position of a descriptive adjective (na't). It is also permissible that it be a subject (mubtada'), with its predicate being ﴿fahum la yu'minun﴾ (so they do not believe).

**Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 6, verses 21–22:**

Allah's words ﴿And who is more unjust﴾ are a *ibtida'* (the subject of a nominal sentence, in grammatical terms) and a *khabar* (its predicate). The meaning is: there is no one more unjust ﴿than one who fabricates against Allah a lie﴾, i.e. invents it, ﴿or denies His signs﴾, meaning the Qur'an and the miracles (*mu'jizat*).

﴿Indeed, the wrongdoers will not prosper.﴾ It has been said that this refers to this world. Then He resumes: ﴿And [mention] the Day We will gather them all together﴾, meaning "remember the Day We gather them." It has also been said that the meaning is: the wrongdoers will not prosper in this world nor on the Day We gather them. On this reading, one does not stop at ﴿the wrongdoers﴾, because what follows is connected to it. It has also been said that it is connected to what comes after, which is ﴿Look﴾ (*unzur*), meaning: look how they lied on the Day We gather them, i.e. how will they lie on the Day We gather them?

﴿Then We will say to those who associated others with Allah: "Where are your partners,﴾ this is a question of exposure (*ifdah*), not of clarification (*ifsah*). [[In manuscript K: "not of clarification (*idah*)."]]

﴿whom you used to claim?"﴾ meaning: that they would intercede for you with Allah according to your claim, and that they would bring you near to Him in nearness. This is a rebuke to them. Ibn 'Abbas said: every "claim" (*za'm*) in the Qur'an is a lie.

**Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 6, verses 21–22:**
