Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 6, verse 23:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Then their fitnah (trial, test) will be nothing﴾. Al-fitnah means al-ikhtibar (testing), meaning: their answer was not, when they were tested with this question, and they saw the realities and the motives [[In MS h, w, j, and ʿ: al-da'awa (claims).]] were removed.

(﴿Except that they said, "By Allah, our Lord, we were not polytheists."﴾) They disavowed shirk and denied it, because they saw His forgiveness and His pardon toward the believers. Ibn ʿAbbas said: Allah, may He be exalted, forgives the ruin of the sincere people, and no sin is too great for Him to forgive. So when the polytheists see this, they say, "Indeed our Lord forgives sins, and does not forgive shirk. So come, let us say: we were people of sins, and we were not polytheists." Then Allah, may He be exalted, says: "Now, since they concealed shirk, seal their mouths," so their mouths are sealed, and their hands speak and their feet bear witness to what they used to earn. At that point the polytheists know that Allah does not leave any statement concealed. This is His saying: ﴿On that Day those who disbelieved and disobeyed the Messenger will wish that the earth were leveled over them, and they will not conceal from Allah any statement﴾ [an-Nisa 42]. Abu Ishaq al-Zajjaj said: The interpretation of this verse is very subtle. Allah, mighty and majestic, informed of the stories of the polytheists and their being tempted by their shirk, then He informed that their fitnah (trial) at the time they saw the realities was only that they disavowed shirk. A parallel to this in language is that you see a person who loves a misguided one, and when he falls into ruin, he disavows him, and it is said: "Your love for him was only that you disowned him." Al-Hasan said: This is specific to the hypocrites, who acted according to their habit in the world, and the meaning of "fitnatuhum" is the outcome of their fitnah, that is their disbelief. Qatadah said: its meaning is their excuse.

In Sahih Muslim, from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, he said: (The servant will meet [Allah], and He will say, "O so-and-so [Ay Ful]?" [[Al-Nawawi said: (with a damma on the fa' and a sukun on the lam), and its meaning is "O so-and-so," and it is a truncation contrary to analogy. It was also said: it is not a truncation but a dialectal form meaning "so-and-so," because it is only said with a sukun on the lam; if it were a truncation they would have made it with a fatha or damma. And "turaabbi'" means "you take a quarter of the booty," meaning: "Did I not make you a chief obeyed, because the king used to take a quarter of the booty in the Jahiliyyah, not his companions." It was also said: its meaning is "I left you at ease, not needing hardship and seeking."]] "Did I not honor you, make you a chief, [and marry you] [[Addition from Sahih Muslim.]], subject to you horses and camels, and leave you to lead and take a quarter?" He will say, "Yes [O my Lord]." [[Addition from Sahih Muslim.]] Then He will say, "Did you think that you would meet Me?" He will say, "No." Then He will say, "Indeed I forget you as you forgot Me." Then he meets the second and says to him the same, and he says the same exactly. Then he meets the third and says to him the same, and he says, "O my Lord, I believed in You, in Your Book, and in Your Messenger, and I prayed, fasted, and gave charity," and he praises himself with the best he can. He said: Then it is said, "Here, then," and then it is said to him, "Now We will send a witness against you," and he reflects within himself, "Who is it that will bear witness against me?" Then his mouth is sealed, and it is said to his thigh, his flesh, and his bones, "Speak," and his thigh, his flesh, and his bones speak of his deeds. This is so that he may have no excuse from himself, and that is the hypocrite, and that is the one with whom Allah is angry.)

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 6, verse 24:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Look how they lied against themselves﴾. The lie of the polytheists was their saying that worshipping idols brings us near to God in nearness (zulfa). Rather, they supposed this, and their supposition being mistaken does not excuse them nor remove the name of lying from them. And the lie of the hypocrites was in their excusing themselves with falsehood and in their denial of their hypocrisy.

(﴿And what they used to fabricate has vanished from them﴾), that is, look how their fabrication vanished from them, meaning it dissolved and became void, what they used to suppose of the intercession of their gods. It was also said: (﴿And what they used to fabricate has vanished from them﴾) means: what they used to worship besides God departed from them, so it did not avail them anything, related from al-Hasan. It was also said: the meaning is that their fabrication escaped them because of their bewilderment and the distraction of their minds.

The looking in His saying (﴿Look﴾) is meant as the looking of reflection (nazar al-i'tibar). Then it was said: (﴿how they lied﴾) means "how they will lie," so the future is expressed by the past, and it is permissible that they lie in the Hereafter, because it is a place of bewilderment, confusion and distraction of the mind. It was also said: it is not permissible that a lie should occur from them in the Hereafter, because it is an abode of recompense for what was in this world, and this is the view of most people of reflection; the lie belongs only to this world. So the meaning of ﴿By God, our Lord, we were not polytheists﴾ according to this view is: we were not polytheists in our own estimation. According to the permissibility that they lie in the Hereafter, His saying ﴿And they will not hide from God any statement﴾ seems to contradict it, but there is no contradiction: they will not hide from God any statement in some situations, when their tongues, hands and feet testify against them for their deeds, and they lie against themselves in some situations before the testimony of the limbs, as previously explained. And God knows best.

Sa'id ibn Jubayr, regarding His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿By God, our Lord, we were not polytheists﴾, said: they made excuses and swore oaths. Likewise said Ibn Abi Najih and Qatadah. It is related from Mujahid that he said: when they saw that sins are forgiven except associating partners with God, and that people are coming out of the Fire, they said: ﴿By God, our Lord, we were not polytheists.﴾ It was also said: ﴿By God, our Lord, we were not polytheists﴾ means: we knew that stones neither harm nor benefit. This, though it is a correct statement, and they have spoken truthfully and not concealed, yet they are not excused by it, for the obstinate one is a disbeliever and not excused.

Then it was said regarding His saying ﴿Then their trial will not be⦅except that they said⦆﴾ there are five readings. Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read "yakun" (will be) with the ya', "fitnatahum" (their trial) in the accusative as the predicate of "yakun", and "illa an qalu" (except that they said) as its subject, meaning except their saying; this is a clear reading. The people of Madinah and Abu 'Amr read "takun" with the ta', "fitnatahum" in the accusative, and "(illa an qalu)" meaning except their statement. Ubayy and Ibn Mas'ud read, instead of "(thumma lam takun)", "wa ma kana" (and it was not), "fitnatuhum illa an qalu" (their trial was only that they said). Ibn 'Amir, 'Asim in the narration of Hafs, al-A'mash in the narration of al-Mufaddal, al-Hasan, Qatadah and others read "(thumma lam takun)" with the ta', "fitnatuhum" in the nominative as the subject of "takun", and "illa an qalu" as the predicate; these are four readings. The fifth: "thumma lam yakun" with the ya', "(fitnatuhum)" in the nominative; "fitnah" is treated as masculine because it means "futun" (trials), and similar to it is His saying: ﴿So whoever receives an admonition from his Lord and desists﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:275].

﴿Wallahi﴾: the waw is the waw of oath. ﴿Rabbuna﴾ is an epithet of God, may He be mighty and majestic, or an apposition. Whoever puts it in the accusative does so as a vocative, meaning "O our Lord," and this is a good reading, because it carries the sense of humility and supplication; however, it separates the oath from its answer by the vocative.

**Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 6, verse 25:**

The words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿And among them are those who listen to you﴾. [The verb was made singular] according to the wording (lafz), referring to the polytheists, the disbelievers of Makkah.[[Addition from Ibn ʿAṭiyya. Abu Ḥayyan: he made the pronoun singular in (yastamiʿu) in accordance with the wording of (man), and plural in (ʿalā qulūbihim) in accordance with its meaning.]]

(And We have placed over their hearts veils) means that We did this to them as a recompense for their disbelief. The meaning is not that they do not hear or do not understand, but since they did not benefit from what they heard, and did not submit to the truth, they were in the position of one who neither hears nor understands. The word (akinna) means coverings, the plural of (kinān), like (asinna) and (sinān), and (aʿinna) and (ʿinān). One says (kanantu al-shayʾa fī kinnihi) when I protected the thing within its covering, and (akantu al-shayʾ) when I concealed it. (Al-kinānah) is well known [meaning a quiver for arrows, and a tribe of Mudar, after whom the land of Kinanah was named].[[Meaning a quiver for arrows, and a tribe of Mudar, after whom the land of Kinanah was named.]] (Al-kannah), with a fatha on the kaf and the nun, is the wife of one's father; it is also said to be the wife of one's son or brother, because she is within his covering.

(That they should not understand it) means that they should not comprehend it, and it is in the accusative position. The meaning is: out of aversion to their understanding it, or lest they understand it.[[In (ج): yafqahūhu.]][[In (ج): yafqahūhu.]]

(And in their ears a heaviness) is coordinated with what precedes it, meaning a weight (waqr). From this one says: (waqirat udhunuhu), with a fatha on the waw, yaqaru waqran, meaning his ear became deaf. The regular verbal noun would be with a vowel on the middle letter, but it came with a sukun. Allah has also (waqara udhunahu, yaqiruhā waqran), and it is said: "O Allah, make his ear deaf (qir udhunahu)." Abu Zayd related from the Arabs: (udhunun mawqurah), in the passive form, so according to this (wuqirat) with a damma on the waw. Ṭalḥah ibn Muṣarrif read (wiqran) with a kasra on the waw, meaning that He placed in their ears what blocked them from hearing the speech, by way of comparison with the load (waqr) of a camel, which is the amount it can bear. (Al-waqr) is the load. From this one says: a palm tree laden (mawqir) or (mawqirah) when it has abundant fruit. A man who is (dhū qirah) is one who is dignified, with a fatha on the waw, and from it one says: (waqura al-rajul), with a damma on the qaf, (waqaran), and (waqara), with a fatha on the qaf, also.

The words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿And if they should see every sign, they would not believe in it﴾. Allah the Exalted informed of their obstinacy, because when they saw the moon split, they said: "It is magic." So Allah, Mighty and Majestic, informed that they rejected the signs without any proof.

The words of Allah the Exalted: (until, when they come to you, they dispute with you). Their dispute was their saying: "You eat what you have slaughtered, but you do not eat what Allah has slaughtered." This is related from Ibn ʿAbbas. (Those who disbelieve say) refers to Quraysh. Ibn ʿAbbas said: they said to al-Naḍr ibn al-Ḥārith: "What does Muhammad say?" He said: "I see him moving his lips, and he says nothing but the fables of the ancients, like what I tell you about the past generations." Al-Naḍr was a man of tales and journeys, and he had heard stories in the lands of the non-Arabs, such as the story of Rustam and Isfandiyar, so he would relate them to them. The singular of (asāṭīr) is (asṭār), like (abyāt) and (abāyīt), from al-Zajjāj.[[Thus in (اوب وهـ وك). In (زوع): anyab wa-anabib. Both are plurals, and plurals of plurals, so let it be considered.]] Al-Akhfash said: its singular is (ustūrah), like (uḥdūthah) and (aḥādīth). Abu ʿUbaydah said: its singular is (isṭārah). Al-Naḥḥas said: its singular is (usṭūr), like (ʿuthkūl).[[Al-ʿuthkūl: the cluster of dates; it is said: the stalk, which is the bunch of ripe dates upon the stalks of the palm cluster.]] It is also said that it is the plural of (asṭār), and (asṭār) is the plural of (saṭr). One says (saṭr) and (saṭar). A (saṭr) is an extended, arranged thing, like a line (saṭr) of a book. Al-Qushayrī said: its singular is (asṭīr). It is also said: it is a plural with no singular, like (madhākīr) and (ʿabādīd),[[Al-ʿabādīd and al-ʿabābīd, without a singular from their own form: groups of people and horses scattered and going in every direction, hills, and distant roads.]] and (abābīl), meaning what the ancients wrote in books. Al-Jawharī and others said: (al-asāṭīr) are falsehoods and empty nonsense.

I say: one of my teachers recited to me:

My night has grown long, and my whisperings have assailed me,
Because of one who came bringing trivialities and falsehoods.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 6, verse 26:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And they forbid it and keep away from it﴾. Al-nahy (forbidding) is restraint, and al-nay' is distance. It is general over all the disbelievers, meaning they forbid following Muhammad ﷺ and keep away from him; this is related from Ibn 'Abbas and al-Hasan. It was also said that it is specific to Abu Talib, who forbade the disbelievers from harming Muhammad ﷺ, yet kept away from belief in him; this too is related from Ibn 'Abbas. The people of the biographies (ahl al-siyar) narrated: The Prophet ﷺ had gone out to the Ka'bah one day and wished to pray. When he entered into the prayer, Abu Jahl (may Allah curse him) said: "Who will stand up to this man and spoil his prayer for him?" Ibn al-Zib'ara stood up, took dung and blood, and smeared it on the face of the Prophet ﷺ. The Prophet ﷺ turned from his prayer and then came to Abu Talib, his uncle, and said: (O uncle, do you not see what has been done to me?) Abu Talib said: "Who did this to you?" The Prophet ﷺ said: "Abd Allah ibn al-Zib'ara." Abu Talib stood up, placed his sword on his shoulder, and walked with him until he came to the people. When they saw Abu Talib approaching, the people began to rise, and Abu Talib said: "By Allah, if a man stands up, I will strike him with my sword," so they sat down until he drew near to them. He said: "O my son, who did this to you?" He said: (Abd Allah ibn al-Zib'ara). Abu Talib took dung and blood and smeared it on their faces, their beards and their garments, and spoke evil to them. Then this verse was revealed: "And they forbid it and keep away from it." The Prophet ﷺ said: (O uncle, a verse was revealed concerning you.) He said: "And what is it?" He said: (It prevents Quraysh from harming me and refuses to let you believe in me.) Abu Talib then said:

By Allah, they will never reach you with their host
until I am laid down buried in the dust.

So proclaim your command; there is no shame upon you,
and rejoice in it, and let your eyes be refreshed.

You called me, and you claimed that you were my sincere counsellor,
and indeed you spoke truly, and before this you were trustworthy.

And you presented a religion of which you know
that it is among the best religions of mankind.

Were it not for reproach, or dread of disgrace,
you would have found me generous in that, certain. [In al-Wahidi and others: "clear" (mubinan).]

They said: "O Messenger of Allah, will Abu Talib's support benefit him?" He said: (Yes, by it the shackle was removed from him, he was not joined with the devils, and he will not enter the pit of snakes and scorpions. His punishment is only in two sandals of fire, from which his brain boils; and that is the least punishment among the people of the Fire.) And Allah revealed to His Messenger: ﴿So be patient as the steadfast of the messengers were patient﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 35]. [See vol. 16, p. 220.]

In Sahih Muslim, from Abu Hurayrah, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said to his uncle: (Say, "There is no god but Allah," and I will testify for you with it on the Day of Resurrection.) He said: "Were it not that Quraysh would reproach me, saying, 'It was only fear that moved him to this,' I would have affirmed it, to comfort your eye." So Allah revealed: ﴿Indeed, you do not guide whom you love, but Allah guides whom He wills﴾ [al-Qasas: 56]. [See vol. 13, p. 299.] This is the well-known narration, "al-jaza'" with jim and zay, meaning fear. Abu 'Ubayd [in K and Y: Abu 'Ubaydah] said: "al-kharʻ" with a dotted kha and an undotted ra, meaning weakness and softness.

Also in Sahih Muslim, from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: (The least punished of the people of the Fire is Abu Talib, who wears two sandals of fire, from which his brain boils.)

As for Abd Allah ibn al-Zib'ara, he embraced Islam in the year of the Conquest, his Islam was good, and he sought pardon from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, who accepted his excuse. He was an excellent poet, and he said praising the Prophet ﷺ, and he has many poems in his praise which abrogate what had passed of his disbelief. Among them is his saying:

Sleep was kept away from me by restlessness and cares,
and the night, with its sheltering canopy, was dark.

Of what reached me, that Ahmad reproached me
concerning him, so I spent the night as if I were feverish.

O best of those on whose joints were carried
a swift, vigorous she-camel, agile of hands, strong. [al-naqah dhat al-sur'ah wa al-nashat, and al-naqah al-sulbah. See vol. 5, p. 206.]

Indeed I apologize to you for what
I did when I was in error, wandering.

In the days when Sahm commanded me to the most misguided course,
and Makhzum commanded me to it,

and I extended the causes of ruin, and the commands of the misguided led me,
and their command is ill-omened.

Today my heart has believed in the Prophet Muhammad,
and whoever errs in this is deprived.

Enmity has passed and its causes have ended,
and bonds and forbearance have come between us.

So forgive, may both my parents be a ransom for you,
my slip; for you are merciful, the one shown mercy.

Upon you is a mark from the Sovereign's sign,
a bright light and a sealed seal.

He gave you, after love, His proof,
honour; and the proof of God is great.

I have indeed testified that your religion is true
in truth, and that you are great among the servants.

And Allah bears witness that Ahmad is chosen,
he is honoured among the righteous.

A lord whose edifice rose from Hashim,
a branch established in the heights and roots. 

It was also said that the meaning of "they forbid it" is: those who listen forbid the Qur'an, "and keep away from it." This is from Qatadah. So the pronoun in "from it" according to the first two views refers to the Prophet ﷺ, and according to Qatadah's view it refers to the Qur'an.

﴿And they destroy none but themselves﴾: "in" (in) is negating, meaning they destroy none but themselves by their persistence in disbelief, and by bearing the burdens of those they turn away from.

"His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And if you could see when they are made to stand before the Fire⦅i.e. when⦆⦅from b, j, ʿ, and y⦆ they are made to stand⦆﴾ tomorrow. ⦅Idh⦆ may be used in the place of ⦅idha⦆, and ⦅idha⦆ in the place of ⦅idh⦆. What is yet to come is spoken of as if it had already happened, because God's report is true and certain, and so He expresses it in the past tense. The meaning of ⦅idh wuqifu⦆ is "they were held back"; one says: "I made him stand (waqaftuhu waqfan), and he stood (waqafa wuqufan)." Ibn al-Sumayqaʿ read ⦅idh waqafu⦆ with a fatha on the waw and the qaf, from al-wuquf (standing). "⦅ʿala al-nar⦆" means they are above it on the Ṣirāt while it is beneath them. It is also said that ⦅ʿala⦆ here carries the sense of ⦅bi⦆, meaning they are made to stand near it while they witness it. Al-Ḍaḥḥak said: "They were gathered," meaning at its gates. It is said: "They were made to stand upon the back of Hell while the Fire is beneath them." It is reported in a narration that all people will be made to stand upon the back of Hell, as if it were the surface of melted fat (ihala),⦅Ihala is melted fat, and matn al-ihala is its surface when it is poured into a vessel; he likens the stillness of Hell before the unbelievers enter it to that.  (Lisan al-ʿArab).⦆ then a caller will call out: "Take your companions, and leave my companions." It is also said that ⦅wuqifu⦆ means they entered it, may God protect us from it, so ⦅ʿala⦆ carries the sense of ⦅fi⦆, meaning they were made to stand in the Fire. The response to ⦅law⦆ is omitted so that the mind may range over every possibility, which makes the warning more forceful. The meaning is: if you could see them in that state, you would see the worst of conditions, or a terrifying sight, or a wondrous matter, and the like of such estimations."

"His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Then they will say, 'Would that we could be returned, and not deny the signs of our Lord, and be among the believers.'﴾ Reading with ⦅raf'⦆ in the three verbs as coordinated (ʿatf) is the reading of the people of Madina, al-Kisa'i, Abu ʿAmr, and Abu Bakr from ʿAsim, with a ⦅ḍamma⦆ (i.e., raf' in all of them, as in Ibn ʿAṭiyya).⦆ Ibn ʿAmir read ⦅nukadhdhiba⦆ with raf' and ⦅wa-nakuna⦆ with naṣb, and all of this falls within the sense of wishing (tamanni), meaning: they wish for return, that they not deny, and that they be among the believers. Sibawayh preferred cutting off (qat') in ⦅wa-la nukadhdhibu⦆, so that it is not included in the wish; the meaning is: "and we do not deny" as a steadfast state of not denying, i.e., we do not deny whether we are returned or not. Sibawayh said: this is like the saying "leave me, and I will not return," meaning I will not return in any case, whether you leave me or not. Abu ʿAmr cited in support of its exclusion from the wish His saying: ﴿And indeed they are liars﴾, because lying does not occur in a wish, but only in a statement. Whoever holds that it is included in the wish says: the meaning is "and indeed they are liars in the world, in their denial of the Resurrection and their denial of the messengers." Hamza and Hafs read ⦅nukadhdhiba⦆ and ⦅nakuna⦆ with naṣb as answers to the wish, since it is not obligatory, and both are included within the wish, in the sense that they wished for return, for abandoning denial, and for being with the believers. Abu Ishaq said: the meaning of ⦅wa-la nukadhdhiba⦆ is: if we are returned, we will not deny. The naṣb in ⦅nukadhdhiba⦆ and ⦅nakuna⦆ is by implied ⦅an⦆, as it is put in the answer to interrogation, command, prohibition, and solicitation, because all of these are not obligatory and have not yet occurred; so the answer with waw is put in the naṣb, as if it were coordinated with the verbal noun of the first verb, as though they said: "Would that there could be for us a return and a freedom from lying, and being among the believers." These two were treated as dependent on the verbal noun of ⦅nuradd⦆, since the meaning shifts to the nominative, and there was no alternative but to imply ⦅an⦆ in it, whereby naṣb completes in both verbs. Ibn ʿAmir read ⦅wa-nakuna⦆ with naṣb as an answer to the wish, like your saying: "Would that you would come to us, and we would honour you," meaning: would that your arrival occurred, and our honouring you occurred; the two preceding verbs are included in the wish. Or he intended: "and we do not honour you," as a cut-off according to what preceded, which is possible. Ubayy read ⦅wa-la nukadhdhiba bi-ayati rabbina abadan⦆ (and we will never deny the signs of our Lord). It is also reported from him and from Ibn Masʿud: ⦅Would that we could be returned, so that we do not deny⦆ with fa' and naṣb; the fa' is used for naṣb in the answer just as waw is, according to al-Zajjaj. Most of the Basran grammarians do not permit the answer except with fa'."

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 6, verse 28:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿But there has become apparent to them what they used to conceal before﴾. "Bal" (but rather) is a turning away from their wishing and their claim to faith, if they were returned. The scholars differed over the meaning of "badā lahum" (there became apparent to them) according to several opinions, after determining who is meant. It was said: the intended are the hypocrites, because the name of disbelief encompasses them, so the pronoun returns to some of those mentioned. Al-Nahhas said: "This is from fine, eloquent speech." It was also said: the intended are the disbelievers, and when the Prophet ﷺ admonished them, they feared and concealed that fear lest their weak followers perceive them, so it would become evident on the Day of Resurrection. For this reason al-Hasan said: "badā lahum" means: what he used to hide from some of them became apparent to some of them. It was also said: rather, there became apparent to them what they used to deny of polytheism, so they say: ﴿By Allah, our Lord, we were not polytheists﴾, then Allah makes their limbs speak and they testify against them to their disbelief; that is when ﴿there became apparent to them what they used to conceal before﴾. This was said by Abu Rawq [[Abu Rawq: (with a fatha on the ra', sukun on the waw, and a qaf after it) is 'Atiyyah ibn al-Harith al-Hamdani al-Kufi. Ibn Sa'd mentioned him in the fifth class and said: he is the author of the tafsir. (al-Tahdhib).]]. It was also said: "badā lahum" refers to what they used to hide of disbelief, meaning their evil deeds appeared, as He said: ﴿And there will appear to them from Allah what they had not reckoned﴾ [Az-Zumar: 47] [[See vol. 15, p. 264.]]. Al-Mubarrad said: there appeared to them the recompense of their disbelief which they used to conceal. It was also said: the meaning is: rather, there became apparent to those who followed the misguided leaders what the misguided leaders used to hide from them concerning the matter of the resurrection and the Last Day, because after it comes: ﴿And they say: there is nothing but our life of this world, and we will not be resurrected﴾.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And if they were returned﴾. It was said: after witnessing the punishment. It was said: before witnessing it.

﴿They would return to what they were forbidden﴾: meaning they would revert and go back to what they were forbidden of polytheism, due to Allah's knowledge concerning them that they would not believe. Iblis witnessed what he witnessed of the signs of Allah, then he obstinately persisted.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And indeed they are liars﴾. This is a report about them and a description of the state they were in during the world, of denying the messengers and rejecting the resurrection, just as He said: ﴿Indeed your Lord will judge﴾ [An-Nahl: 124], making it a description of a future state. It was also said: the meaning is "and indeed they are liars" in what they reported about themselves, namely that they would not lie and would be among the believers. Yahya ibn Wathhab read "wa-law ridduu" with a kasra on the ra', because the original is "rududu," so the kasra of the dal was transferred onto the ra'.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 6, verse 29:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And they say, "There is nothing but our life of this world, and we will not be resurrected."﴾ (Ibtida' and khabar, and "in" (إِنْ) is negating.)

"Wa-ma nahnu" ("nahnu" is the ism of "ma") "bi-mab'uthin" (resurrected) is its khabar (predicate). This is a beginning of information about them concerning what they said in the world. Ibn Zayd said: it falls under His saying: ﴿And if they were returned, they would certainly return to that which they were forbidden.﴾ ﴿And they say, "There is nothing but our life of this world."﴾ That is, they would return to disbelief and occupy themselves with the pleasure of the present state. This is to be understood of the obstinate one, as we explained in the case of Iblis, or it is that Allah [[In b, k, h, and ʿ: the Lord.]] confuses them after they have recognized (the truth), and this is common in reason.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 6, verse 30:

The words of the Exalted: ﴿And if you could see when they are made to stand before their Lord﴾. "Were made to stand" (wuqifu) means they are held back (ḥubisu) "before their Lord" (ʿala rabbihim), meaning before what Allah will decree concerning them. It has also been said that "ʿala" here carries the sense of "ʿind" (near, in the presence of), meaning in the presence of His angels and His recompense. Where no authority belongs to anyone other than Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, one says: "waqaftu ʿala fulan," meaning "I stood in his presence." The answer to "law" (if) is omitted because of the great magnitude of the standing.

﴿He will say: Is this not the truth?﴾ This is a confirmation and a rebuke, meaning: Is this resurrection not real and existing? ﴿They will say: Yes, by our Lord.﴾ They reinforce their acknowledgment with an oath, by saying: "wa-Rabbina" (by our Lord). It has also been said that the angels, by Allah's command, will say to them: Is this resurrection and this punishment not the truth? And they will say: "Yes, by our Lord, it is the truth." ﴿He will say: Then taste the punishment for what you used to deny.﴾

He said, may He be exalted: ﴿Those have lost who denied the meeting with God﴾. It was said: (this means) denying resurrection after death and recompense. The evidence for this is his, peace be upon him, saying: "Whoever swears a false oath to seize by it the property of a Muslim man will meet God while He is angry with him." That is, he will meet His recompense, because the one with whom God is angry does not see Him, according to those who affirm the vision (of God, ru'yah). This was the view of al-Qaffal and others. Al-Qushayri said: "This is not valid, because interpreting "meeting" as "recompense" in one place, on the basis of a specific indication, does not require this interpretation in every place. So "meeting" should be understood in its apparent sense in this verse. The unbelievers denied the Creator (al-Sani'), and one who denies the vision denies existence itself!"

He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿until the Hour comes upon them suddenly﴾. The Resurrection was called "the Hour" because of the swiftness of the reckoning in it. The meaning of "suddenly" (baghtah) is "unexpectedly." It is said: "The matter took them by surprise (baghatahum al-amr yabghatuhum baghtan wa baghtah)." It is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal). According to Sibawayh, it is a verbal noun (masdar) in the place of a circumstantial state, as when you say: "I killed him patiently (qataltuhu sabran)." He cited the line [The verse is by Zuhayr ibn Abi Sulma, and its witness is his saying: "la'ayan bila'in" (laya bilay), which is in the accusative as a verbal noun in the place of a circumstantial state. The sense is: "We carried our young man (on it) reluctantly and with difficulty." He describes a horse as energetic and strongly built. He says: when we lifted the youth onto it to hunt, it refused because of its vigour, so we could only mount him after delay and effort. Al-la'y means delay; al-mahbuk means the strongly built; al-zima' here means the lean one, which is the praised kind; and the root of al-zama' is thirst.

(Shawahid Sibawayh).]:

"Reluctantly, with great difficulty, we carried our young man
upon a horse of tight build, lean of limb, and thirsty."

Sibawayh does not allow this to be used as a model for analogy; one does not say: "So-and-so came suddenly (sur'atan)."

He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿They will say: "Alas for us!"﴾. The address (nida') falls upon "regret" (al-hasrah), though it is not in truth one being addressed, but it indicates the abundance of regret. Similar to this are "O wonder!" (ya lil-'ajab) and "O ease!" (ya lil-rakha'), which are not in truth addresses either, but indicate abundant wonder and ease. Sibawayh said: "It is as if he said: 'O wonder, come, for this is the time of your coming.' Likewise your saying: 'O my regret' [i.e., 'O regret'] (ya hasrati) [i.e., ya hasrata] [from b, j, k, 'a'], 'Come, for this is your time.' Likewise whatever cannot validly be addressed takes this course. This is more eloquent than saying: 'I am amazed (ta'ajjabtu).'" From this is the poet's saying:

"Then how wondrous is it, from her laden howdah!" [A half-line from the Mu'allaqah of Imru' al-Qays, whose full line is: "And on the day I hobbled my mount for the maidens..."]

It was also said: this is an alert to people about the great regret that befalls them, i.e., "O people, be alert to the great regret that is upon me." Thus the address falls upon one who is not, in truth, the one addressed, like your saying: "I will not see you here." So the prohibition falls upon one who is not, in truth, the one prohibited.

He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿over what we neglected concerning it﴾. That is, concerning the Hour, meaning in preparing for it; this is from al-Hasan. "Neglected" (farrarna) means "we wasted," and its root meaning is "to go ahead." It is said: "So-and-so went ahead (farrata), i.e., went forward and reached the water first." From this comes (the hadith): "I shall be your forerunner (farat) at the Pool." From this also is al-farit, meaning one who goes ahead to the water; and from it (comes the supplication for a child): "O God, make him a forerunner (farat) for his parents." So their saying "farrarna" means: we sent forward our incapacity. It was also said: "farrarna" means: we made others the ones who went ahead of us to the obedience of God, while we fell behind.

"Concerning it" (fiha) means: in the world, by leaving work for the Hour. Al-Tabari said: the pronoun ("it") refers to the bargain (al-safqah). This is because, when the loss of their bargain became clear to them, since they had sold faith for unbelief and the Hereafter for this world, they said: ﴿Alas for us, over what we neglected concerning it﴾, i.e., concerning the bargain. Its mention was omitted because the context indicates it, for loss occurs only in a bargain of sale. The evidence is his saying: ﴿so their commerce did not profit﴾ [Al-Baqarah 2:16]. [See vol. 1, p. 210.] Al-Suddi said: "over what we wasted," i.e., of works for Paradise. And in a report from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, from the Prophet (ﷺ), concerning this verse, he said: "The people of the Fire will see their places in Paradise and will say: 'Alas for us!'"

He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿while they bear their burdens upon their backs﴾. That is, their sins, the plural of wizr (burden). "Upon their backs" is a figurative usage (majaz), an extension, and a comparison to one who carries a weight. From it is said: wazara yazir, and wazira yuzar; so one is wazir (bearing a load) and mawzur (burdened). Its root is from al-wazar, which is a mountain. From it is the hadith about the women who went out to a funeral: "Return burdened (mawzurat), not rewarded (ma'jurat)." Abu 'Ubayd said: the common people say ma'zurat, as if it had no basis in his view, since it derives from al-wizr. Abu 'Ubayd said: it is said to a man who spreads out his garment and puts goods in it: "Carry your burden (wizr)," that is, your load. From it comes al-wazir (vizier), because he bears the weights of what is entrusted to him of managing the affairs of governance. The meaning is that sins clung to them, so they became weighed down by them.

He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿Unquestionably evil is what they bear﴾. That is: how wretched is the thing they carry.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 6, verse 32:

There are two issues here. The first concerns His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And the life of this world is nothing but play and amusement﴾, meaning because of the brevity of its duration, as the poet said:

Surely the world is like the dreams of a sleeper, and what good is a life that does not endure?

Consider, when you obtain a pleasure yesterday and spend it, are you not but like a dreamer?

Another said:

So act deliberately, for you are mortal, and strive for yourself, O human.

Whatever has been has not been since it passed, and what is to be has already been. [[There is iqwa' (a defect of rhyme vowel) in this.]]

It is also said: the meaning is that the enjoyment of the worldly life is play and amusement, that is, what they desire in this world has no outcome, so it is in the position of play and amusement. Sulayman ibn 'Abd al-Malik looked into a mirror and said, "I am the young king," and a slave-girl of his said to him:

You would be a fine enjoyment if you could remain, but there is no remaining for a human being.

There is nothing in what has appeared to us of you as a fault, [[In the margin of B: people found fault with him.]] among people, except that you are mortal.

It is also said: the meaning of "play and amusement" is vanity and delusion, as He said: ﴿And the life of this world is only the enjoyment of delusion﴾ [Al 'Imran: 185]. So the purpose of the verse is to refute the disbelievers in their saying: "There is only our life of this world." Play (la'ib) is well known; al-Lu'abah is one who plays much, and al-Mal'ab is the place of play; it is said: la'iba yal'ab. Amusement (lahw) is also well known; everything that occupies you has diverted you (alhaka), and I was diverted by amusement. It is also said: its root is turning away from something, from their saying: lahaytu 'anhu (I turned away from it). Al-Mahdawi said: this is remote, because the one whose meaning is turning away has its third radical as yā', as evidenced by their saying: lihyan, while the third radical of the first is waw.

The second issue: what pertains to the Hereafter is not part of amusement and play, for the reality of play is what brings no benefit, and amusement is what one is distracted by, while what is intended for the Hereafter is outside both. A man disparaged this world in the presence of 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him, and 'Ali said: "The world is a house of truth for one who speaks truly of it, a house of salvation [[In K: trade.]] for one who understands from it, and a house of richness for one who takes provision from it." Mahmud al-Warraq said:

Do not follow the world and its days with blame, even if its circle turns upon you.

Among the nobility of the world and its excellence is that through it the Hereafter is attained.

Abu 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-Barr narrated from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The world is cursed, and cursed is what is in it, except what is in it of the remembrance of Allah, or what leads to the remembrance of Allah, and the scholar and the student are partners in the reward; and the rest of people are rabble with no good in them." It was also recorded by al-Tirmidhi from Abu Hurayrah, and he said: a hasan gharib hadith. It is also narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "Among the humiliation of the world before Allah is that He is disobeyed only in it, and what is with Him is not attained except by abandoning it." Al-Tirmidhi narrated from Sahl ibn Sa'd, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "If the world were equal in Allah's sight to the wing of a mosquito, He would not have given a disbeliever a sip of water from it." The poet said:

Take your enjoyment of the days if you are prudent, for you are between one who forbids and one who commands from them.

If the world leaves a man his religion, then whatever has escaped him is no harm.

The world will not equal the wing of a mosquito, nor the weight of the down [[Al-zaff (with kasra): the small feathers; some specified it to ostrich feathers. In Adab al-Dunya wa'l-Din it is recorded as "wazn dharr" (the weight of an ant).]] of a bird's wing.

He has not approved the world as a reward for a believer, nor has He approved the world as a recompense for a disbeliever. [[So it is in the originals. Rather, the world is the recompense of the disbeliever, due to his saying, peace and blessings be upon him: "The world is a prison for the believer and a paradise for the disbeliever."]]

Ibn 'Abbas said: this is the life of the disbeliever, because he passes it in delusion and falsehood; as for the life of the believer, it is embraced by righteous deeds, so it is not amusement and play. [[Yuzji al-ayyam: he drives the days onward.]]

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And the abode of the Hereafter is better﴾, that is, Paradise, because of its permanence. It was named "the Hereafter" because it is delayed from us, and "the world" because it is near to us. Ibn 'Amir read (wa-la-daru al-akhirah) with one lam, and the idafah (construct) is according to the assumption that the modified noun has been elided and the adjective put in its place; the estimate: wa-la-daru al-hayati al-akhirah. According to the reading of the majority (wa-la-l-daru al-akhirah), the lam is the lam of inception, the dar is in the nominative by the inception, and al-akhirah is made an adjective for it, and the predicate is (khayrun li-lladhina...). It is strengthened by ﴿That is the abode of the Hereafter﴾ [al-Qasas: 83] and ﴿And indeed the abode of the Hereafter, that is the life﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 64]. So "the Hereafter" comes as an adjective of "the abode" in both.

(For those who are mindful) meaning: of shirk.

(Will you not reason?) It is read with yā' and with tā'; that is, will they not reason that the matter is thus, so that they would renounce the world? And Allah knows best.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 6, verse 33–34:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿We certainly know that what they say grieves you﴾. The particle (inna) is given a kasra because of the entry of the lam (lam al-ibtida', the emphatic lam).

Abu Maysara said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) passed by Abu Jahl and his companions, and they said: "O Muhammad, by Allah, we do not deny you, and you are truthful in our sight, but we deny what you have brought." So this verse was revealed: "Indeed, they do not deny you, but it is the wrongdoers who deny the signs of Allah" (6:33). Then He consoled him with His saying: "And messengers were denied before you" (6:34), the verse.

It is read "yukadhdhibunaka" (they deny you) both with light and with intensive (tashdid) forms. It was said: the two have the same meaning, like ḥazantuhu and aḥzantuhu (I grieved him / I made him grieved). Abu Ubayd preferred the light reading, and it is the reading of Ali (may Allah be pleased with him). It is related from him that Abu Jahl said to the Prophet (ﷺ): "We do not deny you, but we deny what you have brought," so Allah, Mighty and Majestic, revealed: "Indeed, they do not deny you."

Al-Nahhas said: Abu Ubayd has been opposed in this. And it is related: "We do not deny you," so Allah, Mighty and Majestic, revealed: "They do not deny you."

What strengthens this is that a man recited to Ibn Abbas "fa-innahum la yukdhibunaka" with the light form, and Ibn Abbas said to him: "fa-innahum la yukadhdhibunaka" (with the intensive form), because they used to call the Prophet (ﷺ) "al-Amin" (the trustworthy).

The meaning of "yukadhdhibunaka" according to the lexicographers is that they attribute to you lying and reject what you have said. The meaning of "la yukdhibunaka" is that they do not find you bringing lies, just as you say: "akdhabtuhu" (I found him a liar), "abkhaltuhu" (I found him stingy), meaning they do not find you a liar if they reflect upon what you have brought. It is also possible that the meaning is: they do not establish against you that you are a liar, because it is said "akdhabtuhu" when you argue against him and demonstrate that he is a liar. And in the intensive form: they do not deny you with proof or evidence, and this is indicated by "but it is the wrongdoers who deny the signs of Allah (with rejection)."

Al-Nahhas said: The view on this is the position of Abu Ubayd, and his argument is binding, because Ali, may Allah honour his face, is the one who related the hadith, and it is authentically established from him that he recited with the light form. Al-Kisa'i related from the Arabs: "akdhabtu al-rajul" when you inform that he has come with a lie and narrated it, and "kadhdhabtuhu" when you inform that he is a liar. Likewise al-Zajjaj said: "kadhdhabtuhu" when you say to him "you lie," and "akdhabtuhu" when you mean that what he brought is a lie.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So they were patient over what they were denied﴾, i.e., so be patient as they were patient.

(And they were harmed until Our help came to them) i.e., Our aid, meaning: so there will come to you what you were promised.

(And there is none who can alter the words of Allah) explains that victory, i.e., what Allah, Mighty and Majestic, has promised, no one can repel. There is no one who annuls His judgment, and no breaking of His promise. "For every term is a decree" (13:38). "Indeed, We will help Our messengers and those who believed" (40:51). "And certainly Our word has preceded for Our servants, the messengers. Indeed, they will be the victorious. And indeed, Our soldiers – they will be the predominant" (37:171–173). "Allah has decreed: 'I and My messengers will surely prevail'" (58:21).

(And there has certainly come to you from the news of the messengers) the subject of (jā'aka) is an implied pronoun; the meaning is: there has come to you from the news of the messengers a report.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 6, verse 33–34:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿We certainly know that what they say grieves you﴾. The particle (inna) is given a kasra because of the entry of the lam (lam al-ibtida', the emphatic lam).

Abu Maysara said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) passed by Abu Jahl and his companions, and they said: "O Muhammad, by Allah, we do not deny you, and you are truthful in our sight, but we deny what you have brought." So this verse was revealed: "Indeed, they do not deny you, but it is the wrongdoers who deny the signs of Allah" (6:33). Then He consoled him with His saying: "And messengers were denied before you" (6:34), the verse.

It is read "yukadhdhibunaka" (they deny you) both with light and with intensive (tashdid) forms. It was said: the two have the same meaning, like ḥazantuhu and aḥzantuhu (I grieved him / I made him grieved). Abu Ubayd preferred the light reading, and it is the reading of Ali (may Allah be pleased with him). It is related from him that Abu Jahl said to the Prophet (ﷺ): "We do not deny you, but we deny what you have brought," so Allah, Mighty and Majestic, revealed: "Indeed, they do not deny you."

Al-Nahhas said: Abu Ubayd has been opposed in this. And it is related: "We do not deny you," so Allah, Mighty and Majestic, revealed: "They do not deny you."

What strengthens this is that a man recited to Ibn Abbas "fa-innahum la yukdhibunaka" with the light form, and Ibn Abbas said to him: "fa-innahum la yukadhdhibunaka" (with the intensive form), because they used to call the Prophet (ﷺ) "al-Amin" (the trustworthy).

The meaning of "yukadhdhibunaka" according to the lexicographers is that they attribute to you lying and reject what you have said. The meaning of "la yukdhibunaka" is that they do not find you bringing lies, just as you say: "akdhabtuhu" (I found him a liar), "abkhaltuhu" (I found him stingy), meaning they do not find you a liar if they reflect upon what you have brought. It is also possible that the meaning is: they do not establish against you that you are a liar, because it is said "akdhabtuhu" when you argue against him and demonstrate that he is a liar. And in the intensive form: they do not deny you with proof or evidence, and this is indicated by "but it is the wrongdoers who deny the signs of Allah (with rejection)."

Al-Nahhas said: The view on this is the position of Abu Ubayd, and his argument is binding, because Ali, may Allah honour his face, is the one who related the hadith, and it is authentically established from him that he recited with the light form. Al-Kisa'i related from the Arabs: "akdhabtu al-rajul" when you inform that he has come with a lie and narrated it, and "kadhdhabtuhu" when you inform that he is a liar. Likewise al-Zajjaj said: "kadhdhabtuhu" when you say to him "you lie," and "akdhabtuhu" when you mean that what he brought is a lie.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So they were patient over what they were denied﴾, i.e., so be patient as they were patient.

(And they were harmed until Our help came to them) i.e., Our aid, meaning: so there will come to you what you were promised.

(And there is none who can alter the words of Allah) explains that victory, i.e., what Allah, Mighty and Majestic, has promised, no one can repel. There is no one who annuls His judgment, and no breaking of His promise. "For every term is a decree" (13:38). "Indeed, We will help Our messengers and those who believed" (40:51). "And certainly Our word has preceded for Our servants, the messengers. Indeed, they will be the victorious. And indeed, Our soldiers – they will be the predominant" (37:171–173). "Allah has decreed: 'I and My messengers will surely prevail'" (58:21).

(And there has certainly come to you from the news of the messengers) the subject of (jā'aka) is an implied pronoun; the meaning is: there has come to you from the news of the messengers a report.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 6, verse 35:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And if their turning away has been grievous to you﴾, i.e., their aversion and their turning away from faith has been great upon you.

(So if you are able) capable (to seek) to seek out (a tunnel in the earth), i.e., a passage through which you may escape to another place. From this comes al-nafqa', the burrow-hole of the jerboa (yarbu') [see vol. 1, p. 178 for its explanation], and from it comes al-munafiq (the hypocrite), which has already been discussed.

(Or a ladder) is coordinated with what precedes it, i.e., a means to the sky. This is a figurative image, because the ladder by which one ascends is a means to the place, and it is masculine. What al-Farra' related about its feminine form is not known. Qatadah said: the ladder is the steps (al-daraj). Al-Zajjaj said: it is derived from al-salama (safety), as if it brings you safely to the place you seek.

(Then you bring them a sign) is coordinated with what precedes it, i.e., so that they may believe, then do it; the answer is left implied because the listener knows it. God commanded His Prophet ﷺ not to let his grief over them become intense if they do not believe, just as he cannot guide them.

(And if God had willed, He would have gathered them upon guidance), i.e., He would have created them believers and disposed them to it. Exalted is He explained that their disbelief is by God's will, as a refutation of the Qadariyya. It has also been said that the meaning is: He would have shown them a sign that compels them to faith, but the Mighty and Majestic willed to reward those among them who believed and did good.

(So do not be among the ignorant) i.e., among those whose grief intensified and who were consumed with regret, until that drove them to excessive distress and to what is not permitted. That is: do not grieve over their disbelief so that you approach the state of the ignorant. It has also been said: the address is to him, but the intended meaning is the community, for the hearts of the Muslims were straitened by their disbelief and their harm.

Al-Qurtubi's commentary on Surah 6, verses 36–37:

Allah's words: ﴿Only those who listen will respond﴾. That is, listening with attentiveness, understanding, and desire for the truth. They are the believers, who accept what they hear, benefit from it, and act upon it. Al-Hasan and Mujahid said this is its meaning, and the sentence is complete there. Then He said: ﴿As for the dead, Allah will raise them﴾. They are the disbelievers, according to al-Hasan and Mujahid. That is, they are in the position of the dead, in that they neither accept nor pay attention to any proof. It was also said: "the dead" means everyone who has died. ﴿Allah will raise them﴾, that is, for the reckoning. According to the first explanation, "raising them" means guiding them to faith in Allah and His Messenger (ﷺ). Al-Hasan said: it means He raises them from their polytheism until they believe in you, O Muhammad, namely at the moment of death, in the state of compulsion in this world.

Allah's words: ﴿They say, "Why has not a sign been sent down to him from his Lord?"﴾ Al-Hasan said: the word *law* (لولا, "why not") here carries the meaning of *hal* (هلا, "why not"). The poet said:

*You count the slaughter of the pregnant she-camel as the best of your glory,*
*O Bani Dawtara, were it not for the armoured warrior who covered them.*

(This is al-Farazdaq boasting in his poetry of the generosity of his father Ghalib, who slaughtered a hundred she-camels in the contest with Suhaym ibn Wathil al-Riyahi at a place called Sawar, a day's journey from Kufa. For this reason Jarir also says: "I was pleased that the Mujashi' do not count, among glory, anything except the slaughter of a she-camel at Sawar." Bani Dawtara is a phrase used of people who do not perform any notable deeds.)

This request from them was obstinacy after the clear proofs had appeared and the argument had been established by the Qur'an, which they were unable to match with a single surah like it, because of its arrangement (في ب وع: الرصف, "al-rasf", meaning the ordering of one thing with another) and its knowledge of the unseen.

Allah's words: ﴿But most of them do not know﴾. That is, they do not know that Allah, Mighty and Majestic, sends down only those signs that serve the benefit of His servants, and that it was in Allah's knowledge to bring forth from their loins peoples who would believe in Him, and He did not intend to annihilate them. It was also said: ﴿But most of them do not know﴾ that Allah is able to send them down. Al-Zajjaj said: they asked that He gather them upon guidance, that is, by compulsion.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 6, verse 38:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And there is no creature (dabbah) on the earth﴾. The meaning of ad-dabbah (creature, that which crawls or walks) and the discussion of it have already been given in "al-Baqarah" [see vol. 2, p. 196]. Its original form is an adjective, from dabba yadibbu, so one is dabb (crawling) when one walks with short, close steps.

(﴿Nor a bird that flies with its two wings﴾) with "ta'ir" in the genitive, as a conjunction with the wording. Al-Hasan and Abdullah ibn Abi Ishaq read "wa la ta'irun" in the nominative, as a conjunction with the position (mahall), and "min" is extra (za'idah), the sense being: "wa ma dabbatin". "Bi-janahayhi" (with its two wings) is an emphasis and a removal of ambiguity, for the Arabs use "flying" (tayaran) of other than birds: they say to a man "tarfi hajati" (hasten my need), meaning "hurry". So He mentioned "with its two wings" so that the statement would be confined to birds, while its use for other things is figurative. It has been said that the balance of a bird's body between its two wings helps it to fly; were it not balanced, it would tilt. So He informed us that flight is by the two wings, and "none holds them up except Allah" [al-Nahl: 79]. The janah (wing) is one of the two sides of a bird by which it is enabled to fly in the air; its origin is inclination to one side, and from it comes "janahat al-safinah" (the ship inclined) when it leaned toward the side of the land, adhering to it, and came to a halt. The "ta'ir" of a person is his deed, and in the revelation: ﴿And every human being We have fastened his ta'ir to his neck﴾ [al-Isra': 13].

(﴿Are communities like you﴾) meaning: they are groups like you in that Allah, Mighty and Majestic, created them, undertook their provision, and dealt justly with them; so you should not wrong them, nor exceed in regard to them what you have been commanded. "Dabbah" applies to everything that crawls, and the mention of what is on the earth was singled out, excluding the sky, because it is what they know and see directly. It has also been said: they are communities like us in glorifying (tasbih) and in indicating (the Creator); the meaning being: there is no creature nor bird but it glorifies Allah, Exalted, and points to His oneness, if the disbelievers would reflect. Abu Hurairah said: they are communities like us in the sense that He will gather the animals on the Day (of Judgement) and will exact retribution for the hornless (sheep) from the horned, then Allah will say to it: "Be dust." This is the view chosen by al-Zajjaj, for he said: (﴿Communities like you﴾) in creation, provision, death, resurrection and retribution, and the meaning of the first saying has entered into this as well. Sufyan ibn Uyaynah said: that is, every kind of creature and bird has in mankind some resemblance to it: among them is one who rushes like the lion, and among them one who is greedy like the pig, and among them one who snarls like the dog, and among them one who struts like the peacock; this is the meaning of resemblance. Al-Khattabi approved of this and said: for you associate with animals and beasts, so take your caution. Mujahid said regarding His saying, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿Communities like you﴾: "They are kinds, having names by which they are known, just as you are known." It has been said other than this, of what is not sound, that they are like us in knowledge, that they will be gathered and given bliss in Paradise, and will be compensated for the pains that befell them in this world, and that the people of Paradise will be familiar with their forms. The sound view is that ﴿communities like you﴾ in being created, indicating the Creator, in need of Him, and provided for by Him, just as your provision is upon Allah. Sufyan's saying is also good, for it is a resemblance that actually exists.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿We have not neglected in the Book anything﴾. That is, in the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawh al-Mahfuz), for in it He recorded what befalls of events. It has been said: that is, in the Qur'an; meaning, We have not left out any matter of the religion without indicating it in the Qur'an, either by a clear, explained indication or by a general one whose explanation is to be received from the Messenger (ﷺ), or from consensus (ijma'), or from analogy (qiyas) established by the text of the Book. Allah, may He be exalted, said: ﴿And We have sent down to you the Book as an explanation of all things﴾ [al-Nahl: 89], and He said: ﴿And We sent down to you the Reminder so that you may explain to the people what has been sent down to them﴾ [al-Nahl: 44], and He said: ﴿And whatever the Messenger gives you, take it, and whatever he forbids you, refrain from it﴾ [al-Hashr: 7]. Thus in this verse and the verse of al-Nahl He summarized what He did not specify, of what He did not mention; so the statement of Allah is true that He did not neglect anything in the Book without mentioning it, either in detail or in principle. And He said: ﴿Today I have perfected for you your religion﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 3].

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Then to their Lord they will be gathered﴾, that is, for recompense, as has preceded in the report of Abu Hurairah. In Sahih Muslim, on his authority, that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The rights will certainly be rendered to their owners on the Day of Resurrection, until the hornless sheep is avenged against the horned sheep." By this it indicates that the animals will be gathered on the Day of Resurrection. This is the view of Abu Dharr, Abu Hurairah, al-Hasan and others. It is related from Ibn Abbas, and Ibn Abbas said in one report: the gathering of the beasts and birds is their death. This was also said by al-Dahhak. The first view is more sound, for the apparent meaning of the verse and the sound report support it, and in the revelation: ﴿And when the wild beasts are gathered﴾ [al-Takwir: 5]. As for the saying of Abu Hurairah, as transmitted by Ja'far ibn Burqan from Yazid ibn al-Asamm from him: "Allah will gather all creation on the Day of Resurrection: the animals, the beasts, the birds and everything; and of His justice that Day He will take for the hornless from the horned, then He will say: 'Be dust.'" That is His saying: ﴿The disbeliever will say: 'Would that I were dust!'﴾ [al-Naba': 40]. Ata said: when they see the children of Adam and their state of distress, they will say: "Praise be to Allah who has not made us like you; there is no Paradise we hope for, nor Fire we fear," then Allah will say to them: "Be dust." At that point the disbeliever will wish that he were dust. A group said: this gathering mentioned in the verse refers to the disbelievers, and what intervened is an interjected statement and the establishing of proofs; as for the hadith, its purpose is an illustration intended to magnify the matter of reckoning, retribution, and the care taken in it, so that it is understood that there is no escape for anyone from it. They supported this with what is in a non-sahih report from some of its transmitters of an addition: "until the hornless sheep is avenged against the horned sheep, and the stone for what it struck the stone, and the stick for what it scratched the stick." They said: thus it is clear that its purpose is an illustration conveying admonition and awe, since inanimate things cannot have their address, reward or punishment understood, and none of the sensible has held this view, and whoever imagines it is among the dull fools. They said: and because the pen does not run over them, so they cannot be held accountable. I say: the sound view is the first, because of the hadith of Abu Hurairah which we mentioned, and even if the pen does not run over them regarding rulings, yet among themselves they are held accountable. It is related from Abu Dharr that he said: Two sheep butted each other in the presence of the Prophet (ﷺ), and he said: "O Abu Dharr, do you know over what they butted?" I said: No. He said: "But Allah knows, and He will judge between them." This is an explicit text. We have expanded upon it in clarity in the book "al-Tadhkirah bi-Ahwal al-Mawta wa-Umur al-Akhirah." And Allah knows best.

[Qur'an 6:39] "Those who deny Our signs are deaf and dumb" — this is a beginning and predicate: that is, they have lost the benefit of their hearing and their sight. So every nation of animals and other creatures is guided to its own interests, while the disbelievers are not guided. This has already been discussed in (al-Baqarah) [[See vol. 1, p. 214.]].

(In darknesses) — that is, the darknesses of disbelief. Abu 'Ali said: it is possible that the meaning is "deaf and dumb" in the Hereafter, so that it is literal rather than a linguistic metaphor.

(Whomever Allah wills to lead astray, He leads him astray) — this indicates that He wills the disbeliever's misguidance and intends it, so that His justice may be carried out in him. Do you not see that He said: (And whomever He wills, He places him upon a straight path) — that is, upon the religion of Islam, so that His grace may be carried out in him. And in this is a refutation of the doctrine of the Qadariyyah. The will refers to those who denied: among them are those whom He misguides and among them those whom He guides.

[Qur'an 6:40] "Say: Have you considered yourselves?" — Nafi' read the two hamzahs with lightening: he drops the vowel of the first onto the letter before it, and pronounces the second between-between (bayna bayn). Abu 'Ubayd related from him that he drops the hamzah and compensates for it with an alif. Al-Nahhas said: according to the grammarians this is an error attributed to him, because the yā' is sākin and the alif is sākin, and two sākins do not come together. Makki said: it has been related from Warsh that he replaced the hamzah with an alif, because the transmission from him is that he lengthens the second, and lengthening can only be fully achieved with substitution; substitution is a derivative of the basic forms, and the basic form is that the hamzah be made between the open hamzah and the alif. This is the practice of everyone who lightened the second except Warsh. The substitution of the hamzah is permissible when a sākin follows it, because the first is a letter of madd and līn; the lengthening arising with the sākin takes the place of a vowel by which one reaches the pronunciation of the second sākin.

Abu 'Amr, 'Asim and Hamzah read (a-ra-ayta-kum) with the two hamzahs made full, and they kept the word in its original form; the original is the hamzah, because the interrogative hamzah entered upon (ra'ayta), so the hamzah is the root letter of the verb, and the yā' is sākin because of the attached pronoun of the nominative. 'Isa ibn 'Umar and al-Kisa'i read (a-ray-ta-kum) with the deletion of the second hamzah. Al-Nahhas said: this is rare in Arabic grammar, and it is permissible only in poetry; the Arabs say: "a-ra-ayta-ka Zayd-an ma sha'nuhu" (have you seen Zayd, what is his condition?).

The school of the Basrans holds that the kaf and the mim are for address, having no place in grammatical analysis; this is the view chosen by al-Zajjaj. The school of al-Kisa'i, al-Farra' and others holds that the kaf and the mim are in the accusative by the verb of seeing falling upon them, and the meaning is "have you seen yourselves?" So when they are for address — an additional particle for emphasis — then (in) in His words "in atakum" is in the accusative position as the object of ra'ayta; and when it is a noun in the accusative position, then (in) is in the position of the second object. The first is from the sight of the eye, since it is transitive to one object; and with the meaning of knowledge it is transitive to two objects.

His words: (Or the Hour comes upon you) — the meaning: or the Hour comes upon you, the Hour in which you will be raised. Then He said: (Will you call upon other than Allah, if you are truthful?) The verse concerns the argument against the polytheists who acknowledged that they had a Creator; that is, you return to Allah in times of hardship, and you will also return to Him on the Day of Resurrection — so why do you persist in polytheism in a state of ease? They used to worship idols and call upon Allah to remove the punishment.

[Qur'an 6:41] "Rather, it is Him you call upon" — "rather" (bal) is a turning away from the first and an affirmation of the second. "Iyyahu" is in the accusative, governed by "tad'una" (you call upon). (Then He removes what you call upon Him for, if He wills) — that is, He removes the harm to which you call Him to remove, if He wills to remove it.

(And you forget what you associate) — it was said: at the descent of the punishment. Al-Hasan said: that is, you turn away from it with the turning away of one who forgets, and that is because of despair of salvation from it, since there is neither harm nor benefit in it. Al-Zajjaj said: the meaning may be "and you abandon." Al-Nahhas said: like His words: "And We had already made a covenant with Adam before, but he forgot" (Ta-Ha 20:115) [[See vol. 11, p. 251.]].

(And you forget what you associate) — it was said: at the descent of the punishment. Al-Hasan said: that is, you turn away from it with the turning away of one who forgets, and that is because of despair of salvation from it, since there is neither harm nor benefit in it. Al-Zajjaj said: the meaning may be "and you abandon." Al-Nahhas said: like His words: "And We had already made a covenant with Adam before, but he forgot" (Ta-Ha 20:115) [[See vol. 11, p. 251.]].

[Qur'an 6:39] "Those who deny Our signs are deaf and dumb" — this is a beginning and predicate: that is, they have lost the benefit of their hearing and their sight. So every nation of animals and other creatures is guided to its own interests, while the disbelievers are not guided. This has already been discussed in (al-Baqarah) [[See vol. 1, p. 214.]].

(In darknesses) — that is, the darknesses of disbelief. Abu 'Ali said: it is possible that the meaning is "deaf and dumb" in the Hereafter, so that it is literal rather than a linguistic metaphor.

(Whomever Allah wills to lead astray, He leads him astray) — this indicates that He wills the disbeliever's misguidance and intends it, so that His justice may be carried out in him. Do you not see that He said: (And whomever He wills, He places him upon a straight path) — that is, upon the religion of Islam, so that His grace may be carried out in him. And in this is a refutation of the doctrine of the Qadariyyah. The will refers to those who denied: among them are those whom He misguides and among them those whom He guides.

[Qur'an 6:40] "Say: Have you considered yourselves?" — Nafi' read the two hamzahs with lightening: he drops the vowel of the first onto the letter before it, and pronounces the second between-between (bayna bayn). Abu 'Ubayd related from him that he drops the hamzah and compensates for it with an alif. Al-Nahhas said: according to the grammarians this is an error attributed to him, because the yā' is sākin and the alif is sākin, and two sākins do not come together. Makki said: it has been related from Warsh that he replaced the hamzah with an alif, because the transmission from him is that he lengthens the second, and lengthening can only be fully achieved with substitution; substitution is a derivative of the basic forms, and the basic form is that the hamzah be made between the open hamzah and the alif. This is the practice of everyone who lightened the second except Warsh. The substitution of the hamzah is permissible when a sākin follows it, because the first is a letter of madd and līn; the lengthening arising with the sākin takes the place of a vowel by which one reaches the pronunciation of the second sākin.

Abu 'Amr, 'Asim and Hamzah read (a-ra-ayta-kum) with the two hamzahs made full, and they kept the word in its original form; the original is the hamzah, because the interrogative hamzah entered upon (ra'ayta), so the hamzah is the root letter of the verb, and the yā' is sākin because of the attached pronoun of the nominative. 'Isa ibn 'Umar and al-Kisa'i read (a-ray-ta-kum) with the deletion of the second hamzah. Al-Nahhas said: this is rare in Arabic grammar, and it is permissible only in poetry; the Arabs say: "a-ra-ayta-ka Zayd-an ma sha'nuhu" (have you seen Zayd, what is his condition?).

The school of the Basrans holds that the kaf and the mim are for address, having no place in grammatical analysis; this is the view chosen by al-Zajjaj. The school of al-Kisa'i, al-Farra' and others holds that the kaf and the mim are in the accusative by the verb of seeing falling upon them, and the meaning is "have you seen yourselves?" So when they are for address — an additional particle for emphasis — then (in) in His words "in atakum" is in the accusative position as the object of ra'ayta; and when it is a noun in the accusative position, then (in) is in the position of the second object. The first is from the sight of the eye, since it is transitive to one object; and with the meaning of knowledge it is transitive to two objects.

His words: (Or the Hour comes upon you) — the meaning: or the Hour comes upon you, the Hour in which you will be raised. Then He said: (Will you call upon other than Allah, if you are truthful?) The verse concerns the argument against the polytheists who acknowledged that they had a Creator; that is, you return to Allah in times of hardship, and you will also return to Him on the Day of Resurrection — so why do you persist in polytheism in a state of ease? They used to worship idols and call upon Allah to remove the punishment.

[Qur'an 6:41] "Rather, it is Him you call upon" — "rather" (bal) is a turning away from the first and an affirmation of the second. "Iyyahu" is in the accusative, governed by "tad'una" (you call upon). (Then He removes what you call upon Him for, if He wills) — that is, He removes the harm to which you call Him to remove, if He wills to remove it.
