The Qur'anic phrase ﴿And We certainly sent [messengers] to communities before you﴾ is a consolation to the Prophet (ﷺ). It contains an ellipsis (*iḍmār*, omission of words understood from context), meaning: "We sent messengers to communities before you." It also contains another ellipsis, indicated by the apparent meaning, whose implied sense is: "they denied, so We seized them."

This verse is connected to what precedes it in the manner of a state connected to a closely related state. These people followed, in opposing their Prophet, the same path that those before them had taken in opposing their prophets, so they were liable to be struck by the same affliction that had struck those who came before them.

The meaning of ﴿al-ba'sā'﴾ (adversity) is calamities affecting wealth, and ﴿al-ḍarrā'﴾ (hardship) is calamities affecting bodies. This is the view of most scholars, though each of the two words may be used in place of the other. God disciplines His servants with adversity and hardship and with whatever He wills: ﴿He is not questioned about what He does﴾ (Al-Anbiya' 21:23).

Ibn 'Aṭiyya said: "Some servants have derived from this verse, for the discipline of their own souls, the use of adversity in the form of dispersing their wealth, and hardship in the form of subjecting their bodies to hunger and nakedness."

I say: This is ignorance on the part of those who do it, and they have made this verse a foundation for it. This is a punishment from God, which He inflicts on whichever of His servants He wills to test with it. It is not permissible for us to test ourselves with it and to match it by analogy (*qiyās*), for food and clothing are the means by which we reach the abode of honour and by which we are saved from the terrors of the Day of Resurrection. In the revelation: ﴿O messengers, eat of the good things and do righteous deeds﴾ (Al-Mu'minun 23:51). And He said: ﴿O you who believe, spend of the good things you have earned﴾ (Al-Baqarah 2:267). And: ﴿O you who believe, eat of the good things We have provided for you﴾ (Al-Baqarah 2:172). So He commanded the believers with what He addressed the messengers with. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) and his Companions used to eat good things, wear the finest garments and adorn themselves with them, and so did the Successors (*tābi'ūn*) after them, and so on onward. This has been explained earlier in (Al-Ma'idah) (See pp. 263 ff. of this volume), and its rulings concerning clothing and other matters will come in (Al-A'raf) (See vol. 7, p. 195). Had things been as they claimed and argued, then God's blessings upon us through crops, gardens, all kinds of fruits and plants, and the cattle which He subjected for us, allowed us to eat their flesh, drink their milk, and find warmth in their wool, along with other blessings He mentioned, would have no great benefit. Had what they held been a virtue, the Messenger of God (ﷺ), his Companions, and those who came after them among the Successors and scholars would have been the most deserving of it. The explanation of the excellence of wealth and its benefit, and the refutation of those who refuse to acquire it, has been given earlier at the end of (Al-Baqarah) (See vol. 3, pp. 417 ff.). The Prophet (ﷺ) also forbade continuous fasting (*wiṣāl*) out of fear of weakness in the body, and he forbade the squandering of wealth, in response to the ignorant rich.

God's words ﴿so that they may humble themselves﴾ mean: so that they may supplicate and abase themselves. The word is derived from *ḍarā'a*, which means humility, and it is said: "He became humble (ḍaraʿa), so he is one who is humble (ḍāriʿ)."

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 6, verses 43–45:

The word of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿Why did they not humble themselves when Our punishment came upon them?﴾ (*Falawla*) is a reproach (*tahdid*), and it is the particle that is followed by a verb, meaning *hallā* ("why not"). This is a rebuke for abandoning supplication, and an announcement about them that they did not humble themselves when the punishment descended. It is also possible that they humbled themselves but in the manner of one who is not sincere, or that they humbled themselves only when the punishment had already overtaken them, and humility in these forms is not beneficial. Supplication is commanded in times of ease and in times of hardship. Allah, the Exalted, said: "Call upon Me, and I will respond to you" (Ghafir 40:60) [See vol. 15, p. 326.]. And He said: "Indeed, those who disdain My worship" (Ghafir 40:60), meaning My supplication, "will enter Hell, humiliated" (Ghafir 40:60). This is a severe warning.

﴿But their hearts became hardened﴾, meaning they became stiff and coarse. This is an expression for disbelief and persistence in disobedience. We ask Allah for well-being.

﴿And Satan made attractive to them what they were doing﴾, meaning he deluded them (*aghwāhum*) [In manuscripts ج, ع, ى: *aghrāhum*, "he enticed them"] toward sins and drove them to them.

The word of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿So when they forgot what they had been reminded of﴾. It is said: why were they blamed for forgetting when it was not their own action? The answer is that *nasū* here means *tarakū*, "they abandoned what they had been reminded of." This is related from Ibn Abbas and Ibn Jurayj, and it is the view of Abu Ali, because one who abandons something out of aversion has placed it in the status of what has been forgotten, as one says "he abandoned it into forgetfulness." Another answer is that they exposed themselves to forgetting, so blame was justified for that, just as blame is justified for exposing oneself to the wrath and punishment of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic.

The meaning of ﴿We opened for them the gates of every thing﴾ is the gates of blessings and goods, meaning We multiplied these for them. The estimate of the grammarians (*ahl al-ʿarabiyya*) is: We opened for them the gates of everything that had been closed to them.

﴿Until, when they rejoiced in what they had been given﴾, its meaning is that they became insolent, exultant, and self-admiring, and they thought that this gift would not perish, and that it indicated Allah's approval of them. ﴿We seized them suddenly﴾, meaning We uprooted them and fell upon them with force. *Baghtatan* means "suddenly," and it is seizing someone unawares and without any prior sign. If someone is seized while he is heedless and unaware, he has been seized suddenly, and the most painful thing is what comes upon one suddenly. It has been said that the reminder that preceded, which they turned away from, took the place of a sign. And Allah knows best. *Baghtatan* is a verbal noun in the position of a circumstantial clause (*ḥāl*), which, according to Sibawayh, is not to be analogized upon, as has already been mentioned. This was a gradual leading on (*istidraj*) from Allah, the Exalted, as He said: ﴿And I give them respite; indeed, My plan is firm﴾ (al-A'raf 7:183) [See vol. 7, p. 329.]. We seek refuge in Allah from His wrath and His plan.

Some scholars said: May Allah have mercy on a servant who reflects upon this verse: ﴿until, when they rejoiced in what they had been given, We seized them suddenly.﴾ Muhammad ibn al-Nadr al-Harithi said: These people were given respite for twenty years. Uqba ibn Amir related that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "When you see Allah giving servants what they wish despite their disobedience, that is only a gradual leading on from Him to them." Then he recited: ﴿So when they forgot what they had been reminded of﴾, the whole verse. Al-Hasan said: By Allah, there is no one whom Allah expands in worldly life and who does not fear that he is being plotted against in it, except that his deeds have diminished and his judgment has weakened. And there is no one whom Allah withholds from, and who does not think that it is good for him in it [In ج: in that], except that his deeds have diminished and his judgment has weakened. And it is reported in a narration that Allah, the Exalted, revealed to Musa (ﷺ): "When you see poverty coming toward you, say: 'Welcome, emblem of the righteous.' And when you see wealth coming toward you, say: 'A sin whose punishment has been hastened.'"

The word of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿then they were suddenly in despair﴾ (*mubslisūn*). The *mublis* is the one who is stunned, grieved, and despairing of good, who cannot produce an answer because of the severity of the bad condition that has befallen him. Al-Ajjaj said:

"O companion, do you recognize a dung-covered abode...?"
"Yes, I recognize it, and it has become *ablas*."

That is, he was bewildered by the terror of what he saw. From this the name Iblis is derived. *Ablasa al-rajul* means he fell silent, and *ablasat al-nāqa* (the she-camel is *mibläs*) means she did not ruminate or [did not] become mounted due to the intensity of her sexual urge, when she wanted the stallion, the camel "*ḍabaʿat*" ("was in heat") with *ḍabʿatan* and *ḍabʿan*.

The word of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿So the last remnant of the people who had done wrong was cut off﴾. *Dābir* means the last. It is said: *dabara al-qawm yadburuhum dabran* when he was the last of them in coming. In a hadith from Abdullah ibn Mas'ud: "Among the people are those who do not come to prayer except as *dabariyyan*" [*Dabariyyan* may be narrated with a fatha or with a sukun on the ba', and it is a relative noun derived from *dabr*, "the end of a thing"; fatha on the ba' is one of the alterations of the relative form (Ibn al-Athir)], meaning at the end of the time. The meaning here is that their descendants and their successors were cut off, so that no remnant of them remained. Qutrub said: It means that they were uprooted and destroyed. Umayya ibn Abi al-Salt said:

"So they were destroyed by a punishment that uprooted their last remnant,
and they could not avert it nor were they helped."

From this comes *tadbīr*, because it is the firm arrangement of the outcomes of affairs.

﴿And praise be to Allah, Lord of the worlds﴾. It has been said: for their destruction. It has also been said: it is an instruction to the believers on how to praise Him. This verse contains proof of the obligation to abandon wrongdoing, because of what follows from cutting off the remnant, leading to an everlasting punishment, along with the fact that the one who cuts it off deserves praise from every praiser.

The commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on Surah 6, verses 46–47:

﴿Say: "Have you considered: if Allah took away your hearing and your sight"﴾. That is, He removed them and tore them away. He used the singular "hearing" (sam'akum) because it is a verbal noun (masdar) that denotes the plural.

(And seals) means He stamped (taba'a). This was discussed earlier in al-Baqarah [[See vol. 1, p. 185.]].

The answer to (in) (in-) is omitted; its implied meaning is: "who could bring it to you?" Its position is in the accusative, because it stands in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal), as when you say: "Strike him if he goes out," meaning "going out." It has been said that what is meant is the meanings subsisting in these limbs. Allah may also take away the limbs and the faculties together, leaving nothing. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Before We obliterate faces﴾ [An-Nisa' 4:47 [[See vol. 5, p. 241.]]]. The verse is an argument against the disbelievers.

(Who is a god other than Allah who could bring it to you?) "Man" (who) is in the nominative as the subject (mubtada'), its predicate is "ilah" (god), and "ghayr" (other than) is its attribute. Likewise "ya'tikum" (bring to you) is in the nominative, being an attribute of "ilah." Its form is that of an interrogative, and the clause of which it is part stands in the position of the two objects of "ra'aytum" (have you considered). The meaning of "ara'aytum" is "a'lamtum" (you know). The pronoun in (bihi) (by it/him) is singular, although the preceding mention was plural, because the meaning is "by the one taken away," so the pronoun refers to the one mentioned. It has also been said that it refers to hearing explicitly, as in His words: ﴿And Allah and His Messenger have more right that they should please Him﴾ [At-Tawbah 9:62 [[See vol. 8, p. 193.]]]. Sight and hearts are included by way of tadmin (implicit inclusion of the sense of one verb in another). It has also been said that the meaning is: "Who is a god other than Allah who could bring it to you by any of these things mentioned?" And it has been said that it refers to the guidance implied by the meaning. 'Abd al-Rahman al-A'raj read (bihi unzur) (look at it) with the "h" vowelled with a damma, following the original form, since the original is that the "h" should be vowelled with a damma, as you say: "ji'tu ma'ahu" (I came with him). Al-Naqqash said: In this verse there is evidence for the preference of hearing over sight, since it is mentioned first here and in other verses. This has already been discussed in full at the beginning of al-Baqarah [[See vol. 1, p. 189.]]. The "turning" (tasrif) of the signs means bringing them from various aspects: by warning, admonition, encouragement, intimidation, and the like.

(Then they turn away) means they turn aside. This is related from Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan, Mujahid, Qatadah and al-Suddi. It is said: "sadafa 'an ash-shay'" when one turns away from a thing, with the verbal noun "sadf" or "sudud," so he is "sadif." "Sadaftuhu" means I met him while turning away from his direction. Ibn al-Riqa' said:

When they recount a story, they say its best part,
and they are turned away from every evil that is to be avoided.

Sadaf in a camel means that its foot tilts from the hand or the foot toward the outer side. So "they turn away" means they are inclined and turn away from the proofs and indications.

﴿Say: "Have you considered: if the punishment of Allah comes upon you suddenly or openly"﴾. Al-Hasan said: "Suddenly" means at night, and "openly" means by day. It has also been said: "suddenly" means unexpectedly. Al-Kisa'i said: One says "baghatahum al-amr yabghatuhum baghtan wa baghtatan" when the matter comes upon them unexpectedly. This has already been mentioned.

(Will anyone be destroyed except the wrongdoing people?) Its parallel is: ﴿Will any be destroyed except the defiantly disobedient people?﴾ [Al-Ahqaf 46:35 [[See vol. 16, p. 222.]]]. That is: will anyone be destroyed except you, because of your polytheism? Here "wrongdoing" (zulm) means polytheism, just as Luqman said to his son: ﴿O my son, do not associate anything with Allah. Indeed, association is a great wrong﴾ [Luqman 31:13 [[See vol. 14, p. 62.]]].

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 6, verse 48:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We send not the messengers except as bearers of good news and warners﴾, meaning: by way of encouragement (tarhib, "encouragement" through promise) and warning (tarhib, "frightening" through threat).

Al-Hasan said: "Bearers of good news" of abundance of provision in this world and reward in the Hereafter. This is indicated by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And if the people of the towns had believed and been mindful of Allah, We would have opened upon them blessings from the heaven and the earth﴾ [[See vol. 7, p. 253.]] [Al-A'raf: 96].

And the meaning of "warners" is those who frighten with the punishment of Allah. So the meaning is: We sent the messengers for this purpose, not for what is demanded of them in the way of signs. They bring signs only in a manner through which their proofs and truthfulness become manifest.

As for His saying: ﴿So whoever believes and makes amends, there will be no fear for them, nor will they grieve﴾, its discussion has already passed.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And those who denied Our signs﴾, i.e., denied the Qur'an and the miracles. It is also said: denied Muhammad, peace be upon him.

﴿Punishment will touch them﴾, i.e., will befall them, ﴿for what they used to defiantly disobey﴾, i.e., disbelieve.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 6, verse 50:

His, the Exalted's, saying: ﴿Say: I do not tell you that I have the treasuries of Allah﴾. This is a response to their saying: "Why has not a sign been sent down to him from his Lord?" [al-An'am: 37]. The meaning is: I do not have the treasuries of His power, so that I may send down what you have proposed of signs, and I do not know the unseen so that I may inform you of it. The khizana (treasury) is that in which a thing is stored, and from it is the hadith: (Indeed, they store up for themselves the udders of their livestock as their provisions. Does one of you love that his storehouse be broken into and his treasury be broken open?). The treasuries of Allah are His capabilities, i.e., I do not have the power to do everything I wish of what you propose. (And I do not know the unseen) also, (and I do not tell you that I am an angel). The people used to imagine that the angels are superior, meaning: I am not an angel, so that I would witness of the affairs of Allah what no human witnesses. Those who hold that the angels are superior to the prophets cited this verse as evidence. The discussion of this has already passed in al-Baqarah [see vol. 1, p. 289 and p. 184], so reflect on it there.

His, the Exalted's, saying: ﴿I only follow what is revealed to me﴾. Its apparent meaning is that he does not decide any matter except where there is revelation. The correct view is that prophets may engage in ijtihad (independent reasoning) and in qiyas (analogical reasoning) upon what is explicitly stated, and qiyas is one of the sources of the Shari'ah. The explanation of this will come in al-A'raf [see vol. 7, p. 171], and the permissibility of the prophets' ijtihad will be discussed in al-Anbiya' [see vol. 11, p. 309], God willing.

His, the Exalted's, saying: ﴿Say: Are the blind and the seeing equal?﴾ That is, the disbelievers and the believers, according to Mujahid and others. It has also been said: the ignorant and the knowing.

(Will you not reflect?) that the two are not equal.

[Commentary of al-Qurtubi on Qur'an 6:51]

Allah's statement: ﴿And warn with it﴾ means: with the Qur'an. And al-indhar (warning) means informing, and it has already been discussed in "al-Baqarah" [[See vol. 1, pp. 289 and 184.]]. It was also said: "with it" means with Allah. It was also said: with the Last Day. He specified "those who fear that they will be gathered" because the proof against them is more binding, for they fear His punishment; not that they doubt the gathering. So the meaning of "fear" is "expect the punishment of the gathering." It was also said: "fear" means "know." If he is a Muslim, he is warned so that he abandons sins; if he is one of the People of the Book, he is warned so that he follows the truth. Al-Hasan said: the intended are the believers. Al-Zajjaj said: it is everyone who affirms the Resurrection, whether believer or disbeliever. It was also said: the verse concerns the polytheists, i.e., warn them of the Day of Resurrection. The first view is more apparent.

(﴿They will have no protector or intercessor besides Him﴾) i.e., besides Allah. This is a refutation of the Jews and Christians in their claim that their father would intercede for them, when they said: ﴿We are the children of Allah and His beloved﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 18]; and of the polytheists, who made their idols intercessors for them with Allah. So Allah informed that intercession does not belong to disbelievers. And whoever says the verse concerns the believers says: the Messenger's intercession for them occurs by Allah's permission, so He is the true Intercessor in that case. In the revelation: ﴿And they do not intercede except for one whom He approves﴾ [al-Anbiya': 28]. ﴿And intercession with Him does not benefit except for one whom He permits﴾ [Saba': 23]. ﴿Who is it that can intercede with Him except by His permission?﴾ [al-Baqarah: 255].

(﴿That perhaps they may fear Allah﴾) i.e., in the future, which is steadfastness upon faith.

The Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on Surah 6, verse 52:

Allah's words: ﴿And do not drive away those who call upon their Lord﴾ [[the rest of the verse, from the manuscripts ج, ب, ك]]. The polytheists (al-Mushrikun) said: "We will not agree to sit with the likes of these," meaning Salman, Suhayb, Bilal and Khabbab, "so drive them away from you." [[In ب, ع, ك, ج and هـ: Hassan.]] They asked that this be put in writing for them. The Prophet (ﷺ) was inclined toward this and called for Ali to write it. The poor believers then stood up and sat off to one side, so Allah revealed the verse. This is why Sa'd, in the authentic hadith, alluded to it when he said: "What Allah willed to happen then befell the heart of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)." The matter will be mentioned later. The Prophet (ﷺ) only leaned toward this out of hope for their conversion and the conversion of their people, and he thought that it would not deprive his Companions of anything or diminish their standing. So he inclined to it, and Allah revealed the verse, forbidding him from what he had intended of driving them away. It was not that he actually drove them away.

Muslim related from Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas, who said: "We were with the Prophet (ﷺ), six men. The polytheists said to the Prophet (ﷺ): 'Drive these away from you, so that they will not be emboldened against us.' He said: 'I was among them, along with Ibn Mas'ud, a man from Hudhayl, Bilal, and two men whose names I will not mention.' What Allah willed to happen then befell the heart of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), so he spoke to himself, and Allah, Mighty and Majestic, revealed: 'And do not drive away those who call upon their Lord in the morning and the evening, seeking His Face.'"

It was said: the meaning of "calling" (al-du'a') is observing the obligatory prayer in congregation. This was said by Ibn Abbas, Mujahid and al-Hasan. It was also said: it means remembrance (dhikr) and recitation of the Qur'an. It may also mean supplication at the beginning and end of the day, so that they begin their day with supplication, desiring success, and end it with supplication, seeking forgiveness.

"Seeking His Face" means seeking His obedience and sincerity in it, that is, they are sincere in their worship and their deeds for Allah, and they direct these toward Him alone and not toward anyone else. It was also said: they seek Allah, who is described as having a Face, as He said: "And there remains the Face of your Lord, Full of Majesty and Honour" [Ar-Rahman: 27]. This is like His saying: "And those who are patient, seeking the Face of their Lord" [Ar-Ra'd: 22].

He singled out the morning and the evening for mention because worldly occupation is dominant among people at those times. Whoever devotes himself to worship during the time of occupation will be even more devoted to it during his time free from occupation.

After this, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) would restrain himself to sit with them, as Allah had commanded him in His words: "And keep yourself patient with those who call upon their Lord in the morning and the evening, seeking His Face. And let not your eyes overlook them" [Al-Kahf: 28]. So he would not rise until they were the ones who began to rise.

Ibn Majah, in his Sunan, has clearly and fully expounded this meaning from Khabbab concerning Allah's words, Mighty and Majestic: "And do not drive away those who call upon their Lord in the morning and the evening," up to His words: "lest you be among the wrongdoers." He said: al-Aqra' ibn Habis al-Tamimi and Uyayna ibn Hisn al-Fazari came and found the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) with Suhayb, Bilal, Ammar and Khabbab, sitting among a group of the weak among the believers. When they saw them around the Prophet (ﷺ), they belittled them. They came to him, spoke to him privately, and said: "We want you to set aside for us a gathering from you, by which the Arabs will recognise our virtue, for the delegations of the Arabs come to you, and we are ashamed for the Arabs to see us sitting with these slaves. So when we come to you, remove them from you, and when we have finished, sit with them if you wish." He said: "Yes." They said: "Then write us a document from you." He said: he called for a sheet and called Ali (may Allah be pleased with him) to write, while we sat in a corner. Then Jibril (peace be upon him) descended and said: "And do not drive away those who call upon their Lord in the morning and the evening, seeking His Face. Nothing of their reckoning falls upon you, and nothing of your reckoning falls upon them, so that you would drive them away and thus be among the wrongdoers." Then he mentioned al-Aqra' ibn Habis and Uyayna ibn Hisn, and said: "And thus We tried some of them by means of others, that they might say: 'Are these the ones on whom Allah has bestowed favour from among us?' Is Allah not best aware of those who are grateful?" [Al-An'am: 53]. Then He said: "And when those come to you who believe in Our signs, say: 'Peace be upon you. Your Lord has prescribed for Himself mercy'" [Al-An'am: 54]. He said: so we drew near to him until we placed our knees against his knee. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) would sit with us, and when he wished to rise, he rose and left us. Then Allah, Mighty and Majestic, revealed: "And keep yourself patient with those who call upon their Lord in the morning and the evening, seeking His Face, and let not your eyes overlook them, desiring the adornment of the life of this world" [Al-Kahf: 28], "and do not obey him whose heart We have made heedless of Our remembrance" [Al-Kahf: 28], meaning Uyayna and al-Aqra', "and who follows his own desire, and whose affair has been [ruin]" [Al-Kahf: 28], that is, destruction. He said: this was the matter of Uyayna and al-Aqra'. Then He set forth for them the parable of the two men and the parable of the life of this world.

Khabbab said: "So we used to sit with the Prophet (ﷺ), and when we reached the hour at which he would rise, we rose and left him until he rose." This was related by Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Yahya ibn Sa'id al-Qattan, who said: Amr ibn Muhammad al-Anqazi [[al-Anqazi: vowelled in al-Qamus as (with a fatha on the qaf) in Lubb al-Lubab; al-Tahdhib says it is with a kasra.]] narrated to us, who said: Asbat narrated to us, from al-Suddi, from Abu Sa'id al-Azdi, who was the reciter of the Azd, from Abu al-Kanud, from Khabbab. [[In ج, ك, ى, ع: Abu Sa'd is also said.]] He also related it from Sa'd, who said: "This verse was revealed about six of us: about me, Ibn Mas'ud, Suhayb, Ammar, al-Miqdad and Bilal." He said: "Quraysh said to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): 'We will not accept being followers of these, so drive them away.' He said: 'What Allah willed to enter the heart of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) from that entered it,' and Allah, Mighty and Majestic, revealed: 'And do not drive away those who call upon their Lord in the morning and the evening,' to the end of the verse." It is also read as (bil-ghudwah), and its explanation will come, God willing, in (al-Kahf). [[See vol. 10, p. 390.]]

Allah's words: ﴿Nothing of their reckoning falls upon you﴾ mean: nothing of their reward, and no provision of their sustenance is your responsibility. Their reward and their provision are with Allah, and your reward and your provision are with Allah, not with anyone else. [[In ك: kafala (guarantee).]]

The first "min" (from) is partitive (lil-tab'id), and the second is additional, for emphasis. Likewise in "and nothing of your reckoning falls upon them." The meaning: since the matter is so, then turn toward them, sit with them, and do not drive them away, out of regard for the right of those who are not on their level in religion and merit. If you did so, you would be a wrongdoer. But He is far above such a thing occurring from him. This is only an explanation of the rulings, and so that the like of it does not happen from others among the people of Islam. This is like His saying: "If you associate partners with Allah, your deeds will surely be nullified" [Az-Zumar: 65], though Allah already knew of him that he would not associate partners and that his deeds would not be nullified.

"So that you would drive them away" is the answer to the negation. "And thus be among the wrongdoers" is put in the subjunctive by the fa' in answer to the prohibition. The meaning: "Do not drive away those who call upon their Lord, and thus you would be among the wrongdoers. And nothing of your reckoning falls upon them, so that you would drive them away," in inverted order. Injustice (zulm) originally means placing a thing in other than its proper place. It has been fully discussed earlier in (al-Baqarah). [[See vol. 1, p. 309.]]

From the force of the verse and the hadith, the prohibition is derived against honouring anyone for his status or his clothing [[In ج, ك, ى, ع, هـ: his parents.]], and against despising anyone for his obscurity or the shabbiness of his clothing.

**Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Qur'an) on Surah 6, verse 53:**

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And thus We tested some of them by means of others﴾, meaning: just as We tested those before you, so We tested these. *Al-fitnah* means testing, that is, We dealt with them as those who test.

(*Li-yaqulu*) is in the subjunctive by the *lam* of purpose (*lam kay*, the particle of purpose), meaning the nobles and the wealthy.

(*A-haʾulaʾi*) means the weak and the poor.

(*Man-na Allahu ʿalayhim min baynina*) Al-Nahhas said: "This is one of the difficult points, because it is asked: how were they tested so that they would say this verse? For if it was a denial, it would be disbelief on their part." There are two answers to this. The first: the meaning is that the wealthy were tested through the poor, whether their rank would be equal before the Prophet (ﷺ), so that they would say, as an interrogative (*istifham*, a question) and not as a denial: "Are these the ones upon whom God has bestowed favour from among us?" The second answer: when they were tested by this, its outcome was that they said it as a denial, and it became like His saying: ﴿So the family of Pharaoh picked him up, that he might become for them an enemy and a grief﴾ [[see vol. 15?, p. 276.]] [Al-Qasas: 8].

(*Alaysa Allahu bi-aʿlama bi-l-shakirin*) concerning those upon whom He has bestowed faith, rather than the leaders whom God knew to be disbelievers. This is an interrogative of affirmation (*istifham taqrir*, a question seeking confirmation), and it is the answer to their saying: "Are these the ones upon whom God has bestowed favour from among us?" It was also said: the meaning is, "Is not God more knowing of who is grateful, [in] accepting Islam when I guide him to it?"

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 6, verse 54:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿When those who believe in Our signs come to you, say: Peace be upon you.﴾ "Al-salam" (peace) and "al-salamah" (safety) have one meaning. The meaning of "salamun 'alaykum" is: may Allah keep you safe in your religion and your persons. It was revealed concerning those whom Allah forbade His Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, from driving away. So whenever he saw them, he would greet them first with the salam and say: "Praise be to Allah who has placed in my community one whom He commanded me to greet first with the salam." Accordingly, the salam was from the Prophet (ﷺ). It is also said that it was from Allah Exalted, that is: convey to them the salam from Us. Under both interpretations, this indicates their virtue and their high standing with Allah Exalted. In Sahih Muslim, on the authority of 'A'idh ibn 'Amr, that Abu Sufyan passed by Salman, Suhayb and Bilal and a group, and they said: "By Allah, the swords of Allah have not taken from the neck of the enemy of Allah what they should have taken." He said: Abu Bakr then said: "Do you say this to the elder and chief of Quraysh?" Then he went to the Prophet (ﷺ) and informed him. He said: "O Abu Bakr, perhaps you have angered them. If you have angered them, you have angered your Lord." So Abu Bakr came to them and said: "O my brothers, have I angered you?" They said: "No, may Allah forgive you, my brother." This is evidence of the elevated rank of these men and their sanctity, as we have explained in the meaning of the verse [[من ج، وع، ك، وه وى.]]. From this is derived the respect due to the righteous and the avoidance of what angers or harms them, for in that is the anger of Allah, that is, the descent of His punishment upon whoever harms any of His friends. Ibn 'Abbas said: the verse was revealed concerning Abu Bakr, 'Umar, 'Uthman and 'Ali [may Allah be pleased with them] [[من ك وى.]]. Fudayl ibn 'Iyad said: a group of Muslims came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: "We have committed sins, so ask forgiveness for us," and he turned away from them, and the verse was revealed. The same is narrated from Anas ibn Malik, in the same wording.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Your Lord has prescribed for Himself mercy﴾. That is, He made this obligatory by His true report and His true promise. The servants are addressed in terms of what they understand: that whoever prescribes something for himself has made it binding upon himself. It is also said: He wrote that in the Preserved Tablet.

(That whoever among you does evil in ignorance) That is, a sin committed without intent. Mujahid said: he does not know the lawful from the unlawful, and from his ignorance he undertakes the matter; so everyone who commits a sin is ignorant in it. This meaning has already passed in "al-Nisa'" [[راجع ج ٥ ص ٩٢.]]. It is also said: whoever prefers the immediate world over the Hereafter is the ignorant one.

(Then indeed He is Forgiving, Merciful) Ibn 'Amir and 'Asim read "anna" (that) with a fatha in "fa-annahu" and likewise in "annahu man 'amila," and Nafi' agreed with them in "annahu man 'amila." The rest read with a kasra in both. Whoever reads with a kasra does so as a resumed sentence (istinaf, a new independent clause), and the clause explains the mercy. "In" (inna), when it enters upon full clauses, takes a kasra, and the rule for what follows the fa' is that it begins a new sentence, so it takes a kasra for that reason. Whoever reads both with a fatha takes the first (annahu) in the position of an accusative as a substitute (badal, apposition) for "mercy," substitution of a thing for the same thing, and "kataba" (prescribed) governs it. It is as if he said: Your Lord has prescribed for Himself that whoever does evil... As for "fa-annahu ghafur" with a fatha, there are two views. The first: it is in the position of a nominative as the subject (mubtada', the topic), with its predicate (khabar) omitted, as if he said: for him is that He is Forgiving, Merciful, because what follows the fa' is a subject, meaning: for him is the forgiveness of Allah. The second: a subject is omitted, and "anna" with what it governs is its predicate, its estimated form being: his matter is that Allah forgives him. This is the preference of Sibawayh, and he did not permit the first; Abu Hatim permitted it. It is also said that "kataba" governs it, that is, your Lord prescribed that He is Forgiving, Merciful. It is narrated from 'Ali ibn Salih and Ibn Harmuz that they read the first with a kasra as a resumed sentence and the second with a fatha, either as a beginning, or as the predicate of a subject, or as governed by "kataba" in the manner previously stated. Whoever reads the first with a fatha, namely Nafi', makes it a substitute for "mercy," and treats the second as a resumed sentence because it follows the fa'. This is a clear reading.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 6, verse 55:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And thus We detail the verses﴾. At-tafsil (detailing) is the clarification by which the meanings become apparent. The meaning is: Just as We have set out for you in this surah Our proofs and Our argumentation against the polytheists, thus do We detail for you the verses concerning everything you need in matters of religion, and We make clear to you Our proofs and arguments concerning every truth that the people of falsehood deny.

Al-Qutabi said: "We detail the verses" means We bring them one after another, and We do not send them down all at once in one connected body.

(And that the way of the criminals may become clear.) It is said: this lam (li-) is connected to a verb, so where is the verb it is connected to? The Kufans said: it is implied, meaning: "And thus We detail the verses, so that We may make clear to you and that [the way of the criminals] may become evident." An-Nahhas said: all of this deletion is unnecessary; the implied sense is: "And thus We detail the verses; We have detailed them." It is also said that the wa (and) introduces a coordination according to meaning, i.e., "so that the truth may become manifest and become clear." It is read with the ya' and with the ta'.

(Sabil, "way," is read with the lam in both the nominative and the accusative.) The reading with ta' is an address to the Prophet ﷺ, meaning: "And that you, O Muhammad, may make clear the way of the criminals." If it is asked: but did the Prophet, upon him be peace, not already know it? The answer, according to az-Zajjaj, is that the address to the Prophet, upon him be peace, is an address to his community, so the meaning is: "And that you [plural] may make clear the way of the criminals." If it is asked: why is the way of the believers not mentioned? There are two answers to this. The first is that it is like His saying: "garments that protect you from the heat" (an-Nahl 16:81), meaning "and that protect you from the cold," which was omitted; similarly the meaning here is "and that the way of the believers may become clear," which was omitted. The second answer is to say: a thing becomes clear (istabana al-shay') and one makes it clear (istabanahu); when the way of the criminals becomes clear, the way of the believers has also become clear. The word sabil is both masculine and feminine: the Tamim treat it as masculine, while the people of the Hijaz treat it as feminine. In the revelation, "if they see the way of right guidance" (al-A'raf 7:146) is masculine, and "why do you bar from the way of Allah" (Al 'Imran 3:99) is feminine. Likewise, (wa-li-tastabina) is read with the ya' and with the ta'; the ta' is an address to the Prophet ﷺ, and what is intended is his community.

**Verse 6:56:** ﴿Say: "I have been forbidden to worship those whom you invoke besides God."﴾ It was said that "tad'una" (you invoke) means "ta'buduna" (you worship). It was also said that it means you call upon them for your urgent affairs in the manner of worship, and by this he meant the idols.

(﴿Say: I will not follow your desires﴾) in what you have demanded of me regarding the worship of these things, and regarding driving away those whom you wish to be driven away.

(﴿Then I would have gone astray﴾), that is, I would have gone astray if I followed your desires.

(﴿And I am not among the guided﴾), that is, on the path of right guidance.

It is read "ḍalaltu" with a fatha and with a kasra on the lam, and both are dialectal forms (lughatān). Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala' [[[from ي, ك.]]] said: "ḍaliltu" with a kasra on the lam is the dialect of Tamim, and it is the reading of Yahya [[[from ك.]]] ibn Wathhab and Talha ibn Musarrif. The first form is the more sound and eloquent, because it is the dialect of the people of the Hijaz, and it is the reading of the majority (al-jumhur). Al-Jawhari said: "al-ḍalal and al-ḍalala are the opposite of al-rashad (right direction), and one says ḍalaltu, adhillu," and God Most High said: ﴿Say: If I go astray, I only go astray to my own detriment﴾ [Saba': 50]. This is the dialect of Najd, and it is the eloquent form, while the people of al-'Aliya say "ḍaliltu, adhillu" with a kasra.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 6, verse 57:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Say: "Indeed, I am upon clear evidence from my Lord"﴾, meaning proof, certainty, argument and demonstration, not upon desire. From this comes the word bayyinah (clear evidence), because it makes the truth clear and manifest.

(And you denied it) meaning, denied the bayyinah, because it carries the sense of bayan (clarification), as He said: "And when the division is attended by the relatives and the orphans and the needy, provide for them from it" [An-Nisa: 8], according to what we explained there [see vol. 5, p. 50]. It was also said that the pronoun refers to the Lord, meaning: you denied my Lord, since His mention has preceded. It was also said: it refers to the punishment. It was said: it refers to the Qur'an.

Concerning the meaning of this verse and the one before it, there is what Mus'ab ibn 'Abd Allah ibn al-Zubayr recited of his own poetry, and he was a poet of good quality, may Allah be pleased with him:

Shall I sit down after my bones have trembled, while death was nearer to me than what is near me?
I dispute with every opposing adversary, and I make his religion a target for my religion.
So I abandon what I know for the opinion of another, and opinion is not like certain knowledge.
And what am I to do with disputation, when it is a thing turned to the left and to the right?
Upright ways have been laid down for us, which lead through every wide path or ravine. [Al-Wajin: the bank of a valley.]
The truth has no obscurity in it, bright like the brightness of the clear dawn.
And there is no substitute for us of the method of Jahm in place of the method of Ibn Amina, the trustworthy.
As for what I know, it has sufficed me, and as for what I do not know, leave me alone.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿What you are hastening for is not with me﴾, meaning the punishment. Because of the extremity of their denial, they used to hasten its descent in mockery, like their saying: "Or you cause the sky to fall upon us in pieces, as you claim" [Al-Isra: 92], and "O Allah, if this is the truth from You, then rain down upon us stones from the sky" [Al-Anfal: 32]. It was also said: what is with me is not among the signs that you propose.

(The decision belongs only to Allah) meaning: the decision regarding the delay or hastening of the punishment belongs only to Allah. It was also said: the decisive judgment between truth and falsehood belongs to Allah.

﴿He relates the truth﴾, meaning He relates the true narratives. With this, those who deny the presence of metaphor (majaz) in the Qur'an have argued. This is the reading of Nafi', Ibn Kathir, 'Asim, Mujahid, al-A'raj and Ibn 'Abbas. Ibn 'Abbas said: Allah, mighty and majestic, said: "We relate to you the best of narratives" [Yusuf: 3] [see vol. 9, p. 119]. The rest read "yaqdi al-haqq" with the dotted dad (ض), and likewise Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, Abu 'Abd al-Rahman al-Sulami and Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab read it; it is written in the Mushaf without a yā'. It should not be stopped upon, and it is from al-qada' (judgment). What supports this is that after it comes "and He is the best of deciders" (wa huwa khayr al-fasilin), and deciding is only judgment, not narrating. This is strengthened by His saying before it: "The decision belongs only to Allah." It is also strengthened by the reading of Ibn Mas'ud: "The decision belongs only to Allah; He judges with the truth" (yaqdi bi al-haqq), where the insertion of the bā' emphasizes the meaning of judging. Al-Nahhas said: this does not necessarily follow, because the meaning of "yaqdi" comes to mean "comes with" and "does," so the meaning is: "He brings the truth," and it is also possible that the meaning is: "He judges the true judgment." Makki said: the reading with the ṣād is more beloved to me, because the two Harams and 'Asim agree on it, and because if it were from al-qada', the bā' would necessarily be present in it, as it appears in the reading of Ibn Mas'ud. Al-Nahhas said: this argument does not necessarily follow, because such a bā' is often omitted.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 6, verse 58:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Say: If I had what you are hastening for﴾ — i.e., of the punishment — ﴿I would surely have decided the matter between you﴾, until the affair is concluded to its end. And "istti'jal" (hastening) is: hastening to seek a thing before its time. "And Allah knows best the wrongdoers" — i.e., the polytheists, and the time of their punishment.

Checked by Abu Ishaq Ibrahim Atfayyish.

The sixth part of Tafsir al-Qurtubi is complete. It is followed, God willing, by the seventh part, whose beginning is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And with Him are the keys of the unseen﴾.

The seventh part.

(In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful)

[Continuation of the commentary on Surah al-An'am]

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 6, verse 59:

There are three issues concerning this.

The first: It has come in a report that when this verse was revealed, twelve thousand angels descended with it. Al-Bukhari narrated from Ibn Umar, from the Prophet (ﷺ), that he said: "The keys of the unseen are five, which none knows but Allah: None knows what the wombs carry except Allah; none knows what will happen tomorrow except Allah; none knows when the rain will come except Allah; no soul knows in what land it will die except Allah; and none knows when the Hour will come except Allah." In Sahih Muslim, from Aisha, she said: "Whoever claims that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) informs of what will happen tomorrow has greatly slandered Allah, and Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Say: None in the heavens and the earth knows the unseen except Allah﴾" [[See vol. 13, p. 225.]]

"Mafatih" is the plural of "maftah" (key), this being the eloquent form. It is also said "miftah," whose plural is "mafatih." And it is the reading of Ibn al-Sumayqa: "mafatih." The "miftah" is an expression for anything that opens a lock, whether sensible, such as a lock on a house, or intelligible, such as reflection.

Ibn Majah in his Sunan and Abu Hatim al-Busti in his Sahih narrated from Anas ibn Malik, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Indeed among people are keys to good, locks against evil, and among people are keys to evil, locks against good. So good tidings to him whom Allah has made the keys of good upon his hands, and woe to him whom Allah has made the keys of evil upon his hands."

In the verse, it is a metaphor for reaching the unseen, just as in the witnessed realm a key is used to reach what is hidden from a person. For this reason some said: it is derived from the people's saying "iftah 'alayya kadha," meaning "give me or teach me what I may reach by it." So Allah the Exalted possesses the knowledge of the unseen, and in His hand are the means that lead to it; no one possesses them except Him. Whomever He wills to inform of them, He informs; and whomever He wills to veil from them, He veils. This does not come as an outpouring from Him except upon His messengers, by the evidence of His saying: ﴿And Allah would not disclose the unseen to you, but Allah chooses from His messengers whom He wills﴾ [[See vol. 4, p. 288.]], and He said: ﴿The Knower of the unseen; He does not reveal His unseen to anyone, except to a messenger whom He has approved﴾ [[See vol. 19, p. 26.]].

It has been said that what is meant by the keys is the treasuries of provision, from as-Suddi and al-Hasan. Muqatil and ad-Dahhak said: the treasuries of the earth. This is a figurative usage, expressed by that through which one reaches them. It has also been said: other than this, of what the meaning of the hadith includes, namely that with Him are the terms and the time of their ending. It has been said: the outcomes of lifespans and the ends of deeds, among other sayings. The first is the preferred view, and Allah knows best.

The second: Our scholars said: Allah the Exalted attributed the knowledge of the unseen to Himself in more than one verse of His Book, except whom He has chosen of His servants. Whoever says, "Rain will fall tomorrow," and asserts it definitively, is a disbeliever, whether he bases it on a sign he claims or not. Likewise, whoever says, "He knows what is in the womb," is a disbeliever. But if he does not assert it definitively, and says: "The nawʾ [[The nawʾ: the setting of a mansion (star) in the west at dawn together with the rising of another from the east opposite it at the same moment; the Arabs used to attribute rains, winds, heat and cold to the one that sets.]] customarily brings down water from Allah," or that it is the cause of water customarily, or that it is the cause of water according to what He has decreed and what has preceded in His knowledge, he does not disbelieve. However, it is recommended for him not to speak of it, for in it there is resemblance to the speech of the people of disbelief, and ignorance of His subtle wisdom, because He sends down rain whenever He wills, sometimes with a certain nawʾ and sometimes without a nawʾ. Allah the Exalted said [[i.e., in the hadith qudsi]]: "Among My servants in the morning are believers in Me and disbelievers [in the star]," as will be explained in "al-Waqi'a" [[See vol. 17, p. 228 onward.]], Allah willing.

Ibn al-Arabi said: Likewise is the saying of the physician: "If the right breast's nipple is darkened, the child is male; if it is on the left breast, it is female; and if the woman finds the right side heavier, the child is female." Whoever claims this as a customary matter, not as a necessary matter in creation, does not disbelieve and is not corrupt. As for whoever claims acquisition of knowledge of the future of one's life, he is a disbeliever. Or whoever reports on general or detailed occurrences, regarding what will be before it is, there is also no doubt of his disbelief.

As for one who reports on eclipses of the sun and moon, our scholars said: he is disciplined but not imprisoned. The reason he is not declared a disbeliever is that a group said it is a matter known through calculation and the determination of stations, as Allah reported in His saying: ﴿And the moon, We have determined for it stations﴾ [[See vol. 15, p. 29.]]. As for his being disciplined, it is because they introduce doubt among the common people, who do not perceive the difference between this and other matters, so they confuse their beliefs and abandon their foundations of certainty. Thus they are disciplined, so that they conceal that knowledge if they have it and do not publicize it.

I say: From this category also is what came in Sahih Muslim from some of the wives of the Prophet (ﷺ) that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Whoever comes to a soothsayer (and asks him about something), his prayer will not be accepted for forty nights."

The ʿarrāf is the diviner and the astrologer who claims knowledge of the unseen. The practice is from ʿarāfa, and its practitioner is an ʿarrāf, one who infers matters through causes and premises he claims to know. Some practitioners of this art may support it with augury, lines, stars and customary causes. This art is ʿiyafa (with a yāʾ). All of these are subsumed under the name kihana (soothsaying), as al-Qadi ʿIyad said. Kihana is the claim to knowledge of the unseen.

Abu Umar ibn Abd al-Barr said in al-Kafi: Among the earnings whose prohibition is agreed upon are interest, the wages of prostitutes, illicit gain, bribery, taking payment for wailing and singing, and payment for soothsaying, claiming the unseen and reporting heavenly news, and for music, play and falsehood altogether.

Our scholars said: Conditions have changed in these times with the coming of the astrologers and soothsayers, especially in the land of Egypt. It has spread among their leaders, followers and rulers to employ astrologers. Indeed many who are affiliated with jurisprudence and religion have been deceived; they came to these soothsayers and diviners, who dazzled them with falsehoods and extracted their wealth, so they gained from their words only mirages and mirage-like illusions, and from their beliefs only corruption and misguidance. All of this is among the major sins, because of the Prophet's saying (peace be upon him): "The prayer will not be accepted for forty nights." How then of one who takes them and spends on them, relying on their statements?

Muslim (may Allah have mercy on him) narrated from Aisha (may Allah be pleased with her), who said: Some people asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) about the soothsayers, and he said: "They are nothing." They said: "O Messenger of Allah, they sometimes tell us something and it turns out to be true!" The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "That word of truth is snatched by the jinn, who whisper it into the ear of his friend (like the clucking of a hen), and they mix with it a hundred lies."

Al-Humaydi said: In the Sahih, there is no other narration from Yahya ibn Urwa, from his father, from Aisha except this one. Al-Bukhari also narrated it from the hadith of Abu al-Aswad Muhammad ibn Abd al-Rahman, from Urwa, from Aisha, that she heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: "The angels descend into the clouds, which is the 'anan,' and they mention the matter decreed in heaven, so the devils steal the hearing and hear it, and convey it to the soothsayers, and they lie with it a hundred lies from their own selves."

This meaning will come in Surah Saba, Allah willing [[See vol. 14, p. 278 onward.]].

The third: The saying of the Exalted: ﴿And He knows what is in the land and the sea﴾. He specified these two by mention because they are the greatest creations adjacent to humans; that is, He knows what perishes on land and sea. It is also said: He knows what is on land of plants, grain and date-pits, and what is in the sea of creatures and the provision of what is in them. ﴿And not a leaf falls but He knows it﴾. Yazid ibn Harun narrated from Nafi, from Muhammad ibn Ishaq, from Nafi, from Ibn Umar, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "There is no seed on the earth, nor fruit on the trees, nor grain in the darknesses of the earth, except that written upon it is: 'In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate: the provision of so-and-so son of so-and-so.'" This is His saying in His perfectly firm Book: ﴿And not a leaf falls but He knows it, nor a grain in the darknesses of the earth, nor anything moist or dry, but it is in a clear Book﴾.

Al-Naqqash narrated from Jafar ibn Muhammad that the "leaf" refers to the miscarried children of Adam's descendants, the "grain" refers to one that is not a miscarriage, the "moist" refers to the living, and the "dry" refers to the dead. Ibn Atiyya said: This is a view that proceeds by way of symbols, and it is not authentically from Jafar ibn Muhammad, and one should not turn to it.

It has been said: The meaning of ﴿And not a leaf falls﴾ is a leaf of a tree: He knows when it falls, where it falls, and how long it turns in the air; and not a grain but He knows when it sprouts, how much it yields, and who eats it. "The darknesses of the earth" are its depths. This is more sound, for it agrees with the hadith and is what the verse requires. And Allah is the Granter of guidance.

It has been said: "in the darknesses of the earth" means the rock that is beneath the seven earths. "Nor anything moist or dry" is read in the genitive, in coordination with the wording. Ibn al-Sumayqa, al-Hasan and others read both with the nominative, coordinating with the position of "min waraqa," so the "min" in this reading is for emphasis.

﴿But it is in a clear Book﴾: that is, in the Preserved Tablet, so that the angels may take lesson from it, not that He, glorified is He, wrote it because of forgetfulness that might befall Him, exalted is He above that. It has also been said: He wrote it while knowing it, to magnify the matter, that is: know that what contains no reward or punishment is written, so how much more so what contains reward and punishment.

The Almighty's words: ﴿It is He who takes your souls by night﴾. That is, He makes you sleep, and He seizes your souls by which you discern. This is not death in reality; rather it is the seizing of the spirits from acting through sleep, just as He seizes them through death. And tawaffi means the taking in full of a thing. "Tuuffiya al-mayyit" means he has taken in full the number of the days of his life. One who sleeps is as if he has taken in full his movements in wakefulness. And al-wafah is death. "Awfaytuka al-mal" and "tawaffaytuhu" [[In manuscripts Z and L: tawaffaytu al-shay'.]]

, and "istawfaytuhu" means when I take it all in full. The poet said [[He is Manzur al-Wabari.]]:

Indeed the sons of al-Ardad are not of any reckoning, and Quraysh has not counted them in number.

It is said: when the spirit leaves the body in sleep, life remains in it, and therefore there is movement and breathing in it. When its lifespan is complete, its spirit leaves and its life is cut off, and it becomes a dead thing that does not move or breathe. Some said: the spirit does not leave it, but the intellect leaves it. It is said: this is a matter whose reality none knows except Allah the Exalted. This is the most sound of the opinions, and Allah knows best.

﴿Then He raises you up therein﴾: that is, during the day, meaning wakefulness.

﴿That a term appointed may be fulfilled﴾: that is, that every person may complete a term appointed for him. Abu Raja' and Talha ibn Musarrif read "Then He raises you up therein that a term appointed may be fulfilled," meaning with Him. And "jaraḥtum" means you earn. It has been mentioned previously in al-Ma'ida [[See vol. 6, p. 66.]]. In the verse there is inversion of order, and the sense is: ﴿It is He who takes your souls by night, then raises you up by day, and knows what you have earned therein﴾; so He put first what is most important, for which the raising up in the day occurs. Ibn Jurayj said: ﴿Then He raises you up therein﴾ means in sleep. The meaning of the verse: His granting respite to the disbelievers is not from heedlessness of their disbelief, for He has counted every thing, known it and recorded it; rather it is so that a term appointed of provision and life may be fulfilled, and then they will return to Him, and He will recompense them. It indicates resurrection and raising by the word "ba'th," since the second creation stands after the first as wakefulness stands after sleep, in that whoever is able to do one is able to do the other.

**Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 6, verses 61–62:**

Allah's words: ﴿And He is the Subjugator over His servants﴾. He means the "above-ness" of rank and standing, not the "above-ness" of place and direction, as was explained earlier at the beginning of the surah. (See vol. 1, p. 1.)

(And He sends over you guardians): that is, from among the angels. "Sending" (al-irsal) in its literal sense means releasing a thing with the message it has been given. So the sending of the angels is with what they carry of the duty of guarding that they were commanded to perform, as He said: ﴿But indeed, over you are guardians﴾. That is, angels who guard the deeds of the servants and guard them from calamities. "Al-hafazah" (the guardians) is the plural of "hafiz" (guardian), like "al-kataba" (the scribes) and "al-katib" (the scribe). It is said that there are two angels by night and two angels by day: one of them records the good and the other the evil. When a person walks, one of them is before him and the other behind him; when he sits, one of them is on his right and the other on his left, based on His saying: ﴿on the right and on the left, seated﴾ (verse). (See vol. 17, p. 8.) It is also said that every person has five angels: two by night, two by day, and the fifth never leaves him, night or day. And Allah knows best.

Umar ibn al-Khattab (may Allah be pleased with him) said:

*Among people is one who lives wretched,*
*foolish of heart, heedless of wakefulness.*

*But if he is faithful and of sound judgment,*
*wary of death, he guards against the guardians.*

*Indeed, people are travelers and residents,*
*and whoever has departed has a lesson for the one who remains.*

Allah's words: ﴿until, when death comes to one of you﴾. He means its causes, as was explained earlier in Surat al-Baqarah. (See vol. 2, p. 137.)

(Our messengers take him in death): in the feminine form for the plural group, as He said: ﴿Our messengers had certainly come to them with clear evidence﴾ and ﴿Messengers had been denied﴾. (See vol. 6, p. 416.) Hamzah recited "tawaffahu rusulunaa" with the masculine form for the plural. Al-A'mash recited "tatawaffahu rusulunaa" with an added taa' and the masculine form. The intended meaning is the assistants of the Angel of Death, as said by Ibn Abbas and others. It is related that they draw the soul out of the body, until, when it is near the moment of seizing it, the Angel of Death seizes it. Al-Kalbi said: the Angel of Death seizes the soul from the body, then hands it over to the angels of mercy if the person was a believer, or to the angels of punishment if he was a disbeliever. It is said that with him are seven angels of mercy and seven angels of punishment. When he seizes a believing soul, he hands it over to the angels of mercy, who give it the glad tidings of reward and ascend with it to the heaven. When he seizes a disbelieving soul, he hands it over to the angels of punishment, who give it the tidings of punishment and terrify it, then they ascend with it to the heaven, and then it is returned to Sijjin, while the spirit of the believer goes to Illiyyin.

The act of causing death ("tawaffi") is sometimes attributed to the Angel of Death, as He said: ﴿Say: The Angel of Death who has been put in charge of you will take you﴾. (See vol. 14, p. 92.) Sometimes it is attributed to the angels, because they carry out that task, as in this verse and others. And sometimes it is attributed to Allah, who is the true One who causes death, as He said: ﴿Allah takes the souls at the time of their death﴾ (see vol. 15, p. 260), ﴿Say: Allah gives you life, then causes you to die﴾ (see vol. 16, p. 172), and ﴿He who created death and life﴾ (see vol. 18, p. 206). So every angel who is commanded does only what he is commanded to do.

Allah's words: ﴿and they do not fail﴾. That is, they do not waste or fall short, meaning they obey the command of Allah. Its root is from "precedence," as was explained before. So the meaning of "farrata" is "he went ahead in weakness." Abu Ubaydah said: they do not delay. Ubayd ibn Umayr recited "la yufrituun" with the lightened form, meaning they do not exceed the limit in what they are commanded to do, whether honoring or humiliating.

(Then they are returned to Allah): that is, Allah returns them through resurrection for the reckoning.

(Their true Master): that is, their Creator, their Provider, their Resurrector, and their Owner. The reading "al-Haqq" with the genitive case (al-khafd) is the recitation of the majority, as a qualifier and attribute of the name of Allah, the Exalted. Al-Hasan recited "al-haqqa" with the accusative case, on the basis of an implied "a'nee" (I mean), or as a verbal noun, meaning "truly."

(Surely to Him belongs the judgment): that is, know and say: judgment belongs to Him alone on the Day of Resurrection, meaning the decision and the final determination.

(And He is the swiftest of reckoners): that is, He does not need thought, deliberation, or counting on fingers. This has been mentioned before. (See vol. 2, p. 435.)

**Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 6, verses 61–62:**

Allah's words: ﴿And He is the Subjugator over His servants﴾. He means the "above-ness" of rank and standing, not the "above-ness" of place and direction, as was explained earlier at the beginning of the surah. (See vol. 1, p. 1.)

(And He sends over you guardians): that is, from among the angels. "Sending" (al-irsal) in its literal sense means releasing a thing with the message it has been given. So the sending of the angels is with what they carry of the duty of guarding that they were commanded to perform, as He said: ﴿But indeed, over you are guardians﴾. That is, angels who guard the deeds of the servants and guard them from calamities. "Al-hafazah" (the guardians) is the plural of "hafiz" (guardian), like "al-kataba" (the scribes) and "al-katib" (the scribe). It is said that there are two angels by night and two angels by day: one of them records the good and the other the evil. When a person walks, one of them is before him and the other behind him; when he sits, one of them is on his right and the other on his left, based on His saying: ﴿on the right and on the left, seated﴾ (verse). (See vol. 17, p. 8.) It is also said that every person has five angels: two by night, two by day, and the fifth never leaves him, night or day. And Allah knows best.

Umar ibn al-Khattab (may Allah be pleased with him) said:

*Among people is one who lives wretched,*
*foolish of heart, heedless of wakefulness.*

*But if he is faithful and of sound judgment,*
*wary of death, he guards against the guardians.*

*Indeed, people are travelers and residents,*
*and whoever has departed has a lesson for the one who remains.*

Allah's words: ﴿until, when death comes to one of you﴾. He means its causes, as was explained earlier in Surat al-Baqarah. (See vol. 2, p. 137.)

(Our messengers take him in death): in the feminine form for the plural group, as He said: ﴿Our messengers had certainly come to them with clear evidence﴾ and ﴿Messengers had been denied﴾. (See vol. 6, p. 416.) Hamzah recited "tawaffahu rusulunaa" with the masculine form for the plural. Al-A'mash recited "tatawaffahu rusulunaa" with an added taa' and the masculine form. The intended meaning is the assistants of the Angel of Death, as said by Ibn Abbas and others. It is related that they draw the soul out of the body, until, when it is near the moment of seizing it, the Angel of Death seizes it. Al-Kalbi said: the Angel of Death seizes the soul from the body, then hands it over to the angels of mercy if the person was a believer, or to the angels of punishment if he was a disbeliever. It is said that with him are seven angels of mercy and seven angels of punishment. When he seizes a believing soul, he hands it over to the angels of mercy, who give it the glad tidings of reward and ascend with it to the heaven. When he seizes a disbelieving soul, he hands it over to the angels of punishment, who give it the tidings of punishment and terrify it, then they ascend with it to the heaven, and then it is returned to Sijjin, while the spirit of the believer goes to Illiyyin.

The act of causing death ("tawaffi") is sometimes attributed to the Angel of Death, as He said: ﴿Say: The Angel of Death who has been put in charge of you will take you﴾. (See vol. 14, p. 92.) Sometimes it is attributed to the angels, because they carry out that task, as in this verse and others. And sometimes it is attributed to Allah, who is the true One who causes death, as He said: ﴿Allah takes the souls at the time of their death﴾ (see vol. 15, p. 260), ﴿Say: Allah gives you life, then causes you to die﴾ (see vol. 16, p. 172), and ﴿He who created death and life﴾ (see vol. 18, p. 206). So every angel who is commanded does only what he is commanded to do.

Allah's words: ﴿and they do not fail﴾. That is, they do not waste or fall short, meaning they obey the command of Allah. Its root is from "precedence," as was explained before. So the meaning of "farrata" is "he went ahead in weakness." Abu Ubaydah said: they do not delay. Ubayd ibn Umayr recited "la yufrituun" with the lightened form, meaning they do not exceed the limit in what they are commanded to do, whether honoring or humiliating.

(Then they are returned to Allah): that is, Allah returns them through resurrection for the reckoning.

(Their true Master): that is, their Creator, their Provider, their Resurrector, and their Owner. The reading "al-Haqq" with the genitive case (al-khafd) is the recitation of the majority, as a qualifier and attribute of the name of Allah, the Exalted. Al-Hasan recited "al-haqqa" with the accusative case, on the basis of an implied "a'nee" (I mean), or as a verbal noun, meaning "truly."

(Surely to Him belongs the judgment): that is, know and say: judgment belongs to Him alone on the Day of Resurrection, meaning the decision and the final determination.

(And He is the swiftest of reckoners): that is, He does not need thought, deliberation, or counting on fingers. This has been mentioned before. (See vol. 2, p. 435.)

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Say: "Who rescues you from the darknesses of the land and the sea?"﴾ That is, from their hardships. It is said: "a dark day" meaning a hard one. Al-Nahhas said: The Arabs say "a dark day" when it is hard, and if they wish to magnify it they say "a day with stars" (dhu kawakib). Sibawayh recited:

"O Banu Asad, do you know our trial,
when a day with stars becomes grim?"

The word "darknesses" is in the plural, referring to the darkness of the land, the darkness of the sea, the darkness of the night, and the darkness of clouds. That is, when you lose your way and fear destruction, you call upon Him: ﴿"If You rescue us from this"﴾ (Nafi' recites "anjaytana") ﴿"from these"﴾ hardships ﴿"we will surely be among the thankful."﴾ That is, among the obedient. So Allah rebukes them for calling upon Him in times of hardship, while in times of ease they call upon others besides Him along with Him, by His saying: ﴿"Then you associate others with Him."﴾

Al-A'mash recited "wa-khifatan" (from fear). Abu Bakr, from Asim, recited "khifyatan" with a kasra on the kha', and the rest recited it with a damma; both are dialects. Al-Farra' added "khufwatan" and "khifwatan," and said: its parallel is "hubyatun," "hibyatun," "hubwatun," and "hibwatun." But the reading of al-A'mash is far-fetched, because the meaning of "tadarru'an" is that you display humility, while "khufyatan" means that you conceal the same. The Kufans recited "li-in anjanaa" (with a nun), and the coherence of the meaning is with the ta', as the people of Medina and the people of Syria recited.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Say: "Allah rescues you from them and from every distress."﴾ The Kufans recited "yunajjikum" with tashdid (doubling), and the rest with takhfif (no doubling). It is said: their meanings are one, like najā, anjaytuhu and najjaytuhu. And it is said: the doubling is for intensification. Al-karb: grief that seizes the soul; from it one says "rajul makrub" (a grieved man). Antarah said:

"And a grieved man, whose distress You removed from him,
with a spear-thrust of Faysal when he called me."

And "al-kurbah" (a distress) is derived from this. His saying, exalted is He: ﴿"Then you associate others with Him."﴾ is a rebuke and reproach, like His saying at the beginning of the surah: ﴿"Then you doubt."﴾ Because when the proof is established after knowledge, sincerity becomes obligatory, and they have substituted for it association, so it is fitting that they be rebuked and reproached on this account, even though they were polytheists before the rescue.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 6, verse 65:

Ay, the One Who is able to deliver you from distress is able to punish you. The meaning of "from above you" (min fawqikum) is stoning, stones, the flood, the Blast (al-sayhah) and the wind, as He did to 'Ad, Thamud, the people of Shu'ayb, the people of Lut and the people of Nuh. This is related from Mujahid, Ibn Jubayr and others.

"Or from beneath your feet" refers to the sinking into the earth (al-khasf) and the quake (al-rajfah), as He did to Qarun and the companions of Madyan. It is also said: "from above you" means the oppressive rulers, and "or from beneath your feet" means the lowly and the evil slaves. This is related from Ibn 'Abbas and also Mujahid.

"Or to confuse you into sects" (aw yalbisakum shiya'an). It is related from Abu 'Abd Allah al-Madani that he read "aw yulbisakum" with a dammah on the yaa', meaning the punishment envelops you and covers you entirely. This is from the verb al-lubs with a dammah on the first letter, whereas the reading with a fathah is from al-labs. The phrase is difficult (mushkil), and the grammatical analysis (i'rab) clarifies it: that is, it confuses your affair for you (yalbisu 'alaykum amrakum), so one of the two objects and the preposition are omitted, as in His words: "And when they measure out to them or weigh for them" [see vol. 19, p. 250]. This confusion occurs by mixing their affair and making them differ in their desires. This is related from Ibn 'Abbas. It is also said: the meaning of "yalbisakum shiya'an" is that He strengthens your enemy until he mixes with you, and when he mixes with you, he has confused you. "Shiya'an" means factions. It is also said: He makes you into factions, so that some of you fight others, through the mixing of their affair and the division of their rulers over the pursuit of worldly gain. This is the meaning of His words: "and makes some of you taste the violence of others" (wa yudhiqa ba'dakum ba's ba'd), that is, through war and killing in strife. This is related from Mujahid. The verse is general concerning both Muslims and disbelievers. It is also said that it refers specifically to disbelievers. Al-Hasan said: it refers to the people of prayer (ahl al-salah). I say: this is the correct view, for it is what is witnessed in existence. The enemy has confused us in our homelands and seized control over our selves and our wealth, along with the strife that prevails over us, with some of us killing others and some of us plundering the wealth of others.

We seek refuge with Allah from the trials, both the apparent and the hidden. It is also related from al-Hasan that he interpreted this regarding what occurred among the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them. Muslim related from Thawban who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Indeed Allah gathered (zawa) the earth for me, so I saw its easts and its wests, and the dominion of my Ummah will reach what was gathered for me of it. I was given the two treasures, the red and the white. I asked my Lord for my Ummah that He not destroy them with a general famine, and that He not give power over them to an enemy from other than themselves, who would destroy their gathering (baydatahum). My Lord said: 'O Muhammad, when I decree a decree, it is not turned back. I have granted you for your Ummah that I will not destroy them with a general famine, and that I will not give power over them to an enemy from other than themselves, who would destroy their gathering [meaning their community, the seat of their authority and the place of their call], even if those from all its regions (aqtar) gathered against them, or he said: from among its regions, until some of them destroy others and some of them take others captive."

An-Nasa'i related from Khabbab ibn al-Aratt, who had witnessed Badr with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), that he kept watch over the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) the whole night until dawn. When the Messenger of Allah finished his prayer and gave the salam, Khabbab came to him and said: "O Messenger of Allah, may my father and mother be your ransom! You prayed tonight a prayer I have never seen you pray like?" The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Indeed, it was a prayer of hope and fear. I asked Allah, Mighty and Majestic, for three things in it, and He gave me two and withheld one. I asked my Lord, Mighty and Majestic, that He not destroy us with what He destroyed the nations with, and He gave it to me. I asked my Lord, Mighty and Majestic, that He not let an enemy from other than us prevail over us, and He gave it to me. I asked my Lord, Mighty and Majestic, that He not confuse us into sects (an yulbisana shiya'an), and He withheld it from me."

I have discussed these reports in the book (al-Tadhkirah), and praise be to Allah. It is also narrated that when this verse was revealed, the Prophet (ﷺ) said to Jibril: "O Jibril, what will be the fate of my Ummah in that case?" Jibril said to him: "I am only a servant like you, so call upon your Lord and ask Him for your Ummah." The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) stood, performed ablution and completed the ablution, prayed and prayed well, then supplicated. Jibril descended and said: "O Muhammad, indeed Allah, Exalted, has heard your statement and has protected them from two matters, which are the punishment from above them and from beneath their feet." He said: "O Jibril, what will be the fate of my Ummah if there are among them divergent desires and one makes the others taste the violence of one another?" Then Jibril descended with this verse: "Alif Lam Mim. Do people think they will be left to say, 'We believe'..." [see vol. 13, p. 323] to the end of the verse.

'Amr ibn Dinar related from Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah who said: When this verse was revealed, "Say: He is able to send upon you a punishment from above you or from beneath your feet," the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "I seek refuge in the Face of Allah." Then when "or to confuse you into sects and make some of you taste the violence of others" was revealed, he said: "These two are easier."

In the Sunan of Ibn Majah, from Ibn 'Umar, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) would not leave these words in the morning: "O Allah, I ask You for well-being in this world and the Hereafter. O Allah, I ask You for pardon and well-being in my religion, my worldly affairs, my family and my wealth. O Allah, conceal my faults, calm my fears, guard me from before me, from behind me, from my right, from my left, and from above me, and I seek refuge in You from being seized from beneath me." Waki' said: meaning the sinking into the earth (al-khasf).

[Allah's words:] "Look how We vary the signs" (unzur kayfa nusarrifu al-ayat), that is, We clarify for them the proofs and the indications.

"So that they may understand" (la'allahum yafqahun): He means the falsehood of what they are upon of shirk and sins.

**Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 6, verses 66–67:**

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿But your people denied it﴾, meaning the Qur'an. Ibn Abi Ablah read "وَكَذَّبَتْ" with a taa' (feminine ending).

(﴿And it is the truth﴾), meaning the true reports.

(﴿Say: I am not a guardian over you﴾). Al-Hasan said: "I am not a keeper of your deeds so that I would repay you for them. I am only a warner, and I have delivered the message." Its parallel is ﴿Nor am I a guardian over you﴾ [[See vol. 9, p. 86.]], meaning: I do not guard your deeds over you. Then it was said that this verse is abrogated (mansukh) by the verse of fighting. It was also said that it is not abrogated, since it was not within his power to make them believe.

(﴿For every news there is a fixed time﴾). For every report there is a reality, meaning that for everything there is a time at which it occurs, without advancing or delaying. It was also said: meaning, for every deed there is a recompense. Al-Hasan said: "This is a threat from God, may He be exalted, to the disbelievers, because they did not acknowledge the Resurrection." Al-Zajjaj said: "It is possible that it is a threat of what will befall them in this world."

(He said) [[From K.]] Al-Suddi said: "On the Day of Badr there became fixed what he had been promising them of punishment." Al-Tha'labi mentioned that he saw in some exegetical works that this verse is beneficial for toothache when it is written on paper and placed on the tooth.
