His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿When you see those who engage in vain talk about Our signs, turn away from them until they engage in a different talk. And if Satan causes you to forget, then do not sit, after the reminder, with the wrongdoing people﴾ (6:68).

On His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿When you see those who engage in vain talk about Our signs, turn away from them﴾, there are two issues.

The first: His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿When you see those who engage in vain talk about Our signs﴾, by denial, rejection and mockery, ﴿turn away from them﴾. The address is directed solely to the Prophet ﷺ. It has also been said that the believers are included in the address along with him, and this is sound, since the reason (ʿillah) is hearing vain talk about the signs of God, and that includes them as well as him. It has also been said that the intended meaning is the Prophet ﷺ alone, because his rising up from the polytheists was difficult for them, whereas the believers were not like that in their presence. So he was commanded to oppose them by rising from them when they mocked and engaged in vain talk, so that they would learn courtesy through this and abandon vain talk and mockery.

Khawd (vain talk, immersion) originally refers to wading into water. It was then used for the deep currents of things that are obscure, by analogy with the depths of water, so the sensory was borrowed for the intellectual. It has also been said that it derives from "mixing": whatever you wade into, you have mixed up, and from this comes "he waded into the water with honey," meaning he mixed it.

God, mighty and majestic, taught His Prophet ﷺ courtesy through this verse, because he used to sit with a group of polytheists, advising them and calling them (to God), and they would mock the Qur'an. So God commanded him to turn away from them with the turning away of one who disapproves. This indicates that when a man knows of another some wrong and knows that he will not accept from him, it is incumbent upon him to turn away from him with the turning away of one who disapproves, and not to engage with him.

Shibl reported from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, regarding His saying: "When you see those who engage in vain talk about Our signs," that he said: they are those who mock the Book of God. God forbade him to sit with them, except if he forgets; then when he remembers, he rises. Warqa' reported from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, who said: they are those who speak falsehood about the Qur'an.

The second: in this verse there is a refutation, from the Book of God, of those who claim that the imams, who are proofs (ḥujaj), and their followers, may mix with the sinful and approve their opinions out of taqiyyah [[Taqiyyah and tuqat have the same meaning. It means that they guard themselves against one another, showing reconciliation and agreement while their inner state is otherwise.]].

Al-Tabari mentioned from Abu Jaʿfar Muhammad ibn ʿAli (may God be pleased with him) that he said: "Do not sit with the people of disputes, for they are the ones who engage in vain talk about the signs of God." Ibn al-ʿArabi said: this is evidence that sitting with the people of major sins is not permissible. Ibn Khuwayz Mindad said: whoever engages in vain talk about the signs of God, his company is abandoned and he is shunned, whether he is a believer or an unbeliever. He said: likewise our companions (the Malikis) prohibited entering the land of the enemy, entering their churches and places of worship, sitting with unbelievers and people of innovation, holding their affection, listening to their speech, or debating them. Some people of innovation said to Abu ʿImran al-Nakhaʿi: "Listen to one word from me," and he turned away from him and said: "Not even half a word." Similarly was reported from Ayyub al-Sakhtiyani. Al-Fudayl ibn ʿIyad said: whoever loves a person of innovation, God nullifies his deeds and removes the light of Islam from his heart; whoever marries his noble daughter to an innovator has severed her kinship; whoever sits with a person of innovation is not given wisdom; and if God, mighty and majestic, knows of a man that he hates a person of innovation, I hope God will forgive him.

Abu ʿAbd Allah al-Hakim reported from ʿAʾishah, may God be pleased with her, who said: the Messenger of God ﷺ said: "Whoever honors a person of innovation has helped in the demolition of Islam." By all of this, the claim of whoever asserts that sitting with them is permissible if they protect their hearing is refuted.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And if Satan causes you to forget, then do not sit, after the reminder, with the wrongdoing people.﴾ On this there are two issues.

The first: His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And if Satan causes you to forget﴾. ("In" [if]) is a conditional particle, and it is usually followed by the heavy nun (nūn al-tawkīd al-thaqīlah), though it may sometimes not be, as in the verse:

*Im yuṣbika ʿaduwwun fī munāwa'atin / yawman faqad kunta tastaʿlī wa tantaṣir*

("If an enemy afflicts you in a contest one day, you were indeed prevailing and victorious.")

Ibn ʿAbbas and Ibn ʿAmir read *yunassiyannaka* with a doubled sīn for intensification. It is said that *nassā* and *ansā* have one meaning (two dialects). The poet said:

*Qālat Sulayma atasrī al-yawma am taqil / wa qad yunassīka baʿḍa al-ḥājati al-kasal*

("Sulayma said: Will you travel today, or will you stay? Laziness may make you forget some of your need.")

The shahid (evidence) is in *yunassīka* with the doubled sīn without the heavy nun, but without *in-mā*.

And Imru' al-Qays said:

*Tunsīnī idhā qumtu sirbālī* [[The full verse, as in Lisan al-ʿArab:

*Wa mithlaki bayḍāʾa al-ʿawāriḍi ṭifla / lāʿūbin tunsī idhā qumtu sirbālī*

The reading in Lisan is *tanāsānī* instead of *tunsīnī*.]]

The meaning: O Muhammad, if Satan makes you forget to rise from them, and you sit with them after the prohibition.

(*Then do not sit after the reminder*): that is, once you are reminded, do not sit ﴿with the wrongdoing people﴾, meaning the polytheists. *Dhikrā* (reminder) is a noun for remembering.

The second: it has been said that this is an address to the Prophet ﷺ, but what is meant is his community. They went to exonerate him, peace be upon him, from forgetting. It has also been said that it is specific to him, and that forgetting is permissible for him. Ibn al-ʿArabi said: even if our companions excuse the statement (of those who say) regarding His saying: "If you associate partners (with God), your deeds will surely be nullified" (39:65) [[See vol. 15, p. 276.]] that it is an address to the community in the name of the Prophet ﷺ, because shirk is impossible for him, there is no excuse for them in this, since forgetting is permissible for him.

He, peace be upon him, said: "Adam forgot, so his descendants forgot." Al-Tirmidhi transmitted it and graded it sound. He also said, informing about himself: "I am only a human like you; I forget as you forget, so when I forget, remind me." He transmitted it in the Sahih, and so he attributed forgetting to himself. He also said, when he heard a man's recitation: "He has indeed reminded me of such-and-such a verse, which I had forgotten."

Scholars differed, once forgetting was permissible for him, on whether it could occur in matters whose path is conveying (the message) of actions and rulings of the Shariah, or not. Al-Qadi ʿIyad reported that the majority of scholars and the leading theoreticians held the former view, as is the apparent meaning of the Qur'an and the hadiths. However, the imams stipulated that God alerts him to this and does not let him persist in it. Then they differed as to whether the alert must come immediately upon the incident (ʿala al-fawr), which is the position of al-Qadi Abu Bakr and most scholars, or whether delay is permissible so long as his life does not wane and his conveying is not cut off; Abu al-Maʿali inclined to this. A group of scholars denied forgetfulness for him in conveying actions and legal acts of worship, just as they unanimously denied it in conveying statements; they explained away the apparent texts that reported this. Abu Ishaq (al-Isfara'ini) inclined to this position. The Batiniyya and a group of the masters of the science of hearts (ahl ʿilm al-qulub) were eccentric and said: forgetting is not permissible for him, and he only feigns forgetfulness deliberately, so that he may establish a sunnah. A great imam of verification, Abu al-Muzaffar al-Isfara'ini, inclined to this in his book *al-Awsat*, but this is an unsound direction, and bringing together two opposites is a remote impossibility.

Ibn ʿAbbas said: When the verse "Do not sit with the polytheists" came down, and this is what is meant by His words, "So turn away from them," the Muslims said: "We cannot enter the mosque and perform the ṭawāf." Then this verse was revealed: "But a reminder" — meaning, if they (the believers) sit with them, then let them remind them.

﴿That perhaps they may fear God﴾ in abandoning what they are engaged in. Then it was said: this was abrogated (naskh) by His words: "And He has already sent down to you in the Book that when you hear the verses of God being disbelieved in and mocked, do not sit with them until they engage in a conversation other than that" [[see vol. 5, p. 417.]]. The concession was only before the conquest (al-fatḥ), and the time was a time of taqiyya (dissimulation under threat). By His words, "And He has already sent down to you in the Book," He alluded to His words: "And leave those who have taken their religion as amusement and diversion." Al-Qushayrī said: The more evident view is that the verse is not abrogated. The meaning is: "You bear no responsibility for the reckoning of the polytheists; your duty is to remind and deter them, and if they refuse, their reckoning is with God." The word "al-dhikrā" is in the accusative position as a verbal noun (maṣdar), and it may also be in the nominative position, meaning: "But what they do is a reminder," i.e., "But upon them is a reminder." Al-Kisāʾī said: the meaning is "But this is a reminder."

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 6, verse 70:

That is, do not set your heart upon them, for they are a people of obstinacy, if you are commanded to admonish them. Qatadah said: this is abrogated; it was abrogated by "Then kill the polytheists wherever you find them" [[See vol. 8, p. 71.]]. The meaning of "play and amusement" (la'iban wa lahwan) is mockery of the religion to which you called them. It was also said: they mocked the religion they were upon, and did not act by it. Mockery is not permitted in any religion. It was also said: "la'iban wa lahwan" means vanity and frivolity, and this has already been mentioned [[See vol. 6, p. 413 and following.]]. The word la'ib (play) has come first in four places in the Qur'an, and I have versified this.

When one asks about play and amusement... and how many a place there is in the Qur'an

There is one instance in al-Hadid and in al-Qital, and in al-An'am there are two instances.

It was also said: the intended meaning of "religion" here is the festival. Al-Kalbi said: God Most High appointed for every people a festival which they venerate and in which they pray to God Most High, and every people made their festival into play and amusement, except the community of Muhammad (ﷺ), for they made it a prayer, a remembrance, and an attendance with almsgiving, like Friday, the Fitr, and the Nahr.

The words of the Most High: ﴿And the life of this world has deceived them﴾, meaning: they knew only the outward appearance of the life of this world.

The words of the Most High: ﴿And remind [them] with it﴾, meaning: with the Qur'an, or with the reckoning.

(Lest a soul be given over to ruin for what it has earned): meaning, it is held in pledge and delivered to destruction, according to Mujahid, Qatadah, al-Hasan, Ikrimah and al-Suddi. The root "ibsal" (giving over to ruin) means delivering a person to destruction; this is the well-known usage in the language. "Absaltu waladi" means I pledged my son as a hostage. Awf ibn al-Ahwas ibn Ja'far said:

And my giving up my sons without a crime... without a bloodshed being spilled [or:] "ba'awnahu" (with the letter ʿayn unpointed, meaning "we absolved him" in the sense of forgiven)... 

"Ba'awnahu" with the unpointed ʿayn means "janaynahu" (I committed an offence on his behalf), and al-ba'w means offence. He had taken on the blood-debt of the two sons of al-Sujayfa on behalf of a wealthy man of Banu Qushayr, and they said: "We will not accept you," so he pledged his sons to them, seeking reconciliation. And al-Nabigha (al-Ja'di) recited:

And we pledged 'Amir at al-Ifaqah, [a place in the land of al-Hazn near Kufa, or a water of Banu Yarbu', and the day of al-Ifaqah is one of the days of the Arabs] for what was in al-Dardaʾ as a pledge, so he was given up.

Al-Dardaʾ: a battalion that belonged to them.

(﴿Besides Allah he will have no protector or intercessor﴾) [see vol. 3, p. 283, p. 273 and vol. 4, p. 109]. (Its meaning has already been explained.) The words of the Most High: ﴿And if he offers every ransom, it will not be accepted from him﴾ — the verse. "Al-ʿadl" is ransom, and this was mentioned in al-Baqarah [see vol. 1, p. 378 and p. 380]. "Al-hamim" is boiling water, and in the revelation: "Boiling water will be poured over their heads" [see vol. 12, p. 25] "etc." "They will go around between it and boiling water, intensely hot" [see vol. 17, p. 175]. The verse is abrogated by the verse of fighting. It was also said: it is not abrogated, because His words "And leave those who have taken their religion as play and amusement" are a threat, like the saying "Leave them to eat and enjoy themselves" [see vol. 10, p. 2]. Its meaning is: do not grieve over them; your duty is only to convey and to remind of the giving over of souls to ruin. Whoever is given over has been delivered and held in pledge. It was also said: its origin is prohibition, from their saying: "This is forbidden (basl) to you," meaning haram, so it is as if they forbade Paradise and Paradise was forbidden to them. The poet said [al-A'sha Maymun]:

Your neighbour is forbidden (basl) to us, prohibited, and our neighbour is lawful to you, and her husband too.

And al-ibsal means prohibition. And al-ibsal means prohibition.

**Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on Surah 6, verses 71–73:**

Allah's words: ﴿Say: "Shall we call upon, besides Allah, that which can neither benefit us"﴾, meaning: that which cannot benefit us if we call upon it [[In manuscript K: "if we hope in it."]].

﴿nor harm us﴾ if we abandon it. He means the idols.

﴿and be turned back on our heels after Allah has guided us﴾, meaning: return to misguidance after guidance. The singular of *a'qab* (heels) is *aqib*, which is feminine, and its diminutive is *uqaybah*. It is said: "So-and-so returned on his heels (*'aqibayh*)" when he turned back. Abu 'Ubaydah said: It is said of one who is turned back from his need without attaining it: "He was turned back on his heels." Al-Mubarrad said: its meaning is that he is given evil after good. Its root is from *al-'aqibah* and *al-'uqba*, which are that which follows something and must come after it. From this comes "And the good end is for the God-fearing" [[This will come on p. 263 of this volume.]]. From it also comes *'aqib al-rajul* (a man's descendants). From it also comes *'uqubah* (punishment), because it follows the sin and results from it.

Allah's words: ﴿like one﴾. The *kaf* (like) is in the accusative position as an attribute of an omitted verbal noun (*masdar*).

﴿whom the devils have enticed in the earth, bewildered﴾, meaning: they lured him away, made his desire seem attractive to him, and called him to it. It is said: *hawa yahwi ila al-shay'* means he hastened toward the thing. Al-Zajjaj said: it is from *hawa yahwa*, from the "desire of the soul" (*hawa al-nafs*), meaning the devil made his desire seem attractive to him. The reading of the majority is *istahwathu* (has enticed him), meaning they carried him away, using the feminine form for the plural noun. Hamzah read *istahwahu al-shayatinu* (the devils have enticed him), using the masculine form for the plural noun. It is reported from Ibn Mas'ud: *istahwahu al-shaytanu* (the devil has enticed him). It is also reported from al-Hasan, and it is the same in the reading of Ubayy. The meaning of *i'tina* (come to us) is "follow us." In the reading of 'Abdullah also: *yad'unahu ila al-huda bayyinan* (they call him to guidance, clearly). Al-Hasan also reported: *istahwathu al-shayatin*. *Hayran* (bewildered) is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (*hal*), and it is not declined because its feminine form is *hayra*, like *sakran* and *sakra*, and *ghadban* and *ghadba*. *Al-hayran* is one who does not find the right direction in his affair. It is said: *hara yahiru harran wa hayrurah* [[We have not found this noun in the lexicon books. In Tafsir al-Razi: "…al-Farra' added *hayranan* and *hayrunah*."]], meaning he wandered in confusion. From this, stagnant water with no outlet is called *ha'ir*, and its plural is *huran*. *Al-ha'ir* is the place (in which) the water becomes confused [[From K.]]. The poet said:

*She treads on two papyrus plants, nourished by a flood*
*in the courtyard of a pool, a deep and rushing pool.* [[Al-'Ayyub: al-Tawil (meter).]]

Ibn 'Abbas said: meaning, the likeness of the idol-worshipper is like that of one whom the ghoul (*ghul*) calls, so he follows it, and in the morning it has thrown him into a place of straying and destruction, so he is bewildered in those wastelands. In the narration of Abu Salih, he said: it was revealed concerning 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Bakr al-Siddiq, who used to call his father to disbelief while his parents called him to Islam and the Muslims. This is the meaning of His words: ﴿who has companions calling him to guidance﴾, but he refuses. Abu 'Umar said: his mother was Umm Rumman bint al-Harith ibn Ghanm al-Kinaniyyah, so he was a full brother of 'A'ishah. 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Bakr witnessed Badr with his people while still a polytheist, and he challenged to single combat, so his father came forward to fight him. It is mentioned that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said to him: "Let me enjoy you with yourself." Then he embraced Islam, his Islam was good, and he accompanied the Prophet ﷺ during the truce of al-Hudaybiyah. This is the statement of the scholars of biography. They said: his name was 'Abd al-Ka'bah, and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ changed his name to 'Abd al-Rahman. He was the eldest son of Abu Bakr. It is said: four generations (*wila'*) did not meet the Prophet ﷺ: a father and his sons, namely Abu Quhafah and his son Abu Bakr and his son 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Bakr and his son Abu 'Atiq Muhammad ibn 'Abd al-Rahman. And Allah knows best.

Allah's words: ﴿And we have been commanded: "That we submit to the Lord of the worlds," and "that you establish the prayer and fear Him."﴾ The *lam* is the *lam* of purpose (*kay*), meaning: we have been commanded in order that we submit, and [we have been commanded] with "that you establish the prayer," because prepositions may be coordinated with one another. Al-Farra' said: the meaning is "we have been commanded to submit," because the Arabs say: "I ordered you to go" (*li-tadhhab*), and "to go" (*bi-an tadhhaba*) with the same meaning. Al-Nahhas said: I heard Abu al-Hasan ibn Kaysan say: it is the *lam* of genitive (*khafd*). The *lam*s are all three: the *lam* of genitive, the *lam* of command, and the *lam* of emphasis, and nothing falls outside them. Islam here means sincerity (*ikhlas*). Establishing the prayer means performing it and being constant in it. It is also possible that "and that you establish the prayer" is coordinated with the meaning, meaning: they call him to guidance and they call him that you establish the prayer, because the meaning of *i'tina* (come to us) is *an i'tina* (that you come to us).

Allah's words: ﴿And He is the One to whom you will be gathered﴾. This is a subject and predicate, and likewise: ﴿He is the One who created the heavens and the earth﴾, meaning: He is the One who must be worshipped, not the idols. The meaning of *bi-al-haqq* (with truth) is with the word of truth, meaning His saying "Be!"

Allah's words: ﴿And on the Day He says "Be," and it is﴾. Meaning: remember the Day He says "Be." Or: fear the Day He says "Be." Or: consider the Day He says "Be." Or: consider the Day He says "Be." It has been said: it is coordinated with the pronoun in His saying "and fear Him." Al-Farra' said: "Be, and it is" is said to be specifically for the Trumpet (*al-sur*), meaning: and on the Day He says to the Trumpet "Be," and it is. It has been said: the meaning is that all He wills of the death and life of people will come to be. According to these two interpretations, His saying "His word is the truth" is a subject and predicate. It has also been said: the saying of Allah "His word" is in the nominative as the subject of *yakun* (it is), meaning what He commands is; "the truth" is its attribute, and the complete sentence on this view is "and it is, His word is the truth." Ibn 'Amir read *fayakuna* (and it is) with the accusative [[In K. In Ibn Khalawayh's Shadhdh: *fayakuna* with the accusative, al-Hasan. In the other principal copies: *fa-nakunu* with *nun*, which is an error.]], and it points to the swiftness of the reckoning and the resurrection. This matter was discussed fully earlier in al-Baqarah [[See vol. 2, p. 89.]].

Allah's words: ﴿On the Day the Trumpet is blown﴾, meaning: and His is the dominion on the Day the Trumpet is blown. Or: His is the truth on the Day the Trumpet is blown. It has been said: it is a substitute for "the Day He says." The *sur* is a horn of light that is blown into. The first blast is for annihilation, and the second for re-creation. It is not the plural of *sura* (form), as some have claimed, meaning it is not blown into the forms of the dead, as we will explain. Muslim transmitted from the hadith of 'Abdullah ibn 'Amr: "…Then the Trumpet is blown, and no one hears it except that he inclines his neck to one side and raises the other [[*Asgha*: he inclined. *Layt* (with a *kasra* on the *lam*): the side of the neck.]]." He said: "The first to hear it will be a man repairing the watering trough of his camels [[That is, plastering and mending it.]]." He said: "The people will be struck senseless. Then Allah will send down—or he said: will cause to descend—rain like a drizzle, and bodies of people will grow from it. Then it will be blown into a second time, and behold, they will stand looking." And he mentioned the hadith. Likewise in the revelation: ﴿Then it was blown into again﴾ [[See vol. 15, p. 177.]], and He did not say "in it" (*fihã*), so it is known that it is not the plural of *sura*. The Ummah is agreed that the one who blows into the Trumpet is Israfil, peace be upon him. Abu al-Haytham said: whoever denies that the *sur* is a horn is like one who denies the Throne, the Balance, and the Bridge, and seeks interpretations for them. Ibn Faris said: the *sur* mentioned in the hadith is like a horn blown into, and *suwar* is the plural of *sura*. Al-Jawhari said: the *sur* is a horn. The poet, a rajiz, said:

*We struck them on the morning of the two hosts,*
*a strong strike, not like the striking of two horns.*

From it is the saying: ﴿On the Day the Trumpet is blown﴾ [[See vol. 13, p. 239.]]. Al-Kalbi said: I do not know what the *sur* is. It is said: it is the plural of *sura*, like *busrah* and *busr*, meaning it is blown into the forms of the dead and the spirits. Al-Hasan read: "On the Day it is blown into the *sur*." The *sawar* (with a *kasra* on the *sad*) is a dialect form of *suwar*, the plural of *sura*. The plural is *siwar*, and *siyar* (with *ya*) is a dialect form of it. 'Amr ibn 'Ubayd said: 'Iyad read "On the Day it is blown into the *sur*," and by this he means the creation. And Allah knows best.

I say: among those who said that the meaning of *sur* in this verse is the plural of *sura* is Abu 'Ubaydah. This, although possible, is rejected by what we have mentioned from the Book and the Sunnah. Also, the Trumpet is not blown twice for the Resurrection; rather it is blown once. Israfil, peace be upon him, blows into the *sur*, which is the horn, and Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, gives life to the forms.

﴿And in the revelation: "So We breathed into it of Our spirit"﴾ [[From J, K and 'A. See vol. 18, p. 302.]].

Allah's words: ﴿Knower of the unseen and the witnessed﴾. With the nominative *'alimu* as an attribute of *alladhi* (He who), meaning: and He is the One who created the heavens and the earth, the Knower of the unseen. It is also possible that it is nominative by supposing a subject. It has been reported from some of them that they read *yanfukhu* (He blows), so the agent may be "Knower of the unseen," because when the blowing into it is by the command of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, it is attributed to Allah, exalted is He. It is also possible that *'alimu* is nominative by taking account of the meaning, as Sibawayh cited:

*"Here I am, [Your] response to the one who pleads for the adversary"* [[This is the first half of a line by al-Harith ibn Nuhayk, whose complete line in Sibawayh's book is: "and one who seeks what the calamities destroy." He described him as one who upheld the proof of the wronged and supported him. *Al-mukhtabit*: the one who seeks what is known. *Tatih*: goes away and perishes.]]

And al-Hasan and al-A'mash read *'alimi* (with the genitive) as an apposition to the pronoun (*ha*) in "to Him" (*lahu*) [[From J and K.]].

Then Allah will send down—or he said: will cause to descend—rain like a drizzle, and bodies of people will grow from it. Then it will be blown into a second time, and behold, they will stand looking." And he mentioned the hadith. Likewise in the revelation: ﴿Then it was blown into again﴾ [[See vol. 15, p. 177.]], and He did not say "in it" (*fihã*), so it is known that it is not the plural of *sura*. The Ummah is agreed that the one who blows into the Trumpet is Israfil, peace be upon him. Abu al-Haytham said: whoever denies that the *sur* is a horn is like one who denies the Throne, the Balance, and the Bridge, and seeks interpretations for them. Ibn Faris said: the *sur* mentioned in the hadith is like a horn blown into, and *suwar* is the plural of *sura*. Al-Jawhari said: the *sur* is a horn. The poet, a rajiz, said:

*We struck them on the morning of the two hosts,*
*a strong strike, not like the striking of two horns.*

From it is the saying: ﴿On the Day the Trumpet is blown﴾ [[See vol. 13, p. 239.]]. Al-Kalbi said: I do not know what the *sur* is. It is said: it is the plural of *sura*, like *busrah* and *busr*, meaning it is blown into the forms of the dead and the spirits. Al-Hasan read: "On the Day it is blown into the *sur*." The *sawar* (with a *kasra* on the *sad*) is a dialect form of *suwar*, the plural of *sura*. The plural is *siwar*, and *siyar* (with *ya*) is a dialect form of it. 'Amr ibn 'Ubayd said: 'Iyad read "On the Day it is blown into the *sur*," and by this he means the creation. And Allah knows best.

I say: among those who said that the meaning of *sur* in this verse is the plural of *sura* is Abu 'Ubaydah. This, although possible, is rejected by what we have mentioned from the Book and the Sunnah. Also, the Trumpet is not blown twice for the Resurrection; rather it is blown once. Israfil, peace be upon him, blows into the *sur*, which is the horn, and Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, gives life to the forms.

﴿And in the revelation: "So We breathed into it of Our spirit"﴾ [[From J, K and 'A. See vol. 18, p. 302.]].

Allah's words: ﴿Knower of the unseen and the witnessed﴾. With the nominative *'alimu* as an attribute of *alladhi* (He who), meaning: and He is the One who created the heavens and the earth, the Knower of the unseen. It is also possible that it is nominative by supposing a subject. It has been reported from some of them that they read *yanfukhu* (He blows), so the agent may be "Knower of the unseen," because when the blowing into it is by the command of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, it is attributed to Allah, exalted is He. It is also possible that *'alimu* is nominative by taking account of the meaning, as Sibawayh cited:

*"Here I am, [Your] response to the one who pleads for the adversary"* [[This is the first half of a line by al-Harith ibn Nuhayk, whose complete line in Sibawayh's book is: "and one who seeks what the calamities destroy." He described him as one who upheld the proof of the wronged and supported him. *Al-mukhtabit*: the one who seeks what is known. *Tatih*: goes away and perishes.]]

And al-Hasan and al-A'mash read *'alimi* (with the genitive) as an apposition to the pronoun (*ha*) in "to Him" (*lahu*) [[From J and K.]].

**Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on Surah 6, verses 71–73:**

Allah's words: ﴿Say: "Shall we call upon, besides Allah, that which can neither benefit us"﴾, meaning: that which cannot benefit us if we call upon it [[In manuscript K: "if we hope in it."]].

﴿nor harm us﴾ if we abandon it. He means the idols.

﴿and be turned back on our heels after Allah has guided us﴾, meaning: return to misguidance after guidance. The singular of *a'qab* (heels) is *aqib*, which is feminine, and its diminutive is *uqaybah*. It is said: "So-and-so returned on his heels (*'aqibayh*)" when he turned back. Abu 'Ubaydah said: It is said of one who is turned back from his need without attaining it: "He was turned back on his heels." Al-Mubarrad said: its meaning is that he is given evil after good. Its root is from *al-'aqibah* and *al-'uqba*, which are that which follows something and must come after it. From this comes "And the good end is for the God-fearing" [[This will come on p. 263 of this volume.]]. From it also comes *'aqib al-rajul* (a man's descendants). From it also comes *'uqubah* (punishment), because it follows the sin and results from it.

Allah's words: ﴿like one﴾. The *kaf* (like) is in the accusative position as an attribute of an omitted verbal noun (*masdar*).

﴿whom the devils have enticed in the earth, bewildered﴾, meaning: they lured him away, made his desire seem attractive to him, and called him to it. It is said: *hawa yahwi ila al-shay'* means he hastened toward the thing. Al-Zajjaj said: it is from *hawa yahwa*, from the "desire of the soul" (*hawa al-nafs*), meaning the devil made his desire seem attractive to him. The reading of the majority is *istahwathu* (has enticed him), meaning they carried him away, using the feminine form for the plural noun. Hamzah read *istahwahu al-shayatinu* (the devils have enticed him), using the masculine form for the plural noun. It is reported from Ibn Mas'ud: *istahwahu al-shaytanu* (the devil has enticed him). It is also reported from al-Hasan, and it is the same in the reading of Ubayy. The meaning of *i'tina* (come to us) is "follow us." In the reading of 'Abdullah also: *yad'unahu ila al-huda bayyinan* (they call him to guidance, clearly). Al-Hasan also reported: *istahwathu al-shayatin*. *Hayran* (bewildered) is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (*hal*), and it is not declined because its feminine form is *hayra*, like *sakran* and *sakra*, and *ghadban* and *ghadba*. *Al-hayran* is one who does not find the right direction in his affair. It is said: *hara yahiru harran wa hayrurah* [[We have not found this noun in the lexicon books. In Tafsir al-Razi: "…al-Farra' added *hayranan* and *hayrunah*."]], meaning he wandered in confusion. From this, stagnant water with no outlet is called *ha'ir*, and its plural is *huran*. *Al-ha'ir* is the place (in which) the water becomes confused [[From K.]]. The poet said:

*She treads on two papyrus plants, nourished by a flood*
*in the courtyard of a pool, a deep and rushing pool.* [[Al-'Ayyub: al-Tawil (meter).]]

Ibn 'Abbas said: meaning, the likeness of the idol-worshipper is like that of one whom the ghoul (*ghul*) calls, so he follows it, and in the morning it has thrown him into a place of straying and destruction, so he is bewildered in those wastelands. In the narration of Abu Salih, he said: it was revealed concerning 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Bakr al-Siddiq, who used to call his father to disbelief while his parents called him to Islam and the Muslims. This is the meaning of His words: ﴿who has companions calling him to guidance﴾, but he refuses. Abu 'Umar said: his mother was Umm Rumman bint al-Harith ibn Ghanm al-Kinaniyyah, so he was a full brother of 'A'ishah. 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Bakr witnessed Badr with his people while still a polytheist, and he challenged to single combat, so his father came forward to fight him. It is mentioned that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said to him: "Let me enjoy you with yourself." Then he embraced Islam, his Islam was good, and he accompanied the Prophet ﷺ during the truce of al-Hudaybiyah. This is the statement of the scholars of biography. They said: his name was 'Abd al-Ka'bah, and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ changed his name to 'Abd al-Rahman. He was the eldest son of Abu Bakr. It is said: four generations (*wila'*) did not meet the Prophet ﷺ: a father and his sons, namely Abu Quhafah and his son Abu Bakr and his son 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Bakr and his son Abu 'Atiq Muhammad ibn 'Abd al-Rahman. And Allah knows best.

Allah's words: ﴿And we have been commanded: "That we submit to the Lord of the worlds," and "that you establish the prayer and fear Him."﴾ The *lam* is the *lam* of purpose (*kay*), meaning: we have been commanded in order that we submit, and [we have been commanded] with "that you establish the prayer," because prepositions may be coordinated with one another. Al-Farra' said: the meaning is "we have been commanded to submit," because the Arabs say: "I ordered you to go" (*li-tadhhab*), and "to go" (*bi-an tadhhaba*) with the same meaning. Al-Nahhas said: I heard Abu al-Hasan ibn Kaysan say: it is the *lam* of genitive (*khafd*). The *lam*s are all three: the *lam* of genitive, the *lam* of command, and the *lam* of emphasis, and nothing falls outside them. Islam here means sincerity (*ikhlas*). Establishing the prayer means performing it and being constant in it. It is also possible that "and that you establish the prayer" is coordinated with the meaning, meaning: they call him to guidance and they call him that you establish the prayer, because the meaning of *i'tina* (come to us) is *an i'tina* (that you come to us).

Allah's words: ﴿And He is the One to whom you will be gathered﴾. This is a subject and predicate, and likewise: ﴿He is the One who created the heavens and the earth﴾, meaning: He is the One who must be worshipped, not the idols. The meaning of *bi-al-haqq* (with truth) is with the word of truth, meaning His saying "Be!"

Allah's words: ﴿And on the Day He says "Be," and it is﴾. Meaning: remember the Day He says "Be." Or: fear the Day He says "Be." Or: consider the Day He says "Be." Or: consider the Day He says "Be." It has been said: it is coordinated with the pronoun in His saying "and fear Him." Al-Farra' said: "Be, and it is" is said to be specifically for the Trumpet (*al-sur*), meaning: and on the Day He says to the Trumpet "Be," and it is. It has been said: the meaning is that all He wills of the death and life of people will come to be. According to these two interpretations, His saying "His word is the truth" is a subject and predicate. It has also been said: the saying of Allah "His word" is in the nominative as the subject of *yakun* (it is), meaning what He commands is; "the truth" is its attribute, and the complete sentence on this view is "and it is, His word is the truth." Ibn 'Amir read *fayakuna* (and it is) with the accusative [[In K. In Ibn Khalawayh's Shadhdh: *fayakuna* with the accusative, al-Hasan. In the other principal copies: *fa-nakunu* with *nun*, which is an error.]], and it points to the swiftness of the reckoning and the resurrection. This matter was discussed fully earlier in al-Baqarah [[See vol. 2, p. 89.]].

Allah's words: ﴿On the Day the Trumpet is blown﴾, meaning: and His is the dominion on the Day the Trumpet is blown. Or: His is the truth on the Day the Trumpet is blown. It has been said: it is a substitute for "the Day He says." The *sur* is a horn of light that is blown into. The first blast is for annihilation, and the second for re-creation. It is not the plural of *sura* (form), as some have claimed, meaning it is not blown into the forms of the dead, as we will explain. Muslim transmitted from the hadith of 'Abdullah ibn 'Amr: "…Then the Trumpet is blown, and no one hears it except that he inclines his neck to one side and raises the other [[*Asgha*: he inclined. *Layt* (with a *kasra* on the *lam*): the side of the neck.]]." He said: "The first to hear it will be a man repairing the watering trough of his camels [[That is, plastering and mending it.]]." He said: "The people will be struck senseless. Then Allah will send down—or he said: will cause to descend—rain like a drizzle, and bodies of people will grow from it. Then it will be blown into a second time, and behold, they will stand looking." And he mentioned the hadith. Likewise in the revelation: ﴿Then it was blown into again﴾ [[See vol. 15, p. 177.]], and He did not say "in it" (*fihã*), so it is known that it is not the plural of *sura*. The Ummah is agreed that the one who blows into the Trumpet is Israfil, peace be upon him. Abu al-Haytham said: whoever denies that the *sur* is a horn is like one who denies the Throne, the Balance, and the Bridge, and seeks interpretations for them. Ibn Faris said: the *sur* mentioned in the hadith is like a horn blown into, and *suwar* is the plural of *sura*. Al-Jawhari said: the *sur* is a horn. The poet, a rajiz, said:

*We struck them on the morning of the two hosts,*
*a strong strike, not like the striking of two horns.*

From it is the saying: ﴿On the Day the Trumpet is blown﴾ [[See vol. 13, p. 239.]]. Al-Kalbi said: I do not know what the *sur* is. It is said: it is the plural of *sura*, like *busrah* and *busr*, meaning it is blown into the forms of the dead and the spirits. Al-Hasan read: "On the Day it is blown into the *sur*." The *sawar* (with a *kasra* on the *sad*) is a dialect form of *suwar*, the plural of *sura*. The plural is *siwar*, and *siyar* (with *ya*) is a dialect form of it. 'Amr ibn 'Ubayd said: 'Iyad read "On the Day it is blown into the *sur*," and by this he means the creation. And Allah knows best.

I say: among those who said that the meaning of *sur* in this verse is the plural of *sura* is Abu 'Ubaydah. This, although possible, is rejected by what we have mentioned from the Book and the Sunnah. Also, the Trumpet is not blown twice for the Resurrection; rather it is blown once. Israfil, peace be upon him, blows into the *sur*, which is the horn, and Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, gives life to the forms.

﴿And in the revelation: "So We breathed into it of Our spirit"﴾ [[From J, K and 'A. See vol. 18, p. 302.]].

Allah's words: ﴿Knower of the unseen and the witnessed﴾. With the nominative *'alimu* as an attribute of *alladhi* (He who), meaning: and He is the One who created the heavens and the earth, the Knower of the unseen. It is also possible that it is nominative by supposing a subject. It has been reported from some of them that they read *yanfukhu* (He blows), so the agent may be "Knower of the unseen," because when the blowing into it is by the command of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, it is attributed to Allah, exalted is He. It is also possible that *'alimu* is nominative by taking account of the meaning, as Sibawayh cited:

*"Here I am, [Your] response to the one who pleads for the adversary"* [[This is the first half of a line by al-Harith ibn Nuhayk, whose complete line in Sibawayh's book is: "and one who seeks what the calamities destroy." He described him as one who upheld the proof of the wronged and supported him. *Al-mukhtabit*: the one who seeks what is known. *Tatih*: goes away and perishes.]]

And al-Hasan and al-A'mash read *'alimi* (with the genitive) as an apposition to the pronoun (*ha*) in "to Him" (*lahu*) [[From J and K.]].

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 6, verse 74:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And when Abraham said to his father Azar﴾. The scholars have discussed this. Abu Bakr Muhammad ibn Muhammad ibn al-Hasan al-Juwayni al-Shafi'i al-Ash'ari said in his book al-Nukat min al-Tafsir: "There is no disagreement among people that the name of Abraham's father was Tarah" [in some manuscripts with the letter jim (with a dot), and in others with the letter ha' (without a dot); and in Jumal it is vocalized by some with the unpointed ha' and by others with the pointed kha'.] "But what is in the Qur'an indicates that his name was Azar." It is also said: Azar, in their language, is a term of blame, as if he said: "And when he said to his father, O erring one, 'Do you take idols as gods?'" And if that is the case, the preferred reading is the nominative (raf'). It is also said: Azar is the name of an idol. In that case its position is accusative (nasb), by way of an implied verb, as if he said: "And when Abraham said to his father, 'Do you take Azar as a god?' 'Do you take idols as gods?'"

I say: What he claimed as consensus is not agreed upon, for Muhammad ibn Ishaq, al-Kalbi and al-Dahhak said: Azar was the father of Abraham, peace be upon him, and Tarikh (Tarikh) is [his other name], like Israel and Jacob, so he had two names, as mentioned earlier. Muqatil said: Azar is a title (laqab), and Tarikh is the name; this was related by al-Tha'labi from Ibn Ishaq al-Qushayri. It may also be the reverse. Al-Hasan said: The name of his father was Azar. Sulayman al-Taymi said: It is an insult and a defect, and its meaning in their speech is "the crooked one." Al-Mu'tamir ibn Sulayman related from his father, who said: "It reached me that it means 'the crooked one,' and it is the harshest word Abraham said to his father." Al-Dahhak said: The meaning of Azar is "the old man, the decrepit" [al-Himm (with a kasra on the ha'): the aged, senile old man. In another manuscript: "al-Harim" (the decrepit), and al-Farra' said likewise] in Persian. Al-Farra' said: It is a word of blame in their language, as if he said "O erring one," for one who reads it in the nominative; or as if he said: "And when Abraham said to his erring father," for one who reads it in the genitive. It is not declined because it is on the pattern of af'al, said al-Nahhas. Al-Jawhari said: Azar is a non-Arabic name, and it is derived from "Azara fulan fulanan" when he helped him, so he is one who supports his people in worshipping idols. It is also said: it is derived from strength, and al-Azr means strength, according to Ibn Faris.

Mujahid and Yaman said: Azar is the name of an idol, and in this interpretation it is in the accusative position, the sense being: "Do you take Azar as a god? Do you take idols?" It is also said: there is inversion (taqdim wa ta'khir) in the speech, the sense being: "Do you take Azar as idols?" I say: On this basis, Azar is a generic noun (ism jins). And God knows best.

Al-Tha'labi said in the book al-'Ara'is: The name of Abraham's father, which his father gave him, was Tarah; but when he came to be in charge of the treasury of Nimrod's gods, he named him Azar [this is probably the correct one, as in the Phoenician language, Izrba'l: the servant (sadin) of the idol Ba'l].

Mujahid said: Azar is not the name of his father; rather it is the name of an idol. He is Abraham ibn Tarah ibn Nahur ibn Sarug ibn Ar'u ibn Falij ibn Eber ibn Shalah ibn Arphaxad ibn Sam ibn Noah, peace be upon him.

As for "Azar" (in this verse), there are readings: "a-izran" with two hamzas, the first fathah and the second kasrah, transmitted from Ibn Abbas. And from him "a-izra" with two fathah hamzas. And it was read in the nominative, and this is narrated from Ibn Abbas. On the first two readings transmitted from him, "tattakhidhu" is without a hamza. Al-Mahdawi said: "a-izran?" It is said that it is the name of an idol, so it is in the accusative under the assumption "do you take izran," and likewise "a-azran." It may also be taken that "a-izran" is derived from al-azr, meaning the back, so it is an object of purpose (maf'ul min ajlihi), as if he said: "For strength do you take idols?" It may also be that izr means wizr (burden), with the waw changed to hamza.

Al-Qushayri said: He mentioned, in the argument against the polytheists, the story of Abraham and his rebuke of his father for worshipping idols. The people most entitled to follow Abraham are the Arabs, for they are his descendants. That is, "and remember when Abraham said..." or "and warn with it, lest a soul be delivered up for what it has earned," remember when Abraham said.

And "Azar" was read as "ya Azaru" (O Azar), as a direct address (nida' mufrad), and this is the reading of Ubayy, Ya'qub and others. This strengthens the view of those who say that Azar is the name of Abraham's father. "Do you take idols as gods?" are two objects of "tattakhidhu" [from ms. K], and it is an interrogative with the sense of denunciation (inkar).

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 6, verse 75:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And thus We showed Abraham the malakut (dominion) of the heavens and the earth﴾. That is, the mulk (kingdom). The waw and the taa' are added for emphasis in the attribute. Similar to it are ar-raghabut, ar-rahabut and al-jabarut. Abu as-Simal (Qa'nab ibn Abi Qa'nab al-'Adawi al-Basri; it is so in the Tabaqat Ilqa' and at-Taj; he has a shadhdh (irregular) reading differing from the common one. In al-Mizan: Abu as-Simak Ma'tab ibn Hilal al-'Adawi al-Basri, who has irregular letters whose transmission is not relied upon nor trusted. In B and J: Ibn as-Simak) recited "malakut" with the lam sukun. According to Sibawayh it is not permissible to delete the fathah because of its lightness, though it may be a dialect. And "nuri" means "araina" (We showed), (so it) has the meaning of the past tense.

It was said: he meant by it what is in the heavens of the worship of the angels and the wonders, and what is on the earth of the disobedience of the children of Adam. So he would supplicate against whomever he saw disobeying, and God would destroy him. God revealed to him: "O Abraham, refrain from My servants; do you not know that among My names is As-Sabur (the Patient)?" 'Ali transmitted its meaning from the Prophet ﷺ.

It was also said: God uncovered for him the heavens and the earth, until the Throne and the lowest of the earths. Ibn Jurayj narrated from al-Qasim from Ibrahim an-Nakha'i, who said: The seven heavens were opened for him, so he looked at them until he reached the Throne, and the earths were opened for him, so he looked at them, and he saw his place in Paradise. That is the meaning of His saying: ﴿And We gave him his reward in this world﴾. (Transmitted from as-Suddi.)

Ad-Dahhak said: He showed him the malakut of the heaven, what He related of the stars, and from the malakut of the earth the seas, the mountains, the trees, and the like of that by which he took evidence. Ibn 'Abbas said something similar. He also said: When he was born he was placed in a sarab (a hollow or a chamber beneath the earth), and his sustenance was placed in the tips of his fingers, so he would suck them. Nimrud the accursed had seen a dream, which was interpreted for him as meaning that his kingdom would be lost at the hands of a boy who would be born, so he ordered that men be separated from women. It was also said: he ordered the killing of every male newborn.

Azar was among those closest to the king Nimrud. Once he sent him on some errand, and he lay with his wife, and she conceived Ibrahim. It was also said: rather, he lay with her in the house of the idols, she conceived, and the idols fell on their faces at that moment. So he took her to one of the ravines until she gave birth to Ibrahim. He dug a sarab for Ibrahim in the earth and placed a rock over its door so that predators would not devour him. His mother would visit him and nurse him, and she would find him sucking his fingers: from one of them honey, from another water, and from another milk. He grew, and was at the level of a boy of three years. When she brought him out of the sarab, people assumed he had been born years earlier. He said to his mother: "Who is my Lord?" She said: "I am." He said: "And who is your lord?" She said: "Your father." He said: "And who is his lord?" She said: "Nimrud." He said: "And who is the lord of Nimrud?" [In K: and who is the lord of Nimrud?] So she slapped him, and she knew that he was the one through whose hands their kingdom would be lost.

The narrative on this is complete in the Qisas al-Anbiya' of al-Kisa'i, and it is a book from which one may take guidance. Some said: his birth was in Harran, but his father moved him to the land of Babil. The majority of the early scholars said: Ibrahim was born in the time of Nimrud ibn Kan'an ibn Sanjarib ibn Kush ibn Sam ibn Nuh. His mention has already passed in "al-Baqarah". The interval between the Flood and the birth of Ibrahim was one thousand two hundred and sixty-three years, and that was three thousand three hundred and thirty years after the creation of Adam.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And that he might be among the certain (muqinin)﴾. That is, and that he might be among the certain, We showed him that, namely the malakut.

God Most High says: ﴿When the night covered him﴾, meaning it concealed him with its darkness. From the same root come *al-jannah* (the garden), *al-jinnah* (madness), *al-junnah* (a shield), *al-janin* (the fetus) and *al-mijann* (a shield), and *al-jinn* (the jinn), all meaning concealment. *Janan al-layl* means the thickening and covering of the night. The poet says [[This is Duraid ibn al-Simma; it is also said to be Khafaf ibn Nadba (from *al-Lisan*).]]:

*"Had it not been for the cover of the night, our charging horses would have overtaken them at Dhu al-Ramth and al-Artha [[al-Ramth (with a kasra): a pasture for camels, and the name of a valley belonging to the Banu Asad. Al-Artha (plural of artah): a tree that grows in sand.]], O Iyad ibn Nashib."*

It is also said *junun al-layl*. It is said both *jannahu al-layl* and *ajannahu al-layl*, two dialectal forms.

﴿He saw a star﴾: This is a separate episode from the account of the showing of the malakut (dominion of the heavens) to him. It is said that he saw this through a crack in the rock placed over the mouth of the *sarab* (an underground chamber). It is also said that when his father brought him out of the *sarab* at sunset, he saw camels, horses and sheep and said, "They must have a lord." He then saw Jupiter or Venus, then the moon, then the sun, and this happened at the end of the month. Muhammad ibn Ishaq said he was fifteen years old. It is also said he was seven years old. And it is said that when he argued with Nimrod, he was seventeen years old.

God Most High says: ﴿He said, "This is my lord"﴾. Its meaning has been disputed in several opinions. It is said that this was said by him during the period of reflection and in his childhood, before the proof was established, and in that state there is neither disbelief nor belief. Those who hold this view cite what was narrated from Ali ibn Abi Talha from Ibn Abbas, who said: "When the night covered him and he saw a star, he said, 'This is my lord,' and he worshipped it until it set. Likewise the sun and the moon. When his reflection was complete, he said, 'I am free of what you associate [with God].'" They take the setting as evidence, since it is the clearest sign of having come into being.

Others said: This cannot be sound. They said: It is impossible for a messenger of God to reach a time at which he is not a monotheist who knows God, and free of every deity other than Him. They said: How can this be imagined of one whom God protected and to whom He gave his right guidance beforehand, and whom He showed His dominion so that he would be among the certain? It is not permissible to describe him as lacking knowledge; rather he knew the Lord from the very first reflection. Al-Zajjaj said: In my view this answer is an error and a mistake by the one who gave it. God Most High has told us that Abraham said: "Keep me and my sons far from worshipping idols," and God, Mighty and Majestic, said: "When he came to his Lord with a sound heart," meaning he never associated anything with Him. He said: In my view, the answer is that he said "This is my lord" according to your claim, since they worshipped idols, the sun and the moon. A parallel to this is God's saying: "Where are My partners" [[See vol. 10, p. 97.]], while He, Mighty and Exalted, is one with no partner; the meaning is "Where are My partners according to your claim." It is also said: When Abraham came out of the *sarab* he saw the light of a star while he was seeking his Lord, and he thought it was His light, so he said, "This is my lord," meaning that its light appeared to him.

﴿Then when it set﴾: he knew that it was not his lord. ﴿When he saw the moon rising﴾ and looked at its light, ﴿he said, "This is my lord. Then when it set, he said, 'If my Lord does not guide me, I will surely be among the misguided people.' Then when he saw the sun rising, he said, 'This is my lord'"﴾; and this is not shirk. He only attributed that light to his lord, and when he saw it disappear, knowledge showed him that it did not deserve that, so he rejected it in his heart and knew that it was something created and not a lord. It is also said that he said "This is my lord" only to establish the proof against his people, so he showed agreement with them. Then when the star set, he established the proof and said: What changes cannot be a lord. They used to venerate the stars, worship them and judge by them.

Al-Nahhas said: Among the best things said on this is what is authentically reported from Ibn Abbas regarding God's saying "Light upon light" [[See vol. 12, p. 255.]]: he said, "Likewise the heart of the believer knows God, Mighty and Majestic, and reasons toward Him with his heart. When he knows Him, he increases in light upon light. Likewise Abraham, peace be upon him, knew God, Mighty and Majestic, with his heart and reasoned toward Him by His signs, so he knew that He had a lord and creator. When God, Mighty and Majestic, made Himself known to him, he increased in knowledge, and so he said: 'Will you dispute with me about God, when He has guided me?'"

It is also said that it is in the sense of interrogation and rebuke, rejecting their action. The meaning is: "Is this my lord, or can the like of this be a lord?" So the hamza of interrogation was omitted. In the revelation there is: ﴿Then if you die, will they be the immortals?﴾ [[See vol. 11, p. 287.]], meaning: "Will they be the immortals?" Al-Hudhali [[He is Abu Khirash; *rafawni* means "they calmed me," from fear.]] said:

*"They calmed me and said, 'O Khuwaylid, do not be frightened,' so I said, while faces were unfamiliar: 'Are they, are they?'"*

Another [[He is Umar ibn Abi Rabi'a.]] said:

*"By your life, I do not know, though I am one who knows, whether they threw the embers in seven or in eight."*

It is also said that the meaning is "This is my lord according to your claim," as God Most High said: ﴿Where are My partners whom you used to claim?﴾ [[See vol. 13, p. 308.]] and He said: ﴿Taste it; indeed you are the mighty, the noble﴾ [[See vol. 16, p. 151.]], meaning "in your own estimation." It is also said that the meaning is "And you say, 'This is my lord,'" so the verb "say" is elided, and such elision is common in the Qur'an. It is also said that the meaning of "This is my lord" is "This is a proof of my Lord."

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿When he saw the moon rising﴾, i.e., appearing. It is said: "bazagha al-qamar" (the moon rose) when it began to rise, and al-bazgh means splitting, as if it splits the darkness with its light. From this comes "bazagha al-bayTar al-dabbah" (the farrier pierced the animal), when he let its blood flow.

(﴿Unless my Lord guides me﴾), i.e., unless He keeps me firm upon guidance. He was already guided, so this may have been said within the period of reflection, or he was asking for steadfastness, given the rational possibility of deviation, as Shu'ayb said: ﴿It is not for us to return to it unless Allah wills﴾ [[See p. 250 of this volume.]]. In the Revelation: ﴿Guide us to the straight path﴾, i.e., keep us firm upon guidance. This has been discussed earlier [[See vol. 1, p. 146.]].

The words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿When he saw the sun rising﴾ is in the accusative as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), because this is a matter of seeing with the eye. "Bazagha, yabzughu" means it rose (ṭalaʿa). "Afala, yafilu ufūlan" means it set (ghāba).

He said "hādhā" (this), though "the sun" is feminine, in accordance with His saying ﴿When it set﴾ (fa-lammā afalat). It was said that the feminization of the sun is for its magnification and greatness, and it is like the Arabs' saying: a man who is nassābah (very knowledgeable in genealogies) and allāmah (very learned). He said "This is my Lord" in the sense of: "This rising one is my Lord." This was said by al-Kisāʾī and al-Akhfash. Others said: that is, "this light." Abu al-Ḥasan ʿAlī ibn Sulaymān said: that is, "this person (shakhṣ)," as al-Aʿshā said:

She stood weeping over his grave: "Who will be mine after you, O ʿĀmir?

You left me in the house a stranger (dhā ghurbah), and whoever has no helper is humbled."

[[The evidence in it is his saying "dhā ghurbah," meaning a person (shakhṣan) who is a stranger.]]

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 6, verse 79:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, I have turned my face﴾, meaning: I have directed my worship and my monotheism solely to Allah, Mighty and Majestic. He mentioned the face because it is the most apparent thing by which a person (is recognized by) [[from K.]] his companion. "Hanifan" (inclining toward the truth).

﴿And I am not of the polytheists﴾: the subject of "ma" (not) and its predicate. When you pause, you say "ana" (I), adding the alif to clarify the vowel, and this is the eloquent dialect. Al-Akhfash said: Among the Arabs there are those who say "an." Al-Kisa'i said: Among the Arabs there are those who say "anah." These are three dialects. In connected speech there are also three dialects: the alif is dropped in continuous speech, since it is an added letter to clarify the vowel in pause. Some Arabs retain the alif in connected speech, as the poet said:

"I am the sword of the tribe, so recognize me" [[This is the first half of a verse; its second half, as in Lisan, root ʾ-n-n, is:

"All together, you have indeed bared the flanks"]]

This is the dialect of some of the Banu Qays and Rabi'ah, according to al-Farra'. Some Arabs say in connected speech "ana fa'altu," like "ʿana fa'altu," which al-Kisa'i reported from some of Qudaah.

**Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 6, verse 80:**

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And his people argued with him.﴾ This is evidence for argumentation and disputation (ḥijāj wa-jidāl). They disputed with him concerning the Oneness of God.

(He said: Do you argue with me concerning God?) Nafi' recited it with a light nun (takhfif al-nun), while the rest of the readers recited it with a doubled nun (tashdid al-nun). There is a difference of report from Ibn 'Amir through the narration of Hisham, concerning this. As for the one who doubled it, he said: the original form has two nuns, the first being the sign of the nominative (raf') and the second being a separator between the verb and the ya' (of the first person). When two identical letters came together in one verb, and that is heavy, the nun was assimilated into the other, so doubling (tashdid) resulted. It is necessary to lengthen the waw so that two quiescent letters do not meet, the waw and the first of the doubled letter, so the lengthening became a separator between the two quiescent letters. As for the one who lightened it, he deleted the second nun, for lightness, because two identical letters came together. The first nun was not deleted because it is the sign of the nominative, for if it were deleted, the nominative would be confused with the jussive (majzum) and the accusative (mansub).

It is related from Abu 'Amr Ibn al-'Ala' that this reading is a grammatical error (lahn). Sibawayh, however, permitted it, saying: "They found the doubling heavy." And he recited:

*tarāhu ka-l-thaghām yu'allu miskan ... yasū'u l-fāliyāti idhā fallanī*

[[The verse is by 'Amr ibn Ma'dikarib, describing his hair and that white hair has overtaken it. Al-thughām: a plant with white flowers, to which white hair is likened. Yu'allu: is perfumed (or drunk) repeatedly, one drink after another; al-'ulal: a second drink after a first.]]

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And I do not fear what you associate with Him.﴾ That is, because it neither benefits nor harms. They had threatened him with the multitude of their gods. ﴿Except that my Lord should will something.﴾ That is, unless God (Allah) gives it life and empowers it, so that he would then fear its harm, and this is the meaning of His saying: ﴿Except that my Lord should will anything.﴾ That is, except that He wills that some disliked thing afflict me for a sin I have committed, so His will is fulfilled. This is an exception that is not from the first (istithna' laysa min al-awwal). The pronoun in "bihi" may refer to God, the Mighty and Majestic, and it may refer to the object of worship. And His saying, "Except that my Lord should will," means that God, the Exalted, does not will that I fear them. Then He said: ﴿My Lord encompasses all things in knowledge.﴾ That is, His knowledge encompasses everything. And it has been mentioned previously [[see vol. 2, p. 84.]].

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 6, verse 81–82:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿How should I fear what you have associated [with Allah], when you do not fear that you have associated with Allah that for which He has not sent down to you any authority?﴾ In "how" (kayfa) there is the meaning of denial. He denounced their frightening him with the idols, while they themselves did not fear Allah, the Mighty and Majestic; that is, "How should I fear [mere] lifeless things, while you do not fear Allah, the One capable of all things?" (for which He has not sent down to you any authority), that is, any proof. This has already been mentioned [[see vol. 4, p. 233.]].

(So which of the two parties is more deserving of security) that is, from the punishment of Allah: the monotheist or the polytheist? Then Allah, judging between them, said: (Those who believe and do not mix their belief with wrongdoing) that is, with polytheism. Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, Ali, Salman and Hudhayfah, may Allah be pleased with them, said so. Ibn Abbas said: it is from the people of Abraham, as a scholar asks and answers himself. It was also said: it is from the words of the people of Abraham, that is, they answered with what is a proof against them; this is what Ibn Jurayj said. In the two Sahihs, from Ibn Mas'ud: when the verse "Those who believe and do not mix their belief with wrongdoing" was revealed, it weighed heavily upon the Companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and they said: "Which of us has not wronged himself?" The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "It is not as you think; it is as Luqman said to his son: 'O my son, do not associate anything with Allah; indeed, association is a great wrong.'" [[see vol. 14, p. 62.]] (And they are guided) that is, in this world.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 6, verse 83:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And that was Our argument which We gave to Abraham﴾. (Tilka) [[In K.]] refers to all of his arguments, until he disputed with them and overcame them with the proof. Mujahid said: it is the statement: "Those who believe and do not mix their belief with wrongdoing" (Q. 6:82). It was also said: his argument against them was that when they said to him, "Do you not fear that our gods will afflict you with madness because you revile them?" [[In K.: "Indeed we fear."]] he said to them, "Do you not fear from them, since you have made the small and the great equal in worship and veneration, so that the great one becomes angry and afflicts you with madness?"

﴿We raise in degrees whom We will﴾, that is, with knowledge, understanding, leadership and kingship. The Kufans read "darajat" (degrees) with tanwin. Similar to this in Surah Yusuf [[See vol. 9, p. 235.]] is the verb being attributed to "man" (whom), because it is in reality the object raised: the implied meaning is "and We raise whom We will to degrees," and then "ila" (to) was omitted. The people of the two Sanctuaries (Mecca and Medina) and Abu 'Amr read it without tanwin, as an idafah (construct), with the verb falling on the degrees; when the degrees are raised, their possessor is raised. This reading is strengthened by His saying, may He be exalted: "Raiser of degrees" (Q. 40:15) [[See vol. 15, p. 298.]], and the saying of the Prophet, peace be upon him: "O Allah, raise his degree." So He attributed the raising to the degrees, and He, there is no god but Him, is the Exalted, the Lofty in His nobility and virtue. The two readings are therefore close in meaning, for whoever has his degrees raised has himself been raised, and whoever is raised has had his degrees raised. So understand.

﴿Indeed your Lord is All-Wise, All-Knowing﴾. He places each thing in its proper place.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 6, verses 84–86:

There are three issues (masa'il) here. The first concerns the words of the Exalted: ﴿And We gave him Isaac and Jacob﴾, meaning as a reward for him for arguing about the religion and sacrificing himself for it. "(Each of them We guided)" means each one of them was rightly guided. "Each" (kullan) is in the accusative governed by "guided" (hadayna), and "Noah" (nuhan) is in the accusative governed by the second "guided" (hadayna).

"(And of his descendants)" means the descendants of Abraham. It was also said that it means the descendants of Noah; this was said by al-Farra', and al-Tabari and many other exegetes adopted it, such as al-Qushayri, Ibn 'Atiyya and others. The first view was stated by al-Zajjaj, and it was objected that among those counted among these descendants are Jonah and Lot, and neither of them was a descendant of Abraham. Lot was the son of his brother, and it was said he was the son of his sister. Ibn 'Abbas said: all these prophets are attributed to the descendants of Abraham, even if some of them were not born to him from either father or mother, because Lot was the son of Abraham's brother. The Arabs call the paternal uncle "father," as Allah related about the sons of Jacob that they said: ﴿We will worship your God and the God of your fathers, Abraham, Isma'il and Isaac﴾, and Isma'il was the paternal uncle of Jacob. Jesus is also counted among the descendants of Abraham, although he was only the son of a daughter. Thus the children of Fatimah, may Allah be pleased with her, are the descendants of the Prophet ﷺ. By this, those who hold that the children of daughters enter into the name "child" hold fast.

The second issue: Abu Hanifa and al-Shafi'i said: whoever endows a waqf upon "his children and the children of his children," the children of his daughters enter into it, however far they descend. Likewise, if he bequeaths to "his relatives" (qaraba), the children of daughters enter into it. For Abu Hanifa, "relatives" means every person with a forbidden (mahram) kinship bond; thus the paternal cousin, the paternal aunt's son, the maternal cousin and the maternal aunt's son drop out, because they are not mahram. Al-Shafi'i said: "relatives" means everyone with a kinship bond, whether mahram or not; so the paternal cousin and others do not drop out for him. Malik said: the children of daughters do not enter into that. Saying "to my relatives and my posterity" is like saying "to my children and the children of my children": it includes the children of sons and whoever traces back to the father's agnatic line and loins, and does not include the children of daughters. A similar view was mentioned from al-Shafi'i earlier in Surah Al 'Imran. The proof for the first two is the saying of the Glorified: ﴿Allah instructs you concerning your children﴾. The Muslims understood from the apparent meaning of the verse only the children of the loins and the children of sons. The Exalted also said: ﴿And for the Messenger and for the near relatives﴾, and the Prophet, peace be upon him, gave to the relatives from among his paternal uncles and not to the children of his maternal uncles. Likewise, the children of daughters are not attributed to him by lineage and do not share a father with him. Ibn al-Qassar said: The proof of those who include daughters' children among the relatives is his saying, peace be upon him, to al-Hasan ibn 'Ali: "Indeed, this son of mine is a master." We know of no one who refuses to say of the children of daughters that they are the children of their mother's father. The meaning requires this, because "walad" (child) is derived from "tawallud" (procreation), and they are necessarily procreated from their mother's father, and procreation through the mother is like procreation through the father. The Qur'an also indicates this; Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And of his descendants, David and Solomon﴾ up to ﴿of the righteous﴾, so He made Jesus among his descendants, though he was the son of his daughter.

The third issue: The discussion of which of these names are not declinable has already been given in Surah An-Nisa'. "Dawud" is not declined because it is a non-Arabic name, and since it is of the form fa'ul, to which the definite article "al-" does not suitably attach, it is not declined. "Ilyas" is non-Arabic. Al-Dahhak said: Ilyas was from the descendants of Isma'il. Al-Qutabi mentioned that he was from the tribe of Yusha' ibn Nun. Al-A'raj, al-Hasan and Qatada read "wa-l-Yasa'" with the alif of wasl (connecting alif). The people of the two Holy Sanctuaries, Abu 'Amr and 'Asim read "wa-l-Yasa'" with a single light lam. The Kufans, except 'Asim, read "wa-l-Layasa'" [with two lams].

Al-Kisa'i also read thus, and he rejected the reading of those who read "wa-l-Yasa'", saying: "It is not said al-yaf'al like al-yahya." Al-Nahhas said: This rejection is not binding, for the Arabs say al-ya'mal and al-yahmad, and if you made Yahya indefinite you would say al-yahya. Abu Hatim rejected those who read "al-Layasa'" and said: "Layasa' is not found." Al-Nahhas said: This rejection is not binding, for Haydar and Zaynab occur in Arabic speech. The truth in this matter is that it is a non-Arabic name, and foreignness is not established by analogy but only by transmission (sama'an), and the Arabs change it considerably, so there is no denying that a name may come in two forms. Makki said: whoever reads with two lams, the original form of the name is Layasa', then the alif and lam entered for definiteness. Had its original form been Yasa', the alif and lam would not have entered it, since they do not attach to Yazid and Yashkur, which are names of two men, because these are definite proper names. But "Layasa'" is indefinite, so the alif and lam enter it for definiteness. The reading with one lam is more beloved to me, because most of the readers follow it. Al-Mahdawi said: whoever reads "al-Yasa'" with one lam, the name is Yasa', and the alif and lam entered as extra letters, like their addition in phrases such as "al-khamsata 'ashar" (fifteen), and in the line:

"We found Yazid ibn al-Walid blessed, strong in bearing the burdens of the caliphate, his shoulder..."

They also added them to the imperfect verb, as in his saying:

"The jerboa is dug out from its nafiqa'... and from its burrow at al-Shaykha, the yataqassa'..."

He means "the one who yataqassa'." Al-Qushayri said: It has been read with a light lam and with a shadda. The meaning is the same, that it is the name of a known prophet, like Isma'il and Ibrahim, but it departs from the pattern of non-Arabic names by the addition of the alif and lam. Some people imagined that al-Yasa' is Ilyas, but this is not so, because Allah mentioned each of them separately. Wahb said: al-Yasa' is the companion of Ilyas, and they were before Zakariyya, Yahya and 'Isa. It was also said: Ilyas is Idris, but this is not correct, because Idris is the grandfather of Noah, and Ilyas is among his descendants. It was also said: Ilyas is al-Khidr. It was said: No, rather al-Yasa' is al-Khidr. "Lut" (Lot) is a non-Arabic name, and it is declined (in the sense of being treated as the lighter form) for its lightness. Its derivation will come in Surah Al-A'raf.

Al-Mahdawi said: whoever reads "al-Yasa'" with one lam, the name is Yasa', and the alif and lam entered as extra letters, like their addition in phrases such as "al-khamsata 'ashar" (fifteen), and in the line:

"We found Yazid ibn al-Walid blessed, strong in bearing the burdens of the caliphate, his shoulder..."

They also added them to the imperfect verb, as in his saying:

"The jerboa is dug out from its nafiqa'... and from its burrow at al-Shaykha, the yataqassa'..."

He means "the one who yataqassa'." Al-Qushayri said: It has been read with a light lam and with a shadda. The meaning is the same, that it is the name of a known prophet, like Isma'il and Ibrahim, but it departs from the pattern of non-Arabic names by the addition of the alif and lam. Some people imagined that al-Yasa' is Ilyas, but this is not so, because Allah mentioned each of them separately. Wahb said: al-Yasa' is the companion of Ilyas, and they were before Zakariyya, Yahya and 'Isa. It was also said: Ilyas is Idris, but this is not correct, because Idris is the grandfather of Noah, and Ilyas is among his descendants. It was also said: Ilyas is al-Khidr. It was said: No, rather al-Yasa' is al-Khidr. "Lut" (Lot) is a non-Arabic name, and it is declined (in the sense of being treated as the lighter form) for its lightness. Its derivation will come in Surah Al-A'raf.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 6, verses 84–86:

There are three issues (masa'il) here. The first concerns the words of the Exalted: ﴿And We gave him Isaac and Jacob﴾, meaning as a reward for him for arguing about the religion and sacrificing himself for it. "(Each of them We guided)" means each one of them was rightly guided. "Each" (kullan) is in the accusative governed by "guided" (hadayna), and "Noah" (nuhan) is in the accusative governed by the second "guided" (hadayna).

"(And of his descendants)" means the descendants of Abraham. It was also said that it means the descendants of Noah; this was said by al-Farra', and al-Tabari and many other exegetes adopted it, such as al-Qushayri, Ibn 'Atiyya and others. The first view was stated by al-Zajjaj, and it was objected that among those counted among these descendants are Jonah and Lot, and neither of them was a descendant of Abraham. Lot was the son of his brother, and it was said he was the son of his sister. Ibn 'Abbas said: all these prophets are attributed to the descendants of Abraham, even if some of them were not born to him from either father or mother, because Lot was the son of Abraham's brother. The Arabs call the paternal uncle "father," as Allah related about the sons of Jacob that they said: ﴿We will worship your God and the God of your fathers, Abraham, Isma'il and Isaac﴾, and Isma'il was the paternal uncle of Jacob. Jesus is also counted among the descendants of Abraham, although he was only the son of a daughter. Thus the children of Fatimah, may Allah be pleased with her, are the descendants of the Prophet ﷺ. By this, those who hold that the children of daughters enter into the name "child" hold fast.

The second issue: Abu Hanifa and al-Shafi'i said: whoever endows a waqf upon "his children and the children of his children," the children of his daughters enter into it, however far they descend. Likewise, if he bequeaths to "his relatives" (qaraba), the children of daughters enter into it. For Abu Hanifa, "relatives" means every person with a forbidden (mahram) kinship bond; thus the paternal cousin, the paternal aunt's son, the maternal cousin and the maternal aunt's son drop out, because they are not mahram. Al-Shafi'i said: "relatives" means everyone with a kinship bond, whether mahram or not; so the paternal cousin and others do not drop out for him. Malik said: the children of daughters do not enter into that. Saying "to my relatives and my posterity" is like saying "to my children and the children of my children": it includes the children of sons and whoever traces back to the father's agnatic line and loins, and does not include the children of daughters. A similar view was mentioned from al-Shafi'i earlier in Surah Al 'Imran. The proof for the first two is the saying of the Glorified: ﴿Allah instructs you concerning your children﴾. The Muslims understood from the apparent meaning of the verse only the children of the loins and the children of sons. The Exalted also said: ﴿And for the Messenger and for the near relatives﴾, and the Prophet, peace be upon him, gave to the relatives from among his paternal uncles and not to the children of his maternal uncles. Likewise, the children of daughters are not attributed to him by lineage and do not share a father with him. Ibn al-Qassar said: The proof of those who include daughters' children among the relatives is his saying, peace be upon him, to al-Hasan ibn 'Ali: "Indeed, this son of mine is a master." We know of no one who refuses to say of the children of daughters that they are the children of their mother's father. The meaning requires this, because "walad" (child) is derived from "tawallud" (procreation), and they are necessarily procreated from their mother's father, and procreation through the mother is like procreation through the father. The Qur'an also indicates this; Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And of his descendants, David and Solomon﴾ up to ﴿of the righteous﴾, so He made Jesus among his descendants, though he was the son of his daughter.

The third issue: The discussion of which of these names are not declinable has already been given in Surah An-Nisa'. "Dawud" is not declined because it is a non-Arabic name, and since it is of the form fa'ul, to which the definite article "al-" does not suitably attach, it is not declined. "Ilyas" is non-Arabic. Al-Dahhak said: Ilyas was from the descendants of Isma'il. Al-Qutabi mentioned that he was from the tribe of Yusha' ibn Nun. Al-A'raj, al-Hasan and Qatada read "wa-l-Yasa'" with the alif of wasl (connecting alif). The people of the two Holy Sanctuaries, Abu 'Amr and 'Asim read "wa-l-Yasa'" with a single light lam. The Kufans, except 'Asim, read "wa-l-Layasa'" [with two lams].

Al-Kisa'i also read thus, and he rejected the reading of those who read "wa-l-Yasa'", saying: "It is not said al-yaf'al like al-yahya." Al-Nahhas said: This rejection is not binding, for the Arabs say al-ya'mal and al-yahmad, and if you made Yahya indefinite you would say al-yahya.
