Abu Hatim rejected those who read "al-Layasa'" and said: "Layasa' is not found." Al-Nahhas said: This rejection is not binding, for Haydar and Zaynab occur in Arabic speech. The truth in this matter is that it is a non-Arabic name, and foreignness is not established by analogy but only by transmission (sama'an), and the Arabs change it considerably, so there is no denying that a name may come in two forms. Makki said: whoever reads with two lams, the original form of the name is Layasa', then the alif and lam entered for definiteness. Had its original form been Yasa', the alif and lam would not have entered it, since they do not attach to Yazid and Yashkur, which are names of two men, because these are definite proper names. But "Layasa'" is indefinite, so the alif and lam enter it for definiteness. The reading with one lam is more beloved to me, because most of the readers follow it. Al-Mahdawi said: whoever reads "al-Yasa'" with one lam, the name is Yasa', and the alif and lam entered as extra letters, like their addition in phrases such as "al-khamsata 'ashar" (fifteen), and in the line:

"We found Yazid ibn al-Walid blessed, strong in bearing the burdens of the caliphate, his shoulder..."

They also added them to the imperfect verb, as in his saying:

"The jerboa is dug out from its nafiqa'... and from its burrow at al-Shaykha, the yataqassa'..."

He means "the one who yataqassa'." Al-Qushayri said: It has been read with a light lam and with a shadda. The meaning is the same, that it is the name of a known prophet, like Isma'il and Ibrahim, but it departs from the pattern of non-Arabic names by the addition of the alif and lam. Some people imagined that al-Yasa' is Ilyas, but this is not so, because Allah mentioned each of them separately. Wahb said: al-Yasa' is the companion of Ilyas, and they were before Zakariyya, Yahya and 'Isa. It was also said: Ilyas is Idris, but this is not correct, because Idris is the grandfather of Noah, and Ilyas is among his descendants. It was also said: Ilyas is al-Khidr. It was said: No, rather al-Yasa' is al-Khidr. "Lut" (Lot) is a non-Arabic name, and it is declined (in the sense of being treated as the lighter form) for its lightness. Its derivation will come in Surah Al-A'raf.

God Most High says: ﴿And of their fathers, their offspring, and their brothers﴾. "Min" (مِنْ) is partitive, meaning: We guided some of their fathers, their offspring, and their brothers. "Wajtabaynahum" (وَاجْتَبَيْنَاهُمْ): Mujahid said, "We purified them." Among the ahl al-lughah (the lexicographers and linguists), it means "We chose them." It is derived from *jabaytu al-ma' fi al-hawd* (جَبَيْتُ الْمَاءَ فِي الْحَوْضِ), meaning "I gathered the water in the basin." Thus *al-ijtiba'* is bringing the one you choose into your special company. Al-Kisa'i said: "*Jabaytu al-ma' fi al-hawd jabyan*" (وَجَبَيْتُ الْمَاءَ فِي الْحَوْضِ جَبًّا), with a short vowel, and *al-jabiyah* is the basin. He said:

*Like the basin of the Iraqi elder, overflowing* (كَجَابِيَةِ الشَّيْخِ الْعِرَاقِيِّ تَفْهَقُ)

[This is the second half of a line by al-A'sha, whose first half, as in the Diwan, is: "He repelled blame from the family of al-Muhalliq, a bowl." *Al-jafnah* is the large bowl; *al-fahaq* is fullness.]

The meanings of *al-istifa'* (election) and *al-hidayah* (guidance) have already been discussed. [See vol. 1, p. 146 and vol. 2, pp. 133–32 1.]

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿That is the guidance of Allah; He guides with it whom He wills of His servants. And if they had associated others with Him, all that they used to do would have been worthless﴾. That is, if they had worshipped other than Me, their deeds would have been nullified (ḥabiṭat), but I protected them. Ḥubūṭ (nullification, invalidation) means annulment. It has already been discussed in al-Baqarah [[See vol. 3, p. 46.]].

His words, Exalted is He: ﴿Those are the ones to whom We gave the Book, and the judgment, and prophethood﴾ are a beginning (ibtida', the subject of a nominal sentence) and its predicate (khabar). "Al-hukm" means knowledge and jurisprudence (fiqh).

(﴿Then if they disbelieve in it﴾) means: in Our signs. ﴿These﴾ means the disbelievers of your time, O Muhammad.

(﴿We have indeed entrusted with it﴾) is the answer to the conditional clause, meaning: We have entrusted with belief in them ﴿a people who are not disbelievers in them﴾. He means the Ansar of Madinah and the Muhajirun of Makkah. Qatadah said: it means the prophets whom God, Mighty and Majestic, related in the Qur'an. Al-Nahhas (al-Nahhas) said: this view is closer to the meaning, because He said after it: ﴿Those are the ones whom God guided, so follow their guidance﴾. Abu Raja' said: they are the angels. It was also said: it is general for every believer among the jinn, humans and angels. The "bi" in "bi-kafirin" is an extra particle (za'idah) for emphasis [[from manuscripts ك and ز.]]

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 6, verse 90:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Those are the ones whom Allah guided, so follow their guidance.﴾ In this are two issues.

The first: His saying, the Exalted: ﴿so follow their guidance.﴾ Iqtida' (following an example) is seeking to conform to another in his action. It has been said: the meaning is, "Be patient as they were patient." And it has been said: the meaning of "so follow their guidance" is monotheism, while the sacred laws (shara'i') differ.

Some scholars have used this verse as evidence for the obligation of following the laws of the prophets in matters where there is no explicit text (nass), as in Sahih Muslim and elsewhere: that the sister of al-Rabi' [[al-Rabi': with a damma on the ra', a fatha on the ba' and a shadda on the following yaa' with a kasra, followed by an unpointed 'ayn. As for Umm al-Rabi', it is with a fatha on the ra', a kasra on the ba' and a light yaa'. See al-Nawawi's commentary on Sahih Muslim, chapter on establishing retaliation for teeth and what is similar to them, where he discusses this story at length.]] Umm Harithah wounded a person, and they brought the dispute to the Prophet ﷺ. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Retaliation, retaliation." Umm al-Rabi' said: "O Messenger of Allah, shall retaliation be taken from so-and-so? By Allah, retaliation shall not be taken from her." The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Glory be to Allah, O Umm al-Rabi', retaliation is the Book of Allah." She said: "By Allah, retaliation shall never be taken from her." He said: "So they did not cease until they accepted the blood-money." Then the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Among the servants of Allah there are those who, if they swear by Allah, He fulfils it for them." The Messenger of Allah ﷺ referred to the saying: ﴿And We prescribed for them therein that the life is for the life...﴾ [[See vol. 6, p. 191.]] — the verse. There is no text in the Book of Allah, the Exalted, on retaliation for a tooth except in this verse, and it is a report about the law of the Torah; nevertheless, he judged by it and referred to it. This is the view of the majority of the companions of Malik and the companions of al-Shafi'i, and that it is obligatory to act upon what is found of it. Ibn Bukayr said: "This is what the principles of Malik require." Many of the companions of Malik, the companions of al-Shafi'i and the Mu'tazilah disagreed on this, citing the saying of the Exalted: ﴿For each of you We have made a law and a way.﴾ [[See vol. 6, p. 209.]] This has no proof in it, because it admits of restriction: except in what is related to you of their reports that did not come in your Book.

In Sahih al-Bukhari, on the authority of al-'Awwam, he said: "I asked Mujahid about the prostration of Sad, and he said: I asked Ibn 'Abbas about the prostration of Sad, and he said: Do you not recite ﴿And of his offspring, Dawud and Sulayman﴾ up to His saying ﴿Those are the ones whom Allah guided, so follow their guidance﴾? And Dawud, peace be upon him, was among those whom your Prophet ﷺ was commanded to follow."

The second issue: Hamzah and al-Kisa'i recited ﴿iqtadi qul﴾ without a ha' when joined. Ibn 'Amir recited ﴿iqtadihi qul﴾. Al-Nahhas said: "This is a grammatical error (lahn), because the ha' is for showing the vowel in pause, and it is not a ha' of a pronoun, nor is a waw or a yaa' after it; likewise it is not permissible to say ﴿fabihudahumu iqtadih qul﴾." Whoever avoids the error and follows the written text (sawad) recites ﴿fabihudahumu iqtadih﴾ and stops without joining, because if he joins with the ha' he commits an error, and if he omits it he opposes the written text. The majority recited with the ha' when joined, out of intention of pausing and out of intention of continuing, following its presence in the script. Ibn 'Ayyash and Hisham recited ﴿iqtadihi qul﴾ with a kasra on the ha', and this is an error that is not permissible in Arabic.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Say: I do not ask you for any wage for it﴾, i.e., a reward for the Qur'an.

﴿It is not but a reminder to the worlds﴾, i.e., the Qur'an.

﴿It is but a reminder to the worlds﴾, i.e., it is an admonition to creation. He attributed the guidance to them, saying: ﴿so follow their guidance﴾, because the guidance occurred through them. And He said: ﴿That is the guidance of Allah﴾, because He is the Creator of the guidance.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 6, verse 91:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿They did not measure God with His true measure﴾, meaning: regarding what is obligatory for Him, what is impossible for Him, and what is permissible for Him. Ibn 'Abbas said: they did not believe that He is capable of everything. Al-Hasan said: they did not magnify Him with His true magnificence. This is from their saying: "So-and-so has qadr" (standing, worth). The explanation of this is that when they said, "God has not sent down anything to any human being," they attributed to God, mighty and majestic, that He does not establish proof against His servants and does not command them with what is good for them. Thus they did not magnify Him with His true magnificence, nor did they know Him with His true knowledge. Abu 'Ubayda said: that is, they did not know God with His true knowledge. Al-Nahhas said: this is a good meaning, because the meaning of "qadartu al-shay'" and "qaddartuhu" is "I knew its measure." It is supported by the saying of the Exalted: ﴿When they said, "God has not sent down anything to any human being"﴾, meaning they did not know Him with His true knowledge, since they denied that He would send a messenger. The two meanings are close. It has also been said: "They did not measure the blessings of God with their true measure." Abu Haywa read "wa ma qadarū Allāha ḥaqqa qadrihi" with a fatha on the dal, and this is a dialect (lugha).

(﴿When they said, "God has not sent down anything to any human being"﴾) Ibn 'Abbas and others said: this refers to the polytheists of Quraysh. Al-Hasan and Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: the one who said it was a Jew, who said, "God did not send down a Book from heaven." Al-Suddi said: his name was Finhas. Also from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, he said: he was Malik ibn al-Sayf, who came to dispute with the Prophet ﷺ, and the Prophet ﷺ said to him: "I adjure you by Him who sent down the Torah to Moses: do you not find in the Torah that God hates the fat rabbi?" He was a fat rabbi. He became angry and said: "By God, God has not sent down anything to any human being." His companions who were with him said to him: "Woe to you! Not even to Moses?" He said: "By God, God has not sent down anything to any human being." So the verse was revealed. Then He said, refuting their statement and rejecting it: ﴿Say: "Who sent down the Book which Moses brought, as a light and guidance for mankind, which you make into scrolls, displaying some and concealing much"?﴾ — that is, into scrolls. "Displaying some and concealing much": this is addressed to the Jews who concealed the description of the Prophet ﷺ and other rulings. Mujahid said: the saying of the Exalted, ﴿Say: "Who sent down the Book which Moses brought"﴾ is addressed to the polytheists; His saying, ﴿which you make into scrolls﴾ is addressed to the Jews; and His saying, ﴿and you were taught what neither you nor your fathers knew﴾ is addressed to the Muslims. This is valid according to the reading of one who reads "yajʿaluna-hu qarāṭīsa yubdūnahā wa yukhfūna" with the ya' (third person). The reading with the ta' (second person) implies that the whole address is to the Jews, and the meaning of "wa 'ullimtum mā lam ta'lamū" is: you were taught what you were not knowing, you and your fathers, as a favour upon them by the sending down of the Torah. The Torah was made into pages, and therefore He said "qarāṭīs tubdūnahā," meaning you display the scrolls. This is a censure of them, and for this reason the scholars disliked writing the Qur'an in separate parts.

(﴿Say: "God"﴾) meaning: say, O Muhammad, "God" (the One) who sent down that Book to Moses and this Book to me. Or: say, "God taught you the Book."

(﴿Then leave them in their discourse, playing﴾) meaning: playing. Had it been an answer to the command, He would have said "yalʿabū." The meaning of the statement is a threat. It has also been said that this is abrogated by fighting. Then it has been said: "tajʿalūnahu" is in the position of an adjective to "nūran wa hudan," so it lies within the relative clause. It may also be a new (independent) clause, the implied sense being: making it into scrolls. As for His saying, "tubdūnahā wa tukhfūna kathīran," it may be an adjective to "qarāṭīs," since an indefinite noun may be described by clauses; and it may be a new clause, as previously mentioned.

This is a Book which We have sent down, blessed (mubarak), meaning it has been blessed, and blessing (barakah) is increase. It is permissible to read it in the accusative in other than the Qur'an as a circumstantial state (hal). Likewise, "confirming what is before it" means confirming the Books sent down before it, for it agrees with them in negating association with God (shirk) and affirming monotheism (tawhid).

"That you may warn the Mother of Towns" means Makkah. The meaning of its being named thus has already been mentioned [see vol. 4, p. 138]. What is meant is its people, so the noun is elided: We sent it down for blessing and warning. "And those around it" means all the horizons.

"Those who believe in the Hereafter believe in it" means the followers of Muhammad (ﷺ), as is shown by His words: "and they guard their prayer." The faith of one who believes in the Hereafter but does not believe in the Prophet (peace be upon him) or in his Book is not considered valid.

**Verse 6:93:** ﴿Who is more unjust than one who fabricates a lie against Allah, or says, "I have been inspired," when nothing has been inspired to him?﴾

Al-Qurtubi: His saying, Most High, ﴿And who is more unjust﴾ is a subject and predicate, meaning: there is no one more unjust.

(than one who fabricates) means: who invents.

(a lie against Allah, or says, "I have been inspired") so he claims to be a prophet, (when nothing has been inspired to him). It was revealed concerning Rahman al-Yamama, al-Aswad al-Ansi, and Sajah, the wife of Musaylima. All of them claimed prophethood and asserted that Allah had inspired them. Qatada said: "We have been told that Allah revealed this about Musaylima." Ibn Abbas also said so.

I say: Of this type is the one who turns away from *fiqh* (jurisprudence, the understanding of the religious law) and the *sunan* (the established practices of the Prophet ﷺ) and what the *salaf* (the early righteous generations) followed of the *sunan*, and then says: "Such-and-such occurred to my mind," or "my heart informed me of such-and-such." They then issue rulings based on whatever comes into their hearts and prevails over them of their thoughts. They claim that this is due to their hearts' purity from impurities and their freedom from other things, so that the divine sciences and the lordly realities are revealed to them. Thus they stand upon the secrets of the universals and know the rulings of the particulars, and they consider themselves independent of the rulings of the universal laws of the Shari'a. They say: "These general legal rulings are only applied to the ignorant and the common people. As for the saints (*awliya'*) and the people of special closeness, they have no need of those texts." It has been transmitted in what they narrate: "Consult your heart, even if the jurists issue you a fatwa" [[In *Kashf al-Khafa* it reads: "Consult your heart, even if people give you a fatwa and issue you rulings." He said: it was narrated by Ahmad, al-Tabarani, Abu Ya'la, and Abu Nu'aym, from Wabisa, as a marfu' (traced to the Prophet ﷺ) hadith.]]. They use as evidence for this al-Khidr, who, they say, became independent, by what was revealed to him of those sciences, of the understanding that Musa had. This statement is heresy (*zandaqa*) and disbelief (*kufr*). Its speaker is to be killed and is not given a chance to repent. No questioning or answering is needed with him, for it necessarily entails the demolition of the rulings and the affirmation of prophets after our Prophet ﷺ. Further elucidation of this meaning will come, if Allah Most High wills, in *al-Kahf* [[See vol. 10, p. 18 and what follows.]].

**Verse 6:93 (continued):** ﴿And who says, "I will send down the like of what Allah has sent down"﴾

"Man" (*man*) is in the genitive position, meaning: and who is more unjust than one who says, "I will send down." The intended person is Abdullah ibn Abi Sarh, who used to write down the revelation for the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, then apostatized and joined the polytheists. According to what the exegetes mention, the cause was that when the verse in *al-Mu'minun* was revealed: ﴿And We created man from an extract of clay﴾ [[See vol. 12, p. 108.]], the Prophet ﷺ summoned him and dictated it to him. When he reached His saying, ﴿Then We produced him as another creation﴾, Abdullah was amazed at the detail of the creation of man and said: ﴿So blessed is Allah, the best of creators﴾. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Thus was it revealed to me." Abdullah then doubted at that point and said: "If Muhammad is truthful, then it was revealed to me as it was revealed to him; and if he is lying, then I have said as he said." He then apostatized from Islam and joined the polytheists, and this is His saying: "And who says, 'I will send down the like of what Allah has sent down.'" This was narrated by al-Kalbi from Ibn Abbas.

Muhammad ibn Ishaq also mentioned it, saying: Shurahbil narrated to me, saying: It was revealed concerning Abdullah ibn Sa'd ibn Abi Sarh: "And who says, 'I will send down the like of what Allah has sent down'". He apostatized from Islam. When the Messenger of Allah ﷺ entered Mecca, he ordered that he be killed, along with Abdullah ibn Khatal and Maqis ibn Subaba, even if they were found under the curtains of the Ka'ba. Abdullah ibn Abi Sarh fled to Uthman, may Allah be pleased with him, who was his foster brother, since his mother had nursed Uthman. Uthman concealed him until he brought him to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ after the people of Mecca had become settled, and asked for his amnesty. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ remained silent for a long time, then said: "Yes." When Uthman left, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "I was silent only so that one of you would stand up and strike his neck." A man from the Ansar said: "Why did you not signal to me, O Messenger of Allah?" He said: "It is not fitting for a prophet to have 'the treachery of the eyes'" [[That is, he conceals in himself something other than what he displays. If he restrains his tongue but signals with his eyes, he has committed treachery.]].

Abu Umar said: Abdullah ibn Sa'd ibn Abi Sarh embraced Islam on the day of the Conquest, and his Islam was good, and nothing objectionable appeared from him after that. He was one of the noble, intelligent, generous men of Quraysh, and the horseman of the Banu Amir ibn Lu'ayy, who was counted among them. Uthman later appointed him governor of Egypt in the year 25 AH. Ifriqiya was conquered at his hands in the year 27 AH, and in the year 31 AH he raided the Asawid from the land of Nubia from there, and he made with them the truce that remains until today.

He also led the raid of al-Sawari [[Ibn al-Athir said in *al-Kamil*: "As for the cause of this raid, when the Muslims had struck the people of Ifriqiya, killed and captured them, Constantine, son of Heraclius, went out with a force the Romans had never gathered since Islam began, and they set out in five hundred or six hundred ships, and the Muslims went out..." etc. It was called the raid of al-Sawari because of the great number of ship masts and their gathering. See vol. 3, p. 9, European edition. And al-Tabari, first part, p. 2865, European edition.]] into the land of the Romans in the year 34 AH. When he returned from his delegations, Ibn Abi Hudhayfa prevented him from entering al-Fustat, so he went to Asqalan and remained there until Uthman, may Allah be pleased with him, was killed. It was also said: rather, he remained in al-Ramla until he died, fleeing from the strife. He prayed to his Lord, saying: "O Allah, make the last of my deeds the dawn prayer." He performed ablution, then prayed. In the first rak'a he recited *Umm al-Qur'an* and *al-'Adiyat* [[In manuscript K: *al-Saffat*.]], and in the second *Umm al-Qur'an* and a surah. Then he gave the salam to his right, then he turned to give the salam to his left, and Allah took his soul. Yazid ibn Abi Habib and others narrated all of this. He did not pledge allegiance to Ali or to Mu'awiya (may Allah be pleased with them both) [[From K and Z.]]. His death came before the people united upon Mu'awiya. It was also said that he died in Ifriqiya, but the correct view is that he died in Asqalan in the year 36 or 37 AH. It was also said: in the year 36 AH.

Hafs ibn Umar narrated from al-Hakam ibn Aban, from Ikrima, that this verse was revealed concerning al-Nadr ibn al-Harith, because he attempted to imitate the Qur'an, saying: "By those that grind with grinding, and those that knead with kneading, and those that bake with baking, and those that morsel with morseling."

**Verse 6:93 (continued):** ﴿If only you could see when the wrongdoers are in the agonies of death﴾

That is, its hardships and its throes. *Al-ghamra* means a hardship. Its origin is a thing that overwhelms other things and covers them. From this comes *ghamarahu al-ma'* (the water overwhelmed him) [[In K: *ghamaza*.]]. Then it was used with the meaning of hardships and adversities, and from this comes *ghamarat al-harb* (the throes of war). Al-Jawhari said: *al-ghamra* is hardship, and its plural is *ghumar*, like *nawba* and *nuwab*. Al-Qutami said, describing the ship of Noah, peace be upon him:

*And the time for those torrents to subside drew near*

And *ghamarat al-mawt* means its hardships.

﴿And the angels extend their hands﴾ is a subject and predicate, and the original form is *basitun* (extending). It was said: with punishment and iron hammers, according to al-Hasan and al-Dahhak. It was also said: for seizing their souls. In the revelation: ﴿If only you could see when the angels take the souls of those who disbelieve, striking their faces and their backs﴾ [[See vol. 8, p. 28.]]. So this verse combines both views. It is said: "He extended his hand toward him with harm" (*basata ilayhi yadahu bil-makruh*).

**(Emit your souls)** means: deliver them from the punishment if you are able to, and this is a rebuke. It was also said: "Bring them out forcibly," because the soul of the believer is eager to leave to meet his Lord, while the soul of the disbeliever is torn out with severe violence. It is said: "O wicked soul, come out in wrath, having incurred wrath, to the punishment of Allah," and this is how it is narrated in the hadith of Abu Hurayra and others. We have treated this in the book *al-Tadhkira*, and praise be to Allah. It was also said: this is like the saying of one who threatens someone he is punishing: "I will surely make you taste the punishment and I will surely bring out your soul." That is because they do not bring out their own souls; rather, the Angel of Death and his helpers seize them. It was also said: this is said to the disbelievers while they are in the Fire. The answer is omitted because of the magnitude of the matter, meaning: and if you saw the wrongdoers in this state, you would see a great punishment. *Al-hawn* and *al-hawan* are the same. ﴿You used to be arrogant﴾ means: you used to exalt yourselves and disdain to accept His signs.

The commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on Surah 6, verse 94:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And you have certainly come to Us alone, as We created you the first time﴾. This is an expression of the gathering (al-hashr). "Furada" is in the accusative position as a circumstantial state (hal, a descriptive state of the subject at the time of the action), and it is not declined because it has the feminine alif (alif al-ta'nith). Abu Haywa read "furadan" with nunation (tanwin, the addition of an "n" sound at the end of a word), and this is the dialect of Tamim, who do not say "furadun" in the nominative position. Ahmad ibn Yahya related "furada" without nunation, and he said: like thalath and rubaa'. "Furada" is the plural of "fardan," like sukara, the plural of sakran, and kusala, the plural of kaslan. It was said: its singular is "fard" with a sukun on the ra', "fard" with a kasra, "fard" with a fatha, and "fareed." The meaning is: you came to Us one by one, each of you alone, without family, without wealth, without child, and without a helper from those who used to accompany you in misguidance, and what you worshipped besides Allah did not benefit you. Al-A'raj read "fardaa" like sakraa and kuslaa, without an alif.

(as We created you the first time): meaning, alone, as you were created. It was also said: naked, as you came out from your mothers' wombs, barefoot, uncircumcised (ghurlan), and bahman (unblemished),[[The ghurl (plural of aghral) is the uncircumcised man. The bahm (plural of baheem) is, in origin, one whose color is not mixed with any other color. The meaning is that there is none among them of the defects and afflictions found in this world, such as blindness, leprosy, lameness, and other things.]] with nothing with them. The scholars said: on the Day of Resurrection, a servant will be gathered with the same limbs he had on the day he was born, so whoever had a limb cut off will have it restored to him on the Day of Resurrection. This is the meaning of His saying "ghurlan," that is, not circumcised, meaning that what was cut off during circumcision will be returned to them.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And you have left behind what We bestowed upon you﴾, that is, what We gave you and made you possess. Al-khawl is what Allah gives a person of servants and blessings.[[In k, ʿ, b: "al-niʿam" (blessings).]]

(behind your backs): that is, behind you.

(And We do not see with you your intercessors): that is, those whom you worshipped and made partners, meaning the idols, that is, My partners. The polytheists used to say that the idols are Allah's partners and our intercessors with Him.

(Your ties have certainly been severed among you): Nafi', al-Kisa'i, and Hafs read it with a fatha as an adverbial accusative (zarf), meaning: your connection has certainly been severed among you. The removal of the connection is indicated by His saying: ﴿And We do not see with you your intercessors whom you claimed﴾. This indicates the severing and the abandonment between them and their partners, since they disowned them and were not with them. Severing them is leaving off their connection with them, so it is good to imply the connection after "taqatta'" because the speech indicates it. In the reading of Ibn Mas'ud there is something that indicates the fatha in it: "laqad taqatta'a ma baynakum." This reading permits only the fatha, because you mentioned the one that is severed, which is "ma." It is as if he said: the connection has certainly been severed among you. It was also said: the meaning is that the matter has certainly been severed among you. The meanings are close. The rest read "baynukum" with a damma, as a noun that is not a zarf, so the verb is attributed to it and it is raised. What makes "bayna" a noun is that the preposition enters upon it, as in His saying: ﴿And between us and you there is a barrier﴾ and ﴿This is the parting between me and you﴾. It is also possible that the reading with the fatha has the meaning of the damma, and it was made accusative because it is used very frequently as an accusative zarf while it is in the position of the nominative. This is the view of al-Akhfash. Accordingly, the two readings have one meaning, so recite whichever of them you wish.

(And what you used to claim has gone astray from you): that is, it vanished.

(what you used to claim): that is, what you used to lie about in this world. It is narrated that this verse was revealed concerning al-Nadr ibn al-Harith. It is also narrated that A'isha (may Allah be pleased with her) recited the saying of Allah, Exalted is He: ﴿And you have certainly come to Us alone, as We created you the first time﴾, and she said: O Messenger of Allah, alas for shame! Will men and women be gathered together, looking at one another's private parts? The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "For every person among them on that Day there is a matter that occupies him" (the men will not look at the women, nor the women at the men, for each is preoccupied with his own concern). This is a sound hadith in the Sahih, which Muslim narrated with this meaning.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 6, verse 95:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, Allah is the splitter of the grain and the date-stone.﴾ He counted among the wonders of His making what their gods cannot do even to the least of it. Al-falq (splitting) means al-shaqq (cleaving): that is, He splits the dead date-stone and brings forth from it a green shoot, and likewise the grain. And from the green shoot He brings forth a dead date-stone and a grain. This is the meaning of ﴿He brings the living out of the dead and brings the dead out of the living﴾, related from al-Hasan and Qatadah. Ibn Abbas and al-Dahhak said: the meaning of faliq is khaliq (Creator). Mujahid said: by al-falq is meant the cleft that is in the grain and in the date-stone. Al-nawa is the plural of nawah (a stone or pit), and it applies to everything that has a pit, such as the mishmish [[kazbarj and ja'far]] and the peach.

(He brings the living out of the dead and brings the dead out of the living): He brings the living human being out of the dead drop of semen, and the dead drop of semen out of the living human being, related from Ibn Abbas. The saying of Qatadah and al-Hasan has already been mentioned, and this was discussed in (Al 'Imran) [[see vol. 4, p. 56.]]. In Sahih Muslim, from Ali: "By Him who split the grain and created the soul, indeed the Prophet, the Unlettered (ﷺ), made a covenant with me that none loves me except a believer, and none hates me except a hypocrite."

(That is Allah) is the subject and predicate.

(So how are you turned away?) From where are you being turned away from the truth, despite what you see of the power of Allah, Majestic and Exalted?

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 6, verse 96:

His statement, exalted is He: ﴿Splitter of the daybreak﴾ is an epithet (na't) of the Name of God, exalted is He; that is, "That is God, your Lord, the Splitter of the daybreak." It was also said that the meaning is that God is the Splitter of the daybreak. Al-subh and al-sabah are the beginning of the day, and likewise al-isbah, that is, the Splitter of the dawn every day, meaning al-fajr (the break of dawn). Al-isbah is the verbal noun (masdar) of asbaha. The meaning is: the one who splits light from darkness and uncovers it. Al-Dahhak said: "Splitter of the daybreak" means the Creator of the day. It is a definite noun (ma'rifah), and according to none of the grammarians is tanwin permissible in it.

al-Hasan and Isa ibn Umar read "fāliqu l-aṣbāḥi" with a fatha on the hamza, which is the plural of subh. Al-A'mash narrated from Ibrahim al-Nakha'i that he read "falaqa l-isbāha" in the form fa'ala, with the hamza kasra and the ha' fatha. Al-Hasan, Isa ibn Umar, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read "wa-ja'ala l-layla sakanan" without an alif. "Al-layla" is put in the accusative (nasb) by taking it as governed by the sense of "fāliq" in both places, since it carries the meaning of "falaqa," because it is a matter that has already occurred; so the first part of the speech is understood in light of its last part. Also, after it come past-tense verbs, namely His saying: "He made for you the stars" and "He sent down water from the sky," so the beginning of the speech is taken to agree with its end. This is strengthened by their consensus on putting "al-shams wa-l-qamar" (the sun and the moon) in the accusative by supposing a verb, and they did not take it as a governed noun in the genitive, as Makki stated, may God have mercy on him.

al-Nahhas said: Yazid ibn Qatib al-Sakuni read "jā'ilu l-layli sakanan wa-l-shamsi wa-l-qamari husbānan" with the genitive, as a conjunction according to the surface form (lafz). I say: Makki, al-Mahdawi and others mean the consensus of the seven readers. And God knows best. Ya'qub, in the transmission of Ruways from him, read "wa-jā'ilu l-layli sākinan." The people of Madinah read "wa-jā'ilu l-layli sakanā," that is, a place of rest.

In the Muwatta', on the authority of Yahya ibn Sa'id, it reached him that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) used to supplicate, saying: "O God, Splitter of the daybreak and Maker of the night a rest, and of the sun and the moon as a reckoning. Settle my debt for me, enrich me from poverty, and let me enjoy my hearing, my sight and my strength in Your way." If it is asked: how did he say "and let me enjoy my hearing and my sight," when in the books of al-Nasa'i, al-Tirmidhi and others it is (and make it the heir from me), and that perishes with the body? It is said to him: there is figurative speech (tajawwuz) in the utterance, and the meaning is: O God, do not let him perish before me. It has also been said that what is meant here by hearing and sight are Abu Bakr and Umar, on the basis of the Prophet's saying, peace be upon him, about them: "They are the hearing and the sight." But this is a remote interpretation; what is meant by them is the two organs.

The meaning of "husbānan" is: according to a reckoning on which the benefits of the servants depend. Ibn Abbas, regarding the saying of the Mighty and Majestic: "And the sun and the moon as a reckoning," said: that is, by calculation. Al-Akhfash said: husbān is the plural of hisab, like shihab and shuhban. Ya'qub said: husbān is the verbal noun of hasibtu l-shay' ahsubuhu husbānan, hisaban and hisbah, and al-hisab is the noun. Others said: God made the course of the sun and the moon by a reckoning that neither increases nor decreases, and by this God, Mighty and Majestic, guided them to His power and His oneness. It was also said: "husbānan" means light (diya'). Husbān in one dialect means fire, and God the Exalted has said: ﴿And He sends upon it a husbān from the sky﴾ [see vol. 10, p. 408]. Ibn Abbas said: fire. And al-husbānah is the small cushion.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 6, verse 97:

His saying, exalted is He: (And it is He who made for you the stars [[In MS K: from the perfection of His power.]]) He shows the perfection of His power, and in the stars there are many benefits. In this verse He mentions some of their benefits, and these are the benefits whose knowledge the Sharia has urged (people) to acquire. In the revelation: "And as a guard against every rebellious devil" [[See vol. 15, p. 64.]] and "We have made them missiles against the devils" [[See vol. 18, p. 210.]]. And "made" (ja'ala) here means "created" (khalaqa).

(We have detailed the signs) i.e., We have made them clear and explained in detail, so that they may be more effective in admonition (i'tibar).

(For a people who know)

He singled them out because they are the ones who benefit [[In MS K: by them.]] from them.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 6, verse 98:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿It is He who produced you from a single soul﴾ means Adam, peace be upon him. This has already been discussed at the beginning of the surah [[See vol. 6, p. 387.]].

(Fa-mustaqarrun) Ibn 'Abbas, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, al-Hasan, Abu 'Amr, 'Isa, al-A'raj, Shayba and al-Nakha'i read it with a kasra on the qaf, while the rest read it with a fatha. It is in the place of a nominative (raf') as the subject of a nominal sentence (mubtada'), except that the implied meaning for those who read the qaf with a kasra is fa-minha mustaqirr (so from her is a settled place), while the reading with a fatha means lahа mustaqarr (for her is a settled place). 'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud said: So for her there is a settled place in the womb and a place of deposit (mustawda') in the earth where she dies. This explanation supports the fatha reading. Al-Hasan said: "fa-mustaqarr" is in the grave. Most of the people of tafsir say: the mustaqarr is what is in the womb, and the mustawda' is what is in the loins (sulb); this was narrated by Sa'id ibn Jubayr from Ibn 'Abbas, and al-Nakha'i said it too. It is also narrated from Ibn 'Abbas: mustaqarr in the earth and mustawda' in the loins. Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: Ibn 'Abbas said to me, "Have you married?" I said, "No." He said: Indeed Allah, mighty and majestic, will bring forth from your back what He has deposited in it. It is also narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that the mustaqarr is one who has been created and the mustawda' is one who has not yet been created; al-Mawardi mentioned this. Also from Ibn 'Abbas: and a mustawda' with Allah. I say: In the revelation there is: ﴿And for you on the earth is a settled place and enjoyment for a time﴾, and the "istida'" (deposit) indicates their being in the grave until they are raised for reckoning. This has already been discussed in al-Baqara [[See vol. 1, p. 321.]].

(We have detailed the signs for a people who understand.) Qatada said: "fassalna" means we made clear and established. (And Allah knows best.)

**Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on Surah 6, verse 99 (part 1 of 2)**

There are seven issues in this verse.

**First:** His saying, ﴿And He it is who sends down water from the sky﴾, meaning rain.

﴿So We bring forth thereby the growth of every thing﴾, meaning every kind of vegetation. It was also said: the provision of every living creature.

﴿So We bring forth from it green [foliage]﴾. Al-Akhfash said: meaning *akhdar* (green), just as the Arabs say, "Arinīhā namiratan urikhā" [[The *ha'* in *arinīhā* refers to the cloud, and *al-thamar* refers to the cloud that has marks like those of a leopard (*namir*). It was also said: small clouds close to one another. Its singular is *namirah*, and *matarah* means *mātirah* (rain-bearing). The meaning is: if you see the sign of a thing, you know what follows it. It is said of a matter whose occurrence is certain when its signs and first indications appear. (From *Fara'id al-La'ali*, vol. 1, p. 252, Beirut edition.)]] *mutarah* (show me the cloud, I will show you the rain). *Al-khidr* [[*Al-khidr*: the green substance in plants, which is the substance of life, and is among the secrets of the power of the Creator, glorified is He.]] means the fresh green herbs. Ibn Abbas said: it means wheat, barley, *al-sult* [[*Al-sult* (pronounced with a vowel like *al-qufl*): a kind of white barley that has no husk.]], maize, rice, and all other grains.

﴿We bring forth from it grain piled up﴾, meaning that some of it is stacked upon other parts, like the ear of grain.

**Second:** His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿And from the palm trees, from their spathe, are clusters hanging low﴾. This is a beginning and a predicate (*mubtada' wa-khabar*). Al-Farra' permitted, outside the Qur'an, *qinwanan daniyatan* (in the accusative) as a coordination with what came before. Sibawayh said: some of the Arabs say *qunwān*. Al-Farra' said: this is the dialect of Qays, while the people of the Hijaz say *qinwān*, and Tamim say *qinyān*; then they all converge on the singular, saying *qinw* and *qanw*.

*Al-Tal'* is the sheath before it splits open to reveal the *al-ighrīd* (the inner flower-cluster). *Al-ighrīd* is also called *tal'*. *Al-tal'* is what is seen of the palm-date cluster. *Al-qinwān* is the plural of *qinw*, and its dual is *qinwān*, like *sinw* and *sinwān* (with a kasra on the *nūn*). The plural came in the form of the dual. Al-Jawhari and others said: the dual of *sinw* is *sinwān* and the plural is *sinwān* (with a damma on the *nūn*). *Al-qinw* is *al-idhq* (the cluster), and its plural is *al-qinwān* and *al-aqnā'*. He said:

*Tawīlat al-aqnā' wa-l-athākil* [[*Al-athākil*: the plural of *al-ithkāl* and *al-uthkūl* (a variant of *al-athkāl* and *al-ushkūl*), which is the cluster in which the *shamārīkh* (the stalks of the dates) are found. This is the second half of a line. Its first half, as in *al-Insan*, is: "Qad abṣarat Su'dā bihā kattā'ilī," and *al-katā'il* is the plural of *kutaylah*, which is a tall palm tree.]]

Others said: *aqnā'* is the plural of paucity (*jam' al-qillah*). Al-Mahdawi said: Ibn Hurmuz read *qanwān* with a fatha on the *qāf*, and it was also transmitted from him with a damma. With the fatha, it is a collective noun that is not broken plural, equivalent to *rakb* according to Sibawayh, and equivalent to *al-bāqir* and *al-jāmil*, because *fi'lān* is not among the patterns of the plural. The damma on the *qāf* is on the basis that it is the plural of *qinw*, which is *al-idhq* (with a kasra on the *'ayn*), and this is *al-kibāsah*, the cluster of the palm tree. *Al-idhq* (with a fatha on the *'ayn*) is the palm tree itself. It was also said: *al-qinwān* is *al-jummār* (the palm heart).

*Daniyah* means near, reachable by one who stands or sits. This is related from Ibn Abbas, al-Bara' ibn 'Azib, and others. Al-Zajjaj said: among them are near ones and among them are distant ones, so it was omitted, and similar to it is ﴿garments that protect you from the heat﴾ [[See vol. 10, p. 159.]]. He singled out the near ones for mention because one of the aims of the verse is to mention power and to bestow favour, and the favour is more evident in what is near at hand.

**Third:** His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿and gardens of grapes﴾, meaning and We brought forth gardens. Muhammad ibn 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Layla and al-A'mash read *wa-jannātun* in the nominative, and this is the sound reading from 'Asim's transmission. Abu 'Ubayd and Abu Hatim rejected this reading, and Abu Hatim even said it was an error (*humḥāl*), because gardens cannot come from palm trees. Al-Nahhas said: the reading is permissible, and the interpretation is not based on this, but it is in the nominative as a beginning, and the predicate is omitted, meaning "and for them are gardens." Just as a group of readers read ﴿and houris with wide, lovely eyes﴾ [[See vol. 17, p. 202.]]. Sibawayh, al-Kisa'i, and al-Farra' permitted this kind of construction, and there are many like it. On this same basis, *wa-ḥūran 'īnan* (in the accusative) was also reported by Sibawayh, who recited:

*Ji'nī bi-mithli Banī Badrin li-qawmihim ... aw mithla Usrati Manzūri ibn Sayyār* [[The line is by Jarir, addressing al-Farazdaq and boasting over him with the nobles of Qays, because they are his maternal relatives. Banu Badr are from Fazara, and among them is the nobility of Qays 'Aylan; Banu Sayyar are from Fazara, from Dhubyan, from Qays. (From *Sharh al-Shawahid* by al-Shantamari.)]]

It was also said: the estimate is "and gardens of grapes, We brought them forth," just as you say, "I honoured 'Abd Allah and his brother," meaning "and his brother I also honoured." As for the olive and the pomegranate, only the accusative is possible for them, by *ijma'* (scholarly consensus). It was also said: *wa-jannātin* in the nominative is coordinated with *qinwān* verbally, even though it is not of the same kind in meaning.

﴿And the olive and the pomegranate, similar and dissimilar﴾, meaning similar in their leaves: the leaf of the olive resembles the leaf of the pomegranate in covering the whole branch and in the size of the leaf, and dissimilar in taste. This is related from Qatadah and others. Ibn Juraij said: "similar" in appearance and "dissimilar" in taste, like two pomegranates whose colour is one but whose taste is different. The pomegranate and the olive are singled out for mention because of their nearness to them and their prominence among them. This is like His saying: ﴿Do they not look at the camels, how they are created?﴾ [[See vol. 20, p. 34.]] He directed them to the camels because they are the most familiar thing to them.

**Fourth:** His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿Look at its fruit when it bears fruit﴾, meaning a look of reflection, not a mere look of sight devoid of contemplation. In the language, *al-thamar* is the produce of trees. Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read *thumurihi* with a damma on the *tha'* and the *mīm*. The rest read it with a fatha on both, as the plural of *thamarah*, like *baqarah* and *baqar*, and *shajarah* and *shajar*. Mujahid said: *al-thamar* means kinds of wealth, and *al-tamar* is the fruit of the palm. It seems that the meaning according to Mujahid's view is: look at the wealth from which the fruit is obtained. So *al-thumur* with two dammas is the plural of *thimār*, which is wealth that bears fruit. It was reported from al-A'mash (in some copies, al-A'raj) *thumrihi*, with a damma on the *tha'* and a sukun on the *mīm*: the damma was dropped because it is heavy, seeking lightness. It is also possible that *thamar* is the plural of *thamarah*, like *badanah* and *badan*. It is also possible that *thamar* is the plural of a plural, so you say *thamarah*, *thimār*, and *thamar*, like *himār* and *humur*. It is also possible that it is the plural of *thamarah* like *khashabah* and *khashab*, not the plural of a plural.

**Fifth:** His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿and its ripening﴾. Muhammad ibn al-Sumayqa' read *wa-yāni'ihi* (with an *alif*), and Ibn Muhaysin and Ibn Abi Ishaq read *wa-yun'ihi* with a damma on the *yā'*. Al-Farra' said: this is the dialect of some people of Najd. It is said: *yana'a al-thamaru yay'a'u* (the fruit ripened), and *al-thamaru yani'un* (the fruit is ripe). And *ay'ana yun'u* (it ripened) and the fruit is *muni'un*. The meaning is: its ripeness. *Yana'a* and *ay'ana* when it ripens and reaches maturity. Al-Hajjaj said in his sermon: "I see heads that have ripened, and the time of their harvest has come." Ibn al-Anbari said: *al-yan'* is the plural of *yani'*, like *rakib* and *rakb*, and *tajir* and *tajr*, and it is the one who has reached maturity and attained full growth. Al-Farra' said: *ay'ana* is more than *yana'a*, and its meaning is red. From this is what is reported in the hadith of *li'an* (mutual cursing): "If she bears him red like the *yanah*," and the *yanah* is a red bead; it is said that it is carnelian or a kind of it.

The verse indicates, for the one who reflects and looks with his eye and his heart, the look of one who contemplates, that changing things must have a changer. This is because He, Exalted is He, said: "Look at its fruit when it bears fruit and its ripening." You see it first as a sheath (*ṭal'*), then as *ighrīd* when the sheath splits open to reveal it. *Al-ighrīd* is also called *ḍaḥk*, then *balah* (unripe dates), then *sayyab* (soft and watery), then *jidāl*, when it turns green and becomes round before it hardens, then *busr* when it becomes large, then *zahw* when it turns red; it is said *azhā yuzhī*. Then *mūkat* when spots of ripening (*irṭāb*) appear on it. If this starts from the stem end, it is *mudhnibah*, and this is *al-tadhnūb*. When it softens, it is *tha'dah*. When the ripening reaches half of it, it is *mujazza'ah*. When it reaches two-thirds of it, it is *ḥulqānah*. When the ripening covers all of it, it is *munsabitah*; it is said *ruṭab munsabit*. Then it dries and becomes dates (*tamr*). So God, Exalted is He, by its movement from state to state, its change, and its coming into existence after it was not, alerted (the reader) to His oneness and the perfection of His power, and that it has a Maker who is powerful and knowing. It also indicates the possibility of resurrection, because plants come into being again after drying out. Al-Jawhari said: *yana'a al-thamaru yay'a'u*, and *yay'a'u yan'an wa-yunū'an*, meaning it ripened.

**Sixth:** Ibn al-'Arabi said: Malik said: *al-ī'nā'* (ripening) is goodness without spoilage or *naqsh* (pricking). Malik said: *naqsh* is when the experts prick the fruit until it becomes soft (*yurṭab*), meaning it is pierced so that air enters it quickly and it softens rapidly. That is not the ripening intended in the Qur'an, nor is it the one to which the Messenger of God (ﷺ) tied (his ruling)

...the sale. Rather, it is what comes from its own nature without effort. In some lands of figs, which are the cold lands, it does not ripen until a stick greased with oil is inserted into its mouth. When it ripens, its sale becomes lawful, because that is the necessity of the air and the custom of those lands. Had it not been so, it would not have ripened at the time of ripeness.

I say: This ripeness (al-yan', the stage of maturity) upon which the permissibility of selling dates depends, by which their eating becomes wholesome and they are safe from blight, occurs at the rising of al-Thurayya (the Pleiades), through the custom that Allah, glory be to Him, has made to flow, and which He has perfected with His knowledge and power.

Al-Mu'alla ibn Asad related from Wuhayb, from 'Asal ibn Sufyan, from 'Ata', from Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "When al-Thurayya rises in the morning, the blight is lifted from the people of the land." Al-Thurayya is the star (the Pleiades), and there is no disagreement about this. Its rising in the morning is on the twelfth night that passes of the month of Ayyar, which is the month of May.

In al-Bukhari: "Kharijah ibn Zayd ibn Thabit informed me that Zayd ibn Thabit would not sell the fruits of his land until al-Thurayya rose, whereupon the yellow was distinguished from the red."

The seventh issue: Those who dropped the rule of calamities (jawa'ih, unforeseen losses) to fruits relied on these reports, and on what is similar to them of the Prophet's (ﷺ) prohibition of selling fruit until its goodness appears (yabdu salahuha, its ripeness becomes evident), and his prohibition of selling fruits until the blight is gone. Uthman ibn Suraqah said: "I asked Ibn 'Umar, 'When is this?' He said: 'The rising of al-Thurayya.'"

Al-Shafi'i said: "It has not been established for me that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) commanded the removal of calamities. Had it been established for me, I would not have disregarded it. The established principle agreed upon is that whoever buys what may lawfully be sold and takes possession of it, the loss is his." He said: "And if I were to hold the removal of calamities, I would apply it to both small and great." This is the view of al-Thawri and the Kufans.

Malik and most of the people of Madinah went to its removal, based on the hadith of Jabir that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) commanded the removal of calamities. It was related by Muslim. 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz used to judge by it, and it is the view of Ahmad ibn Hanbal and all the people of hadith. The Zahiriyyah (Literalists) removed it from the buyer in both small and great amounts, on the generality of the hadith. However, Malik and his companions considered that the calamity must reach one third of the fruit or more; what was less than a third they disregarded and treated as incidental, since no fruit is free from either the small part of its goodness being lost or some slight corruption reaching a small part of it. Asbagh and Ashhab did not look at the fruit but at its value: if the value was a third or more, it was removed from him.

A calamity (jaihah), according to Ibn al-Qasim, is what cannot be prevented. On this basis, theft is not a calamity; so also in the Kitab of Muhammad. In the Kitab it is stated that it is a calamity, and this was related from Ibn al-Qasim, but his companions and people disagreed with him.

Mutarrif and Ibn al-Majishun said: Whatever reaches the fruit from the sky, such as mildew, hail, drought, or heat, or the breaking of trees by what is not the work of a human being, is a calamity. Disagreement arose about drought (al-'atash). According to the narration of Ibn al-Qasim, it is a calamity. The correct view regarding vegetables is that there is a calamity in them, as in fruit.

Whoever sells fruit before its ripeness on condition that it be left on the tree is void, and the sale is annulled and returned, because of the prohibition against it, and because it is consuming people's property wrongfully. This is due to his (ﷺ) saying: "Consider: if Allah withholds the fruit, by what right does one of you take his brother's property?" This is the view of the majority. Abu Hanifah and his companions authenticated it, and they interpreted the prohibition as disapproval (karahah). The majority went to the permissibility of selling it before its ripeness on condition of cutting it. al-Thawri and Ibn Abi Layla prohibited it, holding fast to the prohibition that came concerning this. The majority specified this by clear analogy (qiyas jali), because it is a known item of sale whose possession is valid at the time of the contract, so its sale is valid like other sold items.

The Almighty's words: ﴿They made the jinn partners with God﴾. This mentions another kind of their ignorance. That is, some of them believed that there were partners of God among the jinn. An-Nahhas said: "al-jinna" is the first object and "shuraka'a" is the second object, like ﴿and made you kings﴾ and "wa ja'altu lahu malan mamdudan" (﴿and to whom I granted abundant wealth﴾). Such constructions are common in the Qur'an. The intended meaning is: "They made the jinn partners of God." It is also possible that "al-jinna" is an appositive (badal) for "shuraka'a," and the second object is "lillah." Al-Kisa'i permitted the nominative "al-jinnu" to mean "they are the jinn."

"Wa khalaqahum" is the reading of the majority, meaning: God created those who made partners for Him. It was also said that it means: God created the jinn, who were the partners. Ibn Mas'ud recited "wa huwa khalaqahum" with the added "huwa." Yahya ibn Ya'mur recited "wa khalqahum" with a sukun on the lam, and he said: that is, "they made their creation partners of God," because they used to create a thing and then worship it.

The verse was revealed concerning the polytheists of the Arabs. The meaning of their associating the jinn with God is that they obeyed them in the way they obeyed God, the Mighty and Majestic. This was narrated from al-Hasan and others. Qatada and al-Suddi said: they are those who said that the angels are the daughters of God. Al-Kalbi said: it was revealed concerning the zanadiqa (heretics), who said that God and Iblis are two brothers: God is the creator of humans and animals, and Iblis is the creator of the jinn, the beasts of prey and the scorpions. Close to this is the doctrine of the Magians, who said that the world has two creators: an eternal god, and a second one, a devil, originated from the thought of the eternal god. They claimed that the creator of evil is originated. Likewise the Ha'itiyya of the Mu'tazila (a rationalist theological school), who were followers of Ahmad ibn Ha'it, claimed that the world has two creators: the eternal god, and another that is originated, which God, the Mighty and Majestic, created first and then entrusted with the management of the world, and which will call creatures to account in the Hereafter. Exalted is God above what the wrongdoers and deniers say, a great exaltation.

"Wa kharaqu" is the recitation of Nafi' with shaddah (tashdid), indicating intensification (ta'thir), because the polytheists claimed that God has daughters, who are the angels, and they called them jinn because they are hidden (ijtinan). The Christians claimed that the Messiah is the son of God, and the Jews said: 'Uzayr is the son of God. Thus this became frequent among their disbelief, so the verb was made intensive to match the meaning. Exalted is God above what they say. The rest of the readers recited it with the lighter form (takhfif), indicating diminution (taqlil).

Al-Hasan al-Basri was asked about the meaning of "wa kharaqu lahu" with shaddah, and he said: it is only "wa kharaqu" with takhfif, an Arabic word. When a man lied in the assembly, it was said: "kharaqaha, wa rabbi al-Ka'bah" (he invented it, by the Lord of the Ka'bah). The lexicographers said: the meaning of "kharaqu" is "ikhtalaqu" (they fabricated) and "iftaʿalu" (they made up). "Wa kharaqu" is in the intensive form. Mujahid, Qatada, Ibn Zayd and Ibn Jurayj said: "kharaqu" means "they lied." It is said that the meanings of kharaqa, ikhtaraqa and ikhtalaqa are the same, that is, "ahdatha" (he originated it).

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 6, verse 101:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿The Originator of the heavens and the earth﴾, meaning, the one who brought them into being; so how could it be possible for Him to have a son? "Badi'" (Originator) is the predicate of an implied subject, meaning, "He is the Originator." Al-Kisa'i permitted its genitive case as an adjective of Allah, exalted and mighty is He, and its accusative case in the sense of "Originating the heavens and the earth." This is an error according to the Basrans, because the active participle works like its verb only if it is a complement of "al" (the definite article) in every case; if it is not a complement of "al," it works under two conditions according to the Basrans: that it has the meaning of the present or the future. Al-Kisa'i permitted its working when it refers to the past.

(﴿Where could He have a son?﴾) meaning, from where could He have a son? The offspring of everything is its like, and He has no like.

(﴿And He has no consort﴾), meaning, no wife. (﴿And He created everything﴾) is a general statement whose meaning is particular, meaning, He created the world. His speech and the attributes of His essence do not enter into this. A similar example is His saying: ﴿My mercy encompasses everything﴾, and it did not encompass Iblis nor whoever died in disbelief. A similar example is His saying: ﴿It destroys everything﴾, and it did not destroy the heavens and the earth.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Such is Allah, your Lord; there is no god but Him﴾. "Dhalikum" (that) is in the nominative position as the subject (mubtada', the grammatical subject). "Allahu rabbukum" (Allah, your Lord) is in apposition (badal, substitution). "Khaliqu kulli shay'" (Creator of everything) is the predicate (khabar) of the subject. It is also permissible for "rabbukum" to be the predicate, with "khaliq" as a second predicate, or for there to be an elided subject (mubtada' muqaddar), meaning: "He is the Creator." Al-Kisa'i and the reciters permitted the accusative (nasb) for it.

﴿Eyes cannot perceive Him﴾. God, glorified is He, declares that He is exempt from the attributes of created things, and among them is perception in the sense of encompassing and delimiting, as all other created things are perceived. Vision, however, is established. Al-Zajjaj said: the meaning is that the essence of His reality cannot be reached, just as you say, "I have grasped such-and-such." For reports about seeing Him on the Day of Resurrection have been authentically transmitted from the Prophet (ﷺ). Ibn 'Abbas said: "﴿Eyes cannot perceive Him﴾" refers to this world, and the believers will see Him in the Hereafter, because God informs of this in His words: ﴿Faces that Day will be radiant, looking toward their Lord﴾. [See vol. 19, p. 105.] Al-Suddi also said this. This is the best of what has been said, because of the indication of the revelation and the reports that have come concerning seeing God in Paradise. Its explanation will come in Surah Yunus. [See vol. 8, p. 330.]

It has also been said that ﴿eyes cannot perceive Him﴾ means that they cannot encompass Him, while He encompasses them; this is also reported from Ibn 'Abbas. It has also been said that the meaning is that the eyes of the hearts cannot perceive Him, that is, the intellects cannot perceive Him so as to imagine Him, since ﴿there is nothing like unto Him﴾. [See vol. 16, pp. 7 and 52.] It has also been said that the meaning is that created eyes in this world cannot perceive Him, but He creates for whomever He wills of His honored servants a sight and perception by which he sees Him, as with Muhammad (peace be upon him). For seeing God in this world is rationally possible, since if it were not possible, Moses' request (peace be upon him) would have been impossible, and it is impossible that a prophet should be ignorant of what is permissible for God and what is not. Rather, he asked only for what is permissible and not impossible.

The early generations (al-salaf) differed about whether our Prophet (peace be upon him) saw his Lord. In Sahih Muslim, from Masruq, who said: I was reclining beside 'A'isha, and she said: "O Abu 'A'isha [Abu 'A'isha: the kunya of the Imam Masruq], three things, whoever speaks of any one of them has greatly slandered God." I said: "What are they?" She said: "Whoever claims that Muhammad saw his Lord has greatly slandered God." He said: I had been reclining, so I sat up and said: "O Mother of the Believers, give me time and do not hasten me. Did not God, Mighty and Majestic, say: ﴿And he certainly saw Him at the clear horizon﴾ [See vol. 19, p. 239.] and ﴿And he certainly saw Him in another descent﴾? [See vol. 17, p. 92.]" She said: "I was the first of this Community to ask the Messenger of God (ﷺ) about this, and he said: 'It is only Gabriel. I did not see him in his true form, in which he was created, except on these two occasions. I saw him descending from the sky, filling the vastness of his form between the sky and the earth.'" Then she said: "Have you not heard that God, Mighty and Majestic, says: ﴿Eyes cannot perceive Him, but He perceives the eyes, and He is the Subtle, the All-Aware﴾? Have you not heard God, Mighty and Majestic, say: ﴿And it is not for a human that God should speak to him except by revelation or from behind a veil, or send a messenger﴾ up to His words ﴿Most High, Wise﴾? [See vol. 16, pp. 7 and 52.]" She said: "Whoever claims that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) concealed anything of the Book of God has greatly slandered God, while God says: ﴿O Messenger, deliver what has been revealed to you from your Lord; and if you do not, then you have not conveyed His message﴾. [See vol. 6, p. 242.]" She said: "Whoever claims that he informs of what will happen tomorrow has greatly slandered God, while God says: ﴿Say: None in the heavens and the earth knows the unseen except God﴾." [See vol. 13, p. 225.]

This is the view of 'A'isha, may God be pleased with her, that there was no seeing, and that he only saw Gabriel. Ibn Mas'ud held the same, and likewise Abu Hurayrah, may God be pleased with him, that he saw Gabriel, though two reports from them differ.

Among hadith scholars, jurists, and theologians (al-mutakallimun), a group denied this and rejected the possibility of seeing Him. From Ibn 'Abbas it is reported that he saw Him with his own eye, and this is the well-known position of his. His evidence is God's words: ﴿The heart did not lie about what it saw﴾. [See vol. 17, p. 92.] 'Abd Allah ibn al-Harith said: Ibn 'Abbas and Ubayy ibn Ka'b met, and Ibn 'Abbas said: "As for us, the sons of Hashim, we say that Muhammad saw his Lord twice." Then Ibn 'Abbas said: "Do you wonder that intimate friendship (khullah) was for Abraham, speech for Moses, and vision for Muhammad (ﷺ), and upon them all be peace?" He said: Ka'b then exclaimed "Allahu akbar" until the mountains echoed back to him, then said: "God divided His vision and His speech between Muhammad and Moses, peace be upon them both. He spoke to Moses, and Muhammad (ﷺ) saw Him."

'Abd al-Razzaq reported that al-Hasan used to swear by God that Muhammad certainly saw his Lord. Abu 'Umar al-Talamankί reported this from 'Ikrimah, and some theologians reported it from Ibn Mas'ud, though the first report from him is more famous. Ibn Ishaq reported that Marwan asked Abu Hurayrah: "Did Muhammad see his Lord?" He said: "Yes." Al-Naqqash reported from Ahmad ibn Hanbal that he said: "I say according to the hadith of Ibn 'Abbas: he saw Him with his eye, he saw Him!" until his breath was cut off, meaning Ahmad's breath.

Shaykh Abu al-Hasan al-Ash'ari and a group of his companions held this view, that Muhammad (ﷺ) saw God with his sight and the eyes of his head. This was also said by Anas, Ibn 'Abbas, 'Ikrimah, al-Rabi' and al-Hasan. Al-Hasan used to swear by God, besides whom there is no god, that Muhammad certainly saw his Lord. A group, among them Abu al-'Aliyah, al-Qurazi, and al-Rabi' ibn Anas, said: he saw his Lord only with his heart and inner being. This is also reported from Ibn 'Abbas and 'Ikrimah.

Abu 'Umar said: Ahmad ibn Hanbal said: "He saw Him with his heart," and he shrank from saying that He was seen in this world with the eyes. Malik ibn Anas said: "He was not seen in this world, because He is everlasting, and the everlasting is not seen by the perishable. When they are in the Hereafter and are given everlasting eyes, they will see the Everlasting with the everlasting." Al-Qadi 'Iyad said: This is a fine and graceful statement, and there is no proof in it of impossibility except from the standpoint of weakness of capacity. When God strengthens whomever He wills of His servants and empowers him to bear the burdens of vision, it is not impossible in his case. Some of this will come concerning Moses (peace be upon him) in Surah al-A'raf, God willing. [See p. 278 of this part.]

﴿And He perceives the eyes﴾. That is, nothing is hidden from Him that He does not see and know. He specified "eyes" only for the sake of paronomasia (tajnis) in the speech. Al-Zajjaj said: In this statement is evidence that created beings cannot perceive eyes, that is, they do not know the true nature of sight, or what it is in the eyes by which a person sees and not through his other limbs. Then He said: ﴿And He is the Subtle, the All-Aware﴾, that is, the Gentle toward His servants. It is said: "So-and-so was gentle (lataf) with so-and-so," meaning he dealt with him gently. Gentleness in action is kindness in it. Gentleness (lutf) from God is divine success (tawfiq) and protection ('isma). "He treated him kindly with such-and-such," meaning he was good to him with it. The noun is "lutaf" with a vowel on the first letter. It is said: "A gift (lutafah) came to us from so-and-so," meaning a present. Al-mulatafah is kindness, according to al-Jawhari and Ibn Faris. Abu al-'Aliyah said: The meaning is: Subtle in extracting things, All-Aware of their places. Al-Junayd said: "The Subtle is the One who illuminates your heart with guidance, nourishes your body with food, grants you guardianship in trial, guards you while you are in the blaze, and admits you into the Paradise of refuge." Other things have been said, whose meanings return to the sense of gentleness and similar. The views of the scholars on this will come in Surah al-Shura, God willing. [See vol. 16, p. 16.]

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 6, verse 104:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿There has certainly come to you clear evidences (baṣā'ir) from your Lord﴾, meaning signs and proofs by which one sees and is guided. It is the plural of baṣīrah, which means proof (dalālah). The poet said:

They came, their proofs upon their shoulders... and my proof runs upon it, a swift steed.

[[What appears in the lexicon books is: "They departed ... etc.," and that this verse belongs to al-Asha' al-Ja'fi. He means: they left the blood of their father behind them, meaning they did not avenge it, while I am seeking my vengeance. Al-'Itd (with a vowel on the tā' or its kasra): the steed that is complete in form, swift in its leap, prepared for running, with no unsteadiness or looseness. Al-Wa'a (with a fatha on the wāw and a long vowel): the swift steed of capable build.]]

By al-baṣīrah he means the clear, manifest proof. He described the proof as "coming" to magnify its importance, since it is like an absent thing whose arrival is awaited by the soul, as one says: "Well-being has come when illness has departed, and good fortune has approached while misfortune has turned away."

(So whoever sees, it is for his own self) al-ibṣār is perception by the sense of sight; that is, whoever seeks proof and recognizes the truth, benefit returns to his own self.

(And whoever is blind) does not seek proof, and so he becomes like the blind man; upon his own self his blindness falls.

(And I am not a guardian over you) meaning I have not been commanded to protect you so that you do not destroy yourselves. It was also said: meaning I cannot keep you from the punishment of God. And it was said: "bi-ḥafīẓ" means a watcher, one who counts your deeds over you. Rather, I am only a messenger who conveys to you the messages of my Lord, and He is the Guardian over you; nothing of your actions is hidden from Him.

Al-Zajjaj said: This was revealed before the obligation of fighting, then he was commanded to restrain them by the sword from worshipping idols.

**The Qur'an: "And thus do We vary the verses"**

The kaf in *kadhalika* (thus) is in the accusative position. The meaning is: We vary the verses in the way We have recited them to you, that is, as We have varied the verses concerning promise, threat, admonition and warning in this surah, and We vary them in other surahs.

﴿and that they may say, "You have studied"﴾. The waw in *wa-liyaqulu* is a conjunction coordinating with an implied clause. The meaning is: We vary the verses so that the proof may be established, and so that they may say, "You have studied." It is also said that the meaning is: We varied them so that they would say, "You have studied." In that case the lam is the lam of consequence (*lam al-sayrura*, indicating an outcome that was not necessarily intended).

Al-Zajjaj said: This is like saying, "So-and-so wrote this book for his own destruction," meaning that his affair ended in that outcome. Likewise, when the verses were varied, their affair came to the point where they said, "You have studied and learned from Jabr and Yasar." These two were Christian boys in Makkah, and the people of Makkah said, "He is only learning from them."

Al-Nahhas said: There is another good interpretation of the meaning, namely that "We vary the verses" means We bring them one verse after another, so that they say, "You have studied them with us," and they join the first to the last. This is the literal meaning, whereas what Abu Ishaq said is figurative (*majaz*).

There are seven readings of *darasta* (you have studied). Abu 'Amr and Ibn Kathir read *darasta* with an alif between the dal and the ra, in the pattern of *faa'alta* (*dara-sta*, "you have studied with [others]"). This is the reading of Ali, Ibn Abbas, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Mujahid, Ikrima and the people of Makkah. Ibn Abbas said: The meaning of *darasta* is "you have recited [to them] and they have recited [to you]." Ibn Amir read *darasta* with a fatha on the sin and a sukun on the ta, without an alif, in the pattern of *kharajat*. This is the reading of al-Hasan. The rest read *darasta*, in the pattern of *kharajta*.

According to the first reading, the meaning is "you have studied with the People of the Book, and they have studied with you," that is, you discussed with them and they discussed with you. Sa'id ibn Jubayr said this. The Qur'an indicates this meaning in the words of God reporting about them: ﴿and other people helped him with it﴾, that is, the Jews helped the Prophet (ﷺ) with the Qur'an, and they discussed it with him. All of this is the statement of the polytheists. Similar to it is their saying: ﴿"They are fables of the former peoples. He has had them written down, and they are dictated to him morning and evening."﴾ And also: ﴿When it is said to them, "What has your Lord sent down?" they say, "Fables of the former peoples."﴾

It is also said that the meaning is "you have studied with us" (*darastana*), and so its meaning is the same as *darasta*. This was mentioned by al-Nahhas, who preferred it. The first view was mentioned by Makki. Al-Nahhas claimed that it is figurative, as in the verse of poetry:

*"So for death is what the mother bears"*

[This is the second half of a line; its first half, as in al-Mughni (under the letter lam), is: *"Fa-in yakun al-mawt afnahum"* ("If death has destroyed them").]

As for the one who reads *darasat* (feminine, with the verb agreeing with the feminine noun *ayat*, "verses"), the best that has been said about its reading is that the meaning is: "lest they say, 'They have been effaced and erased,' and Muhammad (ﷺ) does not bring anything other than them." Qatada read *durisat*, meaning "they have been recited." Sufyan ibn 'Uyayna narrated from Amr ibn 'Ubayd, from al-Hasan, that he read *darasat*. Abu Hatim held that this reading is not permissible, saying: "Because verses cannot be studied together." Others said: The reading with this form is permissible, and the meaning is not what Abu Hatim thought. Rather, its meaning is "your community has studied them," that is, "your community has studied with you," even though no mention of it has preceded. This is like the verse: ﴿until it was hidden behind the veil﴾.

Al-Akhfash reported *wa-liyaqulu darasta* and said it has the same meaning as *darasta*, but is more emphatic. Abu al-Abbas reported that it was read *wa-liyaqulu darasta* with the lam pronounced with a sukun, as a command. In this reading there is a sense of threat, that is, "let them say whatever they wish, for the truth is clear," as He, mighty and majestic, said: ﴿So let them laugh little and weep much﴾. As for the one who pronounces the lam with a kasra, it is according to him the lam of purpose (*lam kay*, "in order that").

All these readings return in derivation to one thing: softening and making easy (*al-talyin wa-al-tadhlil*). *Darasta* comes from *darasa yadrusu dirasatan*, which means reading in front of another. It is also said: *darastuhu* means I made him submissive through much reading. Its origin is *darasa al-ta'ama*, meaning he trampled the grain, and *al-diyas* (threshing) is *al-dirас* in the dialect of the people of al-Sham. It is also said: its origin is from *darastu al-thawba adrusuhu darsan*, meaning I wore it out. The garment *darasa darsan*, meaning it became worn out. This also returns to the meaning of submission. It is said that the Idrisi (Idris, peace be upon him) was so named because of his frequent study of the Book of God. One says: *darastu al-kutub*, *tadarastuha* and *iddarastuha*, meaning I studied them. *Darastu al-kitab darsan wa-dirasatan*. *Darasat al-mar'a darsan*, meaning the woman menstruated. It is said that the vagina of a woman is called *Abu Adras*, and this derives from menstruation. *Al-Darsu* also means a hidden path. Al-Asma'i reported: *ba'irun lam yudarras*, meaning a camel that has not been ridden. *Darastu* also derives from *darasa al-manzilu*, meaning it became effaced when it fell into disrepair.

Ibn Mas'ud and his companions, Ubayy, Talha and al-A'mash read *wa-liyaqulu darasa*, meaning Muhammad (ﷺ) studied the verses.

﴿and that We may make it clear to a people who know﴾. That is, the statement and the variation, or the Qur'an.

The Exalted said: ﴿Follow what is revealed to you from your Lord﴾. It means the Qur'an. That is, do not occupy your heart and your thoughts with them, but devote yourself to the worship of Allah. "There is no god but He, and turn away from the polytheists" is abrogated (mansukh).

"The words of Allah, the Exalted: (Had Allah willed, they would not have associated others with Him). He stated explicitly that shirk occurs by His will, and this is a refutation of the doctrine of the Qadariyya (the Qadariyya, the early school that denied divine predestination). As mentioned previously.

(And We have not appointed you a guardian over them) meaning: it is not possible for you to protect them from the punishment of Allah.

(Nor are you a manager over them) meaning: one who takes charge of their affairs concerning their interests, whether for their religion or their worldly life, so that you could be gentle with them in obtaining what is due to them. You are neither a protector in that matter nor a trustee in this; you are only a messenger who conveys. And this was before he was commanded to fight."

**Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 6, verse 108:**

There are five issues in it.

The first: His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And do not revile those whom they invoke besides Allah﴾. It is a prohibition (nahy).

(Then they would revile Allah, ﴿فَيَسُبُّوا اللَّهَ﴾) is the answer to the prohibition. So He, glorified is He, forbade the believers from reviling their idols, because He knew that if they reviled them, the disbelievers would flee and their disbelief would increase. Ibn 'Abbas said: The disbelievers of Quraysh said to Abu Talib, "Either you forbid Muhammad and his companions from reviling our gods and disparaging them, or we will revile his God and insult him." So the verse was revealed.

The second: The scholars said: its ruling remains in this community in every circumstance. Whenever the disbeliever is in a position of strength, and it is feared that he will revile Islam, the Prophet (ﷺ), or Allah, Mighty and Majestic, then it is not permissible for a Muslim to revile their crosses, their religion, or their churches, nor to engage in anything that leads to that, because it amounts to inciting disobedience. And the idols are referred to by ﴿الَّذِينَ﴾ ("those who"), although they do not reason, in accordance with the beliefs of the disbelievers concerning them.

The third: In this verse there is also a kind of conciliation (muwada'ah), and evidence for the obligation of applying the principle of blocking the means (sadd al-dhara'i', i.e., closing avenues that lead to harm). It also contains evidence that the one who is in the right may refrain from his right when exercising it would lead to harm in the religion. And from this meaning is what is related from 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, that he said: "Do not issue a final judgment between relatives, for fear of severing ties." Ibn al-'Arabi said: If the right is obligatory, one takes it in every case; but if it is permissible, then this statement applies to it.

The fourth: His saying, Exalted is He: (﴿عَدْواً﴾), that is, out of ignorance and transgression.
