It is related from the people of Mecca that they read ﴿عَدْواً﴾ with a damma on the 'ayn and the dal and a shaddah on the waw, and this is the reading of al-Hasan, Abu Raja' and Qatadah; it goes back to the first reading, and both have the same meaning: injustice. The people of Mecca also read ﴿عَدُوًّا﴾ with a fatha on the 'ayn and a damma on the dal, meaning "enemy." It is singular but stands for the plural, as He said: "They are an enemy to me, except the Lord of the worlds" [See vol. 13, p. 110.]. And He said: "They are the enemy" [See vol. 18, p. 125.], and it is in the accusative either as a verbal noun (masdar) or as an object of purpose (maf'ul min ajlih).

The fifth: His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Thus We have made appealing to every community their deeds﴾, that is: just as We made their deeds appealing to these people, so likewise We made the deeds of every community appealing to them. Ibn 'Abbas said: We made obedience appealing to the people of obedience, and disbelief appealing to the people of disbelief. This is like His saying: "Thus Allah leads astray whom He wills and guides whom He wills" [See vol. 10, p. 172.]. And in this there is a refutation of the Qadariyyah (those who deny divine decree).

The commentary of al-Qurtubi, *al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Qur'an*, on Surah 6, verse 109:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And they swore by Allah their most emphatic oaths that if a sign came to them, they would surely believe in it.﴾ In this there are two issues.

The first: His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿And they swore﴾, meaning they took oaths. The "jahd" of an oath (its strongest form) is the most emphatic of them, and it is the one made by Allah. So His saying "jahd aymanihim" means the utmost of their oaths, the extent to which their knowledge reached and their ability went. This is because they believed that Allah is the Supreme Deity, and that these idols they worshipped were only [worshipped] under the assumption that they would bring them near to Allah in closeness, as He reported about them in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿We only worship them so that they may bring us near to Allah in closeness﴾ [See vol. 15, p. 123]. They used to swear by their fathers, by the idols, and by other things, and they swore by Allah, Exalted is He. They called it the "jahd" of the oath when the oath was by Allah.

"Jahd" is in the accusative as a verbal noun (masdar), and its governing verb is "aqsamu" according to the view of Sibawayh, because it carries the same meaning. "Al-jahd" (with a fatha on the jim) means hardship; one says, "I did that with jahd." "Al-juhd" (with a damma on the jim) means capacity; one says, "This is my juhd," meaning my capacity. Some scholars treat the two as one and cite His saying: ﴿and those who find nothing but their juhd﴾ [See vol. 8, p. 215]. It is also read "juhdahum" with a fatha, related from Ibn Qutaybah.

The occasion of revelation, as the exegetes mentioned, al-Qurazi, al-Kalbi and others, is that Quraysh said: "O Muhammad, you inform us that Musa struck the rock with his staff and twelve springs gushed forth from it, that Isa used to revive the dead, and that Thamud had a she-camel. So bring us some of these signs so that we may believe you." He said: "What do you wish?" They said: "Make al-Safa into gold for us. By Allah, if you do it, we will all follow you." The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) stood up and supplicated, and Jibril (peace be upon him) came to him and said: "If you wish, al-Safa will become gold for them, but if Allah sends a sign and they do not believe after it, He will surely punish them, so leave them until one of them repents." The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Rather, let one of them repent." Then this verse was revealed.

Allah made clear that whoever is foreknown by the eternal knowledge not to believe, he will not believe, even if he swears that he will surely believe.

The second issue: His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿their most emphatic oaths﴾. It was said: its meaning is with the most severe oaths among them. Here arises an important legal issue, namely a man's saying: "The oaths are binding on him if such-and-such is the case." Ibn al-Arabi said: This form of oath was known at the beginning of Islam in a form other than this one. They used to say: "Upon me is the strongest thing anyone has ever taken from anyone," and Malik said: his wives are divorced. Then this form multiplied until among people it came to a form whose mother is this one. Our shaykh al-Fihri al-Tarsusi used to say: He must feed thirty poor people if he breaks it, because his saying "al-aymanu" (the oaths) is the plural of "yamin" (oath); and if he had said "upon me is an oath" and broke it, we would have obligated him to one expiation (kaffara). If he had said "upon me are two oaths," he would be obligated to two expiations if he broke them. "Al-aymanu" is the plural of "yamin," so he is obligated to three expiations in them.

I say: Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Mughith mentioned in his documents that the shaykhs of Qayrawan disagreed about it. Abu Muhammad ibn Abi Zayd said: He is obligated, regarding his wife, to three divorces, the pilgrimage on foot to Makkah, distributing one third of his wealth, an expiation of an oath, and the freeing of a slave. Ibn Mughith said: Ibn Arfa'a Ra'suhu and Ibn Badr, among the jurists of Toledo, also said this. Shaykh Abu Imran al-Fasi, Abu al-Hasan al-Qabisi and Abu Bakr ibn Abd al-Rahman al-Qarawi said: He is obligated to one single divorce if he had no intention. Among their proofs for this is the narration of Ibn al-Hasan in his hearing from Ibn Wahb, in his saying: "The strongest thing anyone has ever taken from anyone is that upon him is an expiation of an oath." Ibn Mughith said: Those we have named therefore interpreted the speaker's saying "the oaths are binding on him" as one single divorce, because he cannot be in a worse state than one who says: "The strongest thing anyone has ever taken from anyone is that upon him is an expiation of an oath." He said: And we say accordingly.

He said: The earlier scholars argued from the saying of Ibn al-Qasim: Whoever says, "Upon me is the covenant of Allah, its binding pledge and its guarantee, and the strongest thing anyone has ever taken from anyone, regarding a matter that I will not do," and then does it, [Ibn al-Qasim] said: If he did not intend divorce or emancipation and removed them from that, then let it be three expiations. If he had no intention when he swore, then he should make two expiations for his saying "upon me is the covenant of Allah and its binding pledge." He frees a slave, his wives are divorced, he walks to Makkah, and gives away one third of his wealth in charity for his saying "and the strongest thing anyone has ever taken from anyone."

Ibn al-Arabi said: As for the method of evidences, the "alif" and "lam" in "al-aymanu" either intend the category (genus) or a specific reference. If it is for specific reference, then the referent is your saying "by Allah," and so it will be what al-Fihri said. If it is for the category, then divorce is a category, so it enters into it, and its number is not exhausted, because what suffices is that a single meaning enters into each category. For if the entire meaning entered into the category, it would obligate him to give away all his wealth, since giving charity with wealth may be an oath. And Allah knows best.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Say: The signs are only with Allah﴾, meaning: Say, O Muhammad, Allah is the One able to bring them, and He brings them only when He wills. ﴿And what will make you realize﴾, meaning: and what will inform you, your oaths, so the object is omitted. Then He began anew and said: ﴿that when they come, they will not believe﴾, with the "inna" having a kasra. This is the reading of Mujahid, Abu Amr and Ibn Kathir. The reading of Ibn Mas'ud supports this: "And what will make you realize that when they come, they will not believe." Mujahid and Ibn Zayd said: the addressees here are the polytheists, and the speech is complete. He passed judgment upon them that they will not believe, and in the verse after this He informed us that they will not believe. This interpretation resembles the reading of the one who reads "tu'minun" with a ta'.

Al-Farra' and others said: the address is to the believers, because the believers said to the Prophet (ﷺ): "O Messenger of Allah, if the sign were to come down, perhaps they would believe." So Allah, Exalted is He, said: ﴿And what will make you realize﴾, meaning: what will inform you and make you know, O believers. ﴿That﴾ with a fatha, and this is the reading of the people of Madina, al-A'mash and Hamza, meaning: perhaps when they come, they will not believe. Al-Khalil said: "anna" here has the meaning of "la'alla" (perhaps), and Sibawayh related this from him. In revelation: ﴿And what will make you realize that he may purify himself﴾ [See vol. 19, p. 211], meaning: that he purifies himself. It is related from the Arabs: "Go to the market, that you buy something for us," meaning: perhaps you. Abu al-Najm said:

I said to Shaybān: come near to his meeting,
that you feed the people from his roast.

Adi ibn Zayd said:

O blamer, what will make you realize that my death
is by an hour in the day or in the morning of tomorrow?

meaning: perhaps. Durayd [The correct attribution is to Hatim al-Ta'i, as in al-Sihah of al-Jawhari and his Diwan; it is narrated as "la'alli," so there is no evidence in it] ibn al-Simma said:

Show me a horse that died of emaciation, for I
see what you see, or a miser made to live forever.

meaning: perhaps I. [In the manuscripts: "Leave me to roam the lands, for I..."] It is common in Arabic speech that "anna" means "la'alla." Al-Kisa'i related that it is so in the codex of Ubayy ibn Ka'b: "And what will make you realize? Perhaps it [will come]." Al-Kisa'i and al-Farra' said: the "la" is superfluous, and the meaning is: "And what will make you realize that they, if the signs come to the polytheists, will believe?" The "la" is added, just as "la" is added in His saying: ﴿It is forbidden for a city which We have destroyed that they will not return﴾ [See vol. 11, p. 340], because the meaning is: "and it is forbidden for a destroyed city that they return." And in His saying: ﴿What prevented you from not prostrating?﴾ [See p. 165 and p. 390 of this part], meaning: what prevented you from prostrating. Al-Zajjaj, al-Nahhas and others considered the addition of "la" weak and said: it is an error and a mistake, because it is only added where there is no ambiguity. It was also said: there is an omission in the speech, and the meaning is: "And what will make you realize that when they come they will not believe, or they will believe." Then this part was omitted because the listener knows it. Al-Nahhas and others mentioned this.

This is a difficult verse, especially the phrase ﴿And We leave them in their transgression, wandering blindly﴾. It has been said: the meaning is that on the Day of Resurrection We will turn their hearts and their sight over onto the blaze of the Fire and the heat of its embers, just as they did not believe in the world. ﴿And We leave them﴾ refers to the world, meaning We give them respite and do not punish them. So part of the verse concerns the Hereafter and part concerns this world. Its parallel is ﴿Faces that day will be humbled﴾ (see vol. 20, p. 26): ﴿this is in the Hereafter﴾, ﴿labouring, weary﴾ is in this world.

It has also been said: ﴿And We turn [them over]﴾ refers to this world, meaning that We come between them and faith if that sign came to them, just as We came between them and faith the first time, when you called them and displayed the miracle. In the Revelation (al-Tanzil) it says: ﴿Know that Allah comes between a person and his heart﴾ (8:24).

The meaning is: they should have believed when the sign came to them and they saw it with their eyes and recognised it with their hearts. When they do not believe, this is due to Allah turning their hearts and their sight, just as they did not believe in it the first time. The particle ﴿like﴾ (kaf) is attached to an omitted element, meaning: so they will not believe, just as they did not believe in it the first time, that is, the first time the signs came to them, which they were unable to match, such as the Qur'an and others.

It has also been said: ﴿And We turn over the hearts of these people so that they do not believe﴾, just as the disbelievers of the earlier nations did not believe when they saw the signs they had demanded.

And it has been said: there is inversion in the statement, meaning: when the sign comes, they will not believe, just as they did not believe the first time, and We turn their hearts and their sight.

(﴿And We leave them in their transgression, wandering blindly﴾) means: bewildered. This was discussed in al-Baqarah (see vol. 1, p. 209).

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 6, verse 111:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And even if We had sent down to them the angels﴾, so that they saw them face to face.

(And the dead had spoken to them) by Our giving them life.

(And We had gathered together against them everything) that they asked for of the signs. "Qubulan" means face to face (muqabalah), according to Ibn 'Abbas, Qatadah and Ibn Zayd. This is the reading of Nafi' and Ibn 'Amir. It is also said: "in plain sight" (mu'ayanah), when they would believe. Muhammad ibn Yazid said: "qubulan" may mean "direction" (nahiyah), as we say: "li fulan qibala mal" (I have wealth in the direction of so-and-so), so "qubulan" is put in the accusative as an adverb of place (zarf). The rest of the readers read "qubulan" with a damma on the qaf and the ba', and its meaning is "guarantors" (dumana'), so it is the plural of qabil in the sense of kafil, like raghif and rughuf, as He said: ﴿or you bring God and the angels as a guarantee (qabil)﴾, i.e., they would guarantee that. This is from al-Farra'. Al-Akhfash said: it has the sense of "tribe after tribe" (qabil qabil), i.e., group by group. Mujahid said: it is an accusative of circumstance (hal) according to both opinions. Muhammad ibn Yazid said: "qubulan" means face to face (muqabalah), and from it comes: ﴿if his shirt is torn from the front (min qubul)﴾. From it also comes the "qubul" (front) and "dubur" (back) of a man, since it is what lies before him and behind him. From it also comes "qubul" of menstruation. Abu Zayd related: "I met so-and-so qabalan and qibalan and muqabalatan and qibalan," all with the meaning of confronting, so the damma is equal to the kasra in meaning, and both readings are equivalent; this was said by Makki. Al-Hasan read "qubulan" with the damma of the ba' removed because of its heaviness. According to al-Farra's opinion, this involves making speak what does not speak, and guaranteeing what has intellect is a great sign for them. According to al-Akhfash's opinion, it involves the gathering of kinds that is not customary. And "al-hashr" means gathering.

﴿They would not have believed unless God willed﴾. "An" (that) is in a position of exception, not from the first part; i.e., but if He willed that for them. It is also said: the exception is for the people of happiness who had already been decreed in God's knowledge to believe. In this there is consolation for the Prophet (ﷺ).

(But most of them are ignorant) i.e., they are ignorant of the truth. It is also said: they are ignorant that it is not permissible to demand signs after they have seen one sign.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 6, verse 112:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And thus We have appointed for every prophet﴾ — He consoles His Prophet and comforts him, meaning: just as We tested you with these people, so likewise We appointed for every prophet before you (an enemy), i.e., enemies. Then He described them, saying (﴿devils among mankind and jinn﴾). Sibawayh related that *ja'ala* (to appoint, to make) is used in the sense of *wasafa* (to describe). "Enemy" (*'aduwwan*) is the first object. "For every prophet" is in the position of the second object. "Devils among mankind and jinn" is an apposition (*badal*) to "enemy." It is also permissible for "devils" (*shayatin*) to be the first object and "enemy" the second object, as if it were said: We made the devils of mankind and jinn an enemy. Al-A'mash recited "shayatin al-jinn wal-insi" with the jinn placed first. The meaning is the same.

(﴿They inspire one another with varnished speech as deception﴾) This is an expression for what the devils of the jinn whisper to the devils of mankind. It is called *wahy* (inspiration) because it occurs only in secret, and their embellishment (*tamwih*) is called *zukhruf* (ornament) because of their decorating it. From this comes the name *dhahab zukhruf* (gold). Every good thing that is gilded is *zukhruf*, and *al-muzakhraf* is the adorned. *Zakharif al-ma'* are its streaks (ripples). "Deception" (*ghururan*) is in the accusative as a verbal noun (*masdar*), because the meaning of "they inspire one another" is that they deceive them with it, a deception. It is also permissible for it to be in the position of a circumstantial accusative (*hal*), and *al-ghurur* is falsehood. Al-Nahhas said: It is related from Ibn 'Abbas, through a weak chain of narration, that he said concerning the words of Allah, mighty and majestic, "they inspire one another": "With every jinni is a devil, and with every human is a devil. One of them meets the other and says: 'I have led my companion astray by such-and-such, so lead your companion astray by the like of it.' The other says the same. This is the inspiration of one to another." This was also said by 'Ikrimah, al-Dahhak, al-Suddi and al-Kalbi. Al-Nahhas said: The first view is indicated by His words, "Indeed the devils inspire their allies to dispute with you" [[p. 74 of this part.]], and this clarifies the meaning. I say: The authentic Sunnah also indicates it, in the saying of the Prophet, peace be upon him: "There is none of you but a companion from the jinn has been assigned to him." It was asked: "Not even you, O Messenger of Allah?" He said: "Not even I, except that Allah helped me against him, so he has submitted (*aslama*), and he does not command me except with good." It is narrated as *fa-aslamu* with a *damma* and as *fa-aslama* with a *fatha* on the *mim*. The *damma* means "so I am safe from his evil," and the *fatha* means "so he has submitted." He said, "There is none of you," and did not say "nor of the devils," though it is possible that he alluded to one of the two kinds by the other, and so this would be of the type of "garments that protect you from the heat" [[see vol. 10, p. 159.]]. But this is far-fetched, and Allah knows best. 'Awf ibn Malik related from Abu Dharr that the Messenger of Allah, peace be upon him, said: "O Abu Dharr, have you sought refuge in Allah from the evil of the devils of mankind and jinn?" I said: "O Messenger of Allah, do mankind have devils?" He said: "Yes, they are worse than the devils of the jinn." Malik ibn Dinar said: The devil of mankind is more harmful to me than the devil of the jinn, because when I seek refuge in Allah the devil of the jinn departs from me, but the devil of mankind comes to me and drags me to sins openly. 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, heard a woman reciting [[From manuscripts K, A, J. The one who knows says the verse belongs to a littérateur of Basra who saw the women and described their condition, saying: "Indeed women are devils." The verse. A woman answered him: "Indeed women are fragrant herbs." The verse.]]:

Indeed women are fragrant herbs, created for you,
and each of you desires the smelling of herbs.

'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, answered her:

Indeed women are devils, created for us,
we seek refuge in Allah from the evil of devils.

His saying, may He be exalted: (﴿Had your Lord willed, they would not have done it﴾) meaning: they would not have done the inspiring of deceptive speech. ﴿So leave them﴾ is an imperative that carries the sense of threat. Sibawayh said: One does not say *wadhara* or *wada'a* (to leave); they have dispensed with them by *taraka* (to leave). I say: This is only the usual usage. In the revelation there is ﴿And leave those who﴾ [[It should be noted that the verb in "And leave those who" and "leave them" is an imperative, and the author's statement does not fit them. Perhaps there is an error in the text, and infallibility belongs to Allah.]] and ﴿what your Lord has not forsaken (*wada'aka*) you﴾. [[*Wada'aka* with the lightened pronunciation is a reading related from the Prophet, peace be upon him. It is not one of the seven readings.]] In the Sunnah: "Let people cease from abandoning the Friday prayers (*wad'ihim al-jumu'at*)." And the saying: "If they do it, meaning the sins, then they have been forsaken (*tuwuddi'a*) by Him." Al-Zajjaj said: The *waw* is heavy; since *taraka* has no *waw*, it was used in the sense of what has the *waw*, so what has the *waw* was left out. This is the meaning of a statement, though not its exact wording.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 6, verse 113:

God Almighty says: ﴿and so that the hearts of those who do not believe in the Hereafter may incline to it﴾. *Tasgha* means *tamil* (to incline). It is said: *saghawtu asghu saghwan wa sughuwwan*, and *saghaytu asgha*, and *saghaytu* (with kasra) also. From it one says: *sagha yasgha sagan wa sughyan*, and *asghaytu ilayhi asgha'an*, with the same meaning. The poet said:

*You see the fool, with him, turning away from every firm [[In ا, ب, ز, ك and in al-Lisan: "mukarramah" (honoured).]] principle, a deviation, and in him is a leaning towards likening (God to creation).*

It is also said: *asghaytu al-inā'* when I tilt the vessel so that what is in it gathers. Its root meaning is inclining towards a thing for some purpose. From this: *saghat al-nujum*, meaning the stars inclined towards setting. In the Revelation: ﴿Your hearts have certainly inclined﴾. Abu Zayd said: it is said:

*Saghwuhu ma'aka wa sighwuhu, wa saghahu ma'aka*, meaning his inclination is with you. In a hadith: "*fa-asgha lahā al-inā'*", meaning for the cat. And "*Akrimū fulānan fī sāghiyatihi*", meaning among his relatives who incline towards him and seek what he has. And the she-camel "*asghat*" when she inclines her head towards the man, as if she is listening to something when the saddle is fastened on her. Dhu al-Rummah said:

*She inclines her head when he fastens the saddle on her, leaning, until when he settles into her stirrup, she leaps. [[Al-kawr (with damma): the saddle of the camel with its equipment, like a saddle for a horse. Ibn Sayyidah said: many people pronounce the kaf with a fatha, which is an error. Jānihah: inclining, adhering closely. Al-gharz: a strap like a stirrup, into which the man places his foot at the stirrup. He describes his camel as clever and quick in movement.]]*

The *lam* in "*wa-li-tasgha*" is *lam kay* (the lam of purpose), and the governing verb for it is "*yūhī*" (they inspire). Its implied sense: some of them inspire to others in order to deceive them, and so that (the hearts) incline. Some claimed that it is *lam al-amr* (the lam of command), but this is an error, because it should have been "*wa-l-taşgha*" with the alif deleted. Rather, it is *lam kay*. The same applies to "*wa-li-yaqtarifū*". However, al-Hasan read "*wa-li-yarđawhu wa-liyaqtarifū*" with the lam sukun, making it *lam al-amr* carrying a sense of threat, as one says: "do what you wish."

The meaning of "*wa-liyaqtarifū mā hum muqtarifūn*" is: and so that they may acquire what they are acquiring, as related from Ibn Abbas, al-Suddi and Ibn Zayd. It is said: *kharaja yaqtarifu ahlahu*, meaning he went out to earn for his family. *Qarafa fulān hādhā al-amr* when he engaged in it and did it. *Qaraftanī bi-mā ddaʿaytā ʿalayya*, meaning you accused me of suspicion. *Qarafa al-qarḥah* when he peeled off from it (a scab). *Iqtaraf kadhiban* (he fabricated a lie). Ru'bah said:

*The fabrication of a lie, when it is fabricated, has wearied the piety of the pious and the chastity of the chaste. [[In ع: "al-ʿafīf" (the chaste). In او, ب, ج, ك, ز: "al-ḍaʿīf" (the weak).]]*

Its root meaning is cutting off a piece of a thing.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 6, verse 114:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Shall I seek a judge other than Allah?﴾ "Ghayra" (other than) is in the accusative, governed by "abtaghi" (I seek). "Hakaman" (a judge) is in the accusative as a specification (bayan), and if you wish, as a state (hal). The meaning is: Shall I seek for you a judge other than Allah, when He has sufficed you the burden of questioning, in the signs, by what He has sent down to you of the Book, the detailed (al-mufassal), i.e., the clarified (al-mubayyan)? Then it has been said: al-hakam (the arbiter) is more emphatic than al-hakim (the judge), since the name "hakam" is only deserved by one who judges with truth, for it is an attribute of exaltation in praise. Whereas al-hakim is an attribute derived from the verb, so it may be applied to one who judges without truth.

﴿And those to whom We gave the Book﴾ means the Jews and the Christians. It has been said: it refers to those among them who embraced Islam, such as Salman, Suhayb, and Abdullah ibn Salam.

﴿know that it﴾, i.e., the Qur'an,

﴿is sent down from your Lord in truth﴾, meaning that everything in it of promise and threat is true. ﴿So do not be among the doubters﴾, i.e., among those who doubt that they know it is sent down from Allah. Ata' said: "Those to whom We gave the Book" are the leaders of the companions of Muhammad (ﷺ): Abu Bakr, Umar, Uthman, and Ali (may Allah be pleased with them).

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 6, verse 115:

His saying, exalted is He: (And the word of your Lord has been fulfilled) — the reading of the people of Kufa is the singular "kalimatu" (word), while the rest read it in the plural "kalimat" (words). Ibn Abbas said: "the promises of your Lord, so none can alter them." The "words" refer either to the expressions, or to what is connected to them of promise and threat and other things. Qatadah said: "The words are the Qur'an; none can alter it. The distorters do not add to it nor subtract from it."

(In truth and justice) — that is, in what He promised and decreed; there is no one to reverse His decree and no breaking of His promise. Al-Rummani related, from Qatadah... Al-Rummani related from Qatadah: "None can alter them in what He has judged," meaning that although it is possible for the words to be changed and altered in their wording, as the People of the Book altered the Torah and the Gospel, that is of no account. The verse indicates the obligation to follow the implications (dalalat) of the Qur'an, because it is the truth, and it cannot be altered by anything that contradicts it, since it comes from the All-Wise, from Whom nothing of the affairs is hidden (all of it [[from k.]].

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 6, verse 116–117:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And if you obey most of those on earth﴾ means the disbelievers.

(They will mislead you from the way of Allah) means: from the path that leads to the reward of Allah.

(They follow only assumption) "in" here carries the meaning of "má" (not), and likewise (and they only guess) means: they conjecture and estimate. From this comes al-kharsh (guessing, estimating), and its root meaning is cutting. The poet said:

You see the aim of the spear-shafts among us, as if it were ... the measuring of palm-fronds in the hands of the shawatib [[The verse is by Qays ibn al-Khatim. Al-qasd (with a kasra on the qaf and a fatha on the sad, plural qisad): a piece broken off. Al-mirān: spear-plant, or stiff, pliant spears. Al-tadharru': measuring a thing by the forearm (dhira'). Al-kharsan: canes of the palm-frond. Al-shawatib (plural of shatiba): the woman who strips the palm-rib and then passes it to the one who cleans it, who takes off all that is on it with her knife until she leaves it thin, then passes it back to the first, who strips it again on her forearm and measures it. His saying "fina ka'annahu" is the reading in the originals, while in al-Lisan it is "talqa ka'annahu," and in his Diwan it is "tahwa ka'annaha."]]

It means palm-fronds cut lengthwise, from which the kharsh (cane-pieces) are made. It is the plural of kharsh. From it comes the verb kharasa, yakhrusu, al-nakhla kharsan, meaning he estimated it in order to take the tax from it. So the one who guesses (al-kharis) asserts with certainty what it is not permissible to assert with certainty, since there is no certainty with him.

More elaboration on this will come, God willing, in (surah) al-Dhariyat [[See vol. 17, p. 33.]].

(Indeed your Lord knows best) Some people said: "a'lam" here means "ya'lam" (knows), and they cited the saying of Hatim al-Ta'i:

Tayy has made an alliance without us, a pact ... and Allah knows that we were not forsakers of them [[In the originals: "fa-kharafat" and "wa-khawalan" with a waw instead of a dhal. The correction is from Tafsir al-Tabari. Khudhul: plural of khadhul.]]

And the saying of al-Khansa:

Allah [[In b, j, k, z and i: "the people."]] knows that his cup ... will go on the morning of the wind or by night.

But this is not a valid proof, because it does not match "He knows best who are guided," and because it is possible that it remains on its original form.

(Who strays from His path) "man" here means "ay" (which), so it is in the nominative position, and the governing word is "yadillu" (strays). It was said: it is in the accusative position by "a'lam" (knows best), meaning: Indeed your Lord knows best which of the people strays from His path. It was also said: it is in the accusative position by removing the preposition, i.e., "bi-man yadillu" (concerning whoever strays). One of the Basran grammarians said this, and it is good, because of His saying: (and He knows best who are guided), and His saying at the end of al-Nahl: "Indeed your Lord is He who knows best who has strayed from His path, and He knows best who are guided" [[See vol. 10, p. 200.]]. It is also read as "yudillu" (with a damma on the ya and a kasra on the dal), and this is by omitting the object. The first reading is better, because He said: "and He knows best who are guided." If it were from idlal (causing to stray), He would have said: "and He knows best who are the guiders."

(They will mislead you from the way of Allah) means: from the path that leads to the reward of Allah.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 6, verse 118:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So eat of that over which the name of Allah has been mentioned﴾. It was revealed concerning some people who came to the Prophet ﷺ and said: "O Messenger of Allah, we eat what we kill, and we do not eat what Allah has killed?" So it was revealed, "So eat..." up to His saying, "And if you obey them, indeed you are polytheists." At-Tirmidhi and others narrated it. ʿAtaʾ [[In K: Qatadah.]] said: this verse is a command to mention the name of Allah over drink, slaughter, and every food. And His saying, (if you are believers in His signs), meaning: those who take up His rulings and commands; for belief in them entails and requires taking them up and submitting to them.

The Almighty's words: ﴿And what is [the matter] with you that you should not eat of that over which the Name of Allah has been mentioned?﴾ The meaning: what prevents you from eating what you have named your Lord over, even if you have slain it with your own hands.

(And He has detailed) i.e., He has made clear to you the lawful from the unlawful, and doubt and confusion have been removed from you. Here "mā" is an interrogative that implies affirmation (taqrīr). The sense of the sentence is: "And what reason do you have not to eat?" The phrase "an" (that) is in a position of genitive, by way of an implied preposition. It is also permissible that it be in an accusative position, with no preposition implied, the governing element being the sense of the verb in "mā lakum," its estimated meaning being "what prevents you."

Then He made an exception, saying: ﴿except that to which you are compelled﴾, meaning from among everything He has forbidden, such as carrion and other things, as was mentioned previously in [[See vol. 2, p. 224.]] al-Baqarah. This is a disjunctive (munqaṭi') exception.

Nafi' and Ya'qub read "wa-qad faṣṣala lakum mā ḥarrama" with both verbs in the fatḥah (open vowel). Abu 'Amr, Ibn 'Amir and Ibn Kathir read both with ḍammah. The Kufans read "faṣṣala" with fatḥah and "ḥurrima" with ḍammah. 'Aṭiyyah al-'Awfi read "faṣala" with lightening (takhfīf). Its meaning is "became clear and manifest," as in the recitation "Alif. Lam. Ra. A Book whose verses have been perfected, then detailed" [[See vol. 9, p. 2.]], i.e., made clear. Abu 'Ubaydah preferred the recitation of the people of Madinah. It is also said that "faṣṣala" means "explained," and this refers to what He mentioned in Surah al-Ma'idah from His words: "Forbidden to you are carrion, blood, and the flesh of swine" [[See vol. 6, p. 47.]], and so on. I say: this is open to question, since al-An'am is Meccan and al-Ma'idah is Medinan, so how could He refer for explanation to what had not yet been revealed, unless "faṣṣala" carries the meaning of "yufaṣṣilu" (He details). And Allah knows best.

The Almighty's words: ﴿And indeed, many [people] lead [others] astray by their desires without knowledge﴾ [[Reading of Nafi'.]]. The Kufans read "yuḍillūna" from aḍalla. ﴿by their desires without knowledge﴾ refers to the polytheists, who said: "What Allah slaughters with His knife is better than what you slaughter with your knives." ﴿Without knowledge﴾ means without any knowledge they possess concerning the matter of slaughter, since the wisdom in it is the expulsion of the blood that Allah has forbidden to us, unlike what dies of its own accord. For this reason He prescribed dhakāh (ritual slaughter) at a specific place, so that the cut there would be a means of drawing out all the blood in the animal, unlike other organs. And Allah knows best.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 6, verse 120:

His statement, exalted is He: ﴿Abandon the outward and the inward of sin﴾. Concerning this, the scholars (ʿulamāʾ) have many opinions, and their summary returns to the following: the outward is what is done by the body of the things God has forbidden, and the inward is what is held in the heart of opposition to God's command in what He has commanded and forbidden. This level is not reached except by one who fears God and does good, as He said: "Then they feared God and believed, then they feared God and did good" (5:93). This is the third level, according to what was explained earlier in al-Ma'idah [[See vol. 6, p. 293.]]. It was also said: it is what the Jahiliyyah (the Age of Ignorance) practiced, namely visible fornication and taking women as secret companions. What we have mentioned encompasses every sin and (requires every command [[from K.]].

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 6, verse 121:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And do not eat of that over which the name of Allah has not been mentioned, for indeed it is grave disobedience.﴾ In it there are five issues.

The first: Abu Dawud related that he said: The Jews came to the Prophet ﷺ and said: "We eat what we kill, but we do not eat what Allah kills?" So Allah, Mighty and Majestic, revealed: "And do not eat of that over which the name of Allah has not been mentioned," to the end of the verse. And al-Nasa'i related from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His saying, "And do not eat of that over which the name of Allah has not been mentioned," that he said: The polytheists disputed with them [[i.e., the polytheists disputed with the believers.]] and said: "What Allah slaughters, you do not eat, but what you slaughter, you eat." So Allah, glorified is He, said to them: "Do not eat, for you have not mentioned the name of Allah over it."

Here arises a legal-theoretical (usuli) question, which is the second: Namely, whether a general expression that comes in response to a particular cause is restricted to that cause or not. Our scholars said: There is no difficulty in the validity of the claim of generality regarding what the Lawgiver states at the outset, in forms of general expressions. As for what he states as an answer to a question, there is a distinction, as is known in the principles of jurisprudence, except that if he brings it in an independent wording without the question, it joins the first in the validity of the intent toward generality. So His saying, "Do not eat," is apparent in covering carrion, and it includes what has been dedicated to other than Allah by the generality of "over which the name of Allah has not been mentioned," and by the added mention of other than the name of Allah, glorified is He, over it, which requires its prohibition explicitly by the saying: "and that which has been dedicated to other than Allah" [[See vol. 2, p. 216.]].

Whether it includes what a Muslim leaves the invocation of the name over deliberately, in slaughter and at the release of the game (hunting animal), the scholars differed on this according to five opinions. These are (the third issue, the first opinion):

The first: If he leaves it out inadvertently, both are eaten. This is the view of Ishaq and a narration from Ahmad ibn Hanbal. If he leaves it out deliberately, neither is eaten. This is said by Malik and Ibn al-Qasim in the Kitab (al-Mudawwanah), and it is the view of Abu Hanifa and his companions, al-Thawri, al-Hasan ibn Hayy, 'Isa and Asbagh. Sa'id ibn Jubayr and 'Ata' also said it, and al-Nahhas chose it and said: "This is the best, because one who is forgetful is not called a sinner."

The second: If he leaves it out either deliberately or forgetfully, he eats both. This is the view of al-Shafi'i and al-Hasan, and it is related from Ibn 'Abbas, Abu Hurayrah, 'Ata', Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab, Jabir ibn Zayd, Ikrimah, Abu 'Iyad, Abu Rafi', Tawus, Ibrahim al-Nakha'i, 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Layla and Qatadah. Al-Zuhawi related from Malik ibn Anas that he said: "The slaughtered animal over which the invocation was left out, either deliberately or forgetfully, is eaten." And it is related from Rabi'ah also. 'Abd al-Wahhab said: The invocation is a sunnah, so if the slaughterer leaves it out forgetfully, the animal is eaten according to the view of Malik and his companions.

The third: If he leaves it out deliberately or forgetfully [[In k: forgetfully.]], its eating is prohibited. This is said by Muhammad ibn Sirin, 'Abd Allah ibn 'Ayyash ibn Abi Rabi'ah, 'Abd Allah ibn 'Umar, Nafi', 'Abd Allah ibn Zayd al-Khatmi and al-Sha'bi, and Abu Thawr, Dawud ibn 'Ali and Ahmad in one narration also said it.

The fourth: If he leaves it out deliberately, its eating is disliked. This is said by al-Qadi Abu al-Hasan and Shaykh Abu Bakr from our scholars.

The fifth: Ashhab said: The slaughter of one who leaves out the invocation deliberately is eaten, unless he is one who treats it lightly. Al-Tabari said something similar.

(Evidences [[From b, j, k, ʿ and y.]] Allah, the Exalted, said: "So eat of that over which the name of Allah has been mentioned," and He said: "And do not eat of that over which the name of Allah has not been mentioned." So He distinguished the two states and clarified the two rulings. His saying, "Do not eat," is a prohibition for the sake of forbiddenness, and it cannot be taken to mean reprehension, since it covers, in some of its implications, what is purely forbidden; and it cannot be divided, i.e., it cannot be intended to mean prohibition and reprehension together. This is one of the precious principles. As for the forgetful person, no address is directed to him, since addressing him is impossible, so the condition is not obligatory upon him. As for one who deliberately leaves out the invocation, he is in one of three situations: either he leaves it out when he lays the animal down and says: "My heart is filled with the names of Allah and His unity, so I have no need of mentioning it with my tongue," this suffices him, because he has mentioned Allah, majestic is His majesty, and glorified Him. Or he says: "This is not a place for explicit invocation, since it is not an act of worship," so this too suffices him. Or he says: "I will not invoke, and what is the measure of the invocation?" This is one who is careless and a sinner, and his slaughter is not eaten. Ibn al-'Arabi said: "I am surprised at the head of the verifiers, the Imam of the Two Sanctuaries, when he said: 'The mention of Allah is only prescribed in acts of devotion, and slaughter is not an act of devotion.' This contradicts the Qur'an and the Sunnah." The Prophet ﷺ said in the Sahih: "Whatever makes the blood flow and over which the name of Allah has been mentioned, eat." If it is said: "The intended meaning of mentioning the name of Allah is in the heart, because mention is the opposite of forgetfulness, and the locus of forgetfulness is the heart, so the locus of mention is the heart. And al-Bara' ibn 'Azib related: 'The name of Allah is upon the heart of every believer, whether he invokes or does not invoke.'" We say: Mention is by the tongue and by the heart. What the Arabs used to do was invoke idols and standing stones with the tongue, so Allah abrogated that by mentioning Him on the tongues, and this became well known in the Shari'ah, to the extent that Malik was asked: "Does one invoke Allah, exalted is He, when performing ablution?" He said: "Does he intend to slaughter?" As for the hadith that they relied upon, "The name of Allah is upon the heart of every believer," it is a weak hadith. A group of the people of knowledge deduced from it that the invocation over the slaughtered animal is not obligatory, based on His saying, peace be upon him, to people who asked him: "O Messenger of Allah, indeed some people bring us meat and we do not know whether they mentioned the name of Allah over it or not?" The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Invoke the name of Allah over it and eat." Al-Daraqutni related it from 'A'ishah, and Malik related it as a mursal from Hisham ibn 'Urwah from his father, and there was no disagreement about its being mursal.

He interpreted it by saying at its end: "And that was at the beginning of Islam," meaning before the revelation of "And do not eat of that over which the name of Allah has not been mentioned." Abu 'Umar said: This is weak, and within the hadith itself is what refutes it, because he commanded them in it to invoke the name of Allah over eating, which indicates that the verse had already been revealed to him. And among what supports the correctness of what we have said is that this hadith took place in Medina, and the scholars do not differ that His saying, "And do not eat of that over which the name of Allah has not been mentioned," was revealed in Surat al-An'am in Mecca. The meaning of "And indeed it is grave disobedience" is: it is indeed disobedience, according to Ibn 'Abbas. And fisq (grave disobedience) means: departure. It has already been discussed [[See vol. 1, p. 244.]].

The fourth issue: His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And indeed the devils inspire their allies﴾, i.e., they whisper, casting into their hearts the disputing with falsehood. Abu Dawud related from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His saying, "And indeed the devils inspire their allies," that they say: "What Allah slaughters, do not eat it, but what you slaughter, eat it." So Allah revealed, "And do not eat of that over which the name of Allah has not been mentioned." Ikrimah said: By "devils" in this verse is meant the rebellious humans among the Magians of Persia. But Ibn 'Abbas and 'Abd Allah ibn Kathir said: Rather, the devils are the jinn, and the unbelieving jinn are the allies of Quraysh. It is related from 'Abd Allah ibn al-Zubayr that it was said to him: "Al-Mukhtar says: 'It is revealed to me.'" He said: "He spoke the truth: indeed the devils inspire their allies."

(And His saying: [[From k.]] "to dispute with you." It means their saying: "What Allah kills, you do not eat, and what you kill, you eat." And disputation (mujadalah) is the repelling of a statement by way of argument with strength; it is derived from al-ajdal, a strong bird. It was also said: it is derived from al-jadalah, which is the ground, so that he overcomes his opponent with argument, subduing him until he is like one thrown down to the earth. It was also said: it is derived from jadl, which is intense twisting, so that each of them twists the argument of the other until he severs it [[In k: nullifies it.]], and it is true in supporting the truth and false in supporting falsehood.)

The fifth issue: His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And if you obey them﴾, i.e., in permitting carrion, ﴿indeed you would be polytheists﴾. So the verse indicates that whoever deems lawful something that Allah has prohibited becomes a polytheist by it. Allah, glorified is He, has explicitly prohibited carrion, so whoever accepts its permission from another has committed shirk. Ibn al-'Arabi said: A believer becomes a polytheist by obeying a polytheist only if he obeys him in belief. As for if he obeys him in action while his conviction remains sound and steadfast upon monotheism and affirmation, then he is a disobedient sinner, so understand it. This has already passed in al-Ma'idah [[See vol. 6, p. 254 and p. 301.]].

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 6, verse 122:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Is he who was dead and We brought him to life﴾. The majority (al-Jumhur) read the waw with a fatha, and the interrogative hamza (hamzat al-istifham) entered upon it. Al-Musayyabi transmitted from Nafi' ibn Abi Nu'aym "Awa man kana" with the waw sukun. An-Nahhas said: It is permissible that it be taken as conveyed in meaning, i.e., "Look and reflect: shall I seek a judge other than Allah?" ﴿Is he who was dead and We brought him to life﴾. It has been said: its meaning is that he was dead when he was a drop of semen (nutfah), and then We brought him to life by breathing the spirit into him; this was related by Ibn Bahr. Ibn 'Abbas said: "Or is he who was an unbeliever and We guided him." It was revealed concerning Hamzah ibn 'Abd al-Muttalib and Abu Jahl. Zayd ibn Aslam and as-Suddi said: "We brought him to life" refers to 'Umar (may Allah be pleased with him). ﴿Like one whose likeness is in darkness﴾ refers to Abu Jahl (may Allah curse him). The sound view is that it is general, applying to every believer and disbeliever. It has also been said: he was dead through ignorance, and We brought him to life through knowledge. Some scholars recited verses indicating the soundness of this interpretation by one of the poets of Basra (al-Basrah):

And in ignorance, before death, there is a death for its people, so their bodies are graves before the graves.

And whoever has not been given life by knowledge is dead, and for him there is no resurrection until the resurrection.

Light (an-nur) is an expression for guidance and faith. Al-Hasan said: it is the Qur'an. It has been said: it is wisdom. It has been said: it is the light mentioned in the saying: ﴿Their light runs before them and on their right hands﴾ (see vol. 17, pp. 242 and 245), and His saying: ﴿Wait for us, that we may borrow from your light﴾.

﴿Walking with it among the people﴾, i.e., with the light among people. ﴿Like one whose likeness is in darkness﴾, i.e., like one who is in darkness; so the word "mathal" (likeness) is superfluous (za'idah). You say: "I honour your likeness," meaning "I honour you." Similar is His saying: ﴿then the recompense is like what he killed of the cattle﴾ (see vol. 6, p. 306), and ﴿There is nothing like Him﴾ (see vol. 16, p. 7). It has also been said: the meaning is "like one whose likeness is the likeness of one who is in the darkness." And "mathal" and "mithl" are one and the same.

﴿Thus was made attractive to the disbelievers what they used to do﴾, i.e., Satan made the worship of idols attractive to them and made them imagine that they were superior to the Muslims.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 6, verse 123:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And thus We have placed in every town its greatest criminals﴾. The meaning is: Just as We made the disbelievers see as fair what they were doing, so We placed in every town... "mujrimiha" (its criminals) is the first object of "ja'ala" (placed), and "akabira" (greatest) is the second object, with the order inverted. "Ja'ala" here carries the sense of "sayyara" (made/rendered). "Al-akabir" is the plural of "al-akbar" (greatest). Mujahid said: He means the great ones (al-'uzama').

It was also said: the leaders and the great ones. He singled them out for mention because they are most capable of corruption. "Al-makr" (plotting, scheming) is cunning in opposing uprightness; its root meaning is twisting (al-fatl), so the schemer twists a person away from uprightness, that is, turns him away from it. Mujahid said: They would seat four men at every pass (aqaba), driving people away from following the Prophet ﷺ, just as those before them among the earlier nations did with their prophets.

﴿And they plot only against themselves﴾: that is, the consequence of their scheming returns upon them. It is, from Allah, the mighty and majestic, the recompense for the scheming of the schemers, in the form of painful punishment.

﴿And they do not perceive﴾: at the moment, due to the extremity of their ignorance, that the consequence of their scheming returns to them.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 6, verse 124:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿When a sign comes to them, they say, "We will never believe"﴾. He explains another aspect of their ignorance, which is that they said, "We will never believe until we are given prophethood, so that we are given the like of what Musa and Isa were given of signs." A parallel to this is His saying: "Rather, every one of them wants to be given scrolls spread out" [see vol. 19, p. 88]. The pronoun in "jā'athum" (came to them) refers to the great men (al-akabir) who have been mentioned. Al-Walid ibn al-Mughira said: "If prophethood were true, I would be more worthy of it than you, for I am older than you in years and greater than you in wealth." Abu Jahl said: "By Allah, we will never be pleased with him or follow him, unless revelation comes to us just as it comes to him," and so the verse was revealed. It is also said: they did not seek prophethood, but said, "We will not believe you until Jibril and the angels come to us and inform us of your truthfulness." The first view is more sound, because Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Allah knows best where to place His message﴾ [a reading], that is, with whom He entrusts it and who is fit for it. Here "ḥaythu" (where) is not an adverb of place; rather, it is a noun in the accusative which governs the object by way of expansion (ittisa'), meaning: Allah knows the people of the message. The original would have been "Allah knows the places of His message," then the preposition was dropped. It is not permissible for "a'lam" (knows best) to govern "ḥaythu" as an adverb of place, because the meaning would then be "Allah knows in this place," and that is not permissible to attribute to the Creator, the Exalted. Rather, its position is accusative by a hidden verb indicated by "a'lam," and it is a noun, as we have mentioned. "Al-saghar" means humiliation, subjugation and abasement; likewise "al-sughr" (with a dammah). Its verbal noun is "al-saghar" (with a fatha). Its origin is from "al-sighar" (smallness) as opposed to "al-kibar" (greatness), as if abasement makes a person consider himself small. It is also said its origin is from "al-saghar," which is contentment with abasement. One says from it: "saghara yasghuru" (with fatha on the ghayn in the past tense and damma in the future), and "saghira yasghara" (with kasra in the past and fatha in the future) — two dialects — "saghaaran" and "saghaaran." The active participle is "sāghir" and "saghīr." "Al-sāghir" is one who is content with subjugation. "Al-maṣghūrā'" means the small ones. A land "muṣaghgharah" is one whose vegetation has not grown tall [in al-Lisan: its vegetation is small and has not grown], according to Ibn al-Sikkit. ﴿With Allah﴾, that is, "min 'inda Allah" (from Allah), and it has been omitted. It is also said that there is inversion in it, meaning: "Humiliation will befall those who committed crime before Allah." Al-Farra' said: "Humiliation from Allah will befall those who committed crime." It is also said the meaning is: "Humiliation will befall those who committed crime, a humiliation established with Allah." Al-Nahhas said: "This is the best of the opinions, because 'ʿinda' (with) is in its proper place."

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 6, verse 125:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Whomever Allah wills to guide, He expands his breast to Islam﴾. That is, He widens it for him, grants him success, and makes its reward appealing to him. It is said: sharaha means "split open," and its origin is expansion. And Allah sharaha his breast means He widened it through clarity regarding that. And "I sharahtu the matter" means I built it up and clarified it. The Quraysh used to say "sharah an-nisa' sharhan," and this is among the things mentioned earlier concerning expansion and spreading out, namely having intercourse with a woman while she lies on her back. So al-sharh means uncovering: one says "I explained the obscure (sharahtu al-ghamid)," and from it comes tashrih al-lahm (cutting meat into thin slices). The reciter (al-rajiz) said:

"How much you have eaten of liver and rennet, then you stored up for it something sliced."

A piece of it is called sharihah, and every fleshy meat that is stretched out is called sharihah.

﴿And whomever He wills to lead astray﴾, that is, to mislead, ﴿He makes his breast constricted, tight (haraja)﴾. This is a refutation of the Qadariyya. A parallel to this verse from the Sunnah is his saying, peace be upon him: "Whomever Allah wills good for, He gives him understanding in the religion," recorded by the two Sahihs. This is not possible except with the expansion and illumination of the breast. And religion here means the acts of worship, as He said: "Indeed, the religion with Allah is Islam." The implication of this address is that whoever Allah does not will good for, He constricts his breast, removes his understanding far away, and so does not give him understanding. And Allah knows best.

It is narrated that Abdullah ibn Mas'ud said: "O Messenger of Allah, does the breast expand?" He said: "Yes, a light enters the heart." He asked: "Is there a sign of that?" The Prophet ﷺ said: "Turning away from the abode of deception, turning in repentance to the abode of eternity, and preparing for death before death arrives."

Ibn Kathir read "dayyiqan" with lightening (tikhfif), like "hayn" and "layn," both dialects. Nafi' and Abu Bakr read "harajan" with a kasra, and its meaning is constriction. The meaning is repeated, and this is good because the wording differs. The rest read it with a fatha, the plural of harajah, which is also intense constriction; and al-harajah is a thicket of dense trees, its plural being hiraj and harajat. From it comes "fulan yatahharaj," meaning he constricts himself in leaving off his desires for sins, said al-Harawi. Ibn Abbas said: haraj is the place of dense-packed trees, so the heart of the disbeliever is not reached by wisdom, just as the grazing animal cannot reach the place whose trees are densely intertwined. This meaning is also narrated from Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him; Makki, al-Tha'labi and others mentioned it. Every constriction is haraj. Al-Jawhari said: makan harij and haraj means a narrow place, thick with trees, which the grazing animal cannot reach. It was also read "dayyiqan harajan" and "harajan." It has the same status as wahad, wahid, farad, farid, danaf and danif, with one meaning. Others transmitted this from al-Farra'. One says: his breast became harij, yahraj, harajan. Haraj also means sin. Haraj also means a lean she-camel, and it is said: a long one on the face of the earth, from Abu Zayd, so it is a homonym. Haraj is also a wooden frame, its parts tied to one another, on which the dead are carried, from al-Asma'i. This is the saying of Imru' al-Qays:

"If you see me upon a bier of Jabir, on a haraj like a qarr, my shrouds flapping."

Sometimes it is placed over the bier of women. 'Antarah said, describing an ostrich:

"They follow the crest of its head, and it is as if it were a haraj over a bier for them, canopied."

Al-Zajjaj said: haraj is the extreme of narrowness. When one says "fulan harij al-sadr," the meaning is one who has constriction in his breast. When one says "haraj," it is the active participle. Al-Nahhas said: haraj is the active participle, and haraj is a verbal noun described by it, as one says "rajul 'adl" and "ridan."

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿As if he were climbing up into the sky﴾. Ibn Kathir read it with a sukun on the sad, lightened, from al-su'ud, which is ascending. Allah likened the disbeliever in his aversion to faith and his burden of it to one who burdens himself with what he cannot bear, just as climbing into the sky is unbearable. Likewise "yasa''adu," originally "yatasa'adu," with the ta assimilated into the sad; this is the reading of Abu Bakr and al-Nakha'i, except that it carries the sense of doing one thing after another, which is heavier on its doer. The rest read it with a shadda without an alif, and it is like the preceding. Its meaning is that he burdens himself with what he cannot bear, bit by bit, like your saying "yatajarra'" and "yatafawwaq" (tafawwaqa sharabahu: he drank it bit by bit). It is narrated from Abdullah ibn Mas'ud that he read "ka'annama yatasa'adu." Al-Nahhas said: the meaning of this reading and of the reading "yassa''adu" and "yasa'adu" is one. The meaning in both is that the disbeliever, from the constriction of his breast, is as if he wants to climb to the sky while he cannot do so, so it is as if he is seeking that. It was said: the meaning is that his heart nearly climbs to the sky, recoiling from Islam. Thus Allah places the filth upon them, as He placed constriction of the breast in their bodies. The root of rijs in the language is stench. Ibn Zayd said: it is punishment. Ibn Abbas said: al-rijs is the Shaytan, meaning He empowers him over them. Mujahid said: rijs is that in which there is no good. Likewise, rijs according to the people of language is stench. So the meaning of the verse, and Allah knows best, is: He places cursing in this world and punishment in the Hereafter.

﴿upon those who do not believe﴾.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 6, verse 126:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And this is the path of your Lord, straight﴾, meaning: this which you are upon, O Muhammad, and the believers, is the religion of your Lord, with no crookedness in it.

(﴿We have detailed the verses﴾), meaning: We have made them clear, ﴿for a people who take heed﴾.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 6, verse 127:

His, may He be exalted, saying: ﴿For them﴾, that is, for those who remember (al-mutadhakkirin).

(Dar al-Salam) means Paradise, so Paradise is the House of God, just as the Ka'bah is called the House of God. It is also permissible that the "dar" here means "safety" (al-salamah), that is, the place in which one is safe from calamities. And the meaning of (with their Lord) is that it is guaranteed for them by Him; He brings them to it by His grace.

(And He is their Protector) means their Helper and their Supporter.

"And on the Day He will gather them all together" — [[In the reading of Nafi', it is "nahshuruhum" with the nun, as in the originals.]] It is in the accusative governed by an implied verb, meaning: "And on the day We gather them, We will say..."

(jamee'an) is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal). It means that all of creation will be gathered at the station of the Resurrection.

(ya ma'shara al-jinn) is a vocative construction with an annexed noun (nida' mudaf).

(qad istakthartum mina al-ins) means: "You have acquired much of the enjoyment of mankind." The verbal noun is elided, with its object annexed to it, and the preposition as well; what indicates this is His saying: "Our Lord, some of us enjoyed others" (rabbana istamta'a ba'duna bi-ba'din). This refutes the view of those who said that the jinn are the ones who enjoyed mankind, because mankind accepted from them. The correct view is that each one enjoys the other. The grammatical construction is: istamta'a ba'duna ba'dan. The enjoyment of the jinn from mankind is that they took pleasure in men's obedience to them, and men took pleasure in accepting from the jinn, to the point that they committed fornication and drank wine by the jinn's seduction of them. It was also said: when a man passed through a valley on his journey and feared for himself, he would say: "I seek refuge in the lord of this valley from everything I fear." And in the revelation: "And there were men from mankind who sought refuge with men from the jinn, so they increased them in distress" (see vol. 19, p. 8). This is the enjoyment of mankind from the jinn. As for the enjoyment of the jinn from mankind, it is what they used to convey to them of false reports, soothsaying and sorcery. It was also said: the enjoyment of the jinn from mankind is that they acknowledge that the jinn have the power to repel from them what they fear. The meaning of the verse is the rebuke and reproach of the astray and the misleading, and their humiliation in the Hereafter before the eyes of all creatures.

(wa balagha ajalana al-ladhi ajjalta lana) means: meaning death and the grave, "and we have reached the end of our term which You appointed for us," and we arrived regretful.

(qala al-naru mathwakum) means: the place of your residence. al-mathwa is the dwelling.

(khalidina fiha illa ma sha'a Allah) is an exception that is not from the first. Al-Zajjaj said: it refers to the Day of Resurrection, meaning: "abiding in the Fire, except for what God wills" of the duration of their raising from their graves and the length of their time in reckoning; so the exception is disjunctive. It was also said: the exception refers to the Fire, meaning: except for what God wills of punishing you by other than the Fire at some times. Ibn 'Abbas said: the exception is for the people of faith; so "ma" in this case means "man." He also said: this verse requires suspension (waqf) regarding all the disbelievers. Its meaning is that it requires suspension regarding one who has not died, since he may yet embrace Islam. It was also said: "except what God wills" refers to their being in the world without punishment. The meaning of this verse is the meaning of the verse in Hud: "As for those who are wretched, they will be in the Fire," and there it will come in full, God willing. "Indeed your Lord is Wise," in their punishment and in all His acts, "All-Knowing" of the measure of their recompense.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 6, verse 129:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And thus We make some of the wrongdoers allies of others﴾. The meaning: just as We did to these people, of what I have described to you, of some of them enjoying others, I make some of the wrongdoers allies of others, and then some of them will disown others tomorrow. The meaning of "nuwalli" (We make allies, or We appoint as masters) according to this is "naj'alu waliyyan" (We make [someone] a wali, i.e., an ally or guardian). Ibn Zayd said: We empower the wrongdoers among the jinn over the wrongdoers among mankind. And also from him: We empower some of the wrongdoers over others, so that he destroys and humiliates him. This is a threat to the wrongdoer: if he does not refrain from his wrongdoing, God empowers another wrongdoer over him. The verse also includes everyone who wrongs himself [[from manuscript k.]], or wrongs his subjects, or the merchant who wrongs people in his trade, or the thief, and others. Fudayl ibn Iyad said: If you see a wrongdoer taking revenge on a wrongdoer, stop and look at it in wonder. Ibn Abbas said: When God is pleased with a people, He appoints their best as their rulers; when God is angered with a people, He appoints their worst as their rulers. And in a report from the Prophet ﷺ: "Whoever helps a wrongdoer, God will empower him over him." It was also said: The meaning is that We leave some of them to others in what they choose of disbelief, just as We leave them tomorrow to their leaders, who cannot deliver them from the punishment; that is, just as We do this to them in the Hereafter, so We do it to them in this world. It has been said regarding His saying, exalted is He: ﴿We will turn him over to what he has turned to﴾ [[see vol. 5, p. 385]], "We leave him to what he has entrusted himself to." Ibn Abbas said: Its explanation is that when God wills evil for a people [[in k.: suw'an]], He appoints their worst as their rulers. This is indicated by the saying, exalted is He: ﴿And whatever affliction strikes you, it is because of what your hands have earned﴾ [[see vol. 61, p. 30]].

The Almighty said: ﴿O assembly of jinn and humankind, did there not come to you messengers from among you﴾. That is, on the Day when We gather them, We say to them: "Did there not come to you messengers," and the words are elided. They will acknowledge what exposes them. The meaning of "from among you" is in creation, obligation and address.

Since the jinn are among those who are addressed and who reason, He said "from among you." Although the messengers were from humankind, and humankind predominates in address, just as the masculine is given precedence over the feminine.

Ibn 'Abbas said: The messengers of the jinn are those who conveyed to their people what they had heard of the revelation, as He said: ﴿They returned to their people as warners﴾ [see vol. 16, p. 210]. Muqatil and al-Dahhak said: God sent messengers from among the jinn just as He sent them from among humankind. Mujahid said: The messengers are from humankind, and the warners are from the jinn. Then he recited: ﴿to their people as warners﴾ [see vol. 16, p. 210]. This is the meaning of Ibn 'Abbas's statement, and it is the sound view, as will be explained in al-Ahqaf [see vol. 16, p. 210].

al-Kalbi [in K: Muqatil said: this is the meaning of, etc.] said: Messengers used to be sent before Muhammad (ﷺ) to both humankind and the jinn together. I say: This is not sound. Rather, in Sahih Muslim, from the hadith of Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah al-Ansari, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "I have been given five things that no prophet before me was given: every prophet was sent to his own people specifically, and I have been sent to every red and black [person]," and the hadith continues. This will be explained in al-Ahqaf [see vol. 16, p. 210].

Ibn 'Abbas said: Messengers used to be sent to humankind, and Muhammad (ﷺ) was sent to the jinn and humankind. This was related by Abu al-Layth al-Samarqandi. It was also said: A group of the jinn listened to the prophets, then returned to their people and informed them, as was the case with our Prophet, peace be upon him. Thus they are called messengers of God, even though their sending is not explicitly stated. And in the revelation: ﴿From both of them come forth the pearl and the coral﴾ [see vol. 17, p. 161], meaning from one of the two, since pearls and coral come forth from the salt water and not from the sweet. Likewise, the messengers are from humankind and not from the jinn. So the meaning of "from among you" is from one of you. This was permissible because the mention of both had preceded.

It was also said: The word "messengers" was used in the general sense because both humans and jinn are gathered together on the plain of Resurrection, and the reckoning is for them, not for creation in general. When they were in that place under one reckoning regarding reward and punishment, they were addressed that day with a single address, as if they were one group. This is because the beginning of their creation was for worship, and reward and punishment depend on worship. Also, the origin of the jinn is from a smokeless flame of fire, while our origin is from dust, and their creation is different from ours. Among them are believers and disbelievers.

Our enemy Iblis is an enemy to them; he is hostile to their believers and allied with their disbelievers. Among them are sectarian factions: Shi'a, Qadariyya and Murji'a, who recite our Book. God described them in Surah al-Jinn in His words: ﴿And among us are the Muslims, and among us are the unjust. Whoever has submitted, those have sought out the right course. And as for the unjust, they will be fuel for Hell﴾ and ﴿And among us are the righteous, and among us are those other than that; we were of divided ways﴾ [see vol. 19, p. 14], as will be explained there.

"Qussun" is in the place of a nominal qualifier (in the nominative) for "messengers."

﴿They will say: We bear witness against ourselves﴾, that is, we testify that they conveyed the message.

﴿And the worldly life deceived them﴾. It was said: This is an address from God to the believers, meaning that these people were deceived by the worldly life, that is, it deluded them, and they thought it would endure, and they feared its loss if they believed.

﴿And they bore witness against themselves﴾, that is, they acknowledged their disbelief. Muqatil said: This is when the limbs testified against them to their polytheism and to what they used to do [from K].

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 6, verse 131:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿That﴾ is in the position of the nominative according to Sibawayh, meaning: the matter is that. And "inna" is the lightened form of the heavy (inna), meaning: We only did this to them because I did not destroy the towns through their wrongdoing, i.e., through their polytheism, before sending the messengers to them, lest they say: "No bringer of good tidings nor warner came to us." And it has been said: "I did not destroy the towns for the polytheism of those among them who associated partners," so it is like ﴿and no bearer of burdens shall bear the burden of another﴾ [[See vol. 7, p. 157.]]. Had He destroyed them before the sending of the messengers, He would have had the right to do as He wills. Indeed, Jesus said: ﴿If You punish them, they are Your servants﴾ [[See vol. 6, p. 377.]], and this has already been mentioned [[See vol. 16, p. 196.]]. Al-Farra' permitted that "that" (dhalika) be in the position of the accusative, the meaning being: He did that to them, because He would not destroy the towns through wrongdoing.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 6, verse 132:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And for each there are degrees according to what they have done﴾, i.e., of the jinn and of mankind, as He said in another verse: "Those are the ones against whom the word has come into effect, among nations that had passed on before them of jinn and mankind; indeed, they were losers" [al-A'raf 7:38]. Then He said: "And for each there are degrees according to what they have done, and that He may fully repay them their deeds, and they will not be wronged" [al-Ahqaf 46:19]. In this there is an indication that the obedient among the jinn are in Paradise and the disobedient among them are in the Fire, just like mankind, equally. And this is the most sound of what has been said on this matter, so know it. The meaning of "And for each there are degrees" is: for each doer of obedience there are degrees of reward, and for each doer of disobedience there are levels (darkat) of punishment.

(And your Lord is not unaware) of what they do, i.e., He is not heedless and not forgetful. Ghaflah (heedlessness) is that a thing escapes you because you are occupied with something else.

(of what they do) Ibn 'Amir read it with the ta' (ta-ta'malun, "you"), while the rest read it with the ya' (ya'malun, "they").

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 6, verse 133:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And your Lord is the Free of need﴾, meaning: free of need from His creation and from their deeds.

(Possessor of mercy), meaning: toward His friends and the people of His obedience. (If He wills, He can take you away), meaning: by causing death and by eradicating you through punishment.

(And replace you with whom He wills after you), meaning: another creation better and more obedient than you.

(Just as He produced you from the descendants of another people). The kaf (the "like") is in the place of a accusative (naṣb), meaning: He will replace after you whom He wills with a replacement like that by which He produced you. Its parallel is: ﴿If He wills, He can take you away, O people, and bring others﴾ and ﴿If you turn away, He will substitute a people other than you﴾ [[See vol. 16, p. 257.]]. So the meaning is: others will be exchanged in your place, just as you say: "I gave you a garment from your dinar."

Qur'an 6:134: ﴿Indeed, what you are promised is surely coming﴾.

It may be that this is from "awda'tu" (I threatened) in the sense of evil, and its verbal noun is al-iy'ad (threatening). The intended meaning is the punishment of the Hereafter. It may also be from "wa'attu" (I promised), with the meaning being the Hour, in whose coming there is both good and evil, so the good was given precedence. This meaning has been related from al-Hasan.

﴿And you cannot escape﴾: that is, you cannot elude it. It is said: "A'jazani fulan," meaning, so-and-so eluded me and overpowered me.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 6, verse 135:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Say: O my people, act according to your standing⦅makanah⦆﴾. Abu Bakr read it in the plural, "makanatikum". The makanah is the manner (tariqah). The meaning is: remain upon what you are upon, for I too remain upon what I am upon. If it is said: how is it permissible for them to be commanded to persist in what they are upon while they are disbelievers? The answer is that this is a threat, as the Mighty and Majestic said: "So let them laugh a little and let them weep much" [see vol. 8, p. 216]. And what indicates this is "So you will come to know who will have the good outcome of the Abode", meaning the praiseworthy outcome for which its possessor is praised, i.e. who will have victory in the abode of Islam, who will inherit the earth, and who will have the Last Abode, i.e. Paradise. Al-Zajjaj said: "makanatikum" means your established position (tamakkunukum) in the world. Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan and al-Nakha'i said: "on your side (nahiyatikum)". Al-Qutabi said: "on your place (mawdi'ikum)".

(Inni 'amilun) upon my standing (makanati), and it is omitted because the situation indicates it. "Man" in His saying "man takunu lahu 'aqibatu al-dar" is in the accusative position in the sense of "alladhi" (the one who), because knowledge falls upon it. It may also be in the nominative position, because the interrogative does not take effect from what precedes it, so the verb is suspended (mu'allaq), meaning: you will know which of us will have the outcome of the abode, like His saying: "that We may know which of the two parties is better at computing" [see vol. 10, p. 364]. Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read "yakunu" (with the ya').

﴿وَجَعَلُوا لِلَّهِ مِمَّا ذَرَأَ مِنَ الْحَرْثِ وَالْأَنْعَامِ نَصِيبًا﴾ Regarding this, there is one issue. It is said: *dhara'a yadhra'u dhar'an*, meaning "he created." In the speech there is an ellipsis and abbreviation [[In K: *idmar* (an implied element).]], namely: "and they assigned a share for their idols," which is indicated by what follows. This was among the things that Satan adorned for them and made appealing to them, so that [[From K.]] they set aside a portion of their wealth for God, according to their claim, and a portion for their idols. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan, Mujahid, and Qatadah, and the meanings are close. They assigned a part for God and a part for their associates. If what belonged to their associates was spent on maintaining them and their custodians (*sadanah*, the attendants of the idols), it was made up to them from what belonged to God. But if what belonged to God was spent on guests and the needy, they were not compensated for it at all. They said: "God is self-sufficient, while our associates are poor." This was among their ignorances and their assertions. *Za'm* means falsehood. Shurayh al-Qadi said: "Every matter has a kunyah (a euphemistic name), and the kunyah of falsehood is *za'amu* (they claimed)." They lied in these matters because no revelation had come down concerning them.

Sa'id ibn Jubayr narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: "Whoever wishes to know the ignorance of the Arabs, let him recite what comes after the hundred and thirtieth verse of Surat al-An'am up to His words: ﴿Those who have lost are those who killed their children foolishly, without knowledge﴾."

Ibn al-'Arabi said: What he said is a sound statement. They acted on their deficient intellects in arranging what is lawful and unlawful, out of foolishness, without knowledge or justice. Yet what they handled with ignorance concerning the taking of deities is a greater ignorance and a greater crime, for transgressing against God, exalted is He, is greater than transgressing against created beings. The proof that God is one in His essence, one in His attributes, and one in His creation is clearer and more evident than the proof that this is lawful and that is unlawful.

It has been related that a man said to 'Amr ibn al-'As: "You, with the perfection of your minds and the abundance of your intellects, worship stone!" 'Amr replied: "Those are minds that their Creator has deceived." So this which God, glorified is He, informed of concerning the frivolity and ignorance of the Arabs is a matter that Islam has removed, and God has nullified it through the sending of the Messenger, peace be upon him. It would have been apparent to us to cause it to die out so that it does not appear, and to make it forgotten so that it is not mentioned. However, our Lord, blessed and exalted is He, mentioned it by its explicit text and set it forth with its explanation, just as He mentioned the disbelief of the disbelievers. The wisdom in that, and God knows best, is that His decree had already preceded, and His judgment had already been executed, that disbelief and confusion would not cease until the Day of Resurrection.

Yahya ibn Wathhab, al-Sulami, al-A'mash, and al-Kisa'i read *"bi-za'mihim"* with a *damma* on the *zay*. The rest read it with a *fatha*, and both are dialectal forms.

(﴿فَمَا كَانَ لِشُرَكَائِهِمْ فَلَا يَصِلُ إِلَى اللَّهِ﴾) That is: it does not reach the needy.

(﴿سَاءَ مَا يَحْكُمُونَ﴾) That is: evil is the judgment they render. Ibn Zayd said: When they slaughtered what belonged to God, they mentioned the name of the idols over it, and when they slaughtered what belonged to their idols, they did not mention the name of God over it. This is the meaning of ﴿فَمَا كَانَ لِشُرَكَائِهِمْ فَلَا يَصِلُ إِلَى اللَّهِ﴾.
