Their leaving out the mention of God was therefore blameworthy on their part, and it falls within the prohibition of eating what has not had the name of God mentioned over it.

The Qur'an verse (6:137) and the commentary's remarks on it are translated below.

﴿And thus their associates made attractive to many of the polytheists the killing of their children.﴾ The meaning: just as it was made attractive to these people to assign to God a share and to their idols a share, so too their associates made attractive to many of the polytheists the killing of their children. Mujahid and others said: [their associates] made the killing of daughters attractive to them, out of fear of poverty. Al-Farra' (Abu Zakariyya Yahya ibn Ziyad al-Farra', d. 207 AH, grammarian of Kufa) and al-Zajjaj (Abu Ishaq Ibrahim ibn al-Sari al-Zajjaj, d. 311 AH, grammarian) said: "Their associates" here means those who served the idols. It was also said: they are the misguided among men. It was also said: they are the devils. By this he refers to the hidden burying alive (al-wa'd al-khafi, the concealed form of burying daughters alive), which is the burying of a girl alive out of fear of captivity and need, and of having nothing of the support she would bring. The devils were called "associates" because they obeyed them in disobedience to God, so they made them partners with God in the obligation of obeying them. It was also said: in the Jahiliyya a man would swear by God, "If God grants me such-and-such number of boys, I will slaughter one of them," just as 'Abd al-Muttalib did when he vowed to sacrifice his son 'Abd Allah.

Then it was said: there are four readings (qira'at) of this verse. The most sound of them is the reading of the majority: "And thus their associates made attractive to many of the polytheists the killing of their children." This is the reading of the people of the two Sanctuaries (Makka and Madina), the people of Kufa, and the people of Basra. "Their associates" is in the nominative, governed by "zuyyina" (was made attractive), because they are the ones who made it attractive, and they did not kill. "Qatl" (killing) is in the accusative, governed by "zuyyina," and "awladuhum" (their children) is in the genitive, being a construct (mudaf) to the object. The original rule for the verbal noun (masdar) is that it be annexed to its subject, because it is the one who brings the action into being, and because the verbal noun cannot do without the agent while the object can be dispensed with. Here it is annexed to the object in form, but annexed to the subject in meaning, because the sense is: "made attractive to many of the polytheists their killing of their children by their associates," and then the annexed element, which is the subject, was omitted, just as it was omitted in God's words: ﴿Man does not tire of asking for good﴾ (41:49), meaning "of his asking for good." So the hā' (his) is the subject of the asking, meaning: man does not tire of asking for good. Likewise, His words "made attractive to many of the polytheists to kill their children their associates" [mean the same]. Makki (Abu Muhammad Makki ibn Abi Talib al-Qaysi, d. 437 AH, Qur'an scholar) said: this reading is the preferred one, because its grammatical construction (i'rab) is sound and because the community (al-jama'a) follows it.

The second reading: "zuyyina" (with a ḍamma on the zay, i.e., in the passive voice); "li-kathirin min al-mushrikin qatla" (with the noun in the nominative); "awladuhum" (in the genitive); "shurakaʾuhum" (in the nominative). This is the reading of al-Hasan (al-Basri). Ibn 'Amir and the people of Syria read "zuyyina" with a ḍamma on the zay, "li-kathirin min al-mushrikin qatlu awladihim" with "qatlu" in the nominative and "awladihim" in the accusative. "Shurakaʾihim" in the genitive, as Abu 'Ubayd related. Others related from the people of Syria that they read "wa-kadhalika zuyyina" with a ḍamma on the zay, "li-kathirin min al-mushrikin qatlu" in the nominative, "awladihim" in the genitive, and "shurakaʾihim" also in the genitive.

The second reading, the reading of al-Hasan, is permissible: "qatlu" is the subject of the passive verb, and "shurakaʾuhum" is in the nominative by an implied verb indicated by "zuyyina," meaning: their associates made it attractive. On this basis it is also permissible to say "ḍuriba Zaydun ʿAmrun," with the meaning "ḍarabahu ʿAmrun" (Zayd was struck by ʿAmr). Sibawayh (Abu Bishr ʿAmr ibn ʿUthman Sibawayh, d. c. 180 AH, grammarian) recited:

"Labbayka, Yazid, a suppliant for a dispute..."

meaning: "a suppliant makes him weep." Ibn ʿAmir and ʿAsim, in the transmission of Abu Bakr, read: ﴿There glorify Him therein in the mornings and evenings, men﴾ (24:36), with the sense: "men glorify Him." Ibn Abi ʿAbla (Ibrahim ibn Abi ʿAbla) read: ﴿Destroyed were the companions of the trench, the fire fed with fuel﴾ (85:4–5), with the sense: "the fire destroyed them."

Al-Nahhas (Abu Jaʿfar Ahmad ibn Muhammad al-Nahhas, d. 338 AH, grammarian and Qur'an commentator) said: as for what Abu 'Ubayd related from Ibn 'Amir and the people of Syria, it is not permissible in speech or in poetry. The grammarians permitted separating the annexed noun from what is annexed to it only by an adverb of time or place, because such a separation is not considered a true separation; but separating by nouns other than adverbs is a solecism (laḥn). Makki said: this reading is weak because of the separation between the annexed noun and what is annexed to it, since such a separation is only permitted in poetry with adverbs, owing to the latitude they are given; and separation with the object in poetry is remote, so permitting it in the Qur'an is even more remote. Al-Mahdawi (Abu al-'Abbas Ahmad ibn ʿAmmar al-Mahdawi, d. c. 430 AH, Qur'an scholar) said: the reading of Ibn 'Amir is by way of separating the annexed noun from what is annexed to it, and similar to it is the saying of the poet:

"So I thrust her with a short spear, the thrust of Abu Mazada upon the young she-camel."

[Footnote: al-Akhfash (Abu al-Hasan al-Akhfash al-Awsat) cited this line without attributing it to anyone. The word "zajj" here means a thrust, and "mazajja," with a kasra on the mim, is a short spear like the mazarīq. "Qalūṣ," with a fatḥa on the qaf, means a young she-camel. The poet means that he thrust his wife as Abu Mazada thrust the young she-camel. Abu was a man's kunya. Cited in al-ʿAyni's Sharḥ al-Shawāhid al-Kubrā, in the chapter on idafa.]

He means: the thrusting of Abu Mazada the young she-camel. And he recited:

"She passes over what she passes over, and she has torn the shifts of ʿAbd al-Qays from their breasts."

He means: she has torn the shifts of ʿAbd al-Qays' breasts.

Abu Ghanim Ahmad ibn Hamdan al-Nahwi said: the reading of Ibn 'Amir is not permissible in Arabic; it is the slip of a scholar, and when a scholar slips, it is not permissible to follow him. His saying is to be referred back to the consensus (ijma'), and likewise whoever among them slips or errs must be referred back to the consensus, for that is better than persisting in what is not correct. They only permitted a poet, by necessity (ḍarura), to separate the annexed noun from what is annexed to it by an adverb, because such a separation is not considered a true separation, as in the saying:

"As writing is inscribed one day by the hand of a Jew, drawing close or wiping out."

[Footnote: The verse is by Abu Hayya al-Numayri. The evidence in it is the annexation of "kaff" (hand) to "al-yahud" (the Jews) with separation by an adverb. He describes the traces of the abode and likens them to writing in its lines and to inference from them, and he specified the Jews because they are people of a Book. He made some of its writing close together and some of it separated and distant, because the traces of abodes require that description and condition. (From Sharh al-Shawahid.)]

Another said:

"As if the sounds, from their hastening with us, of the rear saddle-frames of the mays were the chirping of young chicks."

[Footnote: This verse is by Dhu al-Rumma. The evidence in it is the annexation of "aswat" (sounds) to "awakhir al-mays" (the rear of the mays saddles) with separation by a prepositional phrase, a necessity of poetry. "Mays" is a tree from which saddles are made. "Iygal" is swift travel. He says: as if the sounds of the rear of the mays saddles, from the violent pace of the camels with us and the jolting of their saddles upon them, were the sounds of chicks. (From Sharh al-Shawahid.)]

Another said:

"When Satidama saw her, she wept. By God, what a fine thing today is the one who blamed her!"

[Footnote: This verse is by ʿUmar ibn Qumaʾa. The evidence in it is the annexation of "dar" (good) to "man" (who) with permissibility of separation by an adverb as a necessity of poetry, when it is not possible to annex "dar" to him. It describes a woman who looked at Satidama, a particular mountain far from her abodes, so it reminded her of her land and she wept out of longing for it. (From Sharh al-Shawahid by al-Shantamari.)]

Al-Qushayri (Abu al-Qasim ʿAbd al-Karim al-Qushayri, d. 465 AH, Sufi and Qur'an scholar) said: some people said this is ugly, and this is impossible, because when the reading is established by mass transmission (tawatur) from the Prophet (ﷺ), it is eloquent, not ugly. This construction occurs in the speech of the Arabs, and in the Mushaf of 'Uthman (the standardized codex compiled under Caliph 'Uthman) "shurakaʾihim" is written with a yāʾ, and this indicates the reading of Ibn 'Amir. The killing is attributed in this reading to the associates, because the associates are the ones who made that attractive and called to it. So the verb is annexed to its agent, as is required in the original construction, but he separated between the annexed noun and what is annexed to it, placed the object first and left it in the accusative as it is, since it is later in meaning, and put the annexed element later and left it in the genitive as it is, since it comes before the killing. The sense is: "And thus was made attractive to many of the polytheists the killing of their associates of their children," that is, that their associates killed their children. Al-Nahhas said: as for what someone other than Abu 'Ubayd related (and this is the fourth reading), it is permissible, on the basis that "shurakaʾahum" is a substitute (badal) for "awladihim," because they are their associates in lineage and inheritance.

﴿That they may bring them to ruin﴾: the lam is the lam of purpose (lam kay). "Al-irda'" means destruction.

﴿And that they may confuse them regarding their religion﴾ which He had approved for them: that is, they command them with falsehood and cast doubt upon them regarding their religion. They were upon the religion of Isma'il, and in it there was the killing of children; so the truth becomes covered over, and by this they confuse them.

﴿Had God willed, they would not have done it﴾: (Exalted is He) explained that their disbelief is by God's will. This is a refutation of the Qadariyya (the early school that affirmed human free will in a way that denied divine predestination). ﴿So leave them and what they invent﴾: he means their saying that God has associates.

Al-Qurtubi, al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Qur'an, commentary on Surah al-An'am (6), verse 138:

He (may He be exalted) mentions another kind of their ignorance. Aban ibn Uthman read "ḥujr" with a ḍamma on the ḥa' and the jim. Al-Hasan and Qatada read "ḥajr" with a fatḥa on the ḥa' and a sukun on the jim; the two are dialectal variants with the same meaning. Also reported from al-Hasan is "ḥujr" with a ḍamma on the ḥa'. Abu Ubayd related from Harun, who said: "Al-Hasan used to put a ḍamma on the ḥa' in "ḥijr" throughout the Qur'an, except in His saying: ﴿a barrier and a forbidding ban﴾ [see vol. 13, p. 58], where he would kassa it here." It is also reported from Ibn Abbas and Ibn al-Zubayr: "wa-ḥarthun ḥirj" (﴿and a tilth [of] restriction﴾), with the rā' before the jim, and likewise in the codex of Ubayy. On this there are two opinions. The first is that it is like jabadha and jadhaba (two forms of the same verb meaning "to pull"). The other opinion, and it is the more sound, is that it derives from al-ḥirj, for al-ḥirj (with a kasra on the ḥa') is a dialectal form of al-ḥaraj (with a fatḥa on the ḥa'), which means constriction and sin, so its meaning is the forbidden. One says "fulan yataḥarraj," meaning he constricts his own self from entering into what is doubtful to him of the forbidden.

Al-ḥijr is a homonymous term (lafẓ mushtarak), and here it has the meaning of "the forbidden," its root meaning being prohibition. The intellect is called ḥijr because it prevents one from ugly deeds. "Fulan is in the ḥijr of the judge," i.e. in his protection. "I placed the child under ḥajr (interdiction)." Al-ḥijr also means intellect; Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Is there in that an oath for one of ḥijr?﴾ [see vol. 20, p. 42]. Al-ḥijr also means the female horse, and al-ḥijr means kinship. He said:

They want to distance him from me, though he is
a man of noble lineage, near to me, and of kinship.

The ḥijr of a person and his ḥajr are two dialectal forms, and the fatḥa is more common. That is, they declared forbidden certain livestock and tilth and dedicated them to their idols, saying: ﴿None may eat of them except whom we wish﴾, and they were the servants of the idols. Then He clarified that this was an arbitrary decree for which no revelation had come, and for this reason He said: ﴿by their claim﴾.

﴿And livestock whose backs have been forbidden﴾: he means what they set free for their gods, as previously mentioned regarding the share. Mujahid said: the intended meaning is the bahira, the wasila and the ham [[The baḥīra: a she-camel that had given birth to five young, the last of which was a male; its ear was slit, its back was left unridden, unladen and unslaughtered, it was not driven away from water it came to, nor prevented from pasture, and if a weary, exhausted traveller met it, he would not ride it. The wasīla: a she-camel that had given birth to ten young in succession; and a she-goat that had given birth to seven young in succession, two she-kids; if in the seventh birth she bore a female and a male, it was said she had "joined" her brother, and then only men, not women, could drink her milk. The ḥāmī: a stallion camel that had covered the counted number of mares, ten times; when it reached that, they said "this is a ḥāmī," meaning it had protected its back, so it was left alone, not benefited from in any way, nor prevented from water or pasture. See vol. 6, p. 335 and following.]].

﴿And livestock over which the name of Allah is not mentioned﴾: he means what they slaughtered for their gods. Abu Wa'il said: they did not perform the Hajj upon them.

﴿Fabricating falsehood against Him﴾: i.e., for the purpose of fabricating against Allah, because they used to say: "Allah has commanded us with this." It is in the accusative as an object of purpose (maf'ul lahu). It was also said: meaning they fabricate fabrication, and its accusative form is because it is a verbal noun (maṣdar).

**Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on Surah 6, verse 139:**

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And they say, "What is in the wombs of these livestock is exclusively for our males."﴾ This is another kind of their ignorance. Ibn ʿAbbas said: "It is the milk. They made it lawful for the males and forbidden to the females." It was also said: "It is the fetuses. They said, 'It is for our males.' Then, if any of it died, both men and women would eat it." The ה (hāʾ) in "خالِصَةٌ" (khāliṣah) is for emphasis on exclusivity (hāʾ al-mubālaghah), and similarly one says "رَجُلٌ عَلَّامَةٌ وَنَسَّابَةٌ" (a man who is very learned and a very expert genealogist), as reported from al-Kisaʾi and al-Akhfash. "خالِصَةٌ" with a raised vowel (marfūʿ) is the predicate (khabar) of the subject (mubtadaʾ), which is "مَا" (mā). Al-Farraʾ said: its feminine form is due to the feminine form of "الْأَنْعَامِ" (al-anʿām, the livestock). This view is considered by some people to be an error, because what is in their wombs is not part of them, so it is not like the saying ﴿يَلْتَقِطْهُ بَعْضُ السَّيَّارَةِ﴾ [[from K.]] [[See vol. 9, p. 133.]] , because "بَعْضُ السَّيَّارَةِ" (some of the caravan) is itself a caravan, and this does not apply here. (Al-Farraʾ said): Indeed, what is in the wombs of the livestock is livestock like them, so the feminine form is used because of their feminine nature; that is, the livestock that are in the wombs of the livestock are exclusively for our males. It was also said: that is, the group of what is in the wombs. It was also said: "مَا" refers to the milks or the fetuses, so the feminine form came according to meaning, and the masculine form according to wording.

For this reason He said ﴿and forbidden to our wives﴾ according to the wording. Had He followed the meaning, He would have said "وَمُحَرَّمَةٌ" (wa-muḥarramah, feminine). What supports this is the reading of al-Aʿmash: "خَالِصٌ" (khāliṣ) without the hāʾ. Al-Kisaʾi said: the meaning of "خَالِصٌ" and "خَالِصَةٌ" is one, except that the hāʾ is for emphasis, as one says "رَجُلٌ دَاهِيَةٌ وَعَلَّامَةٌ" (a man who is very shrewd and very learned), as mentioned earlier. Qatadah read "خَالِصَةً" (khāliṣatan) with a fatha, as a circumstantial state (ḥāl) from the pronoun in the adverbial phrase (ẓarf) which is the relative clause (ṣilah) of "مَا". The predicate of the subject is omitted, as when you say: "الَّذِي فِي الدَّارِ قَائِمًا زَيْدُ" (the one who is in the house standing is Zayd). This is the position of the Basran grammarians. According to al-Farraʾ, it is in the accusative by way of separation (qaṭʿ). The same applies to the reading of Saʿid ibn Jubayr: "خَالِصًا" (khāliṣan). Ibn ʿAbbas read "خَالِصَةٌ" in the construct form (idafah), so it is a second inceptive (mubtadaʾ thānī), and the predicate is "لِذُكُورِنَا" (for our males), and the whole clause is the predicate of "مَا". It is also permissible for "خَالِصَةٌ" to be an apposition (badal) for "مَا". These are five readings.

﴿And forbidden to our wives﴾: that is, "our daughters", according to Ibn Zayd. Others said: "their women." If it is dead (inkāna maytatan), it is read with the yāʾ and the tāʾ, meaning: if what is in the wombs of the livestock is dead [[from K.]], ﴿then they share in it﴾, that is, the men and the women. He said ﴿fīhi﴾ (in it) because the intended meaning of "المَيْتَة" (the dead one) is the animal, and this strengthens the reading with the yāʾ, and He did not say "فِيهَا" (fīhā). "مَيْتَةٌ" (maytatun) with the raised vowel means "takes place" or "occurs". "مَيْتَةً" (maytatan) with the fatha means: if the living being is dead.

﴿He will repay them for their description﴾: that is, for their lying and their fabrication; that is, He will punish them for that. "وَصْفَهُمْ" (waṣfahum) is in the accusative by the removal of the preposition (naḥḍ al-khāfiḍ, i.e., the preposition is dropped), meaning "for their description." In the verse there is evidence that the scholar should learn the view of one who opposes him, even if he does not adopt it, until he knows the corruption of that view and knows how to refute it, because Allah the Exalted informed the Prophet ﷺ and his Companions of the view of those who opposed them among (the people of [[from K. and ʿ.]]) their time, so that they might recognize the corruption of their view.

He informed of their loss through their burying of the daughters (al-wa'd) and their prohibition of the bahirah (a she-camel whose ear was slit and was left free from certain burdens) and other things by their own minds. They killed their children out of foolishness, fearing poverty, and they restricted themselves in their wealth, yet they did not fear poverty. This shows the inconsistency of their opinions.

I say: Among the Arabs there were those who killed their children for fear of poverty, as Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, mentioned in another place. Some of them killed out of foolishness without any proof for their killing, and they were Rabi'ah and Mudar. They would kill their daughters for the sake of tribal zeal (hamiyyah). Some of them said: "The angels are the daughters of Allah," so they attached the daughters to the daughters.

It is narrated that a man from the Companions of the Prophet (ﷺ) was always troubled in the presence of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). He said to him: "Why are you grieved?" He said: "O Messenger of Allah, I committed a sin in the Jahiliyyah, and I fear that Allah will not forgive it for me, even if I embrace Islam!" He said to him: "Tell me about your sin." He said: "O Messenger of Allah, I was one of those who killed their daughters. A daughter was born to me, and my wife interceded with me to leave her, so I left her until she grew up and reached maturity, and she became one of the most beautiful women. They proposed to her, and zeal overcame me, and my heart could not bear that I should marry her off or leave her in the house without a husband. So I said to the woman: 'I want to go to such-and-such tribe to visit my relatives, so send her with me.' She was pleased with that, and she adorned her with garments and jewelry, and she took from me covenants that I would not betray her. I took her to the edge of a well and looked into the well, and the girl sensed that I wanted to throw her into the well. So she clung to me and began to weep and say: 'O father! What are you going to do to me!' So I had mercy on her. Then I looked into the well, and zeal overcame me again. Then she clung to me and began to say: 'O father, do not waste the trust of my mother!' So I kept looking once into the well and once at her, and I had mercy on her, until Satan overcame me. I took her and threw her into the well upside down, and she was calling out from within the well: 'O father, you have killed me!' I stayed there until her voice stopped, and then I returned." Then the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and his Companions wept, and he said: "If I were commanded to punish anyone for what he did in the Jahiliyyah, I would punish you."

There are twenty-three issues concerning this verse.

**First issue:** His words, Exalted is He: ﴿He brought into being﴾, meaning He created ﴿gardens, trellised and untrellised﴾. Trellised means orchards that are propped up and raised. Untrellised means not raised. Ibn 'Abbas said: "Trellised" refers to what spreads over the ground and is supported by nothing, such as vines, crops and watermelons. "Untrellised" refers to what stands on a stalk, such as palm trees and all other trees. It was also said: the trellised are those whose trees are raised. The root meaning of *ta'rish* (trellising) is raising. Ibn 'Abbas also said: the trellised are those that people planted and raised, and the untrellised are the fruits that grow in the wilderness and the mountains. This is supported by the reading of 'Ali (may Allah be pleased with him), "*maghrusat* and *ghayr maghrusat*" (planted and unplanted), with a dotted *ghayn* and an undotted *sin*.

**Second issue:** His words, Exalted is He: ﴿and the date palm and the crops﴾. He singled out these two for mention, although they are included in the gardens, because of the excellence they possess. This was explained earlier in *al-Baqara* at His words, "Whoever is an enemy to Allah and His angels" (2:98), and the verse that follows. ﴿Diverse in its produce﴾ means its taste, some of it good and some of it inferior. He called it *ukul* (produce) because it is eaten. ﴿Its produce﴾ is in the nominative as the subject of a nominal sentence. ﴿Diverse﴾ is its adjective, but since it was placed before it and followed it in the accusative, it was put in the accusative, as you say: "I have a cook as a servant" (*'indi tabbakhan ghulam*). The poet said:

*The evil is widespread and meets you by chance,*
*while the good deeds have a door shut against them.*

It was also said that ﴿diverse﴾ is in the accusative as a *hal* (circumstantial qualifier). Abu Ishaq al-Zajjaj said: this is a difficult point of grammar, because it is said: he created them, yet their produce was not diverse, meaning their fruit. The answer is that Allah, glorified is He, created them by His saying "Creator of all things," so He informed that He created them as diverse in their produce, that is, He created them having diversity determined within them. Sibawayh explained this by saying: "I passed by a man with a falcon, hunting with it tomorrow," in the sense of a *hal*, just as you say, "You will surely enter the house eating and drinking," meaning determining that. A third answer: when He created it, it was diverse in its produce, in the sense that if it had been for him, it would have been diverse in its produce. He did not say "their produce" (the dual), because He was satisfied with repeating the reference to one of them, as in His saying: "And when they see a trade or a diversion, they scatter to it" (62:11), meaning to both of them. This meaning has already been mentioned.

**Third issue:** His words, Exalted is He: ﴿and the olive and the pomegranate﴾ are conjoined to it. ﴿Similar and dissimilar﴾ is in the accusative as a *hal*. In this there are three proofs. The first is what has already been mentioned: the evidence that changing things must have a changer. The second is the favour bestowed on us by Him, glorified is He. If, when He created us, He had wished not to create food for us, He could have; and when He created it, He could have made it not beautiful in appearance and not pleasant in taste; and having created it so, He could have made it not easy to pick. He was not obliged to do that from the outset, since nothing is obligatory upon Him. The third is the proof of power: that water, whose nature is to sink, rises by the power of Allah, the One, Knower of the unseen, from the bottoms of the tree to its tops; and when it reaches the top, leaves appear in it that are not of its kind, and fruit emerges whose nature is a full body, a radiant colour, fresh picking, and a delicious taste. Where, then, are the natures and their kinds? Where are the philosophers and their men? Is it within the power of nature to perfect this perfection, or to arrange this wondrous arrangement? No! Such a thing cannot be complete in minds except by a living, knowing, powerful, willing One. Glory be to Him who has a sign and an end in everything!

The connection of this with what precedes is that when the unbelievers fabricated lies against Allah, associated partners with Him, and declared things lawful and unlawful, He pointed them to His oneness by showing that He is the Creator of things, and that He made these things provisions for them.

**Fourth issue:** His words, Exalted is He: ﴿Eat of its fruit when it bears fruit, and give its due on the day of its harvest﴾. These are two commands, both in the form of *af'al* (imperatives). One of them is permissible, as in His saying, "Disperse in the earth" (62:10). The second is obligatory. In the Law it is not impossible for a permissible matter and an obligatory matter to be joined. He began by mentioning the blessing of eating before the command to give the due, to show that beginning with the blessing came from His bounty before the imposition of obligation.

**Fifth issue:** His words, Exalted is He: ﴿and give its due on the day of its harvest﴾. People differed about the interpretation of this due, what it is. Anas ibn Malik, Ibn 'Abbas, Tawus, al-Hasan, Ibn Zayd, Ibn al-Hanafiyya, al-Dahhak and Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab said: it is the prescribed *zakat* (obligatory alms), the tenth (*'ushr*) and the half-tenth (*nisf al-'ushr*). Ibn Wahb and Ibn al-Qasim reported this from Malik in interpreting the verse, and some of al-Shafi'i's companions said the same. Al-Zajjaj related that it was said regarding this verse that it was revealed in Medina.

Ali ibn al-Husayn, 'Ata', al-Hakam, Hammad, Sa'id ibn Jubayr and Mujahid said: it is a right in wealth other than *zakat*, which Allah enjoined as a recommendation. This was also reported from Ibn 'Umar and Muhammad ibn al-Hanafiyya, and Abu Sa'id al-Khudri reported it from the Prophet (ﷺ). Mujahid said: when you harvest and the needy are present, throw some of the ears of grain to them; when you cut the dates, throw some of the stalks to them; when you thresh and winnow it, throw some of it to them; and when you know its measure, take out its *zakat* from it.

A third view holds that it has been abrogated (*mansukh*) by *zakat*, because this surah is Meccan, and the verse of *zakat* was not revealed until Medina: "Take from their wealth a charity" (9:103), and "Establish prayer and give *zakat*" (2:43). This was reported from Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn al-Hanafiyya, al-Hasan, 'Ata' al-'Awfi, al-Nakha'i and Sa'id ibn Jubayr. Sufyan said: I asked al-Suddi about this verse, and he said: "It was abrogated by the tenth and the half-tenth." I said: "From whom?" He said: "From the scholars."

**Sixth issue:** Abu Hanifa has relied upon this verse, and upon the generality of his (peace be upon him) saying: "On what is watered by the sky, a tenth; and on what is watered by irrigation with a water-wheel (*nadh*) or a bucket, half a tenth." (The *nadh* is watering crops and other things with the water-camel, which is the animal one draws water with.) He uses this to make *zakat* obligatory on everything the earth produces, whether food or otherwise. Abu Yusuf reported from him an exception: firewood, grass, clover, figs, palm fronds, the reed of *dharira* (a reed brought from India, like arrow-reed, red, used for medicine), and sugar cane.

The majority rejected this, relying on the view that the purpose of the hadith is to specify what the tenth is taken from and what the half-tenth is taken from. Abu 'Umar (Ibn 'Abd al-Barr) said: as far as I know, there is no disagreement among scholars that *zakat* is obligatory on wheat, barley, dates and raisins, meaning the six staple grains, and that *zakat* on maize and *sult* (a type of barley) is also not disputed. Another group said: there is no *zakat* on anything other than these. This was reported from al-Hasan, Ibn Sirin and al-Sha'bi. Among the Kufans, Ibn Abi Layla, al-Thawri, al-Hasan ibn Salih, Ibn al-Mubarak and Yahya ibn Adam held it, and Abu 'Ubayd adopted it. It was reported from Abu Musa from the Prophet (ﷺ), and it was Abu Musa's own position: he took *zakat* only from wheat, barley, dates and raisins, as Waki' related from Talha ibn Yahya from Abu Burda from his father.

Malik and his companions said: *zakat* is obligatory on every staple that is stored, and al-Shafi'i said the same. Al-Shafi'i also said: *zakat* is only obligatory on what dries and can be stored, as a staple food. There is nothing on olives because they are a condiment. Abu Thawr said the same. Ahmad gave several views, the clearest of which is that *zakat* is obligatory on everything that Abu Hanifa said, if it is measured by *wasq* (a load of about sixty *sa'*). So he made it obligatory on almonds, because they are measured by volume, but not on walnuts, because they are counted. He argued from the Prophet's (peace be upon him) saying: "There is no charity on less than five *awsuq* of dates or grain." He said: the Prophet (ﷺ) made clear that the place of the obligation is the *wasq*, and specified the quantity from which the due must be given.

Al-Nakha'i held that *zakat* is obligatory on everything the earth produces, even ten bundles of green herbs (*dastaja* of herbs; a *dastaja* is a bundle). The position was reported from him differently. This is also the view of Umar ibn 'Abd al-Aziz, for he wrote that a tenth should be taken from whatever the earth produces, whether little or much. 'Abd al-Razzaq reported it from Ma'mar from Simak ibn al-Fadl, who said: Umar wrote... and he mentioned it. It is also the view of Hammad ibn Abi Sulayman and his student Abu Hanifa.

Ibn al-'Arabi inclined to this in his *Ahkam*, saying: "As for Abu Hanifa, he made the verse his mirror, saw the truth, and began to support and strengthen the Hanafi school." He said in the book *al-Qabas bi-ma 'alayhi al-Imam Malik ibn Anas* (*The Torch on What the Imam Malik ibn Anas Held*): Allah said: "the olive and the pomegranate, similar and dissimilar." People differed on whether *zakat* is obligatory on all that it includes or on some of it, and we have explained that in *al-Ahkam*. The essence is that *zakat* is only attached to staple foods, as we have shown, not to vegetables. Pomegranates, peaches (*firsik*, a kind of peach, or a smooth red variety, or whatever splits around a stone) and citrons were in al-Ta'if, yet the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) neither addressed them nor mentioned them, nor did any of his successors.

I say: even though he did not mention it in *al-Ahkam*, this is the correct position on the question, and vegetables have nothing due on them. As for the verse, scholars have differed over whether it is definitive (*muhkam*), abrogated (*mansukh*), or to be understood as a recommendation (*nadb*). No decisive proof determines one of its possible meanings. Rather, the decisive known matter is what Ibn Bukayr mentioned in his *Ahkam*: that Kufa was conquered after the death of the Prophet (ﷺ) and after the rulings had been established in Medina. Could anyone with the least insight suppose that a law like this was suspended and not acted upon in the land of emigration and the seat of revelation, nor in the caliphate of Abu Bakr, until the Kufans acted upon it? Indeed, this is a calamity for whoever thinks this and holds it!

I say: among what indicates this from the sense of revelation is His saying, Exalted is He: "O Messenger, deliver what has been sent down to you from your Lord, and if you do not, you have not conveyed His message" (5:67). Do you think he would conceal anything he was commanded to convey or to explain? Far be it from him!

And He, Exalted is He, said: "Today I have perfected your religion for you and completed My favour upon you" (5:3). And from the perfection of the religion is that it did not take anything from vegetables. Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah said, as reported by al-Daraqutni: "Indeed the melon patches (*al-maqathi*..."

(Plural of *miqtha'a*, with the *tha'* vowelled either with a fatha or a damma): the place where cucumbers grow.]] It used to be with us, and it would yield ten thousand, yet nothing was due on it. Al-Zuhri and al-Hasan said: the price of vegetables is subject to *zakah* (obligatory almsgiving) when they are sold and their price reaches two hundred dirhams. Al-Awza'i said the same concerning the price of fruits. There is no proof in their view, for the reason we have mentioned. Al-Tirmidhi narrated from Mu'adh that he wrote to the Prophet (ﷺ) asking him about *khadrawat* (vegetables), which are herbs, and he said: "There is nothing due on them." This meaning has also been narrated from Jabir, Anas, Ali, Muhammad ibn Abd Allah ibn Jahsh, Abu Musa and Aisha. Al-Daraqutni (may Allah have mercy on him) recorded their hadiths. Al-Tirmidhi said: "Nothing authentic has been transmitted on this subject from the Prophet (ﷺ)." Some of the companions of Abu Hanifa relied on the hadith of Salih ibn Musa, from Mansur, from Ibrahim, from al-Aswad, from Aisha, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Of what the earth produces of vegetables there is *zakah*." Abu Umar (Ibn Abd al-Barr) said: "No trustworthy transmitter among the students of Mansur narrated it in this form; it is only the saying of Ibrahim." I say: Since the argument from the Sunnah falls away because its chains are weak, nothing remains except what we have mentioned, namely the specification of the general wording of the verse, and the general statement of the Prophet (peace be upon him): "For what the sky waters, a tenth." Abu Yusuf and Muhammad said: There is no *zakah* on any vegetable unless it has a lasting yield, except saffron and the like, which are weighed, and on these *zakah* is due. Muhammad considered that for safflower and flax the seed is the criterion: when the seed of safflower and flax reaches five *awsuq* (plural of *wasq*, a measure), the safflower and flax follow the seed, and a tenth or half a tenth is taken from it. As for cotton, nothing is due on it in his view if it is less than five loads (*haml*), and a load is three hundred *manns* by the Iraqi measure. For woad and saffron, nothing is due on less than five *manns* of them; when either reaches five *manns*, alms are due on it, a tenth or half a tenth. Abu Yusuf said: Likewise sugarcane, from which sugar is made, grown on *'ushr* land rather than *kharaj* land (land subject to land tax): it is treated like saffron. Abd al-Malik ibn al-Majishun required *zakah* on the roots of fruit trees but not on herbs. This is contrary to the position of Malik and his followers, who hold that there is no *zakah* on almonds, walnuts, *aljalawz* (hazelnuts) or the like, even though these can be stored. Likewise, they hold there is no *zakah* on plums, apples, pears, or anything similar that does not dry out and is not stored. They differed regarding figs. The best-known view among the people of the Maghrib who follow the school of Malik is that there is no *zakah* on figs. Only Abd al-Malik ibn Habib held that *zakah* is due on them according to the school of Malik, by analogy with dates and raisins. To this view went a group of scholars from Baghdad among the Malikis, including Isma'il ibn Ishaq and those who followed him. Malik said in the *Muwatta'*: "The Sunnah on which there is no disagreement among us, and what I have heard from the people of knowledge, is that there is no alms on any fruit at all: pomegranates, peaches, figs and whatever resembles them. And whatever does not resemble them, if it is a fruit." Abu Umar said: "He included figs in this category, and I think (Allah knows best) that he did not know that they dry out, are stored and are eaten as staple food. Had he known this, he would not have included them in this category, since they are more similar to dates and raisins than to pomegranates." It has reached me that al-Abhari and a group of his companions used to issue rulings requiring *zakah* on figs, and considered it the school of Malik according to their principles. Figs are measured by volume, so the five *awsuq* and what is similar to it by weight are taken into account, and among them figs are judged by the ruling on dates and raisins taken together. Al-Shafi'i said: "There is no *zakah* on any fruit except dates and grapes, because the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) took alms from these two, and they were a staple food in the Hijaz that could be stored. He said: Walnuts and almonds are sometimes stored, and there is no *zakah* on them, because as far as I know they were not a staple in the Hijaz; they were fruit. There is no *zakah* on olives, because of the saying of Allah, Exalted: ﴿the olive and the pomegranate﴾, where He paired it with the pomegranate, and there is no *zakah* on that. Also, figs are more beneficial than olives as a staple, and there is no *zakah* on them." Al-Shafi'i had an opinion requiring *zakah* on olives, which he stated in Iraq, while the earlier view, which he stated in Egypt, was the other. Thus al-Shafi'i's position on olives fluctuated, whereas the position of Malik on it did not differ. This shows that the verse is, in their view, *muhkam* (not abrogated) and not *mansukh* (abrogated). Both of them, and all the jurists, agreed that there is no *zakah* on pomegranates, although it would have been necessary for them to require *zakah* on it. Abu Umar said: "If the pomegranate was excluded by consensus, then it is clear that the intended meaning is that the verse is not general, and the pronoun refers to some of what was mentioned and not all of it." And Allah knows best.

I say: On this basis, those who make the tithe (*'ushr*, one-tenth) obligatory on vegetables have argued, for He, the Exalted, said: ﴿And give its due on the day of its harvest﴾. The thing mentioned before it is the olive and the pomegranate, and the thing mentioned after it, ﴿...﴾, is a separate clause, which by agreement refers to the last of them. This is the statement of al-Kiya al-Tabari (Ilkiya al-Tabari).

It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: "No pomegranate has ever been pollinated except with a drop of water from Paradise." It is also narrated from 'Ali, may Allah ennoble his face, that he said: "When you eat a pomegranate, eat it with its inner membrane, for it is the tanning of the stomach." Ibn 'Asakir mentioned in *Tarikh Dimashq* (*The History of Damascus*) from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: "Do not break a pomegranate from its top, for in it there is a worm from which leprosy arises."

The benefits of olive oil will come in Surah al-Mu'minun, if Allah the Exalted wills. [Refer to vol. 12, p. 114.]

Among those who said that zakat is obligatory on olives were al-Zuhri, al-Awza'i, al-Layth, al-Thawri, Abu Hanifa and his companions, and Abu Thawr. Al-Zuhri, al-Awza'i and al-Layth said: it is estimated (*yukhraṣu*) as olives, and clear oil is taken. [The meanings of *kharṣ* (estimation) will come in the ninth issue.]

Malik said: it is not estimated, but the tithe is taken after it has been pressed and its measure reaches five *awsuq* (plural of *wasq*, a measure of weight or volume). Abu Hanifa and al-Thawri said: it is taken from its kernel (*ḥabb*).

The seventh issue: His saying, the Exalted, ﴿on the day of its harvest﴾. Abu 'Amr, Ibn 'Amir and 'Asim read *ḥaṣādahu* with a fatha on the *ḥa'*, and the rest read it with a kasra. Both are well-known dialectal forms (*lughatān*). Similar pairs are *al-ṣiram* and *al-ṣaram*, *al-jadhadh* and *al-jidhadh*, and *al-qaṭāf* and *al-qiṭāf*.

The scholars differed about the time when the obligation arises, in three opinions:

The first: it is the time of cutting and gathering (*al-jadhadh*). Muhammad ibn Maslama said this, based on the saying of the Exalted: ﴿on the day of its harvest﴾.

The second: it is the day of ripening (*al-ṭīb*), because before ripening the produce is fodder, not food or sustenance. When it ripens and the eating that Allah has bestowed becomes available, the right that Allah commanded becomes due, since the completion of a blessing makes the thanking of the blessing obligatory. The giving at the harvest then refers to what became due on the day of ripening.

The third: it is after the estimation (*khars*) is complete, because at that point the due portion of zakat is determined, so it becomes a condition for its obligation. Its parallel is the arrival of the collector (*sā'ī*) for sheep, and al-Mughira said this.

The sound view is the first, because of the explicit text of the revelation. The well-known view within the school is the second, and al-Shafi'i said this. The practical difference appears if the owner dies after ripening: the zakat is then paid from his estate, and if he dies before the estimation, it falls on his heirs.

Muhammad ibn Maslama said: the estimation was only brought forward as a concession (*tawsi'a*) to the owners of the fruit. If someone pays his zakat after the estimation and before the cutting, it suffices for him, because he has paid it before it became due.

The scholars differed about the practice of estimation, and this is the eighth issue. Al-Thawri disliked it and did not permit it under any circumstances, saying: "Estimation is not an established practice." He said: "The owner of the orchard is only required to pay the tenth of what comes into his hand for the poor, once it reaches five *awsuq*." Al-Shaybani narrated from al-Sha'bi that he said: "Estimation today is an innovation (*bid'a*)." The majority disagree with this. Then they differed. The majority hold that it is permitted for dates and grapes, based on the hadith of 'Attab ibn Usayd, that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ sent him and commanded him to estimate the grapes as one estimates the date palms, and their zakat would be taken as raisins, just as the zakat of date palms is taken as dates. Abu Dawud narrated it. Dawud ibn 'Ali said: estimation for zakat is permitted for date palms and not permitted for grapes. He rejected the hadith of 'Attab ibn Usayd because it is *munqaṭi'* (with a break in its chain) and does not connect through a sound route. Abu Muhammad 'Abd al-Haqq said this.

The ninth issue: the manner of estimation is that one assesses how many fresh dates (*ruṭab*) are on the palm, and assesses how much would be lost if they were dried into dates (*yutammaru*). [In the manuscript *k*: *tutammaru*, meaning it becomes dates by drying.] Then one counts what remains after the loss, and adds some of it to some of the rest until the orchard (*ḥā'iṭ*, a garden) is complete. The same applies to grapes, in every vine trellis (*dāliya*). [From *k*.]

The tenth issue: one estimator suffices for the estimation, like a judge. If there is more dates than what was estimated, the owner of the orchard is not obliged to pay anything on the excess, because it is a ruling that has already been executed. 'Abd al-Wahhab said this. Likewise, if there is less, the zakat is not reduced. Al-Hasan said: "The Muslims used to be estimated against, and then taken from on that estimation."

The eleventh issue: if the owner of the orchard finds the estimate too high, the estimator gives him the choice between giving what was estimated and taking back his estimate. 'Abd al-Razzaq narrated this, from Ibn Juraij, from Abu al-Zubayr, that he heard Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah say: "Ibn Rawaha estimated forty thousand *wasq*, and he claimed that when he gave the Jews the choice, they took the dates and gave him twenty thousand *wasq*." Ibn Juraij said: "I asked 'Ata': 'Is it right, when the owner of the property finds the estimate too high, that the estimator should give him the choice, as Ibn Rawaha gave the Jews the choice?'" He said: "Indeed, by my life! And what sunna is better than the sunna of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ?"

The twelfth issue: estimation is only done after ripening, because of the hadith of 'A'isha, who said: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ used to send Ibn Rawaha to the Jews, and he would estimate the date palms for them when the first dates ripened, before they were eaten. Then he would give the Jews the choice: they could take them at that estimate or hand them over to him." He ﷺ had only commanded estimation so that the zakat could be counted before the fruit was eaten and distributed. al-Daraqutni narrated it through the hadith of Ibn Juraij, from al-Zuhri, from 'Urwa, from 'A'isha. He said: "Salih ibn Abi al-Akhdar narrated it from al-Zuhri, from Ibn al-Musayyab, from Abu Hurayra, while Malik, Ma'mar and 'Uqayl narrated it as a *mursal* (with a missing companion) from al-Zuhri, from Sa'id, from the Prophet ﷺ."

The thirteenth issue: when the estimator estimates, the ruling is that he should deduct a certain amount from his estimate, based on what Abu Dawud, al-Tirmidhi and al-Busti (Ibn Hibban) narrated in his *Sahih* (in *k*, al-Nasa'i) from Sahl ibn Abi Hathma, that the Prophet ﷺ used to say: "When you estimate, take and leave a third; if you do not leave a third, leave a quarter." This is the wording of al-Tirmidhi. Abu Dawud said: "The estimator leaves a third for the *khurfa* (the fruit gathered for consumption)." Yahya al-Qattan said the same. Abu Hatim al-Busti said that this report has two aspects: one, that he leaves a third or a quarter of the tenth; the other, that he leaves that amount from the dates themselves before the tithe is taken, if the orchard is large enough to bear it.

*Al-khurfa* (with a *ḍamma* on the *kha'*) is what is gathered from the palms when their fruit ripens, that is, what is picked. It is said: "Dates are the *khurfa* of the fasting person," according to al-Jawhari and al-Harawi.

The well-known view of the school of Malik is that the estimator leaves nothing at the time of his estimate from the dates of the palm or the grapes; he estimates all of it. Some Medinese scholars narrated that it is lightened in the estimation and something is left for the *'arāyā* (a form of sale or gift of dates on the palm) and the *ṣila* (gift) and the like.

The fourteenth issue: if a calamity (*jā'iḥa*) befalls the fruit after the estimation and before the cutting, the zakat is dropped from him by the consensus of the scholars, unless what remains of it reaches five *awsuq* or more.

**(15th)** There is no zakat on less than five awsuq (wasq, pl. awsuq: a measure of sixty sa'). This is how it came, explained by the Prophet (ﷺ). In the Book, however, it is general (mujmal). Allah the Exalted says: ﴿O you who have believed, spend from the good things you have earned and from what We have produced for you from the earth﴾ [2:267]. He also says: ﴿and give its due on the day of its harvest﴾ [6:141]. Then the explanation came through the tenth and the half-tenth. Then, since the quantity at which property becomes liable for the due was stated in general terms, He explained it as well, saying: "There is no sadaqah on what is less than five awsuq of dates or grain." It also negates zakat on vegetables, since they are not measured by wasq. Whoever obtains five awsuq of dates or grain from his share is obligated to pay zakat, and likewise for raisins. This is what the scholars call the nisab. It is said: wisq and wasq (with the waw vowelled with kasra or fatha), and it is sixty sa'. The sa' is four mudd, and the mudd is a rittl and a third by the Baghdadi measure. The total of five awsuq in mudd is one thousand two hundred mudd, and by weight it is one thousand six hundred rittl. [[In al-Misbah: the Baghdadi rittl is twelve uqiyyah, the uqiyyah is one and two-thirds astar, the astar is four and a half mithqal, the mithqal is one dirham and three-sevenths of a dirham, the dirham is six danaq, the danaq is eight and two-fifths grains. Accordingly, the rittl is ninety mithqal, which is one hundred and twenty-eight and four-sevenths dirhams.]]

**(16th)** Whoever obtains five awsuq of dates and raisins together is not obligated to pay zakat (by consensus [[from b, z and k]]), because they are two different kinds. Likewise, they agreed that dates are not added to wheat, nor wheat to raisins, nor camels to cattle, nor cattle to goats. Sheep are added to goats by consensus. They differed over combining wheat with barley and spelt (sult), which are:

**(17th)** Malik permitted combining these three only, because they are in the sense of a single kind, being close in benefit and sharing the same place of growth and harvest. Their difference in name does not require a difference in ruling, like buffaloes and cattle, and goats and sheep. Al-Shafi'i and others said: they are not combined, because they are different kinds, their qualities are distinct, their names differ, and their taste differs, and this requires that they be separated. And Allah knows best. Malik said: all pulses (qatani) are one kind and are combined with one another. Al-Shafi'i said: a grain known by its own separate name is not combined with its companion, and they differ in form and taste; each kind is combined with its own kind, its inferior with its superior, like dates and its varieties, raisins black and red, and wheat and its varieties, such as samra and others. This is the view of al-Thawri, Abu Hanifa and his two companions Abu Yusuf and Muhammad, and Abu Thawr. Al-Layth said: all grains are combined, the qutniyyah [[qutniyyah (with the qaf vowelled with damma or kasra): whatever is other than wheat, barley, raisins and dates. In al-Tadhhib: qutniyyah is a general term for grains that are cooked, such as lentils, chickpeas, beans, chickpeas... etc.]] and others, some with others, for zakat. Ahmad ibn Hanbal used to hesitate about combining gold with silver, and about combining grains with one another; then at the end of his life he held the view of al-Shafi'i.

**(18th)** Malik said: what its owner consumed of it after it ripened (badw al-salah) or after it was dried (afrak) is counted against him. What its owner gave away from it at the harvest and gathering, and from the olives at picking, is estimated and counted against him. Most jurists disagree with him on this and do not require zakat except on what came into his hand after threshing. Al-Layth said regarding zakat on grains: it is begun with before expenditure. What he and his household eat of the dried produce is not counted against him, in the same way as what is left for the people of the orchard to eat, so it is not estimated against them. Al-Shafi'i said: the estimator leaves for the owner of the orchard what he and his household will eat fresh (ruṭab), and he does not estimate it against them. What is eaten while still fresh is not counted against him. Abu 'Umar said: al-Shafi'i and those who agree with him argued from Allah's saying: ﴿Eat of its fruit when it bears fruit and give its due on the day of its harvest﴾ [6:141]. They used this verse to show that what is eaten before harvest is not counted. They also cited the words of the Prophet (ﷺ): "When you estimate, leave the third; if you do not leave the third, leave the quarter." What the animals and cattle eat at threshing is not counted against its owner, according to Malik and others.

**(19th)** Whatever is sold of fava beans, chickpeas and lupins while still green, its quantity is estimated when dry, and its zakat is paid in grain. Likewise, what is sold of fruit while still green is considered, estimated and assessed when dry, and its zakat is paid on that estimate in raisins and dates. It is also said: it is paid from its price.

**(20th)** As for what does not become dates from the fruit of the palm, nor raisins from grapes, such as the grapes of Egypt (and its unripe dates) [[2]], and likewise its olives that are not pressed, Malik said: its zakat is paid from its price, and its owner is not charged with anything else. Its price is not required to reach twenty mithqal or two hundred dirhams; rather, one considers whether it is thought to reach five awsuq or more. Al-Shafi'i said: he pays a tenth or half a tenth of it from its best quality in dates, if his household eats it fresh or gives it away. [[from k. In or b: its palms.]]

**(21st)** Abu Dawud narrated from Ibn 'Umar, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "For what is watered by the sky, rivers and springs, or is rain-fed (ba'l), the tenth is due; and for what is watered by irrigation with water-wheels (sawani) or by drawing water (nadh), half a tenth is due, and likewise if it drinks from a flowing channel, a tenth is due." [[Ba'l: what grows of palms in land whose water is near, whose roots have reached the water and which has become independent of sky water and rivers. It is also narrated as 'athari, which is the same as ba'li.]] [[Sawani: plural of saniyah, the camel by which water is drawn.]] Sayh is flowing water over the surface of the earth, said Ibn al-Sikkit. The word sayh is mentioned in the hadith, transmitted by al-Nasa'i. [[We did not find this addition in al-Nasa'i, and Allah knows best.]] If he drinks from a flowing channel but the owner of the land does not own the water and only rents it, then it is like sky water, according to the well-known view of the school. Abu al-Hasan al-Lakhmi held that it is like drawn water. If it is watered once by rain water and once by a water-wheel, Malik said: one looks at which of them brought the crop to completion and gave it life, and whichever was greater, the ruling depends on it. This is the narration of Ibn al-Qasim from him. Ibn Wahb narrated from him: if it is watered for half a year by springs and then the supply stops and the rest of the year it is watered by a water-carrying camel, then he owes half its zakat at a tenth, and the other half at half a tenth. He also said once: its zakat is according to that by which its life was completed. Al-Shafi'i said: each of the two is zakated according to its proportion. An example: if it is watered for two months by irrigation and four months by rain, then two-thirds of a tenth is due for the rain water and a sixth of a tenth for the irrigation. And so with whatever is more or less, by proportion. Bakkar used to issue fatwa by this, according to Qutaybah. Abu Hanifa and Abu Yusuf said: one looks at the predominant source and zakats accordingly, and nothing else is considered. It is narrated from al-Shafi'i. Al-Tahawi said: all agree that if it is watered with rain water for one or two days, that is not considered and no share is assigned to it. This shows that the consideration is the predominant source. And Allah knows best.

I say: this is a collection of the rulings of this verse, and perhaps others will bring more than these, as Allah opens for them. And a collection of the meaning of this verse has already passed in al-Baqarah [[see vol. 3, p. 321]]. And praise be to Allah.

**(22nd)** As for the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "There is no sadaqah on grain or dates until it reaches five awsuq," the hadith, al-Nasa'i transmitted it. Hamzah al-Kinani said: no one mentioned the words "on grain" in this hadith except Isma'il ibn Umayyah, who is a trustworthy Qurashi of the descendants of Sa'id ibn al-'As. He said: this sunnah was not narrated by any of the Companions from the Prophet (ﷺ) except Abu Sa'id al-Khudri. Abu 'Umar said: it is as Hamzah said. This is a great sunnah which all have accepted, and no one narrated it from the Prophet (ﷺ) by a sound, preserved route except Abu Sa'id. Jabir also narrated something like it from the Prophet (ﷺ), but it is gharib; and we have found it from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah with a good chain (isnad).

**(23rd)** Allah the Exalted said: ﴿and do not be wasteful﴾ [6:141]. Israf (wastefulness) linguistically means error. A Bedouin, meaning a people, said: "I sought you and so I missed you (asraftukum)," that is, I missed your place. A poet said:
"One of them said, while the horses were trampling them: 'You have erred,' so we answered: 'We too are in error (sarf).'"
Israf in spending means extravagance (tabdhir). Musrif was the nickname of Muslim ibn 'Uqbah al-Murri, the commander of the Battle of al-Harrah [[near Medina in the time of Yazid ibn Mu'awiyah]], because he committed excess (asraf) in it. 'Ali ibn 'Abd Allah ibn al-'Abbas said:
"They defended my kin on the day the battalions of Musrif came, and the sons of al-Lukay'ah."
[[In al-Lisan: "banu al-lukay'ah," in apposition to the subject of "jaat." Under s-r-f. And in l-k-'a: "banu."]]
The intended meaning of the verse is: do not take a thing without its right and then place it where it has no right. This was said by Asbagh ibn al-Faraj. Similar is the saying of Iyas ibn Mu'awiyah: whatever you exceed the command of Allah with is extravagance (israf). Israf in spending is extravagance (tabdhir). Musrif was the nickname of Muslim ibn 'Uqbah al-Murri, the commander of the Battle of al-Harrah [[near Medina in the time of Yazid ibn Mu'awiyah]], because he committed excess in it. 'Ali ibn 'Abd Allah ibn al-'Abbas said:
"They defended my kin on the day the battalions of Musrif came, and the sons of al-Lukay'ah."
[[In al-Lisan: "banu al-lukay'ah," in apposition to the subject of "jaat." Under s-r-f. And in l-k-'a: "banu."]]
The intended meaning of the verse is: do not take a thing without its right and then place it where it has no right. This was said by Isba' ibn al-Faraj. Similar is the saying of Iyas ibn Mu'awiyah: whatever you exceed the command of Allah with is extravagance (sarf) and excess (israf). Ibn Zayd said: it is addressed to the rulers; it means: do not take beyond your right and what is not obligatory upon people. Both meanings are admitted by the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "The one who exceeds in charity is like the one who withholds it." Mujahid said: if Abu Qubays were gold belonging to a man and he spent it in obedience to Allah, he would not be extravagant; but if he spent a dirham or a mudd in disobedience to Allah, he would be extravagant. In this sense it was said to Hatim: "There is no good in extravagance," and he replied: "There is no extravagance in good."

I say: this is weak, refuted by what Ibn 'Abbas narrated, that Thabit ibn Qays ibn Shammas went to five hundred palms, cut them, then divided them in one day, leaving nothing for his family. Then the verse ﴿and do not be wasteful﴾ was revealed, meaning: do not give all of it. 'Abd al-Razzaq narrated from Ibn Jurayj who said: Mu'adh ibn Jabal cut his palms and kept giving in charity until nothing remained of them, so the verse ﴿and do not be wasteful﴾ was revealed. Al-Suddi said: ﴿and do not be wasteful﴾ means: do not give your wealth away so that you become poor. It is narrated from Mu'awiyah ibn Abi Sufyan that he was asked about the saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿and do not be wasteful﴾, and he said: extravagance is what you withhold from the right of Allah the Exalted.

I say: accordingly, giving away all one's wealth, including setting aside the rights of the poor, falls under the category of extravagance (israf), whereas justice (al-'adl) is the opposite of this. So one gives in charity and retains some, as the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "The best charity is that given from a position of wealth" [[That is, what is given freely, having exceeded one's sufficiency. It was also said: he meant what exceeds one's dependents. The word "zahr" (back/support) may be added in such expressions for emphasis and to strengthen the meaning, as if the charity rests upon a strong back of wealth, from Ibn al-Athir.]], unless one is strong of soul, self-sufficient in God, reliant upon Him, alone with no dependents, in which case he may give away all his wealth. Likewise, one may pay the obligatory right due from him, such as zakat, and whatever rights become binding upon the wealth in some circumstances.

'Abd al-Rahman ibn Zayd ibn Aslam said: extravagance (israf) is what one cannot restore to soundness, while sarf is what one can restore to soundness.

An-Nadr ibn Shumayl said: israf is squandering (tabdhir) and excess (ifrat), while sarf is heedlessness (ghaflah) and ignorance (jahl). Jarir said:

"They gave Hunayda, driven by eight camels, and in their giving there was neither reproach (mann) nor sarf."

That is, heedlessness (ighfal), and it is said: error (khata'). A man who is sarf al-fu'ad is one whose heart is erring and heedless. Tarafa said:

"A man whose heart is sarf sees honey mixed with the water of a cloud, my beloved."

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 6, verse 142:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And of the cattle, some for burden and some for carpeting﴾ is a conjunction (ʿatf) (upon what [[from K.]] preceded), meaning: and He brought into being, from the cattle, some for burden and some for carpeting.

Regarding the word al-anʿam (cattle), the scholars have three opinions. The first: al-anʿam refers specifically to camels, and its explanation will come in Surah al-Nahl [[See vol. 10, p. 68.]]. The second: al-anʿam refers to camels alone, and when there are cows and sheep alongside them, these are also called anʿam. The third, and it is the soundest, said by Ahmad ibn Yahya: al-anʿam is every animal that Allah, mighty and majestic, has made lawful. What confirms the soundness of this is the saying of the Exalted: ﴿Lawful for you are the beasts of cattle, except what is recited to you﴾ [[See vol. 6, p. 33.]], and this has already passed.

Al-hamulah (the burden-bearing animal) is that which is able to bear loads and work, according to Ibn Masʿud and others. Then it was said: the term is restricted to camels. And it was said: it is every animal upon which the tribe (al-hayy) may be carried, whether a donkey, a mule, or a camel, according to Abu Zayd, whether or not loads are on it.

ʿAntarah said:

Nothing alarmed me except the burden-animals of her people ... in the midst of the abodes, nibbling the seed of al-hamhamah.

[[Al-hamhamah (with a kasrah on the ha', also said balkha'): a plant whose seed camels are fed.]]

When the form fa'ulah with a fatha on the fa' carries the sense of the active participle, the masculine and feminine share it, as in your saying: rajul furudah and imra'ah furudah, for the coward and the fearful. And rajul sururah and imra'ah sururah, when neither has performed the Hajj, and it has no plural. When it carries the sense of the passive participle, the masculine and feminine are distinguished by the ta' marbutah, as in al-halubah and al-rakubah. Al-humulah (with a damma on the ha'): the loads. As for al-humul (with a damma, without ta'), these are the camels upon which the litters (hawadij) are carried, whether or not women are in them, according to Abu Zayd.

As for ﴿and carpeting﴾: Al-Dahhak said: the burden-animals are of camels and cattle, and the carpeting is sheep. Al-Nahhas said: he cited in support of the holder of this view the saying: ﴿eight pairs﴾, and said: "eight" is a substitute (badal) for His saying "burden and carpeting."

Al-Hasan said: the burden-animals are camels, and the carpeting is sheep. Ibn ʿAbbas said: the burden-animals are everything that carries loads of camels, cattle, horses, mules and donkeys, and the carpeting is sheep. Ibn Zayd said: the burden-animals are what is ridden, and the carpeting is what is eaten for its meat and milked, such as sheep, weaned young camels and young calves; they were called carpeting because of the slightness of their bodies and their nearness to the farsh, which is the level ground that people tread upon. The rajiz (rhymester) said:

He bequeathed to me burden-animals and carpeting ... I milk them every day, a milking.

[[Mashsha al-naqah yamshuha mashshan: he milked the she-camel.]]

Another said:

And we gathered the carpeting from your cattle ... and the burden-animals and the mother-camels of the young.

Al-Asmaʿi said: I have not heard a plural for it. He said: it may be a verbal noun (masdar) that has been used as a name, from their saying: Allah spread them out (farashaha Allahu farshan), that is, scattered them abroad. And al-farsh is the spread-out goods of the house. And al-farsh is the sown field when it is spread out. And al-farsh is the wide open space. And al-farsh in the foot of the camel is a slight widening, and it is praiseworthy. And iftarasha al-shay' means it spread out, so it is a homonymous word (lafz mushtarak). The saying of the Exalted: ﴿and carpeting﴾ may refer to this. Al-Nahhas said: among the finest of what has been said about the two is that the burden-animals are those made subservient and tractable for carrying, and the carpeting is what Allah, mighty and majestic, has created from hides and wool, that upon which one sits and which is spread out. The rest of the verse has already passed.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 6, verse 143–144:

"And of camels two and of cattle two. Say: has He forbidden the two males or the two females, or that which the wombs of the two females contain? Or were you witnesses when Allah enjoined this upon you? So who is more unjust than one who fabricates a lie against Allah to mislead people without knowledge? Indeed, Allah does not guide the wrongdoing people." (143–144)

In it are three issues.

The first: His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿eight pairs﴾. "Eight" (ثَمانِيَةَ, thamaniyata) is in the accusative by a hidden verb, meaning "and He produced eight pairs," according to al-Kisa'i. Al-Akhfash Sa'id said: it is in the accusative as a substitute (badal) for "ḥamulatan wa farshan." Al-Akhfash 'Ali ibn Sulayman said: it is in the accusative governed by "kulu" (eat), meaning "eat the meat of eight pairs." It may also be in the accusative as a substitute for "mā" (what) on the basis of its position. It may also be in the accusative by the sense of "kulu" as permitted: "eight pairs, two of the sheep (ḍa'n)." The verse was revealed concerning Malik ibn 'Awf and his companions when they said: "What is in the bellies of these livestock is exclusively for our males and forbidden to our wives." So Allah, Mighty and Majestic, alerted His Prophet and the believers through this verse to what He had made lawful for them, lest they be in the position of one who forbids what Allah Exalted has made lawful.

The word "zawj" (pair, zawj) is the opposite of "fard" (single). It is said: "zawj or fard," just as it is said: "khasa' or zaka'," "shaf' (even) or watr (odd)." So the saying "eight pairs" means eight singles. Every single in the Arabic usage requires another, and is called a zawj; thus a male is called zawj and a female is called zawj. The word zawj applies to one and to two; it is said: "they two are zawjan," and "they two are zawj," just as it is said: "they two are siyyan" and "they two are sawa'." You say: "I bought two pigeons (zawjay ḥamām)," meaning a male and a female.

The second: His saying: ﴿of the sheep two﴾, i.e., the male and the female. "Ḍa'n" (sheep): the woolly ones among the goats (ghanam), and it is the plural of ḍa'in. The female is ḍa'ina, and the plural is ḍawa'in. It is said that it is a plural with no singular. It is also said its plural is ḍa'in, like 'abd and 'abid. It is also said: ḍi'in. Just as it is said of sha'ir (barley): shi'ir, the ḍad being kasra by assimilation. Ṭalḥa ibn Muṣarrif read "min al-ḍa'ni ithnayni" with fatḥa on the hamza, and it is a Basran-attested dialect. For the Kufans it is regular in every word whose second letter is a throat letter. Likewise, fatḥa and sukun occur in "al-ma'z" (goats). Abban ibn 'Uthman read "min al-ḍa'ni ithnani wa min al-ma'zi ithnani" with raf' by the inchoative. And in the reading of Ubayy: [see note].

(And of the goats two [[As in the originals. What is in the Shawadh of Ibn Khalawayh is: "min al-ma'zi ithnayni" (Ubayy's reading: "min al-ma'zi ithnayni"), which is correct as in al-Bahr and Ruh al-Ma'ani. Ubayy's reading: "min al-ma'zi ithnayni," as is apparent. His saying: "and it is the reading of the majority" refers to the sukun in al-ma'z.]]) and this is the reading of the majority. Ibn 'Amir and Abu 'Amr read with fatḥa. Al-Nahhas said: in Arabic usage the most common is al-ma'z and al-ḍa'n with sukun. What indicates this is their saying in the plural: ma'iz, which is the plural of ma'z, as one says 'abd and 'abid. Imru' al-Qays said:

And the sons of Shamaja ibn Jarm grant them their goats, "ḥanānaka dhā al-ḥanān"

Similar to it are ḍa'n and ḍa'in. Al-ma'z among the goats is the opposite of the ḍa'n; they are the ones with hair and short tails. It is a collective noun (ism jins), and likewise al-ma'z, al-ma'iz, al-um'uz and al-mi'zá. The singular of al-ma'z is ma'iz, like ṣāḥib and ṣaḥb, and tājir and tajr. The female is mā'iza, which is the she-goat (al-'anz), and the plural is mawā'iz. Amʿaza al-qawm: their goats increased. Al-ma''az is the owner of goats. Abu Muhammad al-Fuq'asi said, describing camels for their abundance of milk and preferring them over sheep in the hardship of times:

They measure a measure that is not diminished, when the goat-herder is content with the licking (of milk).

Al-ma'az is the hardness of the ground. Al-am'az is the hard place with many pebbles, and al-ma'zā' too. And istam'aza al-rajul fi amrihi: he exerted himself.

(Qul ā-dhakarayni) is in the accusative governed by "ḥarrama" (forbade).

(Am al-unthayayni) is conjoined to it. Likewise (amma ishtamalat). The mad (long vowel) is added with the alif of wasl to distinguish interrogation from statement. It is permissible to omit the hamza because "am" indicates interrogation, as the poet said:

Do you depart from the tribe, or do you set out early?

The third: The scholars said: the verse is an argument against the polytheists concerning the matter of the baḥīra and what is mentioned with it, and their saying: "What is in the bellies of these livestock is exclusively for our males and forbidden to our wives." It indicates the establishment of debate in knowledge, because Allah Exalted commanded His Prophet, peace be upon him, to debate them and to show them the corruption of their statement. It also contains the establishment of reasoning by analysis (nazar) and analogy (qiyas). It also contains evidence that when a text (naṣṣ) is present, analogy is nullified.

It is also related: "when a counter-instance (naqḍ) is present," because Allah Exalted commanded them to sound comparison and commanded them to extend their reasoning (ṭard al-'illa). The meaning: say to them, if He has forbidden the males, then every male is forbidden. If He has forbidden the females, then every female is forbidden. If He has forbidden what the wombs of the two females contain, meaning of the sheep and goats, then every newborn is forbidden, male or female. And all of them are newborns, so all of them are then forbidden due to the presence of the cause in them. Thus the invalidity of their cause and the corruption of their statement became clear. Allah the Glorified informed that what they did in this regard was a fabrication against Him. ("Inform me with knowledge") i.e., with knowledge, if you have it, from where is this prohibition which you have invented? They had no knowledge, because they did not read the scriptures. The discussion of "And of the camels two" and what follows is as previously stated. (Or were you witnesses) i.e., (did you) witness Allah forbidding this? When the proof was binding upon them, they resorted to fabrication and said: "Thus Allah commanded." Allah Exalted said: ("So who is more unjust than one who fabricates a lie against Allah to mislead people without knowledge?") He showed that they lied, since they stated what no evidence supports.

The second: His saying: ﴿of the sheep two﴾, i.e., the male and the female. "Ḍa'n" (sheep): the woolly ones among the goats (ghanam), and it is the plural of ḍa'in. The female is ḍa'ina, and the plural is ḍawa'in. It is said that it is a plural with no singular. It is also said its plural is ḍa'in, like 'abd and 'abid. It is also said: ḍi'in. Just as it is said of sha'ir (barley): shi'ir, the ḍad being kasra by assimilation. Ṭalḥa ibn Muṣarrif read "min al-ḍa'ni ithnayni" with fatḥa on the hamza, and it is a Basran-attested dialect. For the Kufans it is regular in every word whose second letter is a throat letter. Likewise, fatḥa and sukun occur in "al-ma'z" (goats). Abban ibn 'Uthman read "min al-ḍa'ni ithnani wa min al-ma'zi ithnani" with raf' by the inchoative. And in the reading of Ubayy: [see note].

(And of the goats two [[As in the originals. What is in the Shawadh of Ibn Khalawayh is: "min al-ma'zi ithnayni" (Ubayy's reading: "min al-ma'zi ithnayni"), which is correct as in al-Bahr and Ruh al-Ma'ani. Ubayy's reading: "min al-ma'zi ithnayni," as is apparent. His saying: "and it is the reading of the majority" refers to the sukun in al-ma'z.]]) and this is the reading of the majority. Ibn 'Amir and Abu 'Amr read with fatḥa. Al-Nahhas said: in Arabic usage the most common is al-ma'z and al-ḍa'n with sukun. What indicates this is their saying in the plural: ma'iz, which is the plural of ma'z, as one says 'abd and 'abid. Imru' al-Qays said:

And the sons of Shamaja ibn Jarm grant them their goats, "ḥanānaka dhā al-ḥanān"

Similar to it are ḍa'n and ḍa'in. Al-ma'z among the goats is the opposite of the ḍa'n; they are the ones with hair and short tails. It is a collective noun (ism jins), and likewise al-ma'z, al-ma'iz, al-um'uz and al-mi'zá. The singular of al-ma'z is ma'iz, like ṣāḥib and ṣaḥb, and tājir and tajr. The female is mā'iza, which is the she-goat (al-'anz), and the plural is mawā'iz. Amʿaza al-qawm: their goats increased. Al-ma''az is the owner of goats. Abu Muhammad al-Fuq'asi said, describing camels for their abundance of milk and preferring them over sheep in the hardship of times:

They measure a measure that is not diminished, when the goat-herder is content with the licking (of milk).

Al-ma'az is the hardness of the ground. Al-am'az is the hard place with many pebbles, and al-ma'zā' too. And istam'aza al-rajul fi amrihi: he exerted himself.

(Qul ā-dhakarayni) is in the accusative governed by "ḥarrama" (forbade).

(Am al-unthayayni) is conjoined to it. Likewise (amma ishtamalat). The mad (long vowel) is added with the alif of wasl to distinguish interrogation from statement. It is permissible to omit the hamza because "am" indicates interrogation, as the poet said:

Do you depart from the tribe, or do you set out early?

The third: The scholars said: the verse is an argument against the polytheists concerning the matter of the baḥīra and what is mentioned with it, and their saying: "What is in the bellies of these livestock is exclusively for our males and forbidden to our wives." It indicates the establishment of debate in knowledge, because Allah Exalted commanded His Prophet, peace be upon him, to debate them and to show them the corruption of their statement. It also contains the establishment of reasoning by analysis (nazar) and analogy (qiyas). It also contains evidence that when a text (naṣṣ) is present, analogy is nullified.

It is also related: "when a counter-instance (naqḍ) is present," because Allah Exalted commanded them to sound comparison and commanded them to extend their reasoning (ṭard al-'illa). The meaning: say to them, if He has forbidden the males, then every male is forbidden. If He has forbidden the females, then every female is forbidden. If He has forbidden what the wombs of the two females contain, meaning of the sheep and goats, then every newborn is forbidden, male or female. And all of them are newborns, so all of them are then forbidden due to the presence of the cause in them. Thus the invalidity of their cause and the corruption of their statement became clear. Allah the Glorified informed that what they did in this regard was a fabrication against Him. ("Inform me with knowledge") i.e., with knowledge, if you have it, from where is this prohibition which you have invented? They had no knowledge, because they did not read the scriptures. The discussion of "And of the camels two" and what follows is as previously stated. (Or were you witnesses) i.e., (did you) witness Allah forbidding this? When the proof was binding upon them, they resorted to fabrication and said: "Thus Allah commanded." Allah Exalted said: ("So who is more unjust than one who fabricates a lie against Allah to mislead people without knowledge?") He showed that they lied, since they stated what no evidence supports.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 6, verse 145 (part 1 of 3):

There are four issues in this verse. The first concerns His, may He be exalted, words: ﴿Say: I find not in what has been revealed to me anything forbidden﴾. In this verse, Allah, mighty and majestic, informs (the Prophet) of what He has forbidden. The meaning is: O Muhammad, I find in what has been revealed to me nothing forbidden except these things, not what you forbid by your own desires. This verse is Meccan. At that time there was nothing forbidden in the Sharia except these things. Then the surah "al-Ma'ida" (the Table) was revealed at Medina, and more forbidden things were added, such as the strangled animal (al-munkhaniqa), the beaten animal (al-mawquda) [[al-Mawquda: a sheep that is beaten until it dies without being slaughtered. Al-Mutaraddiya: an animal that falls from a mountain, or falls into a well, or drops from an elevated place and dies.]], the animal that falls from a height (al-mutaraddiya), the animal gored by another (al-natiha), wine (khamr), and other things.
