The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) also forbade at Medina the eating of every animal with fangs among beasts of prey, and every bird with talons.

The scholars have differed over the ruling (hukm) and interpretation (ta'wil) of this verse, and their views are as follows.

The first view is what we have already pointed to: this verse is Meccan (Makki, revealed in Mecca), and every prohibition that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) made, or that comes in the Book joined to it, is an additional ruling from Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, upon the tongue of His Prophet, peace be upon him. Most of the people of knowledge (ahl al-'ilm), of reflection (nazar), jurisprudence (fiqh) and transmitted report (athar), hold this view. Its parallel is the prohibition (nikah, i.e. its prohibition) of marrying a woman together with her paternal aunt or her maternal aunt, alongside His saying: "And lawful for you is what is beyond that" [cf. vol. 5, p. 124]; and His ruling concerning the oath with one witness, alongside His saying: "But if they are not two men, then a man and two women" [cf. vol. 3, p. 391].

It has also been said that the verse is abrogated (mansukhah, i.e. superseded by a later ruling) by His saying (peace be upon him): "Eating any animal with fangs from among the predators is forbidden." Mālik narrated it, and it is a sound hadith.

It has been said that the verse is definitive (muhkam, i.e. not abrogated), and that nothing is forbidden except what is in it. This view is reported from Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn 'Umar and 'A'ishah, but the opposite has also been reported from them. Mālik said: "No prohibition is clear except what is mentioned in this verse."

Ibn Khuwayz Mindad said: this verse includes the permissibility of every animal and other things, except what is excluded in the verse: carrion, flowing blood and the flesh of swine. For this reason we say that the flesh of predators and of all animals other than humans and swine is permitted.

Ilkiya al-Tabari said: Al-Shafi'i built upon it the permissibility of everything that is left unmentioned, taking it from this verse, except what evidence indicates otherwise.

It has also been said that the verse is an answer to one who asked about a specific thing, so the answer was particular to it. This is the view of al-Shafi'i. Al-Shafi'i narrated from Sa'id ibn Jubayr that he said: "In this verse there are things that they asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) about, and he answered them regarding the prohibited ones among those things."

It has also been said: the meaning is, "I do not find in what has been revealed to me," i.e. in this state, the state of revelation and the time of its descent; then it is not impossible that a revelation occurs after that prohibiting other things.

Ibn al-'Arabi claimed that this verse is Madinan (revealed in Medina), though according to most scholars it is Meccan. It was revealed upon the Prophet (ﷺ) on the day when there was revealed to him: "Today I have perfected your religion for you" [Qur'an 5:3], and no abrogating (nasikh) revelation came after it, so it is definitive; therefore nothing is forbidden except what is in it. To this I incline. I (al-Qurtubi) say: This is what I have seen from others too.

Abu 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-Barr reported a consensus that Surah al-An'am is Meccan, except His saying, Exalted is He: "Say: Come, I will recite to you what your Lord has forbidden you," the three verses. Much Qur'an and abundant Sunnah were revealed after it. The prohibition of wine was revealed in Medina in Surah al-Ma'idah. They also agreed that his prohibition (peace be upon him) of eating every animal with fangs from among the predators was only issued by him in Medina. Isma'il ibn Ishaq said: All of this indicates that it was a matter that occurred in Medina after the revelation of His saying: "Say: I do not find in what has been revealed to me anything forbidden," because that is Meccan.

I (al-Qurtubi) say: This is the source of the disagreement among the scholars. A group deviated from the apparent meaning of the hadiths that came with the prohibition of eating every animal with fangs from among the predators, because they came later than it, and the restriction (hasr) in it is apparent, so taking by it is more appropriate, since it is either abrogating what preceded it or preponderant over those hadiths.

As for those who hold the prohibition, it became clear to them and was established for them that Surah al-An'am is Meccan, revealed before the Hijrah, and that this verse was intended as a refutation of the pagans (Jahiliyyah) regarding the prohibition of the bahirah, the sa'ibah, the wasilah and the ham. Then after that He prohibited many things, such as domestic donkeys, the flesh of mules and others, every animal with fangs from among the predators, and every bird with talons.

Abu 'Umar said: It follows from the view of one who says "nothing is forbidden except what is in it" that what has not had the name of Allah mentioned over it deliberately would not be forbidden, and that wine, which is forbidden according to the community of Muslims, would be made lawful. The consensus of the Muslims on the prohibition of grape wine is clear evidence that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) found, in what was revealed to him, a prohibition other than what is in Surah al-An'am, from what was revealed after it of the Qur'an.

The transmission from Mālik has differed concerning the flesh of predators, donkeys and mules. Once he said: they are forbidden, because of what came of his prohibition (peace be upon him) concerning that; and this is the sound position from him, according to what is in the Muwatta'. Another time he said: they are disliked (makruhah), and this is the apparent position in the Mudawwanah, in accordance with the apparent meaning of the verse, and because of what was reported from Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn 'Umar and 'A'ishah regarding its permissibility. This is also the view of al-Awza'i.

Al-Bukhari narrated, through 'Amr ibn Dinar, who said: I said to Jabir ibn Zayd: "They claim that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) forbade the flesh of domestic donkeys?" He said: "al-Hakam ibn 'Amr al-Ghifari used to say that among us in Basra, but Ibn 'Abbas, the sea of knowledge, refused that, and he recited: 'Say: I do not find in what has been revealed to me anything forbidden.'"

It was reported from Ibn 'Umar that he was asked about the flesh of predators, and he said: "There is no harm in it." It was said to him: "What about the hadith of Abu Tha'labah al-Khushani [Hadith of Abu Tha'labah: it was narrated that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'Eating every animal with fangs from among the predators is forbidden.']?" He said: "We do not abandon the Book of Allah, our Lord, for the saying of a Bedouin who urinates on his shins." [In the manuscripts: "for the saying" in place of "for the hadith".]

Al-Sha'bi was asked about the flesh of the elephant and the lion, and he recited this verse. Al-Qasim said: 'A'ishah used to say, when she heard people saying that every animal with fangs from among the predators is forbidden: "That is lawful," and she would recite this verse, "Say: I do not find in what has been revealed to me anything forbidden." Then she said: "If the cooking pot's water was yellower than blood, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) would see it and would not forbid it."

The correct position in this matter is what we began by mentioning, and that what came of the prohibitions after this verse is joined to it and linked to it.

The judge Abu Bakr ibn al-'Arabi pointed to this in his Qabas, contrary to what he mentioned in his Ahkam. He said: It was reported from Ibn 'Abbas that this verse is among the last of what was revealed. Our Baghdadi companions said: everything other than it is lawful, but eating predators is disliked. Among the jurists of the regions, including Mālik, al-Shafi'i, Abu Hanifah and 'Abd al-Malik, eating every animal with fangs from among the predators is forbidden. It is not impossible that an addition should occur after His saying, "Say: I do not find in what has been revealed to me anything forbidden," by evidence that comes concerning it, as the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "The blood of a Muslim man is not lawful except by one of three [things]," and he mentioned disbelief, adultery and killing. Then our scholars said: the causes of killing are ten, by the evidence that came. The Prophet (ﷺ) only reports what has reached him of knowledge from the Creator, exalted is He, and He erases what He wills, establishes, abrogates and advances.

It is established from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "Eating every animal with fangs from among the predators is forbidden." It has also been reported that he forbade eating every animal with fangs from among the predators and every bird with talons. Muslim narrated from Ma'n, from Mālik: "He forbade eating every bird with talons." The first is more sound, and the prohibition of every animal with fangs from among the predators is the explicit school (madhhab) position. Mālik also gave it a chapter heading in the Muwatta' when he said: "The prohibition of eating every animal with fangs from among the predators." Then he mentioned the hadith and followed it with: "And this is the practice among us." Thus he informed us that practice agreed with the report.

Al-Qushayri said: Mālik's saying, "This verse is among the last of what was revealed," does not prevent us from saying: the prohibition of some of these things was established after this verse. Allah has made lawful the good things and forbidden the foul ones, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) forbade eating every animal with fangs from among the predators, and eating every bird with talons, and forbade the flesh of domestic donkeys in the year of Khaybar.

What indicates the soundness of this interpretation is the consensus on the prohibition of excrement, urine, disgusting insects, and donkeys, which are not mentioned in this verse.

The second point: His saying, Exalted is He: "forbidden" (muharraman). Ibn 'Atiyyah said: The word "prohibition" (tahrim), when it comes upon the tongue of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), is suitable to end the thing mentioned at the furthest limit of prohibition and restraint, and it is also suitable, linguistically, to stop short of that limit within the scope of disapproval and the like. So where there is an indicator of acceptance by the Companions who interpreted it, and all of them agreed, and the wordings of the hadiths did not vary concerning it, it is necessary by the Law that its prohibition has reached the furthest limit of prohibition and restraint, and it is joined to swine, carrion and blood. This is the nature of the prohibition of wine.

But where there is an indicator of variation in the wordings of the hadiths, and the imams differed about it although they knew the hadiths, such as his saying (peace be upon him): "Eating every animal with fangs from among the predators is forbidden." The prohibition by the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) of eating every animal with fangs from among the predators is reported, and then the Companions and those after them differed about whether that is forbidden. So for this reason it is permissible for one who examines it to take the word "prohibition" to mean restraint, which is disapproval and the like.

And where there is an indicator of interpretation, such as his (peace be upon him) prohibition of the flesh of domestic donkeys, some of the Companions present interpreted it as because it is impure; some interpreted it so that the people's beasts of burden would not perish; and some interpreted it as an absolute prohibition. The disagreement in the community about the prohibition of its flesh is established, so it is permissible for a scholar who examines it to take the word "prohibition" to mean restraint, which is disapproval and the like, according to his own ijtihad (independent reasoning) and qiyas (analogy).

I (al-Qurtubi) say: This is a fine conclusion on this subject and on the cause of the disagreement, as previously stated.

It has been said: The donkey is not eaten, because it displayed its foul essence when it mounted a male and committed sodomy, so it was called rijs (filth). Muhammad ibn Sirin said: No animal does the deed of the people of Lot except the swine and the donkey. Al-Tirmidhi mentioned it in Nawadir al-Usul.

The third point: 'Amr ibn Dinar narrated from Abu al-Sha'tha', from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: The people of the Jahiliyyah used to eat some things and leave other things, so Allah sent His Prophet (peace be upon him), revealed His Book, made lawful what is lawful and forbade what is forbidden. What He made lawful is lawful, what He forbade is forbidden, and what He was silent about is forgiven. And he recited this verse, "Say: I do not find..." to the end of the verse. He meant that whatever prohibition has not been made clear is permitted by the apparent meaning of this verse.

Al-Zuhri narrated from 'Ubayd Allah ibn 'Abd Allah ibn 'Abbas that he recited "Say: I do not find in what has been revealed to me anything forbidden," and said: "Only the eating of carrion is forbidden, that part of it which is eaten, which is the flesh. As for the hide, the bone, the wool and the hair, they are lawful."

Abu Dawud narrated from Miqdam ibn Talib, from his father, who said: "I accompanied the Prophet (ﷺ) and I did not hear any prohibition concerning the creeping things of the earth." The creeping things (hashrah) are the small land animals, such as lizards, jerboas, hedgehogs, and the like. The poet said:

"We have eaten the locusts (rubba), O Umm 'Amr,
and whoever is a stranger among you eats the creeping things."

[Manuscript variants: in one manuscript the word is "al-dabba" in place of "al-rubba"; the editor notes that the poem's word is "al-rubba", as in the other manuscripts, lisan and taj, and in them "gharīban bi-ard" appears in place of "gharīban ladaykum".]

That is, whatever crawls and moves about. The *ruba* (plural *ruba*, singular *rubya*) is the field mouse. Al-Khattabi said: That he said, "I did not hear any prohibition regarding it," is no proof that it is permissible, since it is possible that someone else heard a prohibition.

People differ regarding the jerboa (*al-yarbu'*), the *wabr* [[The *wabr* (with a sukun on the ba'): a small animal about the size of a cat, grey or white, one of the desert creatures, with beautiful eyes and great shyness, found in the lowlands. Its plural is *wabar*.]] and similar creatures among the crawling things. 'Urwah, 'Ata', al-Shafi'i and Abu Thawr permitted the jerboa. Al-Shafi'i said: "There is no harm in the *wabr*." Ibn Sirin, al-Hakam and Hammad disliked it, as did the Ahl al-Ra'y (the jurists of opinion). The Ahl al-Ra'y disliked the hedgehog. Malik ibn Anas was asked about it and said: "I do not know." Abu 'Amr related: Malik also said, "There is no harm in eating the hedgehog." Abu Thawr did not regard it as objectionable, and he related this from al-Shafi'i. Ibn 'Umar was asked about it, so he recited, "Say: I do not find in what has been revealed to me anything forbidden..." [the verse], and an old man present said: "I heard Abu Hurayrah say: it was mentioned in the presence of the Prophet (ﷺ), and he said: 'It is a foul one among the foul things.'" Ibn 'Umar said: "If the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said this, then it is as he said." Abu Dawud reported it.

Malik said: There is no harm in eating the *dabb* (spiny lizard), the jerboa and the *warl* [[The *warl*: a creature resembling the *dabb*, but larger, found in sands and deserts.]]. In his view, eating snakes is permissible when they have been slaughtered (*dhukkiyat*, i.e. ritually slaughtered), and this is the view of Ibn Abi Layla and al-Awza'i. Likewise the vipers, scorpions, mice and the *'azaya* [[The *'azaya*: a creature like the white-spotted gecko.]] and the hedgehog and the frog. Ibn al-Qasim said: "There is no harm in eating the small creeping things of the earth, its scorpions and its worms, according to the view of Malik, because he said: its dying in water does not spoil it." Malik also said: There is no harm in eating the young of bees, the worms of cheese and dates, and the like.

The argument in its favour is the hadith of Milqam [[In al-Dhahabi's *Tadhhib*: Ibn al-Talab.]] ibn Talib, and the saying of Ibn 'Abbas and Abu al-Darda': "What Allah has made lawful is lawful, what He has made unlawful is unlawful, and what He has kept silent about is pardoned." 'A'ishah said regarding the mouse: "It is not unlawful," and she recited, "Say: I do not find in what has been revealed to me anything forbidden..."

Among the scholars of Madinah there is a group who do not permit eating any of the small creeping things of the earth and its crawling creatures, such as snakes, lizards, mice and the like. According to them, whatever it is permissible to kill may not be eaten, and ritual slaughter (*dhakah*) does not make it lawful for them. This is the view of Ibn Shihab, 'Urwah, al-Shafi'i, Abu Hanifah and his companions, and others.

According to Malik and his companions, no beast of prey of the wild is permitted, all of them, nor the domestic cat nor the wild cat, because it is a predator (*sab'*). He said: The hyena is not eaten, nor the fox. There is no harm in eating all birds of prey: the vulture, the eagles and the like, whether or not they feed on carrion. Al-Awza'i said: All birds are lawful, except that they dislike the *rakham* (a vulture). Malik's argument is that he did not find any of the people of knowledge who disliked eating birds of prey, and he denied the hadith from the Prophet (ﷺ) that "he forbade eating every bird that has talons."

It is related from Ashhab that he said: "There is no harm in eating the elephant if it is ritually slaughtered," and this is the view of al-Sha'bi, but al-Shafi'i prohibited it. The Nu'man (Abu Hanifah) and his companions disliked eating the hyena and the fox. Al-Shafi'i permitted this. It is related from Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas that he used to eat hyenas. Malik's argument is the general prohibition against eating every animal with fangs among the predators, and he did not single out one predator from another. The hadith about the hyena, which al-Nasa'i recorded permitting its consumption, is not something to set against the hadith of prohibition, because it is a report transmitted by 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi 'Ammar alone, and he is not known for transmitting knowledge, nor is he among those whose reports are relied upon when they contradict one who is more reliable than him.

Abu 'Umar said: The prohibition of eating every animal with fangs among the predators has been related through mutawatir (widely transmitted) chains. It has been transmitted by a group of reliable, trustworthy imams, and it is inconceivable that they should be opposed by a report like the hadith of Ibn Abi 'Ammar.

Abu 'Umar said: The Muslims are agreed that it is not permissible to eat the monkey, because the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) forbade eating it, and it is not permissible to sell it, because there is no benefit in it. He said: I do not know of anyone who permitted eating it, except what 'Abd al-Razzaq related from Ma'mar from Ayyub. Mujahid was asked about eating the monkey and said: "It is not among the beasts of grazing (*bahimat al-an'am*)."

I say: Ibn al-Mundhir mentioned that he said: "We have it related from 'Ata' that he was asked about a monkey killed in the sacred precinct (*haram*), and he said: 'Two just men shall judge concerning it.'" He said: According to the school of 'Ata', eating its flesh is permissible, because the compensation (*jaza'*) is not obligatory upon one who kills other than game. In *Bahr al-Madhhab* by al-Ruwayani, according to the school of Imam al-Shafi'i: al-Shafi'i said: It is permissible to sell the monkey, because it can be trained and benefited from for guarding goods. Al-Kashfali related from Ibn Shurayh that it is permissible to sell it because it can be benefited from. It was said to him: "And what is the benefit of it?" He said: "Children rejoice in it." Abu 'Umar said: The dog, the elephant and every animal with fangs are, in my view, like the monkey. The proof lies in the saying of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), not in the saying of anyone else.

Some people claimed that among the Arabs there was no one who ate dog meat except a people from Fak'as. Abu Dawud related from Ibn 'Umar, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) forbade eating the *jallalah* (an animal that feeds on filth) and drinking its milk. In another narration: "concerning the *jallalah* among camels: that one should not ride it or drink from its milk." Al-Halimi Abu 'Abd Allah said: As for the *jallalah*, it is the animal that eats excrement, of beasts and of chickens that are left to feed freely (*mukhallah*). The Prophet (ﷺ) forbade their meat. The scholars said: Whatever shows the smell of excrement in its flesh or its taste is forbidden, and whatever does not show it is lawful.

Al-Khattabi said: This is a prohibition of purity and cleanliness, because when it feeds on the *jallah* (excrement), the stench of its smell is found in its flesh. This applies when most of its fodder is of that kind. But if it grazes on pasture, eats grain, and occasionally gets some excrement along with that, then it is not a *jallalah*; it is rather like the free-range chicken and similar animals that may occasionally come across something of that kind, while most of their food and fodder comes from elsewhere, so eating them is not disliked. Abu Hanifah's companions, al-Shafi'i and Ahmad said: It is not eaten until it has been confined for some days and fed other fodder, and when its flesh is good, it is eaten. It has been related in a hadith that "cattle are fed for forty days and then their flesh is eaten." Ibn 'Umar used to confine chickens for three days and then slaughter them. Ishaq said: There is no harm in eating them after their flesh has been washed thoroughly. Al-Hasan did not regard it as objectionable to eat the flesh of the *jallalah*, and likewise Malik ibn Anas.

Under this heading comes the prohibition of throwing excrement onto the land. It is related from some of them who said: "We used to rent out the land of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and we would stipulate on whoever rented it that he should not throw excrement onto it." It is related from Ibn 'Umar that he would rent out his land and stipulate that it should not be fertilised with dung (*ya'dimu*: he improved the land with manure, which is fertiliser). In one version, "that it should not be defiled with excrement." It is also related that a man used to sow his land with excrement, and 'Umar said to him: "You are the one who feeds people what comes out of them."

They differed concerning eating horses. al-Shafi'i permitted them, and this is the sound view; Malik disliked them. As for the mule, it is born of a cross between the donkey and the mare. One of its parents is permitted or disliked, namely the mare, and the other is forbidden, namely the donkey. So the ruling of prohibition prevails, because when permissibility and prohibition are combined in a single thing, the ruling of prohibition prevails. The explanation of this question will come, God willing, in more detail in *al-Nahl* [[See vol. 10, p. 73 onward.]]. The ruling on locusts will come in *al-A'raf* [[See p. 268 onward of this volume.]]. The majority of the later and earlier scholars hold that eating the rabbit is permissible. It has been reported from 'Abd Allah ibn 'Amr ibn al-'As that he forbade it, and from Ibn Abi Layla that he disliked it. 'Abd Allah ibn 'Amr said: "It was brought to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) while I was sitting, and he did not eat it, nor did he forbid eating it." And he claimed that it menstruates. Abu Dawud reported this. al-Nasa'i related a mursal report from Musa ibn Talhah who said: "A rabbit was brought to the Prophet, which a man had roasted, and he said: 'O Messenger of Allah, I saw blood in it.' So the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) left it and did not eat it, and he said to those present: 'Eat, for if I desired it, I would have eaten it.'"

I say: There is nothing in this that indicates its prohibition. It is rather like his saying (peace be upon him): "It was not in the land of my people, so I find myself disliking it." Muslim related in his *Sahih* from Anas ibn Malik, who said: "We passed by Marr al-Zahran and startled a rabbit, and they ran after it and grew weary. I ran until I caught it, and I brought it to Abu Talhah, who slaughtered it, and he sent its hind leg and thigh to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). I brought it to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and he accepted it."

The fourth point: His saying, "over a person who eats it" means: an eater who eats it. It is related from Ibn 'Amir that he read *uhiya* with a fatha on the hamza. 'Ali ibn Abi Talib read *yattaʻimuhu* with a heavy ta', intending *yatatta'imuhu*, which was assimilated. 'A'ishah and Muhammad ibn al-Hanafiyyah read *'ala ta'imin yat'amuhu* with a past verb. "Unless it be carrion" was read with the ya' and the ta', meaning: unless the thing, or the body, or the soul is dead. *Yakuna* was read with ya', and *maytatan* with a raised case, in the sense of "there occurs or comes about a dead thing." *Al-masfuh* is that which flows out and runs, and this is what is forbidden; anything else is pardoned. Al-Mawardi related that blood which is not flowing: if it has veins on which it congeals, such as the liver and the spleen, it is lawful, because of the saying of the Prophet (peace be upon him): "Two carrions and two bloods have been made lawful for us," the hadith. If it has no veins on which it congeals, but is with the flesh, then there are two opinions regarding its prohibition: one is that it is forbidden, because it is among the flowing blood or part of it; and the mention of "flowing" was made in order to exempt the liver and the spleen from it. The second is that it is not forbidden, because the prohibition is restricted to the flowing blood. I say: This is the sound view.

'Imran ibn Hudayr said: I asked Abu Mijlaz about meat that is smeared with blood, and about a cooking pot whose redness is from blood, and he said: "There is no harm in it; Allah only forbade the flowing blood." 'A'ishah and others said something similar, and the scholars are agreed upon it. 'Ikrimah said: "Were it not for this verse, the Muslims would follow the veins as the Jews follow them." Ibrahim al-Nakha'i said: "There is no harm in blood in a vein or in marrow." This has already been discussed, and the ruling on one who is compelled is mentioned in *al-Baqarah* [[See vol. 2, p. 216 onward.]]. And Allah knows best.

**Six issues arise in it.**

**The first issue** concerns His words, may He be exalted: ﴿And to those who were Jews We forbade every animal with claws﴾. When God, mighty and majestic, mentioned what He had forbidden to the community of Muhammad (ﷺ), He followed it with mention of what He had forbidden to the Jews. This is because it refutes their claim that God had not forbidden anything to them, and that they had only forbidden for themselves what Israel (Ya'qub) had forbidden for himself. The meaning of "Jews" (hadu) has already been discussed in al-Baqarah [[See vol. 1, p. 432.]]. This prohibition upon those who were Jews was only an imposed trial and punishment. The first of the forbidden things mentioned for them is "every animal with claws" (kull dhi zufur).

Al-Hasan read *zufr* with the *fa'* sukun. Abu al-Simmal read *zifr* with a kasrah on the *zay* and sukun on the *fa'*. Abu Hatim rejected the reading with a kasrah on the *zay* and sukun on the *fa'*, and he did not mention this reading, though it is a dialectal form. There is also *zifr* with kasrah on both. The plural is *azfar*, *uzfur* and *azafir* [[In the originals: "...*azafir* and *azafirah*, like *darib* and *darib*..." The phrase "like *darbah* and *dawarib*" is an error by the copyists.]], as al-Jawhari said. Al-Nahhas added from al-Farra' *azafir* and *azafirah*. Ibn al-Sikkit said: one says *rajul azfar bayyin al-zufr* if he has long nails, just as one says *rajul ash'ar* for a man with long hair.

Mujahid and Qatadah said: "animal with claws" refers to whatever does not have split toes among beasts and birds, such as camels, ostriches, geese and ducks. Ibn Zayd said: camels only. Ibn 'Abbas said: "animal with claws" refers to the camel and the ostrich, because the ostrich has claws like the camel. It was also said that it means every animal with talons among birds and every animal with hooves among quadrupeds. The hoof is called a claw by metaphor (*istiʿarah*). Al-Tirmidhi al-Hakim said: the hoof is a claw and the talon is a claw, except that this is on its own scale and that is on its own scale, and there is no metaphor here. Do you not see that both are cut and trimmed, and both are of one kind: a soft, pliable bone? Its origin is a nourishment that grows and is cut, like a human nail. The hoof was named so because it digs (*yahfir*) the ground by its striking upon it. The talon was named *mikhlab* because it tears (*yakhlub*) birds with the tips of those spikes. It was named *zufr* because it seizes things with its claw, i.e. the human or the bird triumphs (*yazfar*) with it.

**The second issue** concerns His words: ﴿And of cattle and sheep We forbade them their fat﴾. Qatadah said: this means the *thurub* (the fat around the internal organs) and the fat of the two kidneys. Al-Suddi also said so. *Thurub* is the plural of *tharb*, which is the thin fat that lies on the paunch. Ibn Jurayj said: every fat was forbidden to them that was not mixed with bone or lying upon bone, and the fat of the flank and the tail was permitted to them, because it lies on the rump.

**The third issue** concerns His words: ﴿except what their backs carry﴾. The word *mā* (what) is in the accusative position by way of exception (*istithna'*). *Zuhuruhuma* (their backs) is in the nominative, raised by *ḥamalat* (carried).

﴿Or the entrails﴾ is in the nominative position, conjoined to *al-zuhur* (the backs); that is, "or what their entrails carry." The *alif* and *lam* (in *al-hawaya*) substitute for the possessive pronoun. On this view, the entrails are among what is permitted.

﴿Or what is mixed with bone﴾: *mā* is in the accusative position, conjoined to *mā ḥamalat* as well. This is the most correct of what has been said about it, and it is the view of al-Kisa'i, al-Farra' and Ahmad ibn Yahya. Analysis requires that a thing be conjoined to what immediately precedes it, unless its meaning would not be sound or some evidence indicates otherwise.

It was also said that the exception in permitting is only what the backs carry, and that ﴿or the entrails or what is mixed with bone﴾ is conjoined to what is forbidden. The meaning would then be: their fats were forbidden to them, or the entrails, or what is mixed with bone, except what the backs carry, for that is not forbidden. Al-Shafi'i used this verse as evidence that whoever swears not to eat fat breaks his oath by eating the fat of the backs, because God, mighty and majestic, excepted what is on their backs from the total of the fat.

**The fourth issue** concerns His words: ﴿or the entrails﴾. *Al-Hawaya* means *al-mabaʿir* (the intestines/bowels), according to Ibn 'Abbas and others. It is the plural of *mabʿar*, named so because dung (*al-baʿr*) gathers in it, and it is *al-zibl* (dung). The singular of *al-hawaya* is *hawaya'*, like *qaṣʿa'* and *qawaṣiʿ*. It was also said: *hawiyah*, like *dhariba* and *dawarib*. It was also said: *hawiyyah*, like *safinah* and *safa'in*.

Abu 'Ubaydah said: *al-hawaya* is what is coiled (*tahawwā*) from the belly, i.e. curved around; it is *munhawiyah*, i.e. rounded. It was also said that *al-hawaya* are the reservoirs of milk, which connect to the intestines, and these are the *masarin* (the bowels). It was also said that *al-hawaya* are the intestines on which the fats lie. Outside this context, *al-hawaya* is a covering wrapped around the camel's hump. Imru' al-Qays said:

*They made them hawaya and sat upon them as saddles,*
*and they lightened from the weaving of the patterned Iraqi cloth.*

God, may He be exalted, informed us that He had written the forbidding of this in the Torah, refuting their lies. Its text in it reads: "Forbidden to you are the carrion, the blood, the flesh of swine, every animal that does not have a split hoof, and every fish that does not have *safasiq*" [[Thus in MS. Z. Perhaps the intended meaning is "ways/patterns." In MS. K: *saqashiq*. In MS. Y: *shafashiq*.]] — that is, whiteness. Then God abrogated (*naskh*) all of that by the law of Muhammad, permitted to them what had been forbidden to them of animals, removed the hardship through Muhammad, peace be upon him, and obligated creation to the religion of Islam in its permitting and forbidding, its commands and its prohibitions.

**The fifth issue:** If they slaughter their livestock and eat what God permitted them in the Torah, and leave what He forbade to them (from K), is it permitted for us? Malik said in the *Kitab Muhammad*: it is forbidden. In the *Sama' al-Mabsut* he said: is it permitted? Ibn Nafi' also held this view. Ibn al-Qasim said: I dislike it.

The reasoning of the first view is that they hold it religiously forbidden and do not intend it at the time of *dhakah* (ritual slaughter), so it is forbidden like blood. The reasoning of the second view, which is the sound one, is that God, mighty and majestic, lifted that prohibition with Islam, and their belief in it has no effect, because it is a corrupt belief. This was said by Ibn al-'Arabi.

I say: What confirms its soundness is what the two *Sahihs* narrate from 'Abd Allah ibn Mughaffal, who said: "We were besieging the castle of Khaybar, when a man threw a bag containing fat, so I leapt to take it. Then I turned and saw the Prophet (ﷺ), and I was ashamed before him." This is the wording of al-Bukhari. The wording of Muslim: 'Abd Allah ibn Mughaffal said: "I obtained a bag of fat on the day of Khaybar." He said: "So I clasped it and said: I will not give any of this to anyone today." He said: "So I turned and saw the Messenger of God (ﷺ) smiling." Our scholars said: his smiling, peace be upon him, was only because he saw how greedily Ibn Mughaffal sought to take the bag and how attached he was to it, and he neither ordered him to discard it nor forbade him.

The permissibility of eating it is the position of Abu Hanifah, al-Shafi'i and the general body of scholars, except that Malik disliked it because of the disagreement concerning it. Ibn al-Mundhir reported from Malik that he forbade it, and the senior students of Malik adopted this view. Their support is what preceded, and the hadith is a proof against them. If they slaughtered every animal with claws... Asbagh said: whatever was forbidden in the Book of God among their slaughtered animals is not permitted to be eaten, because they hold it religiously forbidden. Ashhab and Ibn al-Qasim said the same, while Ibn Wahb permitted it. Ibn Habib said: whatever was forbidden to them, and we know that from our Book, is not permitted to us from their slaughtered animals; and whatever we do not know to be forbidden except from their statements and their own reasoning, is not forbidden to us from their slaughtered animals.

**The sixth issue** concerns His words: ﴿That﴾, i.e. that prohibition. *Dhalika* (that) is in the nominative position, i.e. "the matter is that."

﴿We recompensed them for their rebellion﴾, i.e. for their injustice, as a punishment for them for killing the prophets, barring them from the way of God, taking usury, and devouring people's wealth falsely. In this is evidence that prohibition only comes as a result of sin, because it is a restriction, so one does not turn from the broader permission to it except when there is a sanction.

﴿And indeed We are truthful﴾ in Our report about these Jews concerning what We forbade them of meats and fats.

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And if they deny you﴾. It is a conditional clause (shart), and its answer (jawab) is ﴿Then say: Your Lord is possessed of vast mercy﴾, meaning: from the vastness of His mercy, He forbears toward you and does not punish you in this world. Then He prepared for them the punishment in the Hereafter, so He said: ﴿And His punishment will not be turned away from the guilty people﴾. It was also said: the meaning is, "And His punishment will not be turned away from the guilty people" if He wills it to descend in this world.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 6, verse 148:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿The ones who associated partners [with Allah] will say﴾. Mujahid said: it means the disbelievers of Quraysh.

(They said) ﴿Had Allah willed, we would not have associated [others with Him], nor would our fathers, nor would we have forbidden anything﴾. He means the baheera, the saiba and the wasila. Allah, Mighty and Majestic, informed of the unseen what they would say, and they thought that this was a support for them when the proof had become binding upon them and they had become certain of the falsehood of what they were upon. The meaning is: had Allah willed, He would have sent a messenger to our fathers, who would have forbidden them from associating partners with Allah and from forbidding what He had made lawful for them, so they would have desisted, and we would have followed them in that. So Allah refuted them by saying: ﴿Do you have any knowledge that you can bring out for us?﴾, that is, do you have evidence that this is so? ﴿You only follow conjecture﴾ in this statement.

﴿And you are only guessing﴾, so that you may deceive your weak-minded followers into thinking that you have a proof.

His saying "nor our fathers" is a conjunction (ʿatf) upon the nūn in "ashrakna" (we associated). He did not say "nahnu wa-la ābāʾunā" (we and not our fathers), because the word "wa-la" (nor) served in place of emphasizing the pronoun (tawkid al-mudmar), and for this reason it is good to say: "Mā qumtu wa-la Zayd" (I did not stand, nor Zayd).

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 6, verse 149:

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Say: Then to Allah belongs the conclusive proof﴾. That is, the proof that cuts off the excuse of the one being argued against, and removes doubt from whoever considers it. Its conclusive proof, according to this, is His making clear that He is One, and His sending the messengers and prophets. He made Tawhid (the oneness of God) clear through reflection on the created beings, He supported the messengers with miracles (mu'jizat), and His command binds every person who is accountable (mukallaf). As for His knowledge, His will and His speech, these are unseen (ghayb), which no servant can perceive, except whomever He chooses from among the messengers. For the obligation (taklif) it is sufficient that the servant be in such a state that, if he wished to do what he was commanded, he would be able to do it. The Mu'tazilah have confused the matter by the saying: ﴿If Allah had willed, we would not have associated anything with Him﴾. They said: Allah has blamed those who made their polytheism dependent upon His will. Their reliance on this is false, because Allah the Exalted only blamed them for abandoning their striving (ijtihad) in seeking the truth. They only said that as a form of mockery and play. A parallel to it is: ﴿And they said: If the Most Merciful had willed, we would not have worshipped them﴾ [[See vol. 16, p. 73.]]. Had they said it out of exaltation, reverence and knowledge of Him, He would not have censured them, because Allah the Exalted says: ﴿If Allah had willed, they would not have associated﴾ [[See pp. 60 and 66 of this volume.]], and ﴿They would not have believed unless Allah willed﴾ [[See pp. 60 and 66 of this volume.]], and ﴿If He had willed, He would have guided you all﴾ [[See vol. 10, p. 81.]]. Similar examples are many. So the believers say it out of their knowledge of Allah the Exalted.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 6, verse 150:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Say: Bring forth your witnesses﴾ means: Say to these polytheists, "Bring your witnesses to testify that God has forbidden what you have forbidden." "Halumma" (come, bring) is a word of calling to something, and it is used in the same form for the singular and the plural, and for the masculine and the feminine, according to the people of the Hijaz. But in the dialect of Najd they say: halumma (dual), halummu (plural masculine), halummi (feminine), inflecting it with the marks found in all other verbs. The Qur'an came in the dialect of the Hijaz. God, exalted is He, said: ﴿And those who say to their brethren, "Come hither to us"﴾ [[See vol. 14, p. 151.]] meaning: "Halumma" means: come forward, or draw near. And "halumma al-ta'am" means: bring the food. The meaning here is: "Bring your witnesses." The letter mim is given a fatha because of the meeting of two quiescent letters, as you say: "rudda ya hadha" (return, O this man); it is not permissible to make it damma or kasra. According to al-Khalil, the original is "ha" with "lam" added to it, then the alif was dropped due to frequent use. Others said the original is "hal" with "lam" added to it. It was also said: it keeps its own form and indicates the meaning of "hat" (bring). In Kitab al-Ayn by al-Khalil: its origin is "hal a'um" (do I intend you?), meaning "hal aqsiduka," and then their frequent use of it became such that what is meant by its saying is "ihdur" (be present). Just as "ta'ala" (come up) originally was said by one who is high to one who is low, but their frequent use of it became such that the one who is low says to the one who is high, "ta'ala."

(So if they testify) meaning: some of them testify for others, (then do not testify with them) meaning: do not affirm the rendering of testimony except from a Book or upon the tongue of a Prophet, and they have nothing of that.

**Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on Surah 6, verses 151–153 (part 1 of 4)**

﴿And do not approach the property of the orphan, except in the way that is best, until he reaches his maturity. Give full measure and weight with justice. We do not burden any soul beyond its capacity. And when you speak, be just, even if it concerns a near relative. And fulfil the covenant of Allah. This He has enjoined upon you, so that you may remember.﴾ (152)

﴿And this is My path, straight, so follow it. And do not follow other ways, lest they separate you from His way. This He has enjoined upon you, so that you may be mindful of Allah.﴾ (153)

There are fourteen issues in it.

**The first issue:** His saying, ﴿Say: Come, I will recite﴾. That is: come forward and read with certainty, as my Lord has revealed to me, not by conjecture or by falsehood as you claim. Then He explained that by saying, ﴿that you associate nothing with Him﴾. It is said to a man, *ta'āl* (come), meaning "come forward"; to a woman, *ta'ālī*; to two men or two women, *ta'āliyā*; to a group of men, *ta'ālaw*; and to a group of women, *ta'ālena*. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿So come, I will provide for you﴾. They made "coming forward" a kind of rising up and elevation, because the one commanded to come forward, in the original form of this verb, was as if he had been sitting, and so it was said to him, *ta'āl*, that is: raise your body by standing and come forward. They extended its use until they applied it to both the one standing and the one walking. Ibn al-Shajari said this.

**The second issue:** His saying, ﴿what your Lord has forbidden﴾. The most likely reading of *mā* is that it is a relative pronoun (*khabariyyah*) in the accusative position, governed by *atlu* (I will recite). The meaning is: "Come, I will recite what your Lord has forbidden to you." If you attach *ʿalaykum* (to you) to *ḥarrama* (forbade), that is the most likely reading, because it is the closest, and it is the choice of the Basrans. If you attach it to *atlu* (I will recite), it is also good, because it is the earlier, and this is the choice of the Kufans. The implied meaning in this view is: "I will recite to you what your Lord has forbidden."

﴿That you associate nothing with Him﴾ is in the accusative position, by an implied verb from the same root as the first one, meaning: "I will recite to you that you should not associate," that is, "I will recite to you the prohibition of associating partners with Allah." It may also be governed by the sense of urging contained in *ʿalaykum* (upon you), with *ʿalaykum* then being detached from what precedes it, meaning: "Upon you is abandoning association, and upon you is kindness to the two parents, and that you do not kill your children, and that you do not approach indecencies." This is like saying, "Upon you is your own affair," meaning, "Keep to yourself." Just as He said: ﴿Upon you is your own soul﴾. Ibn al-Shajari said all of this. Al-Nahhas said: *an* (that) may be in the accusative position as a substitute for *mā* (what), meaning: "I will recite to you the prohibition of associating partners." Al-Farra' preferred that *lā* (not) be a prohibition, because after it comes ﴿and﴾.

**The third issue:** This verse is a command from Allah the Exalted to His Prophet, peace be upon him, to call all creation to listen to the recitation of what Allah has forbidden. Likewise, it is obligatory upon the scholars after him to convey to the people and to explain to them what Allah has forbidden them from what is permitted. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿You shall make it clear to the people and not conceal it﴾. Ibn al-Mubarak mentioned: Isa ibn Umar informed us, from Amr ibn Murrah, that he told them: Rabi' ibn Khaytham said to a companion of his: "Would it please you to be given a document from the Prophet (ﷺ) whose seal has not been broken?" He said, "Yes." He said, "Then read: ﴿Say: Come, I will recite what your Lord has forbidden to you﴾," and he read to the end of the three verses. [Al-Qurtubi notes:] In *al-Taqrib* it is stated: "al-Rabi' ibn Khaytham" is pronounced with a *ḍamma* on the *mīm* and a *fatḥa* on the *thāʾ*, but in *al-Khulasa* it is with a *fatḥa* on the *mīm* and *thāʾ*, with a silent *yāʾ* between them. [From *Tahdhib*.]

Ka'b al-Ahbar said: This verse is the opening of the Torah: "In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. Say: Come, I will recite what your Lord has forbidden to you," and so on. [Earlier, Ka'b also said that the beginning of Surah al-An'am is the opening of the Torah.]

Ibn Abbas said: These are the clear verses (*muhkamat*) which Allah mentioned in the surah of "Al 'Imran" [in some manuscripts: al-An'am], upon which the laws of all creation have agreed, and which have never been abrogated in any religious community. It has also been said that they are the Ten Words revealed to Musa (Moses).

**The fourth issue:** His saying, ﴿and to the parents, kindness﴾. Kindness to the parents means righteousness towards them, guarding and protecting them, obeying their commands, removing any slavery from them, and refraining from exercising authority over them. *Iḥsānan* (kindness) is in the accusative as a verbal noun (*maṣdar*), and its governing verb is an implied verb of the same root. Its estimated form is: "And be kind to the parents, with kindness."

**The fifth issue:** His saying, ﴿and do not kill your children out of poverty﴾. *Imlāq* means poverty; that is, do not bury alive your daughters (from *al-mawʾūda*, the buried girl), fearing destitution, for I provide for you and for them. Some of them used to do this to both females and males, fearing poverty, as is apparent from the verse. *Amlaqa* means he became poor, and *amlaqahu* means he made him poor; it is both intransitive and transitive. Al-Naqqash related from Mu'arrij that he said: *al-imlāq* means hunger, in the dialect of Lakhm. Mundhir ibn Sa'id mentioned that *al-imlāq* means spending, and it is said: *amlaqa mālahu*, meaning he spent his wealth. It is also reported that Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, said to his wife: "Spend from your wealth as much as you wish" [using the same root]. A man is called *malaq* if he gives with his tongue what is not in his heart. So *al-malaq* is a homonymous term (*lafẓ mushtarak*), whose explanation will come in its proper place.

**The sixth issue:** This verse may be used as evidence by those who forbid *al-ʿazl* (coitus interruptus), because burying alive removes an existing child and offspring, and *al-ʿazl* prevents the very origin of offspring, so the two are similar. However, taking a life is a greater sin and a more hideous act. For this reason, some of our scholars said that from the Prophet's saying, peace be upon him, about *al-ʿazl*, "That is the hidden burying alive," it is understood that it is disliked (*karāha*), not forbidden (*taḥrīm*). A group of the Companions and others held this view. Another group of the Companions, the Successors, and jurists held that it is permissible, based on his saying, peace be upon him: "There is no blame upon you if you do not do it, for it is only by decree (*al-qadar*)," meaning: there is no sin upon you for not doing it. Al-Hasan and Muhammad ibn al-Muthanna understood from it a prohibition and a deterrence from *al-ʿazl*. The first interpretation is more preferable, because of his saying, peace be upon him: "When Allah wills to create something, nothing can prevent it."

Malik and al-Shafi'i said: It is not permissible to practise *al-ʿazl* with a free woman except with her permission. It seems they regarded ejaculation as part of her pleasure and of her right concerning offspring. They did not hold this for a woman owned by right of possession (*al-mawṭūʾa bi-milk al-yamīn*), since he may practise *al-ʿazl* with her without her permission, because she has no right in any of the matters mentioned.

**The seventh issue:** His saying, ﴿and do not approach indecencies, what is apparent of them and what is hidden﴾. A parallel is His saying: ﴿and leave off the outward and the inward of sin﴾. So His saying "what is apparent" is a prohibition against all kinds of indecencies, which are acts of disobedience. "What is hidden" is what the heart has resolved upon in opposition. "Apparent" and "hidden" are two states that together cover all the categories of things to which they are applied. *Mā ẓahara* (what is apparent) is in the accusative as an apposition (*badal*) to *al-fawāḥish* (indecencies), and *mā baṭana* (what is hidden) is conjoined to it.

**The eighth issue:** His saying, ﴿and do not kill the soul which Allah has forbidden, except by right﴾. The *alif* and *lām* in *al-nafs* (the soul) are for defining the genus, like their saying: "Love of the dirham and the dinar has ruined people." A similar example is His saying: ﴿Indeed, mankind was created anxious﴾ [see vol. 18, p. 289]. Do you not see His saying, "except the praying ones"? Likewise His saying: ﴿By time. Indeed, mankind is in loss﴾ [see vol. 20, p. 178], because He said: ﴿except those who believe﴾.

This verse is a prohibition against killing a soul that is forbidden to be killed, whether it is a believer or a covenanted non-Muslim, except by the right which makes killing it obligatory. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "I have been commanded to fight the people until they say, 'There is no god but Allah.' Whoever says, 'There is no god but Allah,' has protected his property and his life, except by its right, and their reckoning is with Allah." This right has several aspects: among them is withholding the zakat and abandoning the prayer. Abu Bakr al-Siddiq fought those who withheld zakat, and in the revelation: ﴿But if they repent, establish prayer, and give zakat, then let them go on their way﴾ [see vol. 8, p. 71]. This is clear. The Prophet (ﷺ) also said: "The blood of a Muslim man is not lawful except by one of three: a married adulterer, a life for a life, and one who abandons his religion and separates from the community." He, peace be upon him, also said: "If two caliphs are pledged allegiance, then kill the other of them." Narrated by Muslim. [Meaning: repel the other by killing him, if repelling him is not possible without that.] Abu Dawud narrated from Ibn Abbas, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever you find doing the deed of the people of Lut, kill the one who does it and the one it is done to." The explanation of this will come in *al-A'raf* [see vol. 7, p. 74 and p. 243 of this part].

In the revelation: ﴿The only recompense for those who wage war against Allah and His Messenger and strive upon the earth to cause corruption is that they be killed﴾ [see vol. 6, p. 147], (the verse). And He said: ﴿And if two groups of the believers fight, [make peace between them]﴾ [see vol. 16, p. 315], (the verse). Likewise, whoever splits the unity of the Muslims, opposes the leader of their community, divides their word, and strives upon the earth to cause corruption by plundering the families and wealth, rebelling against the ruler, and refusing his judgement, is to be killed. This is the meaning of His saying: ﴿except by right﴾.

He, peace be upon him, also said: "The believers' blood is equal in value, and the lowest of them may undertake a protection on their behalf. A Muslim is not to be killed for a disbeliever, nor a covenanted person during his covenant, and the people of two religions do not inherit from one another." Abu Dawud and al-Nasa'i narrated from Abu Bakr, who said: I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: "Whoever kills a covenanted person outside of his *kunh*, Allah forbids him Paradise." [*Kunh al-amr* is its reality; it is also said its time and measure; it is also said its ultimate end, meaning: whoever kills him at other than his proper time or beyond the limit within which killing him is permitted (from *al-Nihaya*).] In another narration of Abu Dawud, he said: "Whoever kills a man of the dhimmis will not smell the fragrance of Paradise, though its fragrance is found from a distance of seventy years." In al-Bukhari, in this hadith it is: "from a distance of forty years." He narrated it from the hadith of Abdullah ibn Amr ibn al-As.

**The ninth issue:** His saying, ﴿that﴾, refers to these prohibited things. The *kāf* and *mīm* are for address, and they have no place in i'rab (grammatical inflection).

**The tenth issue:** His saying, ﴿He has enjoined upon you﴾. *Waṣiyya* (injunction) is an emphatic command that is within one's ability. The *kāf* and *mīm* are in the accusative position, because it is a pronoun placed for address. In *waṣṣā* there is a subject pronoun that refers back to Allah. Maṭar al-Warraq related from Nafi', from Ibn Umar, that Uthman ibn Affan, may Allah be pleased with him, looked over his companions and said: "Why would you kill me? I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: 'The blood of a Muslim man is not lawful except by one of three: a man who commits adultery after being *muhsan* (married), for which the penalty is stoning; or who kills intentionally, for which the penalty is retaliation (*qawad*); or who apostatizes after his Islam, for which the penalty is execution.' By Allah, I have not committed adultery in the Jahiliyya or in Islam, nor have I killed anyone for which I would retaliate against myself, nor have I apostatized since I embraced Islam. I bear witness that there is no god but Allah and that Muhammad is His servant and Messenger. That is what I have mentioned to you, which He enjoined upon you, so that you may understand!"

**The eleventh issue:** His saying, ﴿And do not approach the property of the orphan, except in the way that is best﴾. That is: by that which is good for it and for its growth (in another copy: its management). This is achieved by preserving the principal and growing its returns. This is the best of the opinions on this matter, for it is comprehensive. Mujahid said: ﴿And do not approach the property of the orphan except in the way that is best﴾ means by trading with it, and do not buy from it nor borrow from it.

**The twelfth issue:** His saying, ﴿until he reaches his maturity (ashuddahu)﴾.

Its meaning: its strength. It may be in the body, and it may be in knowledge gained through experience, and both aspects must be present. The term al-ashudd (maturity, full strength) is here stated without qualification, but the description of the orphan's condition has come in Surah an-Nisa' in a qualified form, where He says: ﴿And test the orphans until they reach marriageable age; then if you perceive in them sound judgment﴾ [[See vol. 5, p. 33.]]. Thus He combined strength of body, which is reaching marriageable age, with strength of understanding, which is perceiving sound judgment. For if the orphan were enabled to take his property before the attainment of understanding and after the attainment of physical strength, he would squander it on his desires and remain a pauper with no wealth. The orphan was singled out for this condition because people neglect him and fathers are absent from their children, so attending to the fatherless one is more fitting. (Al-ihtibal: seizing the opportunity, seeking it, and taking care of it; that is, attending to the affairs of the orphan is more appropriate.)

Reaching ashudd does not permit approaching his property except in the best manner, because the sanctity of property applies to the adult as well. The orphan was mentioned specifically because his guardian is God (his opponent is God). The meaning is: ﴿And do not approach the property of the orphan except in the best manner﴾ permanently, until he reaches his full strength. There is an ellipsis in the speech: when he reaches his full strength and sound judgment is perceived in him, then hand over his property to him.

The scholars differed concerning the ashudd of the orphan. Ibn Zayd said: it is his reaching puberty. The people of Madina said: it is his reaching puberty together with the perception of his sound judgment. According to Abu Hanifa: twenty-five years. Ibn al-Arabi said: "I am astonished at Abu Hanifa, for he holds that prescribed quantities are not established by analogy or reasoning, but only by transmission, and yet he establishes them through weak hadiths. But he lived in the Dar al-Darb, so many deceivers gathered around him; had he lived in the mine, as God destined for Malik, nothing would have come forth from him except the pure gold of religion." (In one manuscript: "al-madhhab," and in another: "al-dhahab." He means by Dar al-Darb: Baghdad; and by the mine: the mine of the Shari'a and its source, the illuminated Madina.)

It has been said that the end of middle age is the gathering point of ashudd, as Suhaym ibn Wathil said:

*A brother of fifty, in whom my full strength has gathered,*
*and experience with the affairs has refined me.*

[[A mujaddad man (with dal and dhal): one who has tested affairs, known them, and mastered them. Mudawarat al-shu'un: handling and treating affairs.]]

It is narrated as "najjadhani" with dal and dhal. Ashudd is a singular noun with no plural, like al-anuk, which is lead. It has also been said that its singular is shadd, like fals and aflus. Its origin is from shadda al-nahar, meaning it rose high; one says: "I came to him at shadd al-nahar and madd al-nahar" (at the height of the day). Muhammad ibn al-Dabbi used to recite the verse of 'Antara:

*My memory of him is of the day, as if his chest and head were dyed with 'alzam.*

[[Al-labban (with fatha on the lam): the chest. In another text: "al-banan," which is a variant. Al-'alzam (with kasra on the ayn and lam, and sukun on the zay): a red dye; it is also said to be al-wasma, a tree with leaves used for dyeing.]]

Another poet said:

*A woman of tall stature, long-armed, sahuq, circles around him at shadd al-nahar.*

[[Al-sahuq: a tall woman.]]

Sibawayh used to say: its singular is shiddah. Al-Jawhari said: this is sound in meaning, because one says: "the boy reached his shiddah," but the pattern fi'lah is not pluralized as af'ul. As for an'um, it is the plural of nu'm, from their saying: "a day of bu's and a day of nu'm." As for the view of those who said its singular is shadd, like kalb and aklub, and shidd like dhi'b and adhu'ub, that is merely analogy, just as they say for the singular of al-ababil: ibbul, by analogy with ijjul, though it is not something heard from the Arabs. Abu Zayd said: "Asabatni shudda 'ala fu'la," meaning hardship. One says "ashadda al-rajul" when he has a strong mount.

The twelfth issue: God's saying: ﴿And give full measure and weight with justice﴾, meaning with moderation in taking and giving during buying and selling. Qist means justice.

﴿We do not burden any soul except according to its capacity﴾, meaning its ability in giving full measure and weight. This implies that these commands apply only to what falls within human ability to guard against and avoid. As for what cannot be avoided, such as the slight variation between the two measures, which is beyond human capacity, it is pardoned. It has also been said that kayl means the measuring vessel; one says: "this is such-and-such a measure," and for this reason it is joined with "weight." Some scholars said: when God, glory be to Him, knew that many of His servants find it hard to be content giving others what is not obligatory upon them, He commanded the giver to render to the rightful owner his due right, and did not require him to give more, because of the hardship to his soul in giving more. He commanded the claimant to take his right, and did not require him to be content with less, because of the hardship to his soul in deficiency.

In the Muwatta' of Malik, from Yahya ibn Sa'id, it reached him that Abdullah ibn Abbas said: "Embezzlement never appeared among a people without God casting terror into their hearts; fornication never spread among a people without death becoming widespread among them; no people diminished the measure and weight without their provision being cut off; no people judged by other than the truth without bloodshed spreading among them; and no people broke a covenant without God giving their enemy power over them." [[Narrated by al-Tabarani as a hadith from Ibn Abbas.]] Ibn Abbas also said: "You, O assembly of non-Arabs, have been entrusted with two matters by which those before you were destroyed: the measure and the weight." [[From manuscript K.]]

The thirteenth issue: God's saying: ﴿And when you speak, be just﴾, which includes rulings and testimony. "Even if it concerns a near relative," meaning even if the right is against people like your own relatives, as has been mentioned in an-Nisa' [[See vol. 5, p. 410.]].

(And fulfil the covenant of God.) This is general over all that God has enjoined upon His servants. It may also be intended to include all agreements made between two people. That covenant is attributed to God because He commanded its preservation and fulfilment. (So that you may remember.)

...so that you may take heed. **Fourteenth issue:** His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And that this is My straight path, so follow it﴾. This is a great verse, and it is conjoined to what came before it. When He forbade and commanded, He here warned against following other than His way. In it He commanded following His path, as we will explain with the sound hadiths and the sayings of the early generation (al-salaf).

"And that" (*wa-anna*) is in the accusative position (*nasb*, the grammatical case of the object), meaning: "and recite that this is My path." This is related from al-Farra' and al-Kisa'i. Al-Farra' said: It is also permissible for it to be in the genitive position (*khafd*), meaning: "He enjoined it upon you, and [He enjoined] that this is My path." Its estimated construction according to al-Khalil and Sibawayh is: "and because this is My path," as in His saying: ﴿And that the mosques belong to God﴾ [[See vol. 19, p. 19.]].

Al-A'mash, Hamza and al-Kisa'i read *wa-inna hadhā* with a kasra on the hamza, as a resumption (*isti'nāf*, a new independent clause), meaning: "The one mentioned in the verses is My path, straight." Ibn Abi Ishaq and Ya'qub read *wa-an hadhā* with the light form. The light form (*mukhaffafa*) is like the heavy form (*mushaddada*), except that it contains the pronoun of the matter and the affair, meaning: "and that it is this." So it is in the nominative position (*raf'*), though the accusative is also permissible. It is also permissible for it to be a redundant particle (*zā'ida*) for emphasis, as in His mighty and majestic saying: ﴿When the bearer of good tidings came﴾ [[See vol. 9, p. 259.]].

*Al-sirāt* (the path) is the way that is the religion of Islam. *Mustaqīman* (straight) is in the circumstantial accusative (*hāl*), and its meaning is: level, upright, with no crookedness in it. So He commanded following His path, which He laid down through the tongue of His Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ), and prescribed, and whose end is Paradise. From it branch off other paths. Whoever takes the main road is saved, and whoever leaves for those other paths, they lead him to the Fire. God the Exalted said: ﴿And do not follow the (other) ways, lest they separate you from His way﴾ — meaning, they incline you away.

Al-Darimi Abu Muhammad related in his *Musnad* with a sound chain: Affan informed us, Hammad ibn Zayd narrated to us, Asim ibn Bahdala narrated to us, from Abu Wa'il, from Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) drew a line for us one day, then said: "This is the way of God." Then he drew lines to his right and lines to his left, then said: "These are paths; on each path there is a devil calling to it." Then he recited this verse.

Ibn Majah also related it in his *Sunan* from Jabir ibn Abd Allah, who said: We were with the Prophet (ﷺ), and he drew a line, and drew two lines to his right and two lines to his left, then he placed his hand on the middle line and said: "This is the way of God." Then he recited this verse: ﴿And that this is My straight path, so follow it, and do not follow the (other) ways, lest they separate you from His way﴾.

These paths include Judaism, Christianity, Zoroastrianism, and all the other religious communities, as well as the people of innovations (*bid'a*) and misguided views among the people of desires and of deviation in the subsidiary matters, and others among the people of excessive deepening in disputation and plunging into theology. All of these are prone to error and are a source of corrupt belief. Ibn Atiyya said: I say: and this is the correct view.

Al-Tabari mentioned in his book *Adab al-Nufus*: Muhammad ibn Abd al-A'la al-San'ani narrated to us, saying: Muhammad ibn Thawr narrated to us, from Ma'mar, from Aban, that a man said to Ibn Mas'ud: What is the straight path? He said: Muhammad (ﷺ) left us at its lower end, and its extremity is in Paradise, and on its right are *jawād* (roads) and on its left are *jawād*, and there are men there calling whoever passes by them. Whoever takes one of those *jawād* ends up in the Fire, and whoever takes the path ends up in Paradise. Then Ibn Mas'ud recited: ﴿And that this is My straight path﴾ to the end of the verse. [*Al-jawād* (with a doubled *dāl*) means the roads; its singular is *jādda*, which is the middle of the road. It was said: its main part; it was also said: its center.]

Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud also said: Learn knowledge before it is taken away, and its taking away is that its people depart. Beware of excessive stringency (*tanaṭṭu'*), of over-deepening (*ta'ammuq*), and of innovations (*bida'*) [[Al-Raghib defined innovation as: "In religion, the introduction of a saying whose speaker and doer did not follow the example of the Lawgiver and his noble earlier followers and firm foundations."]]. Hold fast to the ancient (*al-'atīq*) [[*Al-'atīq*: the old, the first.]]. Related by al-Darimi.

Mujahid said concerning His saying: ﴿And do not follow the (other) ways﴾: "The innovations." Ibn Shihab said: This is like His saying: ﴿Indeed, those who divided their religion and became sects﴾ to the end of the verse [[See p. 149 of this volume.]]. So flee, flee! And salvation, salvation! And hold fast to the straight path and the upright way, which the righteous early generation (*al-salaf al-salih*) trod, and in which is the profitable trade.

The leading scholars (*al-a'imma*) related from Abu Hurayra who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "What I have commanded you, take it; and what I have forbidden you, refrain from it."

Ibn Majah and others related from al-Irbad ibn Sariya who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) admonished us with an admonition from which eyes shed tears and hearts trembled. We said: O Messenger of God, this is surely the admonition of one bidding farewell; so what do you charge us with? He said: "I have left you upon the white (path) [[*Al-bayḍā'*: he (ﷺ) means the religion and the clear proof that admits no doubt whatsoever. ]], its night is like its day; none deviates from it after me except one who is destined to perish. Whoever of you lives will see much disagreement. So hold fast to what you know of my Sunna and the Sunna of the rightly-guided rightful caliphs after me. Bite onto it with the molars. Beware of newly introduced matters, for every innovation is misguidance. And obey, even if an Abyssinian slave is set over you, for the believer is like the docile camel: wherever it is led by its tether, it follows." Related by al-Tirmidhi in similar meaning, and he graded it sound.

Abu Dawud related: Ibn Kathir narrated to us, saying: Sufyan informed us, saying: A man wrote to Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz asking about predestination (*qadar*), and he wrote back: "To proceed: I enjoin upon you the fear of God, moderation in His command, the following of the Sunna of the Messenger of God (ﷺ), and abandoning what the innovators have introduced after its Sunna was already established, for they have spared you its burden. So keep to the community (*jamā'a*), for it is, by God's permission, a safeguard for you. Know that people have not introduced any innovation except that before it there passed what is evidence against it or a lesson concerning it. The Sunna was only laid down by one who knew what lies in opposing it of error, slip, foolishness and excessive deepening. So be content for yourself with what those people were content with for themselves, for they stopped on knowledge, and they refrained with penetrating insight, and they were stronger in uncovering matters, and more deserving of the excellence they were in. If the guidance is what you are upon, then you have preceded them to it; and if you say that it came into being after them, then none has introduced it except one who followed other than their way and turned himself away from them. For they are the foremost; they spoke about it with what suffices and described what heals. Whoever falls short of them is negligent, and whoever goes beyond them is excessive. Some people fell short of them and became harsh, and others went too far from them and became extreme. Yet they, between that, were upon the straight path." And he related the hadith.

Sahl ibn Abd Allah al-Tustari said: Hold to imitating the traces (*athar*) and the Sunna, for I fear that soon a time will come when, if a person mentions the Prophet (ﷺ) and following him in all states, they will blame him, shun him, disown him, humiliate him and belittle him.

Sahl said: Innovation only appeared at the hands of the people of the Sunna, because they associated with them and debated with them, so their sayings became known and spread among the common people, and one who had not heard them heard them. If they had left them alone and not spoken to them, each of them would have died with what was in his breast, not made it manifest, and carried it with him to his grave.

Sahl also said: None of you introduces an innovation until Iblis introduces for him a worship, so he worships by it; then he introduces for him an innovation. When he speaks the innovation and calls people to it, that service (*khadhma*) is taken from him [[Thus in MS B; in MSS J and K: *al-khidma* (the service).]].

Sahl said: I know of no hadith related about innovators more severe than this hadith: "God has forbidden Paradise to the one who holds an innovation." He said: So the Jew and the Christian are more hopeful than they are.

Sahl said: Whoever wishes to honor his religion should not enter upon the ruler, nor be alone with women, nor dispute with the people of desires. He also said: Follow and do not innovate, for you have been sufficed.

In the *Musnad* of al-Darimi: Abu Musa al-Ash'ari came to Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud and said: O Abu Abd al-Rahman, I saw in the mosque just now something that I disapproved of, though I have seen nothing but good, praise be to God. He said: What is it? He said: If you live, you will see it. He said: I saw in the mosque people sitting in circles, waiting for the prayer, and in each circle was a man, and in their hands were pebbles, and he would say to them: "Say *takbir* (Allahu akbar) a hundred times," and they would say it a hundred times. Then he says: "Say *tahlil* (la ilaha illa Allah) a hundred times," and they say it a hundred times. And he says: "Say *tasbih* (subhan Allah) a hundred times," and they say it a hundred times. He said: What did you say to them? He said: I said nothing to them, awaiting your opinion and awaiting your command. He said: Why did you not order them to count their evil deeds, and guarantee them that none of their good deeds would be lost? Then he went on, and we went with him until he came to one of those circles, and he stood over them and said: "What is this that I see you doing?" They said: O Abu Abd al-Rahman, pebbles with which we count the *takbir*, the *tahlil* and the *tasbih*. He said: Then count your evil deeds, and I guarantee you that none of your good deeds will be lost. Woe to you, O community of Muhammad! How swiftly is your destruction! These are the companions of your Prophet (ﷺ), numerous, and these are his garments not yet worn out, and his vessels not broken. By Him in whose hand my soul is, you are either upon a religion more guided than the religion of Muhammad, or you are opening a door of misguidance! They said: By God, O Abu Abd al-Rahman, we intended only good. He said: How many is the one who intends good but will not attain it.

From Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz: a man asked him about something concerning the people of desires and innovations, and he said: "Hold to the religion of the Bedouins and of the boy in the Quranic school, and abstain from anything other than that."

Al-Awza'i said: Iblis said to his allies: From what direction do you come to the children of Adam? They said: From every direction. He said: Do you come to them from the direction of seeking forgiveness (*istighfar*)? They said:

Hayhat! That is something tied to tawhid. [Iblis] said: "I will surely plant in them something for which they will not seek forgiveness from God." He said: "So he planted among them the desires (al-ahwa')." Mujahid said: "I do not know which of the two blessings upon me is greater: that He guided me to Islam, or that He protected me from these desires." Al-Sha'bi said: "They were named the people of desires (ahl al-ahwa') only because they fall (yahwun) into the Fire." All of this is from al-Darimi.

Sahl ibn 'Abd Allah was asked about praying behind the Mu'tazila, and about marrying them and marrying their women. He said: "No, and no honor! They are disbelievers [[It is not among the principles of the People of the Sunnah to declare disbelief in the People of the Qibla over an error in interpretation. So let it be considered.]]. How can one be a believer who says: the Qur'an is created, there is no created Paradise and no created Fire, there is no Path (sirat) for God and no intercession, no one among the believers of the community of Muhammad (ﷺ) who enters the Fire will come out of it, there is no punishment of the grave, no Munkar and Nakir, no seeing of our Lord in the Hereafter and no 'ziyada' (extra vision), that the knowledge of God is created, and they do not regard the ruler or the Friday prayer [as valid]; and they declare disbelief in whoever believes in these things."

Al-Fudayl ibn 'Iyad said: "Whoever loves the person of an innovation, God will nullify his deeds and remove the light of Islam from his heart." Sufyan al-Thawri said: "Innovation is more beloved to Iblis than disobedience: disobedience can be repented of, but innovation cannot be repented of." Ibn 'Abbas said: "Looking at a man of the People of the Sunnah who calls to the Sunnah and forbids innovation is an act of worship." Abu al-'Aliyya said: "Hold to the first matter upon which they were before they split." 'Asim al-Ahwal said: "I related this to al-Hasan, and he said: 'By God, he has advised you and spoken truthfully.'"

The meaning of the saying of the Prophet (peace be upon him) has already passed in "Al 'Imran": "The Children of Israel divided into seventy-two sects, and this community will divide into seventy-three..." the hadith [[See vol. 4, p. 159.]]. Some of the knowledgeable scholars have said: "The sect that was added to the sects of the community of Muhammad (ﷺ) are people who oppose the scholars and hate the jurists, and that never happened in the earlier nations."

Rafi' ibn Khadij narrated that he heard the Messenger of God (ﷺ) say: "There will be among my community people who disbelieve in God and in the Qur'an while they are unaware, just as the Jews and Christians disbelieved." I said: "May I be your ransom, O Messenger of God! How is that?" He said: "They affirm some parts and deny other parts." I said: "May I be your ransom, O Messenger of God! And how do they speak?" He said: "They make Iblis an equal to God in His creation, His power and His provision, and they say: good is from God and evil is from Iblis." He said: "They disbelieve in God, then they recite the Book of God upon that, so they disbelieve in the Qur'an after faith and knowledge?" He said: "What my community meets from them of enmity, hatred and disputation: those are the heretics (zanadiqa) of this community." And he mentioned the hadith.

It has passed in "al-Nisa'" and in this surah the prohibition of sitting with the people of innovations and desires, and that whoever sits with them has the same ruling as they do, when He said: "And when you see those who engage in vain talk concerning Our signs..." [[See p. 12 of this part.]] "the verse." Then He explained in surah "al-Nisa'", which is Madani, the punishment of whoever does that and opposes what God commanded, when He said: "And He has already revealed to you in the Book..." the verse [[See vol. 5, p. 417.]]. So He joined those who sit with them to them. A group of the imams of this community went this way, and ruled according to the implications of these verses regarding the gatherings of the people of innovation, regarding companionship and association with them: among them Ahmad ibn Hanbal, al-Awza'i and Ibn al-Mubarak. They said concerning a man whose habit is sitting with the people of innovation: "He is forbidden from sitting with them; if he desists, well and good; otherwise he is joined to them," meaning in ruling.

'Umar ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz applied the hadd penalty to the gatherings of wine-drinkers, and recited: "Indeed, you would then be like them." It was said to him: "He says: I sit with them in order to separate from them and refute them." He said: "He is forbidden from sitting with them; if he does not desist, he is joined to them."
