**Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on Surah 6, verses 151–153 (part 1 of 4)**

﴿And do not approach the property of the orphan, except in the way that is best, until he reaches his maturity. Give full measure and weight with justice. We do not burden any soul beyond its capacity. And when you speak, be just, even if it concerns a near relative. And fulfil the covenant of Allah. This He has enjoined upon you, so that you may remember.﴾ (152)

﴿And this is My path, straight, so follow it. And do not follow other ways, lest they separate you from His way. This He has enjoined upon you, so that you may be mindful of Allah.﴾ (153)

There are fourteen issues in it.

**The first issue:** His saying, ﴿Say: Come, I will recite﴾. That is: come forward and read with certainty, as my Lord has revealed to me, not by conjecture or by falsehood as you claim. Then He explained that by saying, ﴿that you associate nothing with Him﴾. It is said to a man, *ta'āl* (come), meaning "come forward"; to a woman, *ta'ālī*; to two men or two women, *ta'āliyā*; to a group of men, *ta'ālaw*; and to a group of women, *ta'ālena*. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿So come, I will provide for you﴾. They made "coming forward" a kind of rising up and elevation, because the one commanded to come forward, in the original form of this verb, was as if he had been sitting, and so it was said to him, *ta'āl*, that is: raise your body by standing and come forward. They extended its use until they applied it to both the one standing and the one walking. Ibn al-Shajari said this.

**The second issue:** His saying, ﴿what your Lord has forbidden﴾. The most likely reading of *mā* is that it is a relative pronoun (*khabariyyah*) in the accusative position, governed by *atlu* (I will recite). The meaning is: "Come, I will recite what your Lord has forbidden to you." If you attach *ʿalaykum* (to you) to *ḥarrama* (forbade), that is the most likely reading, because it is the closest, and it is the choice of the Basrans. If you attach it to *atlu* (I will recite), it is also good, because it is the earlier, and this is the choice of the Kufans. The implied meaning in this view is: "I will recite to you what your Lord has forbidden."

﴿That you associate nothing with Him﴾ is in the accusative position, by an implied verb from the same root as the first one, meaning: "I will recite to you that you should not associate," that is, "I will recite to you the prohibition of associating partners with Allah." It may also be governed by the sense of urging contained in *ʿalaykum* (upon you), with *ʿalaykum* then being detached from what precedes it, meaning: "Upon you is abandoning association, and upon you is kindness to the two parents, and that you do not kill your children, and that you do not approach indecencies." This is like saying, "Upon you is your own affair," meaning, "Keep to yourself." Just as He said: ﴿Upon you is your own soul﴾. Ibn al-Shajari said all of this. Al-Nahhas said: *an* (that) may be in the accusative position as a substitute for *mā* (what), meaning: "I will recite to you the prohibition of associating partners." Al-Farra' preferred that *lā* (not) be a prohibition, because after it comes ﴿and﴾.

**The third issue:** This verse is a command from Allah the Exalted to His Prophet, peace be upon him, to call all creation to listen to the recitation of what Allah has forbidden. Likewise, it is obligatory upon the scholars after him to convey to the people and to explain to them what Allah has forbidden them from what is permitted. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿You shall make it clear to the people and not conceal it﴾. Ibn al-Mubarak mentioned: Isa ibn Umar informed us, from Amr ibn Murrah, that he told them: Rabi' ibn Khaytham said to a companion of his: "Would it please you to be given a document from the Prophet (ﷺ) whose seal has not been broken?" He said, "Yes." He said, "Then read: ﴿Say: Come, I will recite what your Lord has forbidden to you﴾," and he read to the end of the three verses. [Al-Qurtubi notes:] In *al-Taqrib* it is stated: "al-Rabi' ibn Khaytham" is pronounced with a *ḍamma* on the *mīm* and a *fatḥa* on the *thāʾ*, but in *al-Khulasa* it is with a *fatḥa* on the *mīm* and *thāʾ*, with a silent *yāʾ* between them. [From *Tahdhib*.]

Ka'b al-Ahbar said: This verse is the opening of the Torah: "In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. Say: Come, I will recite what your Lord has forbidden to you," and so on. [Earlier, Ka'b also said that the beginning of Surah al-An'am is the opening of the Torah.]

Ibn Abbas said: These are the clear verses (*muhkamat*) which Allah mentioned in the surah of "Al 'Imran" [in some manuscripts: al-An'am], upon which the laws of all creation have agreed, and which have never been abrogated in any religious community. It has also been said that they are the Ten Words revealed to Musa (Moses).

**The fourth issue:** His saying, ﴿and to the parents, kindness﴾. Kindness to the parents means righteousness towards them, guarding and protecting them, obeying their commands, removing any slavery from them, and refraining from exercising authority over them. *Iḥsānan* (kindness) is in the accusative as a verbal noun (*maṣdar*), and its governing verb is an implied verb of the same root. Its estimated form is: "And be kind to the parents, with kindness."

**The fifth issue:** His saying, ﴿and do not kill your children out of poverty﴾. *Imlāq* means poverty; that is, do not bury alive your daughters (from *al-mawʾūda*, the buried girl), fearing destitution, for I provide for you and for them. Some of them used to do this to both females and males, fearing poverty, as is apparent from the verse. *Amlaqa* means he became poor, and *amlaqahu* means he made him poor; it is both intransitive and transitive. Al-Naqqash related from Mu'arrij that he said: *al-imlāq* means hunger, in the dialect of Lakhm. Mundhir ibn Sa'id mentioned that *al-imlāq* means spending, and it is said: *amlaqa mālahu*, meaning he spent his wealth. It is also reported that Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, said to his wife: "Spend from your wealth as much as you wish" [using the same root]. A man is called *malaq* if he gives with his tongue what is not in his heart. So *al-malaq* is a homonymous term (*lafẓ mushtarak*), whose explanation will come in its proper place.

**The sixth issue:** This verse may be used as evidence by those who forbid *al-ʿazl* (coitus interruptus), because burying alive removes an existing child and offspring, and *al-ʿazl* prevents the very origin of offspring, so the two are similar. However, taking a life is a greater sin and a more hideous act. For this reason, some of our scholars said that from the Prophet's saying, peace be upon him, about *al-ʿazl*, "That is the hidden burying alive," it is understood that it is disliked (*karāha*), not forbidden (*taḥrīm*). A group of the Companions and others held this view. Another group of the Companions, the Successors, and jurists held that it is permissible, based on his saying, peace be upon him: "There is no blame upon you if you do not do it, for it is only by decree (*al-qadar*)," meaning: there is no sin upon you for not doing it. Al-Hasan and Muhammad ibn al-Muthanna understood from it a prohibition and a deterrence from *al-ʿazl*. The first interpretation is more preferable, because of his saying, peace be upon him: "When Allah wills to create something, nothing can prevent it."

Malik and al-Shafi'i said: It is not permissible to practise *al-ʿazl* with a free woman except with her permission. It seems they regarded ejaculation as part of her pleasure and of her right concerning offspring. They did not hold this for a woman owned by right of possession (*al-mawṭūʾa bi-milk al-yamīn*), since he may practise *al-ʿazl* with her without her permission, because she has no right in any of the matters mentioned.

**The seventh issue:** His saying, ﴿and do not approach indecencies, what is apparent of them and what is hidden﴾. A parallel is His saying: ﴿and leave off the outward and the inward of sin﴾. So His saying "what is apparent" is a prohibition against all kinds of indecencies, which are acts of disobedience. "What is hidden" is what the heart has resolved upon in opposition. "Apparent" and "hidden" are two states that together cover all the categories of things to which they are applied. *Mā ẓahara* (what is apparent) is in the accusative as an apposition (*badal*) to *al-fawāḥish* (indecencies), and *mā baṭana* (what is hidden) is conjoined to it.

**The eighth issue:** His saying, ﴿and do not kill the soul which Allah has forbidden, except by right﴾. The *alif* and *lām* in *al-nafs* (the soul) are for defining the genus, like their saying: "Love of the dirham and the dinar has ruined people." A similar example is His saying: ﴿Indeed, mankind was created anxious﴾ [see vol. 18, p. 289]. Do you not see His saying, "except the praying ones"? Likewise His saying: ﴿By time. Indeed, mankind is in loss﴾ [see vol. 20, p. 178], because He said: ﴿except those who believe﴾.

This verse is a prohibition against killing a soul that is forbidden to be killed, whether it is a believer or a covenanted non-Muslim, except by the right which makes killing it obligatory. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "I have been commanded to fight the people until they say, 'There is no god but Allah.' Whoever says, 'There is no god but Allah,' has protected his property and his life, except by its right, and their reckoning is with Allah." This right has several aspects: among them is withholding the zakat and abandoning the prayer. Abu Bakr al-Siddiq fought those who withheld zakat, and in the revelation: ﴿But if they repent, establish prayer, and give zakat, then let them go on their way﴾ [see vol. 8, p. 71]. This is clear. The Prophet (ﷺ) also said: "The blood of a Muslim man is not lawful except by one of three: a married adulterer, a life for a life, and one who abandons his religion and separates from the community." He, peace be upon him, also said: "If two caliphs are pledged allegiance, then kill the other of them." Narrated by Muslim. [Meaning: repel the other by killing him, if repelling him is not possible without that.] Abu Dawud narrated from Ibn Abbas, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever you find doing the deed of the people of Lut, kill the one who does it and the one it is done to." The explanation of this will come in *al-A'raf* [see vol. 7, p. 74 and p. 243 of this part].

In the revelation: ﴿The only recompense for those who wage war against Allah and His Messenger and strive upon the earth to cause corruption is that they be killed﴾ [see vol. 6, p. 147], (the verse). And He said: ﴿And if two groups of the believers fight, [make peace between them]﴾ [see vol. 16, p. 315], (the verse). Likewise, whoever splits the unity of the Muslims, opposes the leader of their community, divides their word, and strives upon the earth to cause corruption by plundering the families and wealth, rebelling against the ruler, and refusing his judgement, is to be killed. This is the meaning of His saying: ﴿except by right﴾.

He, peace be upon him, also said: "The believers' blood is equal in value, and the lowest of them may undertake a protection on their behalf. A Muslim is not to be killed for a disbeliever, nor a covenanted person during his covenant, and the people of two religions do not inherit from one another." Abu Dawud and al-Nasa'i narrated from Abu Bakr, who said: I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: "Whoever kills a covenanted person outside of his *kunh*, Allah forbids him Paradise." [*Kunh al-amr* is its reality; it is also said its time and measure; it is also said its ultimate end, meaning: whoever kills him at other than his proper time or beyond the limit within which killing him is permitted (from *al-Nihaya*).] In another narration of Abu Dawud, he said: "Whoever kills a man of the dhimmis will not smell the fragrance of Paradise, though its fragrance is found from a distance of seventy years." In al-Bukhari, in this hadith it is: "from a distance of forty years." He narrated it from the hadith of Abdullah ibn Amr ibn al-As.

**The ninth issue:** His saying, ﴿that﴾, refers to these prohibited things. The *kāf* and *mīm* are for address, and they have no place in i'rab (grammatical inflection).

**The tenth issue:** His saying, ﴿He has enjoined upon you﴾. *Waṣiyya* (injunction) is an emphatic command that is within one's ability. The *kāf* and *mīm* are in the accusative position, because it is a pronoun placed for address. In *waṣṣā* there is a subject pronoun that refers back to Allah. Maṭar al-Warraq related from Nafi', from Ibn Umar, that Uthman ibn Affan, may Allah be pleased with him, looked over his companions and said: "Why would you kill me? I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: 'The blood of a Muslim man is not lawful except by one of three: a man who commits adultery after being *muhsan* (married), for which the penalty is stoning; or who kills intentionally, for which the penalty is retaliation (*qawad*); or who apostatizes after his Islam, for which the penalty is execution.' By Allah, I have not committed adultery in the Jahiliyya or in Islam, nor have I killed anyone for which I would retaliate against myself, nor have I apostatized since I embraced Islam. I bear witness that there is no god but Allah and that Muhammad is His servant and Messenger. That is what I have mentioned to you, which He enjoined upon you, so that you may understand!"

**The eleventh issue:** His saying, ﴿And do not approach the property of the orphan, except in the way that is best﴾. That is: by that which is good for it and for its growth (in another copy: its management). This is achieved by preserving the principal and growing its returns. This is the best of the opinions on this matter, for it is comprehensive. Mujahid said: ﴿And do not approach the property of the orphan except in the way that is best﴾ means by trading with it, and do not buy from it nor borrow from it.

**The twelfth issue:** His saying, ﴿until he reaches his maturity (ashuddahu)﴾.

Its meaning: its strength. It may be in the body, and it may be in knowledge gained through experience, and both aspects must be present. The term al-ashudd (maturity, full strength) is here stated without qualification, but the description of the orphan's condition has come in Surah an-Nisa' in a qualified form, where He says: ﴿And test the orphans until they reach marriageable age; then if you perceive in them sound judgment﴾ [[See vol. 5, p. 33.]]. Thus He combined strength of body, which is reaching marriageable age, with strength of understanding, which is perceiving sound judgment. For if the orphan were enabled to take his property before the attainment of understanding and after the attainment of physical strength, he would squander it on his desires and remain a pauper with no wealth. The orphan was singled out for this condition because people neglect him and fathers are absent from their children, so attending to the fatherless one is more fitting. (Al-ihtibal: seizing the opportunity, seeking it, and taking care of it; that is, attending to the affairs of the orphan is more appropriate.)

Reaching ashudd does not permit approaching his property except in the best manner, because the sanctity of property applies to the adult as well. The orphan was mentioned specifically because his guardian is God (his opponent is God). The meaning is: ﴿And do not approach the property of the orphan except in the best manner﴾ permanently, until he reaches his full strength. There is an ellipsis in the speech: when he reaches his full strength and sound judgment is perceived in him, then hand over his property to him.

The scholars differed concerning the ashudd of the orphan. Ibn Zayd said: it is his reaching puberty. The people of Madina said: it is his reaching puberty together with the perception of his sound judgment. According to Abu Hanifa: twenty-five years. Ibn al-Arabi said: "I am astonished at Abu Hanifa, for he holds that prescribed quantities are not established by analogy or reasoning, but only by transmission, and yet he establishes them through weak hadiths. But he lived in the Dar al-Darb, so many deceivers gathered around him; had he lived in the mine, as God destined for Malik, nothing would have come forth from him except the pure gold of religion." (In one manuscript: "al-madhhab," and in another: "al-dhahab." He means by Dar al-Darb: Baghdad; and by the mine: the mine of the Shari'a and its source, the illuminated Madina.)

It has been said that the end of middle age is the gathering point of ashudd, as Suhaym ibn Wathil said:

*A brother of fifty, in whom my full strength has gathered,*
*and experience with the affairs has refined me.*

[[A mujaddad man (with dal and dhal): one who has tested affairs, known them, and mastered them. Mudawarat al-shu'un: handling and treating affairs.]]

It is narrated as "najjadhani" with dal and dhal. Ashudd is a singular noun with no plural, like al-anuk, which is lead. It has also been said that its singular is shadd, like fals and aflus. Its origin is from shadda al-nahar, meaning it rose high; one says: "I came to him at shadd al-nahar and madd al-nahar" (at the height of the day). Muhammad ibn al-Dabbi used to recite the verse of 'Antara:

*My memory of him is of the day, as if his chest and head were dyed with 'alzam.*

[[Al-labban (with fatha on the lam): the chest. In another text: "al-banan," which is a variant. Al-'alzam (with kasra on the ayn and lam, and sukun on the zay): a red dye; it is also said to be al-wasma, a tree with leaves used for dyeing.]]

Another poet said:

*A woman of tall stature, long-armed, sahuq, circles around him at shadd al-nahar.*

[[Al-sahuq: a tall woman.]]

Sibawayh used to say: its singular is shiddah. Al-Jawhari said: this is sound in meaning, because one says: "the boy reached his shiddah," but the pattern fi'lah is not pluralized as af'ul. As for an'um, it is the plural of nu'm, from their saying: "a day of bu's and a day of nu'm." As for the view of those who said its singular is shadd, like kalb and aklub, and shidd like dhi'b and adhu'ub, that is merely analogy, just as they say for the singular of al-ababil: ibbul, by analogy with ijjul, though it is not something heard from the Arabs. Abu Zayd said: "Asabatni shudda 'ala fu'la," meaning hardship. One says "ashadda al-rajul" when he has a strong mount.

The twelfth issue: God's saying: ﴿And give full measure and weight with justice﴾, meaning with moderation in taking and giving during buying and selling. Qist means justice.

﴿We do not burden any soul except according to its capacity﴾, meaning its ability in giving full measure and weight. This implies that these commands apply only to what falls within human ability to guard against and avoid. As for what cannot be avoided, such as the slight variation between the two measures, which is beyond human capacity, it is pardoned. It has also been said that kayl means the measuring vessel; one says: "this is such-and-such a measure," and for this reason it is joined with "weight." Some scholars said: when God, glory be to Him, knew that many of His servants find it hard to be content giving others what is not obligatory upon them, He commanded the giver to render to the rightful owner his due right, and did not require him to give more, because of the hardship to his soul in giving more. He commanded the claimant to take his right, and did not require him to be content with less, because of the hardship to his soul in deficiency.

In the Muwatta' of Malik, from Yahya ibn Sa'id, it reached him that Abdullah ibn Abbas said: "Embezzlement never appeared among a people without God casting terror into their hearts; fornication never spread among a people without death becoming widespread among them; no people diminished the measure and weight without their provision being cut off; no people judged by other than the truth without bloodshed spreading among them; and no people broke a covenant without God giving their enemy power over them." [[Narrated by al-Tabarani as a hadith from Ibn Abbas.]] Ibn Abbas also said: "You, O assembly of non-Arabs, have been entrusted with two matters by which those before you were destroyed: the measure and the weight." [[From manuscript K.]]

The thirteenth issue: God's saying: ﴿And when you speak, be just﴾, which includes rulings and testimony. "Even if it concerns a near relative," meaning even if the right is against people like your own relatives, as has been mentioned in an-Nisa' [[See vol. 5, p. 410.]].

(And fulfil the covenant of God.) This is general over all that God has enjoined upon His servants. It may also be intended to include all agreements made between two people. That covenant is attributed to God because He commanded its preservation and fulfilment. (So that you may remember.)

...so that you may take heed. **Fourteenth issue:** His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And that this is My straight path, so follow it﴾. This is a great verse, and it is conjoined to what came before it. When He forbade and commanded, He here warned against following other than His way. In it He commanded following His path, as we will explain with the sound hadiths and the sayings of the early generation (al-salaf).

"And that" (*wa-anna*) is in the accusative position (*nasb*, the grammatical case of the object), meaning: "and recite that this is My path." This is related from al-Farra' and al-Kisa'i. Al-Farra' said: It is also permissible for it to be in the genitive position (*khafd*), meaning: "He enjoined it upon you, and [He enjoined] that this is My path." Its estimated construction according to al-Khalil and Sibawayh is: "and because this is My path," as in His saying: ﴿And that the mosques belong to God﴾ [[See vol. 19, p. 19.]].

Al-A'mash, Hamza and al-Kisa'i read *wa-inna hadhā* with a kasra on the hamza, as a resumption (*isti'nāf*, a new independent clause), meaning: "The one mentioned in the verses is My path, straight." Ibn Abi Ishaq and Ya'qub read *wa-an hadhā* with the light form. The light form (*mukhaffafa*) is like the heavy form (*mushaddada*), except that it contains the pronoun of the matter and the affair, meaning: "and that it is this." So it is in the nominative position (*raf'*), though the accusative is also permissible. It is also permissible for it to be a redundant particle (*zā'ida*) for emphasis, as in His mighty and majestic saying: ﴿When the bearer of good tidings came﴾ [[See vol. 9, p. 259.]].

*Al-sirāt* (the path) is the way that is the religion of Islam. *Mustaqīman* (straight) is in the circumstantial accusative (*hāl*), and its meaning is: level, upright, with no crookedness in it. So He commanded following His path, which He laid down through the tongue of His Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ), and prescribed, and whose end is Paradise. From it branch off other paths. Whoever takes the main road is saved, and whoever leaves for those other paths, they lead him to the Fire. God the Exalted said: ﴿And do not follow the (other) ways, lest they separate you from His way﴾ — meaning, they incline you away.

Al-Darimi Abu Muhammad related in his *Musnad* with a sound chain: Affan informed us, Hammad ibn Zayd narrated to us, Asim ibn Bahdala narrated to us, from Abu Wa'il, from Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) drew a line for us one day, then said: "This is the way of God." Then he drew lines to his right and lines to his left, then said: "These are paths; on each path there is a devil calling to it." Then he recited this verse.

Ibn Majah also related it in his *Sunan* from Jabir ibn Abd Allah, who said: We were with the Prophet (ﷺ), and he drew a line, and drew two lines to his right and two lines to his left, then he placed his hand on the middle line and said: "This is the way of God." Then he recited this verse: ﴿And that this is My straight path, so follow it, and do not follow the (other) ways, lest they separate you from His way﴾.

These paths include Judaism, Christianity, Zoroastrianism, and all the other religious communities, as well as the people of innovations (*bid'a*) and misguided views among the people of desires and of deviation in the subsidiary matters, and others among the people of excessive deepening in disputation and plunging into theology. All of these are prone to error and are a source of corrupt belief. Ibn Atiyya said: I say: and this is the correct view.

Al-Tabari mentioned in his book *Adab al-Nufus*: Muhammad ibn Abd al-A'la al-San'ani narrated to us, saying: Muhammad ibn Thawr narrated to us, from Ma'mar, from Aban, that a man said to Ibn Mas'ud: What is the straight path? He said: Muhammad (ﷺ) left us at its lower end, and its extremity is in Paradise, and on its right are *jawād* (roads) and on its left are *jawād*, and there are men there calling whoever passes by them. Whoever takes one of those *jawād* ends up in the Fire, and whoever takes the path ends up in Paradise. Then Ibn Mas'ud recited: ﴿And that this is My straight path﴾ to the end of the verse. [*Al-jawād* (with a doubled *dāl*) means the roads; its singular is *jādda*, which is the middle of the road. It was said: its main part; it was also said: its center.]

Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud also said: Learn knowledge before it is taken away, and its taking away is that its people depart. Beware of excessive stringency (*tanaṭṭu'*), of over-deepening (*ta'ammuq*), and of innovations (*bida'*) [[Al-Raghib defined innovation as: "In religion, the introduction of a saying whose speaker and doer did not follow the example of the Lawgiver and his noble earlier followers and firm foundations."]]. Hold fast to the ancient (*al-'atīq*) [[*Al-'atīq*: the old, the first.]]. Related by al-Darimi.

Mujahid said concerning His saying: ﴿And do not follow the (other) ways﴾: "The innovations." Ibn Shihab said: This is like His saying: ﴿Indeed, those who divided their religion and became sects﴾ to the end of the verse [[See p. 149 of this volume.]]. So flee, flee! And salvation, salvation! And hold fast to the straight path and the upright way, which the righteous early generation (*al-salaf al-salih*) trod, and in which is the profitable trade.

The leading scholars (*al-a'imma*) related from Abu Hurayra who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "What I have commanded you, take it; and what I have forbidden you, refrain from it."

Ibn Majah and others related from al-Irbad ibn Sariya who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) admonished us with an admonition from which eyes shed tears and hearts trembled. We said: O Messenger of God, this is surely the admonition of one bidding farewell; so what do you charge us with? He said: "I have left you upon the white (path) [[*Al-bayḍā'*: he (ﷺ) means the religion and the clear proof that admits no doubt whatsoever. ]], its night is like its day; none deviates from it after me except one who is destined to perish. Whoever of you lives will see much disagreement. So hold fast to what you know of my Sunna and the Sunna of the rightly-guided rightful caliphs after me. Bite onto it with the molars. Beware of newly introduced matters, for every innovation is misguidance. And obey, even if an Abyssinian slave is set over you, for the believer is like the docile camel: wherever it is led by its tether, it follows." Related by al-Tirmidhi in similar meaning, and he graded it sound.

Abu Dawud related: Ibn Kathir narrated to us, saying: Sufyan informed us, saying: A man wrote to Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz asking about predestination (*qadar*), and he wrote back: "To proceed: I enjoin upon you the fear of God, moderation in His command, the following of the Sunna of the Messenger of God (ﷺ), and abandoning what the innovators have introduced after its Sunna was already established, for they have spared you its burden. So keep to the community (*jamā'a*), for it is, by God's permission, a safeguard for you. Know that people have not introduced any innovation except that before it there passed what is evidence against it or a lesson concerning it. The Sunna was only laid down by one who knew what lies in opposing it of error, slip, foolishness and excessive deepening. So be content for yourself with what those people were content with for themselves, for they stopped on knowledge, and they refrained with penetrating insight, and they were stronger in uncovering matters, and more deserving of the excellence they were in. If the guidance is what you are upon, then you have preceded them to it; and if you say that it came into being after them, then none has introduced it except one who followed other than their way and turned himself away from them. For they are the foremost; they spoke about it with what suffices and described what heals. Whoever falls short of them is negligent, and whoever goes beyond them is excessive. Some people fell short of them and became harsh, and others went too far from them and became extreme. Yet they, between that, were upon the straight path." And he related the hadith.

Sahl ibn Abd Allah al-Tustari said: Hold to imitating the traces (*athar*) and the Sunna, for I fear that soon a time will come when, if a person mentions the Prophet (ﷺ) and following him in all states, they will blame him, shun him, disown him, humiliate him and belittle him.

Sahl said: Innovation only appeared at the hands of the people of the Sunna, because they associated with them and debated with them, so their sayings became known and spread among the common people, and one who had not heard them heard them. If they had left them alone and not spoken to them, each of them would have died with what was in his breast, not made it manifest, and carried it with him to his grave.

Sahl also said: None of you introduces an innovation until Iblis introduces for him a worship, so he worships by it; then he introduces for him an innovation. When he speaks the innovation and calls people to it, that service (*khadhma*) is taken from him [[Thus in MS B; in MSS J and K: *al-khidma* (the service).]].

Sahl said: I know of no hadith related about innovators more severe than this hadith: "God has forbidden Paradise to the one who holds an innovation." He said: So the Jew and the Christian are more hopeful than they are.

Sahl said: Whoever wishes to honor his religion should not enter upon the ruler, nor be alone with women, nor dispute with the people of desires. He also said: Follow and do not innovate, for you have been sufficed.

In the *Musnad* of al-Darimi: Abu Musa al-Ash'ari came to Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud and said: O Abu Abd al-Rahman, I saw in the mosque just now something that I disapproved of, though I have seen nothing but good, praise be to God. He said: What is it? He said: If you live, you will see it. He said: I saw in the mosque people sitting in circles, waiting for the prayer, and in each circle was a man, and in their hands were pebbles, and he would say to them: "Say *takbir* (Allahu akbar) a hundred times," and they would say it a hundred times. Then he says: "Say *tahlil* (la ilaha illa Allah) a hundred times," and they say it a hundred times. And he says: "Say *tasbih* (subhan Allah) a hundred times," and they say it a hundred times. He said: What did you say to them? He said: I said nothing to them, awaiting your opinion and awaiting your command. He said: Why did you not order them to count their evil deeds, and guarantee them that none of their good deeds would be lost? Then he went on, and we went with him until he came to one of those circles, and he stood over them and said: "What is this that I see you doing?" They said: O Abu Abd al-Rahman, pebbles with which we count the *takbir*, the *tahlil* and the *tasbih*. He said: Then count your evil deeds, and I guarantee you that none of your good deeds will be lost. Woe to you, O community of Muhammad! How swiftly is your destruction! These are the companions of your Prophet (ﷺ), numerous, and these are his garments not yet worn out, and his vessels not broken. By Him in whose hand my soul is, you are either upon a religion more guided than the religion of Muhammad, or you are opening a door of misguidance! They said: By God, O Abu Abd al-Rahman, we intended only good. He said: How many is the one who intends good but will not attain it.

From Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz: a man asked him about something concerning the people of desires and innovations, and he said: "Hold to the religion of the Bedouins and of the boy in the Quranic school, and abstain from anything other than that."

Al-Awza'i said: Iblis said to his allies: From what direction do you come to the children of Adam? They said: From every direction. He said: Do you come to them from the direction of seeking forgiveness (*istighfar*)? They said:

Hayhat! That is something tied to tawhid. [Iblis] said: "I will surely plant in them something for which they will not seek forgiveness from God." He said: "So he planted among them the desires (al-ahwa')." Mujahid said: "I do not know which of the two blessings upon me is greater: that He guided me to Islam, or that He protected me from these desires." Al-Sha'bi said: "They were named the people of desires (ahl al-ahwa') only because they fall (yahwun) into the Fire." All of this is from al-Darimi.

Sahl ibn 'Abd Allah was asked about praying behind the Mu'tazila, and about marrying them and marrying their women. He said: "No, and no honor! They are disbelievers [[It is not among the principles of the People of the Sunnah to declare disbelief in the People of the Qibla over an error in interpretation. So let it be considered.]]. How can one be a believer who says: the Qur'an is created, there is no created Paradise and no created Fire, there is no Path (sirat) for God and no intercession, no one among the believers of the community of Muhammad (ﷺ) who enters the Fire will come out of it, there is no punishment of the grave, no Munkar and Nakir, no seeing of our Lord in the Hereafter and no 'ziyada' (extra vision), that the knowledge of God is created, and they do not regard the ruler or the Friday prayer [as valid]; and they declare disbelief in whoever believes in these things."

Al-Fudayl ibn 'Iyad said: "Whoever loves the person of an innovation, God will nullify his deeds and remove the light of Islam from his heart." Sufyan al-Thawri said: "Innovation is more beloved to Iblis than disobedience: disobedience can be repented of, but innovation cannot be repented of." Ibn 'Abbas said: "Looking at a man of the People of the Sunnah who calls to the Sunnah and forbids innovation is an act of worship." Abu al-'Aliyya said: "Hold to the first matter upon which they were before they split." 'Asim al-Ahwal said: "I related this to al-Hasan, and he said: 'By God, he has advised you and spoken truthfully.'"

The meaning of the saying of the Prophet (peace be upon him) has already passed in "Al 'Imran": "The Children of Israel divided into seventy-two sects, and this community will divide into seventy-three..." the hadith [[See vol. 4, p. 159.]]. Some of the knowledgeable scholars have said: "The sect that was added to the sects of the community of Muhammad (ﷺ) are people who oppose the scholars and hate the jurists, and that never happened in the earlier nations."

Rafi' ibn Khadij narrated that he heard the Messenger of God (ﷺ) say: "There will be among my community people who disbelieve in God and in the Qur'an while they are unaware, just as the Jews and Christians disbelieved." I said: "May I be your ransom, O Messenger of God! How is that?" He said: "They affirm some parts and deny other parts." I said: "May I be your ransom, O Messenger of God! And how do they speak?" He said: "They make Iblis an equal to God in His creation, His power and His provision, and they say: good is from God and evil is from Iblis." He said: "They disbelieve in God, then they recite the Book of God upon that, so they disbelieve in the Qur'an after faith and knowledge?" He said: "What my community meets from them of enmity, hatred and disputation: those are the heretics (zanadiqa) of this community." And he mentioned the hadith.

It has passed in "al-Nisa'" and in this surah the prohibition of sitting with the people of innovations and desires, and that whoever sits with them has the same ruling as they do, when He said: "And when you see those who engage in vain talk concerning Our signs..." [[See p. 12 of this part.]] "the verse." Then He explained in surah "al-Nisa'", which is Madani, the punishment of whoever does that and opposes what God commanded, when He said: "And He has already revealed to you in the Book..." the verse [[See vol. 5, p. 417.]]. So He joined those who sit with them to them. A group of the imams of this community went this way, and ruled according to the implications of these verses regarding the gatherings of the people of innovation, regarding companionship and association with them: among them Ahmad ibn Hanbal, al-Awza'i and Ibn al-Mubarak. They said concerning a man whose habit is sitting with the people of innovation: "He is forbidden from sitting with them; if he desists, well and good; otherwise he is joined to them," meaning in ruling.

'Umar ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz applied the hadd penalty to the gatherings of wine-drinkers, and recited: "Indeed, you would then be like them." It was said to him: "He says: I sit with them in order to separate from them and refute them." He said: "He is forbidden from sitting with them; if he does not desist, he is joined to them."

**Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on Surah 6, verses 151–153 (part 1 of 4)**

﴿And do not approach the property of the orphan, except in the way that is best, until he reaches his maturity. Give full measure and weight with justice. We do not burden any soul beyond its capacity. And when you speak, be just, even if it concerns a near relative. And fulfil the covenant of Allah. This He has enjoined upon you, so that you may remember.﴾ (152)

﴿And this is My path, straight, so follow it. And do not follow other ways, lest they separate you from His way. This He has enjoined upon you, so that you may be mindful of Allah.﴾ (153)

There are fourteen issues in it.

**The first issue:** His saying, ﴿Say: Come, I will recite﴾. That is: come forward and read with certainty, as my Lord has revealed to me, not by conjecture or by falsehood as you claim. Then He explained that by saying, ﴿that you associate nothing with Him﴾. It is said to a man, *ta'āl* (come), meaning "come forward"; to a woman, *ta'ālī*; to two men or two women, *ta'āliyā*; to a group of men, *ta'ālaw*; and to a group of women, *ta'ālena*. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿So come, I will provide for you﴾. They made "coming forward" a kind of rising up and elevation, because the one commanded to come forward, in the original form of this verb, was as if he had been sitting, and so it was said to him, *ta'āl*, that is: raise your body by standing and come forward. They extended its use until they applied it to both the one standing and the one walking. Ibn al-Shajari said this.

**The second issue:** His saying, ﴿what your Lord has forbidden﴾. The most likely reading of *mā* is that it is a relative pronoun (*khabariyyah*) in the accusative position, governed by *atlu* (I will recite). The meaning is: "Come, I will recite what your Lord has forbidden to you." If you attach *ʿalaykum* (to you) to *ḥarrama* (forbade), that is the most likely reading, because it is the closest, and it is the choice of the Basrans. If you attach it to *atlu* (I will recite), it is also good, because it is the earlier, and this is the choice of the Kufans. The implied meaning in this view is: "I will recite to you what your Lord has forbidden."

﴿That you associate nothing with Him﴾ is in the accusative position, by an implied verb from the same root as the first one, meaning: "I will recite to you that you should not associate," that is, "I will recite to you the prohibition of associating partners with Allah." It may also be governed by the sense of urging contained in *ʿalaykum* (upon you), with *ʿalaykum* then being detached from what precedes it, meaning: "Upon you is abandoning association, and upon you is kindness to the two parents, and that you do not kill your children, and that you do not approach indecencies." This is like saying, "Upon you is your own affair," meaning, "Keep to yourself." Just as He said: ﴿Upon you is your own soul﴾. Ibn al-Shajari said all of this. Al-Nahhas said: *an* (that) may be in the accusative position as a substitute for *mā* (what), meaning: "I will recite to you the prohibition of associating partners." Al-Farra' preferred that *lā* (not) be a prohibition, because after it comes ﴿and﴾.

**The third issue:** This verse is a command from Allah the Exalted to His Prophet, peace be upon him, to call all creation to listen to the recitation of what Allah has forbidden. Likewise, it is obligatory upon the scholars after him to convey to the people and to explain to them what Allah has forbidden them from what is permitted. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿You shall make it clear to the people and not conceal it﴾. Ibn al-Mubarak mentioned: Isa ibn Umar informed us, from Amr ibn Murrah, that he told them: Rabi' ibn Khaytham said to a companion of his: "Would it please you to be given a document from the Prophet (ﷺ) whose seal has not been broken?" He said, "Yes." He said, "Then read: ﴿Say: Come, I will recite what your Lord has forbidden to you﴾," and he read to the end of the three verses. [Al-Qurtubi notes:] In *al-Taqrib* it is stated: "al-Rabi' ibn Khaytham" is pronounced with a *ḍamma* on the *mīm* and a *fatḥa* on the *thāʾ*, but in *al-Khulasa* it is with a *fatḥa* on the *mīm* and *thāʾ*, with a silent *yāʾ* between them. [From *Tahdhib*.]

Ka'b al-Ahbar said: This verse is the opening of the Torah: "In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. Say: Come, I will recite what your Lord has forbidden to you," and so on. [Earlier, Ka'b also said that the beginning of Surah al-An'am is the opening of the Torah.]

Ibn Abbas said: These are the clear verses (*muhkamat*) which Allah mentioned in the surah of "Al 'Imran" [in some manuscripts: al-An'am], upon which the laws of all creation have agreed, and which have never been abrogated in any religious community. It has also been said that they are the Ten Words revealed to Musa (Moses).

**The fourth issue:** His saying, ﴿and to the parents, kindness﴾. Kindness to the parents means righteousness towards them, guarding and protecting them, obeying their commands, removing any slavery from them, and refraining from exercising authority over them. *Iḥsānan* (kindness) is in the accusative as a verbal noun (*maṣdar*), and its governing verb is an implied verb of the same root. Its estimated form is: "And be kind to the parents, with kindness."

**The fifth issue:** His saying, ﴿and do not kill your children out of poverty﴾. *Imlāq* means poverty; that is, do not bury alive your daughters (from *al-mawʾūda*, the buried girl), fearing destitution, for I provide for you and for them. Some of them used to do this to both females and males, fearing poverty, as is apparent from the verse. *Amlaqa* means he became poor, and *amlaqahu* means he made him poor; it is both intransitive and transitive. Al-Naqqash related from Mu'arrij that he said: *al-imlāq* means hunger, in the dialect of Lakhm. Mundhir ibn Sa'id mentioned that *al-imlāq* means spending, and it is said: *amlaqa mālahu*, meaning he spent his wealth. It is also reported that Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, said to his wife: "Spend from your wealth as much as you wish" [using the same root]. A man is called *malaq* if he gives with his tongue what is not in his heart. So *al-malaq* is a homonymous term (*lafẓ mushtarak*), whose explanation will come in its proper place.

**The sixth issue:** This verse may be used as evidence by those who forbid *al-ʿazl* (coitus interruptus), because burying alive removes an existing child and offspring, and *al-ʿazl* prevents the very origin of offspring, so the two are similar. However, taking a life is a greater sin and a more hideous act. For this reason, some of our scholars said that from the Prophet's saying, peace be upon him, about *al-ʿazl*, "That is the hidden burying alive," it is understood that it is disliked (*karāha*), not forbidden (*taḥrīm*). A group of the Companions and others held this view. Another group of the Companions, the Successors, and jurists held that it is permissible, based on his saying, peace be upon him: "There is no blame upon you if you do not do it, for it is only by decree (*al-qadar*)," meaning: there is no sin upon you for not doing it. Al-Hasan and Muhammad ibn al-Muthanna understood from it a prohibition and a deterrence from *al-ʿazl*. The first interpretation is more preferable, because of his saying, peace be upon him: "When Allah wills to create something, nothing can prevent it."

Malik and al-Shafi'i said: It is not permissible to practise *al-ʿazl* with a free woman except with her permission. It seems they regarded ejaculation as part of her pleasure and of her right concerning offspring. They did not hold this for a woman owned by right of possession (*al-mawṭūʾa bi-milk al-yamīn*), since he may practise *al-ʿazl* with her without her permission, because she has no right in any of the matters mentioned.

**The seventh issue:** His saying, ﴿and do not approach indecencies, what is apparent of them and what is hidden﴾. A parallel is His saying: ﴿and leave off the outward and the inward of sin﴾. So His saying "what is apparent" is a prohibition against all kinds of indecencies, which are acts of disobedience. "What is hidden" is what the heart has resolved upon in opposition. "Apparent" and "hidden" are two states that together cover all the categories of things to which they are applied. *Mā ẓahara* (what is apparent) is in the accusative as an apposition (*badal*) to *al-fawāḥish* (indecencies), and *mā baṭana* (what is hidden) is conjoined to it.

**The eighth issue:** His saying, ﴿and do not kill the soul which Allah has forbidden, except by right﴾. The *alif* and *lām* in *al-nafs* (the soul) are for defining the genus, like their saying: "Love of the dirham and the dinar has ruined people." A similar example is His saying: ﴿Indeed, mankind was created anxious﴾ [see vol. 18, p. 289]. Do you not see His saying, "except the praying ones"? Likewise His saying: ﴿By time. Indeed, mankind is in loss﴾ [see vol. 20, p. 178], because He said: ﴿except those who believe﴾.

This verse is a prohibition against killing a soul that is forbidden to be killed, whether it is a believer or a covenanted non-Muslim, except by the right which makes killing it obligatory. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "I have been commanded to fight the people until they say, 'There is no god but Allah.' Whoever says, 'There is no god but Allah,' has protected his property and his life, except by its right, and their reckoning is with Allah." This right has several aspects: among them is withholding the zakat and abandoning the prayer. Abu Bakr al-Siddiq fought those who withheld zakat, and in the revelation: ﴿But if they repent, establish prayer, and give zakat, then let them go on their way﴾ [see vol. 8, p. 71]. This is clear. The Prophet (ﷺ) also said: "The blood of a Muslim man is not lawful except by one of three: a married adulterer, a life for a life, and one who abandons his religion and separates from the community." He, peace be upon him, also said: "If two caliphs are pledged allegiance, then kill the other of them." Narrated by Muslim. [Meaning: repel the other by killing him, if repelling him is not possible without that.] Abu Dawud narrated from Ibn Abbas, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever you find doing the deed of the people of Lut, kill the one who does it and the one it is done to." The explanation of this will come in *al-A'raf* [see vol. 7, p. 74 and p. 243 of this part].

In the revelation: ﴿The only recompense for those who wage war against Allah and His Messenger and strive upon the earth to cause corruption is that they be killed﴾ [see vol. 6, p. 147], (the verse). And He said: ﴿And if two groups of the believers fight, [make peace between them]﴾ [see vol. 16, p. 315], (the verse). Likewise, whoever splits the unity of the Muslims, opposes the leader of their community, divides their word, and strives upon the earth to cause corruption by plundering the families and wealth, rebelling against the ruler, and refusing his judgement, is to be killed. This is the meaning of His saying: ﴿except by right﴾.

He, peace be upon him, also said: "The believers' blood is equal in value, and the lowest of them may undertake a protection on their behalf. A Muslim is not to be killed for a disbeliever, nor a covenanted person during his covenant, and the people of two religions do not inherit from one another." Abu Dawud and al-Nasa'i narrated from Abu Bakr, who said: I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: "Whoever kills a covenanted person outside of his *kunh*, Allah forbids him Paradise." [*Kunh al-amr* is its reality; it is also said its time and measure; it is also said its ultimate end, meaning: whoever kills him at other than his proper time or beyond the limit within which killing him is permitted (from *al-Nihaya*).] In another narration of Abu Dawud, he said: "Whoever kills a man of the dhimmis will not smell the fragrance of Paradise, though its fragrance is found from a distance of seventy years." In al-Bukhari, in this hadith it is: "from a distance of forty years." He narrated it from the hadith of Abdullah ibn Amr ibn al-As.

**The ninth issue:** His saying, ﴿that﴾, refers to these prohibited things. The *kāf* and *mīm* are for address, and they have no place in i'rab (grammatical inflection).

**The tenth issue:** His saying, ﴿He has enjoined upon you﴾. *Waṣiyya* (injunction) is an emphatic command that is within one's ability. The *kāf* and *mīm* are in the accusative position, because it is a pronoun placed for address. In *waṣṣā* there is a subject pronoun that refers back to Allah. Maṭar al-Warraq related from Nafi', from Ibn Umar, that Uthman ibn Affan, may Allah be pleased with him, looked over his companions and said: "Why would you kill me? I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: 'The blood of a Muslim man is not lawful except by one of three: a man who commits adultery after being *muhsan* (married), for which the penalty is stoning; or who kills intentionally, for which the penalty is retaliation (*qawad*); or who apostatizes after his Islam, for which the penalty is execution.' By Allah, I have not committed adultery in the Jahiliyya or in Islam, nor have I killed anyone for which I would retaliate against myself, nor have I apostatized since I embraced Islam. I bear witness that there is no god but Allah and that Muhammad is His servant and Messenger. That is what I have mentioned to you, which He enjoined upon you, so that you may understand!"

**The eleventh issue:** His saying, ﴿And do not approach the property of the orphan, except in the way that is best﴾. That is: by that which is good for it and for its growth (in another copy: its management). This is achieved by preserving the principal and growing its returns. This is the best of the opinions on this matter, for it is comprehensive. Mujahid said: ﴿And do not approach the property of the orphan except in the way that is best﴾ means by trading with it, and do not buy from it nor borrow from it.

**The twelfth issue:** His saying, ﴿until he reaches his maturity (ashuddahu)﴾.

Its meaning: its strength. It may be in the body, and it may be in knowledge gained through experience, and both aspects must be present. The term al-ashudd (maturity, full strength) is here stated without qualification, but the description of the orphan's condition has come in Surah an-Nisa' in a qualified form, where He says: ﴿And test the orphans until they reach marriageable age; then if you perceive in them sound judgment﴾ [[See vol. 5, p. 33.]]. Thus He combined strength of body, which is reaching marriageable age, with strength of understanding, which is perceiving sound judgment. For if the orphan were enabled to take his property before the attainment of understanding and after the attainment of physical strength, he would squander it on his desires and remain a pauper with no wealth. The orphan was singled out for this condition because people neglect him and fathers are absent from their children, so attending to the fatherless one is more fitting. (Al-ihtibal: seizing the opportunity, seeking it, and taking care of it; that is, attending to the affairs of the orphan is more appropriate.)

Reaching ashudd does not permit approaching his property except in the best manner, because the sanctity of property applies to the adult as well. The orphan was mentioned specifically because his guardian is God (his opponent is God). The meaning is: ﴿And do not approach the property of the orphan except in the best manner﴾ permanently, until he reaches his full strength. There is an ellipsis in the speech: when he reaches his full strength and sound judgment is perceived in him, then hand over his property to him.

The scholars differed concerning the ashudd of the orphan. Ibn Zayd said: it is his reaching puberty. The people of Madina said: it is his reaching puberty together with the perception of his sound judgment. According to Abu Hanifa: twenty-five years. Ibn al-Arabi said: "I am astonished at Abu Hanifa, for he holds that prescribed quantities are not established by analogy or reasoning, but only by transmission, and yet he establishes them through weak hadiths. But he lived in the Dar al-Darb, so many deceivers gathered around him; had he lived in the mine, as God destined for Malik, nothing would have come forth from him except the pure gold of religion." (In one manuscript: "al-madhhab," and in another: "al-dhahab." He means by Dar al-Darb: Baghdad; and by the mine: the mine of the Shari'a and its source, the illuminated Madina.)

It has been said that the end of middle age is the gathering point of ashudd, as Suhaym ibn Wathil said:

*A brother of fifty, in whom my full strength has gathered,*
*and experience with the affairs has refined me.*

[[A mujaddad man (with dal and dhal): one who has tested affairs, known them, and mastered them. Mudawarat al-shu'un: handling and treating affairs.]]

It is narrated as "najjadhani" with dal and dhal. Ashudd is a singular noun with no plural, like al-anuk, which is lead. It has also been said that its singular is shadd, like fals and aflus. Its origin is from shadda al-nahar, meaning it rose high; one says: "I came to him at shadd al-nahar and madd al-nahar" (at the height of the day). Muhammad ibn al-Dabbi used to recite the verse of 'Antara:

*My memory of him is of the day, as if his chest and head were dyed with 'alzam.*

[[Al-labban (with fatha on the lam): the chest. In another text: "al-banan," which is a variant. Al-'alzam (with kasra on the ayn and lam, and sukun on the zay): a red dye; it is also said to be al-wasma, a tree with leaves used for dyeing.]]

Another poet said:

*A woman of tall stature, long-armed, sahuq, circles around him at shadd al-nahar.*

[[Al-sahuq: a tall woman.]]

Sibawayh used to say: its singular is shiddah. Al-Jawhari said: this is sound in meaning, because one says: "the boy reached his shiddah," but the pattern fi'lah is not pluralized as af'ul. As for an'um, it is the plural of nu'm, from their saying: "a day of bu's and a day of nu'm." As for the view of those who said its singular is shadd, like kalb and aklub, and shidd like dhi'b and adhu'ub, that is merely analogy, just as they say for the singular of al-ababil: ibbul, by analogy with ijjul, though it is not something heard from the Arabs. Abu Zayd said: "Asabatni shudda 'ala fu'la," meaning hardship. One says "ashadda al-rajul" when he has a strong mount.

The twelfth issue: God's saying: ﴿And give full measure and weight with justice﴾, meaning with moderation in taking and giving during buying and selling. Qist means justice.

﴿We do not burden any soul except according to its capacity﴾, meaning its ability in giving full measure and weight. This implies that these commands apply only to what falls within human ability to guard against and avoid. As for what cannot be avoided, such as the slight variation between the two measures, which is beyond human capacity, it is pardoned. It has also been said that kayl means the measuring vessel; one says: "this is such-and-such a measure," and for this reason it is joined with "weight." Some scholars said: when God, glory be to Him, knew that many of His servants find it hard to be content giving others what is not obligatory upon them, He commanded the giver to render to the rightful owner his due right, and did not require him to give more, because of the hardship to his soul in giving more. He commanded the claimant to take his right, and did not require him to be content with less, because of the hardship to his soul in deficiency.

In the Muwatta' of Malik, from Yahya ibn Sa'id, it reached him that Abdullah ibn Abbas said: "Embezzlement never appeared among a people without God casting terror into their hearts; fornication never spread among a people without death becoming widespread among them; no people diminished the measure and weight without their provision being cut off; no people judged by other than the truth without bloodshed spreading among them; and no people broke a covenant without God giving their enemy power over them." [[Narrated by al-Tabarani as a hadith from Ibn Abbas.]] Ibn Abbas also said: "You, O assembly of non-Arabs, have been entrusted with two matters by which those before you were destroyed: the measure and the weight." [[From manuscript K.]]

The thirteenth issue: God's saying: ﴿And when you speak, be just﴾, which includes rulings and testimony. "Even if it concerns a near relative," meaning even if the right is against people like your own relatives, as has been mentioned in an-Nisa' [[See vol. 5, p. 410.]].

(And fulfil the covenant of God.) This is general over all that God has enjoined upon His servants. It may also be intended to include all agreements made between two people. That covenant is attributed to God because He commanded its preservation and fulfilment. (So that you may remember.)

...so that you may take heed. **Fourteenth issue:** His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And that this is My straight path, so follow it﴾. This is a great verse, and it is conjoined to what came before it. When He forbade and commanded, He here warned against following other than His way. In it He commanded following His path, as we will explain with the sound hadiths and the sayings of the early generation (al-salaf).

"And that" (*wa-anna*) is in the accusative position (*nasb*, the grammatical case of the object), meaning: "and recite that this is My path." This is related from al-Farra' and al-Kisa'i. Al-Farra' said: It is also permissible for it to be in the genitive position (*khafd*), meaning: "He enjoined it upon you, and [He enjoined] that this is My path." Its estimated construction according to al-Khalil and Sibawayh is: "and because this is My path," as in His saying: ﴿And that the mosques belong to God﴾ [[See vol. 19, p. 19.]].

Al-A'mash, Hamza and al-Kisa'i read *wa-inna hadhā* with a kasra on the hamza, as a resumption (*isti'nāf*, a new independent clause), meaning: "The one mentioned in the verses is My path, straight." Ibn Abi Ishaq and Ya'qub read *wa-an hadhā* with the light form. The light form (*mukhaffafa*) is like the heavy form (*mushaddada*), except that it contains the pronoun of the matter and the affair, meaning: "and that it is this." So it is in the nominative position (*raf'*), though the accusative is also permissible. It is also permissible for it to be a redundant particle (*zā'ida*) for emphasis, as in His mighty and majestic saying: ﴿When the bearer of good tidings came﴾ [[See vol. 9, p. 259.]].

*Al-sirāt* (the path) is the way that is the religion of Islam. *Mustaqīman* (straight) is in the circumstantial accusative (*hāl*), and its meaning is: level, upright, with no crookedness in it. So He commanded following His path, which He laid down through the tongue of His Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ), and prescribed, and whose end is Paradise. From it branch off other paths. Whoever takes the main road is saved, and whoever leaves for those other paths, they lead him to the Fire. God the Exalted said: ﴿And do not follow the (other) ways, lest they separate you from His way﴾ — meaning, they incline you away.

Al-Darimi Abu Muhammad related in his *Musnad* with a sound chain: Affan informed us, Hammad ibn Zayd narrated to us, Asim ibn Bahdala narrated to us, from Abu Wa'il, from Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) drew a line for us one day, then said: "This is the way of God." Then he drew lines to his right and lines to his left, then said: "These are paths; on each path there is a devil calling to it." Then he recited this verse.

Ibn Majah also related it in his *Sunan* from Jabir ibn Abd Allah, who said: We were with the Prophet (ﷺ), and he drew a line, and drew two lines to his right and two lines to his left, then he placed his hand on the middle line and said: "This is the way of God." Then he recited this verse: ﴿And that this is My straight path, so follow it, and do not follow the (other) ways, lest they separate you from His way﴾.

These paths include Judaism, Christianity, Zoroastrianism, and all the other religious communities, as well as the people of innovations (*bid'a*) and misguided views among the people of desires and of deviation in the subsidiary matters, and others among the people of excessive deepening in disputation and plunging into theology. All of these are prone to error and are a source of corrupt belief. Ibn Atiyya said: I say: and this is the correct view.

Al-Tabari mentioned in his book *Adab al-Nufus*: Muhammad ibn Abd al-A'la al-San'ani narrated to us, saying: Muhammad ibn Thawr narrated to us, from Ma'mar, from Aban, that a man said to Ibn Mas'ud: What is the straight path? He said: Muhammad (ﷺ) left us at its lower end, and its extremity is in Paradise, and on its right are *jawād* (roads) and on its left are *jawād*, and there are men there calling whoever passes by them. Whoever takes one of those *jawād* ends up in the Fire, and whoever takes the path ends up in Paradise. Then Ibn Mas'ud recited: ﴿And that this is My straight path﴾ to the end of the verse. [*Al-jawād* (with a doubled *dāl*) means the roads; its singular is *jādda*, which is the middle of the road. It was said: its main part; it was also said: its center.]

Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud also said: Learn knowledge before it is taken away, and its taking away is that its people depart. Beware of excessive stringency (*tanaṭṭu'*), of over-deepening (*ta'ammuq*), and of innovations (*bida'*) [[Al-Raghib defined innovation as: "In religion, the introduction of a saying whose speaker and doer did not follow the example of the Lawgiver and his noble earlier followers and firm foundations."]]. Hold fast to the ancient (*al-'atīq*) [[*Al-'atīq*: the old, the first.]]. Related by al-Darimi.

Mujahid said concerning His saying: ﴿And do not follow the (other) ways﴾: "The innovations." Ibn Shihab said: This is like His saying: ﴿Indeed, those who divided their religion and became sects﴾ to the end of the verse [[See p. 149 of this volume.]]. So flee, flee! And salvation, salvation! And hold fast to the straight path and the upright way, which the righteous early generation (*al-salaf al-salih*) trod, and in which is the profitable trade.

The leading scholars (*al-a'imma*) related from Abu Hurayra who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "What I have commanded you, take it; and what I have forbidden you, refrain from it."

Ibn Majah and others related from al-Irbad ibn Sariya who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) admonished us with an admonition from which eyes shed tears and hearts trembled. We said: O Messenger of God, this is surely the admonition of one bidding farewell; so what do you charge us with? He said: "I have left you upon the white (path) [[*Al-bayḍā'*: he (ﷺ) means the religion and the clear proof that admits no doubt whatsoever. ]], its night is like its day; none deviates from it after me except one who is destined to perish. Whoever of you lives will see much disagreement. So hold fast to what you know of my Sunna and the Sunna of the rightly-guided rightful caliphs after me. Bite onto it with the molars. Beware of newly introduced matters, for every innovation is misguidance. And obey, even if an Abyssinian slave is set over you, for the believer is like the docile camel: wherever it is led by its tether, it follows." Related by al-Tirmidhi in similar meaning, and he graded it sound.

Abu Dawud related: Ibn Kathir narrated to us, saying: Sufyan informed us, saying: A man wrote to Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz asking about predestination (*qadar*), and he wrote back: "To proceed: I enjoin upon you the fear of God, moderation in His command, the following of the Sunna of the Messenger of God (ﷺ), and abandoning what the innovators have introduced after its Sunna was already established, for they have spared you its burden. So keep to the community (*jamā'a*), for it is, by God's permission, a safeguard for you. Know that people have not introduced any innovation except that before it there passed what is evidence against it or a lesson concerning it. The Sunna was only laid down by one who knew what lies in opposing it of error, slip, foolishness and excessive deepening. So be content for yourself with what those people were content with for themselves, for they stopped on knowledge, and they refrained with penetrating insight, and they were stronger in uncovering matters, and more deserving of the excellence they were in. If the guidance is what you are upon, then you have preceded them to it; and if you say that it came into being after them, then none has introduced it except one who followed other than their way and turned himself away from them. For they are the foremost; they spoke about it with what suffices and described what heals. Whoever falls short of them is negligent, and whoever goes beyond them is excessive. Some people fell short of them and became harsh, and others went too far from them and became extreme. Yet they, between that, were upon the straight path." And he related the hadith.

Sahl ibn Abd Allah al-Tustari said: Hold to imitating the traces (*athar*) and the Sunna, for I fear that soon a time will come when, if a person mentions the Prophet (ﷺ) and following him in all states, they will blame him, shun him, disown him, humiliate him and belittle him.

Sahl said: Innovation only appeared at the hands of the people of the Sunna, because they associated with them and debated with them, so their sayings became known and spread among the common people, and one who had not heard them heard them. If they had left them alone and not spoken to them, each of them would have died with what was in his breast, not made it manifest, and carried it with him to his grave.

Sahl also said: None of you introduces an innovation until Iblis introduces for him a worship, so he worships by it; then he introduces for him an innovation. When he speaks the innovation and calls people to it, that service (*khadhma*) is taken from him [[Thus in MS B; in MSS J and K: *al-khidma* (the service).]].

Sahl said: I know of no hadith related about innovators more severe than this hadith: "God has forbidden Paradise to the one who holds an innovation." He said: So the Jew and the Christian are more hopeful than they are.

Sahl said: Whoever wishes to honor his religion should not enter upon the ruler, nor be alone with women, nor dispute with the people of desires. He also said: Follow and do not innovate, for you have been sufficed.

In the *Musnad* of al-Darimi: Abu Musa al-Ash'ari came to Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud and said: O Abu Abd al-Rahman, I saw in the mosque just now something that I disapproved of, though I have seen nothing but good, praise be to God. He said: What is it? He said: If you live, you will see it. He said: I saw in the mosque people sitting in circles, waiting for the prayer, and in each circle was a man, and in their hands were pebbles, and he would say to them: "Say *takbir* (Allahu akbar) a hundred times," and they would say it a hundred times. Then he says: "Say *tahlil* (la ilaha illa Allah) a hundred times," and they say it a hundred times. And he says: "Say *tasbih* (subhan Allah) a hundred times," and they say it a hundred times. He said: What did you say to them? He said: I said nothing to them, awaiting your opinion and awaiting your command. He said: Why did you not order them to count their evil deeds, and guarantee them that none of their good deeds would be lost? Then he went on, and we went with him until he came to one of those circles, and he stood over them and said: "What is this that I see you doing?" They said: O Abu Abd al-Rahman, pebbles with which we count the *takbir*, the *tahlil* and the *tasbih*. He said: Then count your evil deeds, and I guarantee you that none of your good deeds will be lost. Woe to you, O community of Muhammad! How swiftly is your destruction! These are the companions of your Prophet (ﷺ), numerous, and these are his garments not yet worn out, and his vessels not broken. By Him in whose hand my soul is, you are either upon a religion more guided than the religion of Muhammad, or you are opening a door of misguidance! They said: By God, O Abu Abd al-Rahman, we intended only good. He said: How many is the one who intends good but will not attain it.

From Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz: a man asked him about something concerning the people of desires and innovations, and he said: "Hold to the religion of the Bedouins and of the boy in the Quranic school, and abstain from anything other than that."

Al-Awza'i said: Iblis said to his allies: From what direction do you come to the children of Adam? They said: From every direction. He said: Do you come to them from the direction of seeking forgiveness (*istighfar*)? They said:

Hayhat! That is something tied to tawhid. [Iblis] said: "I will surely plant in them something for which they will not seek forgiveness from God." He said: "So he planted among them the desires (al-ahwa')." Mujahid said: "I do not know which of the two blessings upon me is greater: that He guided me to Islam, or that He protected me from these desires." Al-Sha'bi said: "They were named the people of desires (ahl al-ahwa') only because they fall (yahwun) into the Fire." All of this is from al-Darimi.

Sahl ibn 'Abd Allah was asked about praying behind the Mu'tazila, and about marrying them and marrying their women. He said: "No, and no honor! They are disbelievers [[It is not among the principles of the People of the Sunnah to declare disbelief in the People of the Qibla over an error in interpretation. So let it be considered.]]. How can one be a believer who says: the Qur'an is created, there is no created Paradise and no created Fire, there is no Path (sirat) for God and no intercession, no one among the believers of the community of Muhammad (ﷺ) who enters the Fire will come out of it, there is no punishment of the grave, no Munkar and Nakir, no seeing of our Lord in the Hereafter and no 'ziyada' (extra vision), that the knowledge of God is created, and they do not regard the ruler or the Friday prayer [as valid]; and they declare disbelief in whoever believes in these things."

Al-Fudayl ibn 'Iyad said: "Whoever loves the person of an innovation, God will nullify his deeds and remove the light of Islam from his heart." Sufyan al-Thawri said: "Innovation is more beloved to Iblis than disobedience: disobedience can be repented of, but innovation cannot be repented of." Ibn 'Abbas said: "Looking at a man of the People of the Sunnah who calls to the Sunnah and forbids innovation is an act of worship." Abu al-'Aliyya said: "Hold to the first matter upon which they were before they split." 'Asim al-Ahwal said: "I related this to al-Hasan, and he said: 'By God, he has advised you and spoken truthfully.'"

The meaning of the saying of the Prophet (peace be upon him) has already passed in "Al 'Imran": "The Children of Israel divided into seventy-two sects, and this community will divide into seventy-three..." the hadith [[See vol. 4, p. 159.]]. Some of the knowledgeable scholars have said: "The sect that was added to the sects of the community of Muhammad (ﷺ) are people who oppose the scholars and hate the jurists, and that never happened in the earlier nations."

Rafi' ibn Khadij narrated that he heard the Messenger of God (ﷺ) say: "There will be among my community people who disbelieve in God and in the Qur'an while they are unaware, just as the Jews and Christians disbelieved." I said: "May I be your ransom, O Messenger of God! How is that?" He said: "They affirm some parts and deny other parts." I said: "May I be your ransom, O Messenger of God! And how do they speak?" He said: "They make Iblis an equal to God in His creation, His power and His provision, and they say: good is from God and evil is from Iblis." He said: "They disbelieve in God, then they recite the Book of God upon that, so they disbelieve in the Qur'an after faith and knowledge?" He said: "What my community meets from them of enmity, hatred and disputation: those are the heretics (zanadiqa) of this community." And he mentioned the hadith.

It has passed in "al-Nisa'" and in this surah the prohibition of sitting with the people of innovations and desires, and that whoever sits with them has the same ruling as they do, when He said: "And when you see those who engage in vain talk concerning Our signs..." [[See p. 12 of this part.]] "the verse." Then He explained in surah "al-Nisa'", which is Madani, the punishment of whoever does that and opposes what God commanded, when He said: "And He has already revealed to you in the Book..." the verse [[See vol. 5, p. 417.]]. So He joined those who sit with them to them. A group of the imams of this community went this way, and ruled according to the implications of these verses regarding the gatherings of the people of innovation, regarding companionship and association with them: among them Ahmad ibn Hanbal, al-Awza'i and Ibn al-Mubarak. They said concerning a man whose habit is sitting with the people of innovation: "He is forbidden from sitting with them; if he desists, well and good; otherwise he is joined to them," meaning in ruling.

'Umar ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz applied the hadd penalty to the gatherings of wine-drinkers, and recited: "Indeed, you would then be like them." It was said to him: "He says: I sit with them in order to separate from them and refute them." He said: "He is forbidden from sitting with them; if he does not desist, he is joined to them."

Allah's words ﴿Then We gave Moses the Book﴾: this has two objects.

﴿Perfectly﴾ (tamaman) is either an object of purpose (maf'ul min ajlihi, an object indicating the reason for the action) or a verbal noun (masdar, the noun derived from the verb).

﴿Upon him who did good﴾ (ʿala alladhi ahsan) is read with both the accusative (naṣb) and the nominative (raf'). As for the reading with the nominative, which is the reading of Yahya ibn Yaʿmur and Ibn Abi Ishaq, the meaning is: perfectly, upon that which is best. Al-Mahdawi said: "This is remote, because of the omission of the subject (mubtada') that refers back to alladhi." Sibawayh reported from al-Khalil that he heard: "Ma ana bi-alladhi qa'ilun laka shay'an" (I am not one who will say anything to you). As for the reading with the accusative, it is taken as a past verb within the relative clause (silah, the clause that completes the relative pronoun). This is the view of the Basrans. Al-Kisa'i and al-Farra' permitted that it be a noun functioning as a qualifier (na't) of alladhi. They also permitted "marartu bi-alladhi akhika" (I passed by the one who is your brother), with both of them treating alladhi as qualified by a definite noun or something close to it. Al-Nahhas said: "This is impossible according to the Basrans, because it is a qualifier of the noun before it is complete, and the meaning for them is: upon the one who does good."

Mujahid said: "Perfectly, upon the good-doer, the believer." Al-Hasan said regarding the meaning of "perfectly upon him who did good": "Among them there were good-doers and non-good-doers, so Allah sent down the Book perfectly upon the good-doers." The evidence for the correctness of this view is that Ibn Mas'ud read: "Perfectly upon those who did good" (ʿala alladhina ahsanu).

It is also said: the meaning is: We gave Moses the Torah in addition to what Moses already knew, of what Allah had taught him before the Torah was sent down to him.

Muhammad ibn Yazid said: the meaning of "perfectly upon him who did good" is: perfectly upon him whom Allah, Mighty and Majestic, had favoured Moses (ﷺ) with, of the messengership and other things.

Abd Allah ibn Zayd said: its meaning is upon the favour of Allah, exalted is He, toward His prophets, peace be upon them (from the messengership [from manuscripts B, J and K] and other things).

Al-Rabi' ibn Anas said: "Perfectly upon Moses' goodness, from his obedience to Allah, Mighty and Majestic." Al-Farra' also said this.

Then it is said: "Thumma" (then) indicates that the second action came after the first, while the story of Moses (ﷺ) and his receiving the Book was before this. So it is said: "thumma" here means "wa" (and), that is, "and We gave Moses the Book," because both are conjunctions. It is also said: the sense of the sentence is: "then We had given Moses the Book before Our sending down the Qur'an upon Muhammad (ﷺ)."

It is also said: the meaning is: say, "Come, I will recite to you what your Lord has forbidden to you," then "I will recite what We gave Moses, perfectly." The word ﴿and detailed explanation﴾ (wa tafsilan) is conjoined to it. Likewise ﴿and guidance and mercy﴾ (wa huda wa rahmah). ﴿And this is a Book﴾ is an inceptive sentence (mubtada') and predicate (khabar). ﴿We have sent it down, blessed﴾ (anzalnahu mubarak) is a qualifier (na't), meaning abundant in good. It is permissible outside the Qur'an to read "mubarakan" as a circumstantial state (hal).

﴿So follow it﴾ means: act upon what is in it. ﴿And fear Allah﴾ means: fear its distortion. ﴿That you may be shown mercy﴾ means: so that you may be those who hope for mercy, and so you will not be punished.
